transcript: Montessori and Waldorf. It's not the same, babe. Montessori and Waldorf get lumped together, usually by people in Amazon descriptions, but they're just trying to sell you an aesthetic. Philosophically, these are two totally different worlds. If I had to sum up the difference, I would say Montessori nurtures the soul and Waldorf awakens the imagination. So here's the cliff notes. Let's talk classroom setup. Montessori is rooted in real world experiences. The classroom is meticulously prepared by a teacher so it feels clean and calm and purposeful. Every material and work serves a purpose, whether the child knows it or not. Children use real tools to do real stuff and they have access to everything in the environment to follow their own interests and curiosity. Once the children are in the classroom, the role of the teacher is to step back and observe the children in the prepared environment. This means the children are learning to trust their capabilities and who they are at their core. It's incredibly empowering and it helps them learn who they are as individuals. In a Montessori classroom, creativity comes from within the child through hands-on exploration and experimentation. Now Waldorf is a full send on imagination and creativity. Their world is warm and magical and story-rich. Think watercolor paintings, crochet, knitting, poetry, beeswax, modeling, puppet shows, stories of gnomes and fairies and enchanted palaces. The role of a teacher is highly involved and directive, especially in the group rhythm, transitions. While the teachers may observe informally, it's more about guiding the flow and the energy of the group. It acts as a model rather as an instructor. They'll demonstrate tasks like baking and handiwork, storytelling with purposeful movement and reverence. Okay, now that we got that out of the way, let's talk academics. In a Montessori classroom, language and math are embedded into the whole environment, just like an art project or a puzzle. These materials are designed to spark interest and invite exploration starting as early as two and a half years old. Concepts are presented in an immersive and sensorial way that often feels like a game. These works are developmentally aligned, tapping into the child's physical and practical understanding of the world around them. It literally builds words and numbers with materials experimenting with quantities and decoding phonetic sounds through hands-on experience. Waldorf, on the other hand, delays formal academics until around age seven. This is based on the belief that early childhood should be protected and not rushed. Children knit and crochet to build dexterity for writing, all while absorbing an incredible lexicon through oral stories and deep poetry. It's about honoring the natural perceived rhythm of development. And for many neurotypical children, that can work beautifully. However, with children that have specific language delays or learning differences, like dyslexia, delaying early exposure to reading can make it harder to catch and support challenges until much later. Now, as a Montessori teacher, my personal opinion is that I don't think one cancels out the other. You can foster imagination and creativity while also giving children access to language and math. But honestly, that might be the key philosophical difference between the two. So what's the one thing that both Waldorf and Montessori absolutely have in common? It's a deep respect for the child. It's different philosophies, and that's okay, because we're all different too.

caption: ✨Waldorf and Montessori: What’s the Difference?! ✨ Sometimes I forget how niche we get around here with the Montessori comedy. Not everyone knows the nuances of these two beautiful—but very different—philosophies. Honestly, I had no idea what a Montessori classroom even was until I had my son. Now it’s something that has profoundly changed my life. That said, one of my biggest pet peeves (and I know many Montessori and Waldorf educators feel this) is how often these two approaches get lumped together. Usually because, let’s be honest, they both use natural materials and create dreamy, beautiful spaces for children. But aesthetically similar ≠ philosophically the same. I deeply respect both approaches. I even borrow from Waldorf’s sense of whimsy and creativity when designing Montessori works. The thing I love most about Montessori? You can do almost anything—it’s all in the presentation. Since it’s hard to capture the full depth of both philosophies in one video, I pulled some of the most accurate visuals I could find to tell a cohesive story. If you recognize a photo or classroom, please let me know so I can credit the original creators! author: mamaelisa03
title: Moving from 'Why' to Solutions in Parenting
summary: A mother explains why asking young children 'why did you do that?' is ineffective due to their developing impulse control. She suggests a two-step approach: stating what you observe and immediately focusing on a solution to help the child fix the situation.
key_points: Young children lack the impulse control to explain their actions, so asking 'why' is often unproductive.
Step 1: State what you observe (e.g., 'I see water on the floor').
Step 2: Focus on a solution (e.g., 'Let's clean it up').
Avoid shaming phrases like 'Who am I talking to?' or 'You don't listen' as they cause children to shut down.
Model problem-solving by asking 'What is the next step to fix this?'

author: thecrispyrn
title: NICU nurse: why to skip the Haakaa colostrum collector kit
summary: A NICU nurse warns against using the Haakaa silicone colostrum collector containers because their large surface area causes significant wastage of thick colostrum. She recommends hand expressing into a small cup and drawing the milk into 1 ml syringes for storage and feeding instead.
key_points: Thick colostrum sticks to large container surfaces, causing wastage.
Do not mix freshly expressed (warm) colostrum with already-chilled milk.
Hand express into a small cup and draw up with a 1 ml syringe.
Syringes are cost-effective, easy to store, and allow for direct feeding with minimal loss.

caution: The advice to use syringes for colostrum collection is standard, but always consult your healthcare provider regarding your specific colostrum harvesting plan.

transcript: As a NICU nurse, I am begging you, do not put your precious drops of colostrum in these. I was caring for a baby who had an unexpected NICU stay, and his mom was awesome and had already collected some colostrum during her pregnancy, and she had used this kit. The design is just really poor for storing a liquid where drops matter. The surface area at the inside is really large, and colostrum is really thick, so there's a lot that gets stuck on the sides of the container. It's also a lot of material for what ends up being a very tiny amount, and you'll need a new container for every time that you express colostrum. The kit doesn't come with that many containers. You don't want to mix warm and cold milk together, so adding your colostrum in over time and then freezing it when it's full is not a safe option, especially for a newborn. If you want to collect your colostrum, hand express into a small cup or silberette and then draw it up with a 1 ml syringe. And this is a lot more cost effective and easily stored. Then when it's in a syringe, you can easily give it to your baby into a bottle with a pacifier or just straighten them out through the syringe. This way, almost all of it will go straight to your baby. I'm Ellie. I make content on parenting and life with my time with a baby. If this was helpful, follow for more.

title: Navigating the First Weeks Postpartum
summary: A new mother shares her experience with the challenging first weeks at home, including concerns about postpartum depression and breastfeeding difficulties. She emphasizes the importance of preparation, open communication with partners, and seeking professional support.

Prepare for the postpartum period by taking courses and reading.
If a newborn is lethargic or struggling to feed, seek professional help immediately.
Lactation consultants can provide critical support for feeding challenges.

author: verbal.to.visual
title: Parenting for confidence, not comfort: Anxiety + Bravery = Confidence
summary: A whiteboard animation summarises Katherine Hecht's TED talk. 'Parenting for comfort' (shielding kids from fear) burdens parents, teaches that hard feelings are emergencies, and doesn't work. Instead, parent for confidence: A (anxiety) + B (bravery) = C (confidence), creating mild adventures, modelling bravery, celebrating brave acts and using a gradual 'bravery ladder', as with a boy afraid of bees.
key_points: Shielding kids from every fear sends the message that hard feelings are an emergency.
Teach the ABC: 'It's okay to be scared' (anxiety) + 'I can handle this' (bravery) = 'What else am I capable of?' (confidence).
Create opportunities for small, safe fears through adventure.
Stay calm when they're scared - lend them your nervous system.
Model bravery by doing scary things yourself, including your own fears (e.g. public speaking).
Celebrate brave actions, even small ones.
Use a gradual exposure 'bravery ladder' (bee pictures, videos, a dead bee in a jar, real bees).
scripts: It's okay to be scared.
I can handle this.
What else am I capable of?

ill.caption: Whiteboard summary: parenting for comfort vs parenting for confidence, with the formula Anxiety + Bravery = Confidence.

transcript: do we raise kids who can handle hard things? That's a question that Katherine Hecht explored in a recent TED talk, starting with the story of Sammy, who is afraid of bees. As a parent, it's natural to want to protect your kids from their fears, an approach that Hecht calls parenting for comfort, which she says is the single most natural, well-meaning, and deeply flawed thing that we do. Here are the problems with parenting for comfort. First of all, it places an incredible burden on parents. Always in vigilant protection mode, attempting to control another person's emotional experience. It also teaches kids that hard feelings are an emergency, and sends the message that this feeling is a problem. And the third problem, it doesn't work. When you send your kid off into the world, they will find that discomfort is a side effect of being alive. So you'll be doing them a disservice if you try to shield them from it at every turn. So So instead of planning indoor summer vacations to avoid exposure to bees at all cost, what do you do? Hecht proposes a simple equation. A plus B equals C. Anxiety plus bravery equals confidence. When facing a situation that makes you anxious, you tell yourself, it's okay to be scared. And then you decide to act anyway by telling yourself, I can handle this. After responding to anxiety with bravery, you will naturally ask yourself, what else? I capable of? Anchoring your approach to those ABCs is called parenting for confidence, and you can support your kids at each step of it. You can create opportunities for anxiety through adventure. Go back to outdoor fun in the summer. Create experiences where your kids might get a little bit scared, and by remaining calm in those situations, you help your kids stay calm. You lend them your nervous system and provide them with a steady anchor, and then be the bravery you wish to see in your child. Do the scary thing. The thing that your kid is scared of, but then maybe also the thing that you are scared of. If that's public speaking, get up and share your thoughts at the next community event. And then be sure to celebrate when confidence building actions take place. Even if it's just a high five for enjoying watermelon outside in the summer for the first time in years. In Sammy's case, they followed those ABCs up a bravery ladder with exposure first to bee pictures, then bee videos, then a dead bee in a jar, and then real bees. And he kept it going from there, donning a beekeeper suit and pulling honey out of a hive. And here's the thing about bravery. It's contagious. It makes others feel more capable of tackling their own fears, as we saw a group of kids gather on the stage to share the fears that they had overcome. And this is not a trivial matter, because as Hecht said, brave kids the ones who will change the world. Confidence doesn't come from praise or protection, it comes from practice.

author: pedsdoctalk
title: Pediatrician: if partner gives a night bottle, you still need to pump
summary: Dr. Mona, a pediatrician and IBCLC, explains that newborns feed every 2-3 hours around the clock, and that if you want to breastfeed, any feed replaced by a bottle (formula or expressed milk) in the early weeks needs milk removal by pumping to protect supply. Milk production is supply-and-demand: unremoved milk signals the body to make less and can lead to engorgement, clogged ducts and mastitis. She adds a rapid list of normal newborn feeding facts.
key_points: Newborns eat every 2-3 hours including nights; very young babies may need waking to feed.
The first 6-8 weeks are the supply 'setup phase'; if a feed is replaced by a bottle, pump at that time to protect supply.
Milk not removed = signal to make less; also risk of engorgement, clogged ducts, mastitis.
Losing up to 7-10% of birth weight in the first 3-5 days is normal.
8-12 feeds in 24 hours is normal; cluster feeding is common (around day 2 and weeks 2, 3, 6, and up to 3 months).
A 5-minute feed doesn't mean low supply; some babies are efficient.
Colostrum is real milk; supply often regulates at 6-12 weeks — less leaking doesn't mean less milk.
Judge supply by diapers and weight gain, not pump output; you don't need a big freezer stash.

onscreen: Pediatrician Reacts: What No One Tells You About Newborn Feeding
caption:
A lot of people are surprised by this one. If you're planning to breastfeed, anytime your baby gets a bottle in the early weeks, you still need to pump to protect your supply. So while the idea of a partner doing the night feed sounds dreamy, it might not be the break you were hoping for. Because if milk isn't being removed, your body thinks it isn't needed. That's how supply dips, clogged ducts, and mastitis can sneak up on you.

And that's just one of many feeding curveballs in the newborn phase. A few more worth knowing:
✔️ Babies can lose up to 7-10% of birth weight in the first few days. That's normal. 
✔️ A 5-minute feed doesn't mean low supply. Some babies are just efficient. 
✔️ Cluster feeding around day 2 and weeks 2, 3, and 6 is real, and it can be a lot. 
✔️ Colostrum is real milk. Small in volume, huge in value. 
✔️ Supply often regulates around 6-12 weeks. Less leaking doesn't mean less milk. 
✔️ Your pump output is not the best measure of your supply. Diapers and weight gain are.

Your baby also might not follow the "every 3 hours" script. They might want to feed 12 times in 24 hours, cluster for 3 hours straight in the evening, or latch and pop off six times before actually settling. That's messy and unpredictable and still completely normal.

Want to go even deeper? I sat down with Melissa Mancini (@buildingamotherhood), a registered nurse and certified lactation consultant, on @thepedsdoctalkpodcast. We cover the physiology behind breastfeeding, why cluster feeding happens, feeding on demand vs. scheduling, when to introduce a pacifier, how to handle pain, whether nipple shields are okay, and how to prep for pumping when you go back to work. It is one of the most thorough, practical breastfeeding conversations I have had, and I think every expecting or new parent should hear it.

title: Perineal massage from 34 weeks to reduce birth tearing
summary: A pelvic floor physiotherapist demonstrates (with an anatomical diagram and a pelvic wand) how to do perineal massage to prepare for birth. She explains where to apply pressure, using sweeping motions and sustained holds to mimic crowning while breathing and relaxing the pelvic floor. The caption cites research that it reduces severe tears and episiotomy rates; she did it and had no tear.
key_points: Start from around 34 weeks, at least 3-4 times per week (check with your care team first).
Use a finger/thumb, a partner's help, or a pelvic/perineal wand if reaching is hard.
Insert to between the first and second knuckle to reach the muscles at the vaginal entrance.
Use water-based lube with a tool, or a natural oil with fingers.
Do sweeping motions down the sides, then press and hold: start with 10 seconds, build to 30 seconds, even 1-2 minutes.
Breathe through the stinging/burning stretch and let the pelvic floor relax — don't force through pain.
Caption claims: up to 64% less risk of 3rd/4th-degree tears and ~21% fewer episiotomies.

author: peds_slp
title: Picky eater mealtime mistakes and what to do instead
summary: A pediatric speech-language pathologist doing feeding therapy role-plays common picky-eater mistakes and alternatives. Instead of open-ended 'what do you want?', pressure, bribes and the clean-plate rule, she recommends limited choices, small portions with mostly safe foods, eating together, talking about the food, and playful no-pressure food exploration.
key_points: Don't ask an open-ended 'What do you want to eat?' - offer limited choices instead (e.g. orange or blue spoon).
Serve small portions: about 80% preferred/safe foods and 20% new/unfamiliar foods.
Eat the same food with your child.
Talk about the food and narrate your thoughts (e.g. 'My carrots look like sticks - I wonder if they're crunchy').
Encourage touching and playing with food with no pressure to eat (e.g. 'painting' with carrot sticks and dip, smelling the dip).
Avoid pressure ('open up, take a bite'), dessert bribes ('eat your carrots to get a cookie') and the 'clean plate club'.
Don't force a child to sit at the table until the plate is empty.

author: doctor.bing
title: Praise effort, not intelligence, to build resilience
summary: A neurologist explains that praising children for being 'smart' can lead to a fear of failure. Instead, parents should praise the process—effort, strategy, and persistence—to foster a growth mindset and help children handle challenges.
key_points: Praising intelligence teaches that success is based on talent, which can cause children to freeze when they struggle.
Praising effort and strategy teaches that struggle is a normal part of learning.
Focus on how the child approached the problem rather than just the outcome.
Normalize difficulty by telling children that learning is supposed to feel challenging sometimes.
Small changes in language help rewire the brain to handle stress and setbacks better.
scripts: That was really hard, but I really love how you kept going.
Learning is supposed to be difficult, it's supposed to be challenging sometimes.
transcript: Science shows that the way we praise kids can literally shape how their brain handles failure, challenge, and stress for the rest of their lives. And let me explain. As a neurologist and a father, this matters because learning is not just about intelligence. It is about how the brain responds when something gets hard. One way that I see this play out later in people's lives is with patients recovering from stroke, brain injury, or chronic neurologic symptoms where progress depends less on raw ability and more on how their brain responds to setbacks. When we praise kids for being smart or for things coming easily, the brain quietly learns that success equals talent. And later when they struggle, that same brain is more likely to freeze up and avoid challenges or even feel defeated. But when we praise the process, the effort and the strategy, and even the struggle itself, something very different happens and the kids strengthen their brain circuits involved in persistence, problem solving, and emotional regulation. The child then learns that effort is something they can control and that struggle is a normal part of learning. This is what some people call a growth mindset, but from a brain perspective, it's really about resilience. Kids become more willing to try hard things and bounce back when they do not get it right the first time, which sets the foundation for how they handle challenges later in life. Practically, parents can, instead of saying, you're so smart, say something like, that was really hard, but I really love how you kept going. Praise how they approach the problem and not just the outcome. And normalize struggle by saying, learning is supposed to be difficult, it's supposed to be challenging sometimes. And those small changes over time can shape how a brain approaches lifelong challenges.
onscreen: How we praise kids can rewire their brains
caption: How you praise a child teaches their brain how to handle challenge failure and stress. Effort focused praise builds resilience adaptability and long term learning. Small words can make a big difference. #BrainHealth #LearnOnTikTok #TikTokLearningCampaign  #Neuroscience #MentalResilience

title: Pregnancy warning signs that alarm a labor & delivery triage nurse

key_points: Severe headache with blurry vision — possible preeclampsia; get seen urgently.
Intensely itchy palms and soles with no rash — possible cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP).
Bright red bleeding (not just light pink/brown spotting, which can be normal late in pregnancy).
Baby moving less than usual — reduced fetal movement should be checked the same day.
One lower leg swollen, red (and painful) — possible blood clot (DVT).
Any fall during pregnancy (e.g. down the steps) should be reported and assessed.
When in doubt, call or go to L&D triage — your midwife/OB would rather see you.

author: therapyjeff
title: Protecting boys from online radicalisation
summary: Therapist Jeff Guenther provides five actionable strategies for parents to prevent their sons from being groomed by extremist online content. He emphasizes the importance of emotional literacy, modeling healthy masculinity, and fostering real-world connections.
key_points: Interrupt the 'victim story' by teaching the difference between discomfort and oppression.
Teach emotional literacy so boys can name their feelings instead of turning to blame.
Model healthy masculinity by showing that strength includes kindness and sensitivity.
Teach digital literacy to help boys understand algorithms and propaganda.
Build offline belonging through activities like bands, D&D, woodworking, or volunteering.
transcript: Parents of white boys don't want your kid radicalized online? Do these five things. One, interrupt the victim story. At some point, your son may say he feels attacked for just being white or male. Don't roll your eyes, but also don't coddle him either. Extremist groups that are just a podcast away groom boys by telling them the lie that they're the real victims of feminism or diversity. That victim story is one of the earliest hooks, turning isolation into blame that's easy to weaponize. The best prevention is early conversation, teaching the difference between discomfort and oppression, and offering healthier narratives about belonging and fairness. Two, teach emotional literacy. If your son can't name or regulate his feelings, he's way more likely to turn rejection into rage. Teach him how to say, I feel lonely, instead of girls are the problem. Feelings don't disappear just because you ignore them. They leak out as blame and turn into resentment and contempt, and then far worse. Three, model healthy masculinity. If all he hears is man up and don't cry, he's going to find belonging in toxic online spaces that reward cruelty because if you won't let him be vulnerable, he'll settle for being violent. Show him that strength includes kindness, sensitivity, and respect, or Reddit will happily show him the opposite. Four, teach digital literacy. Stop pretending he's just gaming. He's also in Discord servers, YouTube rabbit holes, and TikTok feeds being told who to hate. Teach him what algorithms are and how propaganda works or the internet will raise him for you. Five, build belonging that isn't online, please. Isolation is rocket fuel for radicalization. If your kid doesn't feel connected in the real world, he's going to go looking for belonging on Discord, YouTube, and anonymous forums full of rage. And those places will happily hand him an identity built on cruelty. So here's the bottom line. Get your sons off Discord. Don't give them weapons. Give them belongings. Sign them up for bands, D&D groups, improv classes, woodworking, archery, volunteering. Whatever makes him feel connected and creative. Talk to him about the feelings he's feeling before some manosphere influencer does it for you. Because if you don't shape his world, the algorithm will, and you're not going to like the result.

author: johannakulp.lcsw
title: Responding when your child says something about their body
summary: A body-image therapist explains what she did when her child said they had a big stomach: instead of immediately refuting it, she asked what they meant. The child turned out to be neutral about it, showing that a quick 'No, you're not big!' would have introduced negativity. She offers a three-step rubric: validate, inquire, then refute or reinforce.
key_points: Don't jump straight to refuting ("No, you're not big!") – it implies that being big is bad.
Step 1 – Validate: reflect back what you heard ("I think I'm hearing you say you have a big stomach").
Step 2 – Inquire with open questions: "What makes you say that?" / "What does that mean to you?"
Step 3 – Refute or reinforce only after you understand the child's meaning.
Often kids are describing their body neutrally; the parent may be the one adding shame.
Reinforce body neutrality/positivity: all bodies have different shapes.

What do you mean by that?
What makes you say that?
What does that mean to you?
Bodies are so cool, right? We all have different shapes. I love my stomach. I love your stomach.

caption:
When your child makes a comment about their body that feels negative, what’s the best response?

Avoid jumping straight to refuting like, “No, you’re not big!”

Instead, get curious. Ask gentle, open-ended questions to understand what’s underneath the comment: 👉 “What makes you say that?” 👉 “What does that mean to you?”

This allows you to really hear their perspective, learn where the belief is coming from, and support or challenge them more effectively.

Refuting and reinforcing comes last—not first. Listening comes first.

key_points: Ask your employer: many private companies give a bonus or aid at birth.
Bucharest: newborn incentive of 2,500 lei via DGASMB (payments heavily delayed; the legal term is one year).
Bucharest: 'Voucher Materna' — 2,000 lei in two instalments for pregnancy tests and medical services, including at many private clinics; apply while still pregnant.
'Bebe de București' store (at the voucher pick-up location) gives virtual coins for cleaned, sterilised second-hand clothes, toys, books, cots and strollers.

Maternity leave: 126 calendar days (63 before, 63 after birth); only 42 days after birth are mandatory before switching to child-raising leave; paid 85% of average income; file via employer with the medical certificate, or at CASMB if not employed.

Child-raising leave: until the child is 2 (3 for a child with disability), 85% of average net income of 12 months in the last 2 years; at least 2 months are reserved for the other parent and are lost if not taken; file at AJPIS or the local town hall.
Child allowance (alocație): 719 lei/month until age 2; file at AJPIS or the local town hall.

Deci dacă încă nu s-a născut bebelușul, puteți beneficia și de acestea. Există de altfel un magazin numit Bebe de București, care se află chiar în cadrul locului de unde se preiau și voucherele. Aceștia îți dau din partea lor niște monede virtuale din care poți să-ți cumperi orice produs sau în magazin. Sunt produse SH aduse de părinți, curățate, sterilizate de la haine, la jucării, la cărți, pătuțuri, cărucioare și așa mai departe. Depinde de perioada în care nimeriți. Cert este că noi am profitat de acest aspect și de asemenea vom aduce o mulțime de hăinuțe și jucării acolo, odată ce Ilan nu va mai avea nevoie de ele, tocmai pentru a susține acest sistem. Apoi, concediul de maternitate. 126 de zile calendaristice, 63 prenatal, 63 postnatal. Singurele obligatorii dintre acestea sunt 42 de zile după naștere pentru a putea intra în concediul de creștere copii. Indemnizația aceasta este în quantum de 85% din media veniturilor, iar actele se depun la CASMB dacă nu ești angajată. Altfel, direct la angajator cu certificatul obținut de la medic. Urmează concediul de creștere copil, care este până la 2 ani ai copilului sau 3 în cazul unui copil cu handicap. Indemnizația este de 85% din media veniturilor nete, realizate în ultimele 12 luni din ultimii 2 ani. Cel puțin 2 luni dintre acestea sunt rezervate celuilalt părinte. Dacă acesta nu își exercită acest drept, cele 2 luni din păcate se pierd. Dosarul se depune în acest caz la AJPIS sau la primăria din localitatea de domiciliu. Pentru alocație unde indemnizația este de 719 lei până la 2 ani, documentele se depun la AJPIS sau primăria localității de domiciliu de asemenea. Dacă vreți și aveți nevoie în următorul clip, vă arăt exact ce acte sunt necesare, unde se depun și în ce ordine ca să nu pierdeți timp și drumuri degeaba. Dacă vă interesează acest aspect, scrieți-mi în comentarii acte și îl fac cât mai repede pentru voi.

author: stefaniaelenam
title: Romanian nursery and kindergarten: rights and regulations
summary: A Romanian mother shares essential legal information for parents enrolling children in nursery or kindergarten, including the right to a 10-day adaptation period and regulations regarding healthy food in schools. She also discusses the emotional challenge of letting go of control and trusting the childcare environment.
key_points: Article 17 of the Romanian nursery methodology allows parents up to 10 working days to accompany their child during the adaptation period.
Law 123/2008 (Art. 10) prohibits the sale or distribution of unhealthy foods in schools.
Ministry of Health Order 541/2025 provides a specific list of foods not recommended for children in educational settings, including high-sugar, high-fat, and high-salt items.
Childcare settings often have limited staff-to-child ratios, meaning parents must accept that their specific home routines may not be followed exactly.
If a child is happy and thriving, minor differences in care routines are usually not grounds for changing the facility.

author: lorifullbright
title: Safety phrases to replace when talking to children
summary: A crime reporter with three decades of experience suggests replacing common safety phrases like 'stranger danger' and 'good touch/bad touch' with more accurate concepts. She emphasizes teaching children about 'tricky people' and 'uncomfortable touch' to better protect them from known abusers and empower them to set body boundaries.
key_points: Replace 'stranger danger' with 'tricky people' because most abusers are known to the child.
Teach children to identify 'tricky' behaviors like asking for secrets or setting conditions for affection.
Replace 'good touch/bad touch' with 'uncomfortable touch' because abusive touch can feel physically pleasant.
Establish a 'no secrets' rule regarding physical touch.
Do not force children to hug relatives to teach them they have control over their own bodies.
Offer alternatives to hugging, such as fist bumps or waves, to respect the child's boundaries.
caution: This advice is based on professional experience in crime reporting and aligns with modern body safety education.

author: thebodysafetyexpert
title: Script: what to say if you find porn on your child's device
summary: A child sexual abuse prevention educator models a calm, shame-free conversation after finding pornography on a child's iPad. She reassures the child they are not in trouble, asks how they found it, explains what pornography is and that it isn't real or healthy, takes responsibility as the adult, and invites questions. The caption notes the average age of first exposure is about 11, with many exposed at 5-7.
key_points: Stay calm: no shame, no blame - exposure is not the child's fault (being shown porn by others is a form of abuse).
Start gently, e.g. while they're doing a calm activity like drawing.
Ask how it happened: popped up, searched, or someone showed them - this tells you whether someone else is involved.
Explain in age-appropriate words that porn is made by adults for adults and shows bodies/relationships in unreal, unhealthy ways.
Normalise their feelings (confused, upset, curious, laughing).
Take responsibility for not protecting them better; then improve device filters and supervision.
Invite questions and become the go-to source on bodies, sex and relationships rather than the internet.

author: cassiemomcoach
title: Simple respectful discipline: child cleans up the mess she made
summary: A parent coach describes her 6-year-old deliberately dumping crumbs in the car. Instead of shaming, lecturing or removing TV, she calmly said the child would vacuum it at home, didn't engage when the child protested, then helped set up the vacuum and thanked her afterwards. She stresses that discipline can be simple, warm and still hold limits.
key_points: Approach with curiosity and assume good intentions rather than that your child is 'bad'.
Use a related consequence: the child cleans up the mess they made.
Avoid unrelated punishments (no TV, time-out) and shaming ('Why are you so bad?').
If they protest, stay calm — they can have feelings while you hold the boundary.
Follow through later at a calm moment and help them get started.
Thank them for taking responsibility, then move on.
Prevent repeats: temporarily skip crumbly snacks in the car until trust is rebuilt.
scripts: Oh, it looks like you put your crumbs on the ground. When we get home, you can be in charge of vacuuming those up.
Hey, let's go vacuum the car.
Thank you for taking responsibility for that mess you made. That's really important in our family.

author: The Considerate Momma
title: Student-Led Conflict Resolution Method
summary: An explanation of a student-led conflict resolution technique used in schools that can also be applied at home. The method focuses on cooling down, using 'I' statements, active listening, and collaborative problem-solving.
key_points: Designate a 'peace table' or 'peace mat' for resolving conflicts.
Step 1: Take a breather to cool down.
Step 2: Use 'I feel [emotion] when [action]' statements to avoid blame.
Step 3: Practice active listening by reflecting back what the other person said.
Step 4: Brainstorm solutions together.
Step 5: Take accountability and thank the other person.
scripts: I feel [emotion] when [action].
I heard you say that when this happened, you felt [emotion].
transcript: The way my daughter's school handles conflict resolution should be studied and utilized in every school, everywhere, all the time. And really, honestly, this could be used for sibling rivalry at home too. It is absolutely brilliant. They start teaching this as young as four years old. Just imagine if someone had given you these skills at four years old, how differently you would handle conflict as an adult, how much more maturely and peacefully and respectfully you would be able to resolve conflict with someone else, anyone else for that matter as an adult. I'm also not going to tell you the name of my daughter's school. Okay. I got a lot of eyeballs on my content and I don't really want people to know where my daughter's going to school. Okay. It is a private school. It is a mixed age group and there are multiple branches around the United States. At least I don't know if they're in other countries yet or not, but you can do your research and then you can just implement this. If you know a principal, a superintendent, a teacher, if you want to utilize this at home, utilize it. So when there is conflict inside the classroom, it is student led. The teachers do not get involved. They have taught the students to go grab another student. So if there are two students in conflict, they will go grab a peace table or peace mat leader to come and help them resolve the conflict. So the teachers are encouraging the students to be part of mediating and like the negotiation, the conflict resolution, all this kind of stuff. So a child is either going to be leading a peace table or they're going to be participating in it and it builds skills either way. Brilliant. So let's say we got two students, they're having a conflict. They go over to one student and they ask, can you please lead a peace table? And that child will say yes or no. They keep going until they find someone that says yes. So they all go over to a peace table or a peace mat and the leader will say, okay, let's take a few minutes to number one, cool down. We're just going to take a breather, take a minute to cool down. Then step two, they're going to look to one of the students and they're going to say, okay, share how you feel. But they have taught them to use the phrase, I feel blank when blank, not when you blank, I feel blank when blank. So what this is teaching children is to not pass the blame of their emotions and reactions onto someone else. Emotional maturity looks like taking responsibility for your own emotions and just sharing, hey, when this happened, I felt this about it. Then the next step is for them to repeat what they heard the other person say. This is something called active and reflective listening, but they're just teaching the children to say, okay, I heard you say when this happened, you felt this. You are validating the other person's experience, whether you agree with it or not. You're just saying, okay, I hear you saying that when this happened, you felt this about it. Okay, I can listen and I can understand that and I can reflect that back to you. Then the next step is to come up with a solution together. They get to brainstorm and think about, okay, how can we avoid this in the future? Just them brainstorming about this is absolutely brilliant, okay? They are learning to utilize the part of their brain that helps them resolve conflict. Then the last step is that they take accountability and thank the other person for coming and resolving conflict with them peacefully. Send this video to somebody because I think that it could change the lives of a lot of people. More people need to know this stuff.

author: Marcel Lu
title: Teaching Children About Consent and Boundaries
summary: This video explains why it is important to respect a child's 'no' regarding physical affection. It argues that pressuring children to hug or kiss adults can undermine their ability to set boundaries and understand consent in the future.
key_points: Forcing physical affection teaches children that others' feelings matter more than their own boundaries.
Children should not be guilted or shamed for refusing physical contact, even with family members.
Teaching consent helps children understand that their body belongs to them.
Respecting a child's 'no' helps them develop healthy boundaries for adulthood.

caution: None.

It's just a hug. No, you're trying to make her feel bad for saying no. Well, I came all the way here and I can't even get a hug? Well, she's not ready for a hug right now. Really? It's just a hug. Well, if it's just a hug, then as an adult, you should be good without it. Also, it's kind of creepy to manipulate a child for not giving you affection. Gosh, you're so sensitive. or you're not sensitive enough to be curious about the inner world of a child what is wrong with you what could possibly happen it's just a hug if an authority figure teaches a child they owe physical affection what does that teach them as they grow up it can make them more vulnerable to manipulation and abuse that's why as her dad i'll never teach my daughter she owes anyone a hug or a kiss and And yes, even family members.
onscreen: When adults don’t respect kids’ boundaries
Come here, give grandpa a hug
Well, if it's just a hug, then as an adult, you
caption:
Comment “BOUNDARIES” and I’ll send you 25 calm, confident boundary scripts you can use when someone crosses your boundaries.

Anyway here is the lesson behind today’s post.

Some people hear this conversation and think:

“It’s just a hug.”

But it’s never just about the hug.

It’s about what a child learns when an adult responds to their “no.”

When we guilt, shame, or pressure children into giving physical affection, we unintentionally teach them that:

• Other people’s feelings matter more than their own boundaries.
• Saying “no” makes them responsible for someone else’s emotions.
• They should ignore their discomfort to keep adults happy.

Those lessons don’t stay in childhood.

They often become the adults who struggle to set boundaries, feel guilty saying no, and tolerate unhealthy relationships because they were taught that love is conditional to how much they can please others.

Teaching a child that their body belongs to them isn’t disrespectful.

It isn’t rude & it isn’t making them “soft.”

It’s teaching consent.

As parents, our job isn’t to raise children who are obedient at all costs.

Our job is to raise children who know their voice matters, their “no” is respected, and they never owe anyone physical affection, not even family.

Because one day, that lesson could protect them in ways we can’t imagine.

caption:
Part 1: If I had daughters I would play this game with them too to help teach enthusiastic consent AND help practice setting boundaries. 

I first posted this game nearly 3 years ago and I thought it was time to refill and show how even three years later we’re still using the body language game to help teach our kids how to protect themselves and protect others. 

We talk about how even if someone isn’t saying “no” with their words, they might be saying “no”, “I don’t like this”, or “I’m uncomfortable” with their body language. That means we stop.

We also reverse the roles so they can practice protecting their own bodies too. We also practice using our voice to say “no”, “stop”, and “I don’t like that.”

We talk about standing up for others, asking for help from a trusted adult, and “reading” body language in other situations, Like if he sees a kid on the playground alone and looking sad, what could he do? What is their body language saying about how they’re feeling?

I take special care to point out what my body language is saying during the day and to point out what I see their body language telling me even when their words aren’t speaking.

title: Teaching a child about social rejection
summary: A mother uses a simple flower-picking activity to teach her son that not being chosen by others does not define his worth. She explains that rejection is a normal part of life and that his value remains intact regardless of others' opinions.
key_points: Use physical objects like flowers to demonstrate abstract social concepts.
Not being picked by others does not mean there is something wrong with you.
Mean words from others reflect their perspective, not the truth about the child.
Some people are only meant to be in our lives for a short time.
Reassure the child of their inherent worth and beauty.
scripts: Just because this flower was picked does that mean that these two are ugly or something is wrong with them? That's the same with you.
That doesn't mean it's true about you.
You are still amazing, you are still loving, you are still kind, you are still wonderful in the way that the lord made you to be.

title: Teaching children the true meaning of fairness
summary: This video provides a simple 10-minute lesson to teach children that fairness does not mean everyone gets the same thing, but rather that everyone gets what they need to be successful. It uses relatable examples like injuries and school supplies to illustrate this concept.
key_points: Fairness means everyone gets what they need to be successful.
Giving everyone the same thing is not always fair.
Use simple demonstrations, like the band-aid example, to explain the concept.
Apply the concept to daily life, such as school supplies or extra help.
Review this concept regularly to reinforce understanding.

author: alimariehere_
title: Teaching children to acknowledge when parents are busy
summary: A mother shares a strategy to reduce frustration when children demand immediate attention while she is busy. By teaching them to add 'after you're done' to their requests, children learn patience and courtesy.
key_points: Teach children to acknowledge when you are busy by adding 'after you're done' to requests.
This helps children understand that others are not always instantly available.
Be consistent and calm when teaching this boundary.
Always thank and praise the child when they use the phrase correctly.
scripts: After you're done, could you help me with this?

author: drlauriesantos
title: Teaching kids autonomy by allowing them to disappoint you
summary: This video argues that parents should encourage children to prioritize their own judgment over people-pleasing. By reframing 'disappointing others' as 're-appointing' oneself as the decision-maker, children can develop autonomy and avoid the trap of living to please others.
key_points: Notice when a child avoids a choice to avoid disappointing an adult.
Give children explicit permission to disappoint others, including parents, when following their own judgment.
Reframe 'disappointing' others as 're-appointing' yourself as the decision-maker of your life.
Aim to break the pattern of living to avoid disappointing parents.
scripts: You got to disappoint your counselor. You got to disappoint everybody so you don't have to disappoint yourself.

caption: What if letting your child disappoint you is one of the greatest gifts you can give them? Glennon Doyle shows us that when kids learn it’s okay to let others down, they develop the autonomy and resilience to become their own person. When we teach our children to reframe disappointment as a good thing, we empower them to see setbacks as opportunities to learn, trust their own judgment, and build the resilience to chart their own path. And this insight isn’t just for kids— many adults still live to avoid disappointing others (especially their parents). But sometimes by disappointing others, we can reclaim our autonomy as the decision-maker of our own lives. Sign up for The Science of Well-Being for Parents at DrLaurieSantos.com/Parents, and listen to this episode of The Happiness Lab with Glennon Doyle and Abby Wambach wherever you get your podcasts!

author: codependencykate
title: The BEND method for parental emotional regulation
summary: A marriage and family therapist explains that secure attachment only requires being attuned to your child about 30% of the time, provided you repair after ruptures. She introduces the 'BEND' method (Behavior, Emotion, Need, Desire) to help parents process their own reactions and practice self-compassion instead of shame.
key_points: Secure attachment requires attunement only about 30% of the time if you repair mistakes.
Relationships are built on repair, not perfection.
Self-compassion is the primary skill for life satisfaction and parenting.
BEND method: Behavior (notice it), Emotion (identify it), Need (find the unmet need), Desire (what you want instead).
All unwanted behavior points to an unmet need.
scripts: I'm noticing I'm yelling. Okay. Let's take a break.
caution: None.

ill.caption: Whiteboard summary: self-compassion and curiosity plus BEND (Behavior, Emotions, Need, Desire) to process a parent's reactions.

transcript: Studies show that you only have to get parenting right 30% of the time to have a securely attached child. I'm going to show you the two skills that you need to get that 30% right. My name's Kate. I'm a marriage and family therapist. I help people restore their relationships. And recently I've been doing videos on estrangement. So if you're a new parent, you maybe have a complicated relationship with your parents. You realize the things that they do. They did not do right. I'm going to teach you exactly the two things that you need to do right. And this is totally within your control. And I think you're going to be really excited when you learn this stuff. Here we go. The first one is self-compassion. Self-compassion has been identified as the number one skill that leads to overall life satisfaction and relationship happiness. You're probably very good at compassion with your friends. You're very good at listening to them, holding space with them, validating them, understanding them. Maybe you're not so good about that with yourself. Maybe you're really hard on yourself. Maybe you had a really critical parent. Maybe you had a really neglectful parent. But the good news is, is that it's not your voice. You weren't born with it. You weren't. You learned it. And that means you need to make space for your real voice to emerge because that is the real you. The real you is self-compassionate. It is curious and it is courageous. What you need to do is when you notice that shaming voice, maybe after you yell at your kids. And I'm going to show you exactly how to process it when you do that, because relationships are not about perfection and not making mistakes. They're about repair and repair builds trust. author: shesnotcrazyseries
title: The physical and social cost of pregnancy for partners
summary: A man explains the biological and social toll pregnancy takes on a mother, emphasizing that she builds the baby from her own body's resources. He urges partners to be present, share the mental load, and prioritize the mother's well-being over just the baby's.
key_points: Pregnancy is physically demanding as the baby draws nutrients like calcium and iron from the mother's body.
Mothers often face career stagnation and loss of physical ease while being expected to 'glow'.
Partners should ask how the mother is doing, not just the baby.
The partner's presence and emotional support are crucial to reducing the mother's burden.
scripts: How are you doing?
I'm here to carry the worry with you.
caution: The biological claims about nutrient depletion are generally accurate but should be discussed with an OB-GYN regarding prenatal nutrition.
transcript: I'm going to mansplain the cost of pregnancy to you. Stay with me. Most men think pregnancy is the waiting room. She's tired, she's big, she's glowing, and then the real event happens at the end. That's the surface. Underneath it, she's paying for this. In a currency, men never have to spend, and we mostly never see the bill. Here's the first thing nobody told us. She's not growing the baby alongside her body. She's building it out of her body. If the baby needs calcium and she's short, it comes out of her bones. If it needs iron, it comes out of her blood. If it needs omega-3s to build the brain, she donates them from hers. She is taking herself apart, literally, to make someone else. That's not a metaphor. That's the biology. And she can't put it down. 40 weeks no night off no version of her that isn't pregnant until it's over but here's the cost we never really count while she's doing this she's often still expected to perform like nothing's happening still at work and quietly watching her career slow while his keeps moving still feeling less safe in her own body more vulnerable more dependent in a world that doesn't make room for it. Still losing the ease she used to take for granted, the easy sleep, the easy movement, the body that just did what she asked. And on top of it all, she's handed a script. Smile. Glow. Say it's the happiest time of your life. Don't be difficult about it. So she pays in her bones, in her blood, in her career, in her safety, in her ease. And then she's asked to look grateful while she does it. Now, none of this means it isn't beautiful. Of course it is. Of course you're excited about your baby. I'm not taking that from anyone. Both things are true at once. It's a gift and it costs her everything to give it. So here's the job. The biggest cost you can add or take away is you. Doing all of that beside a man who's checked out, who thinks it's just pregnancy, who isn't really there, that's the heaviest weight on the pile. And it's the one that you can lift today. Don't ask how the baby's doing. Ask how she's doing. Carry the worry so it isn't only hers. Be the safe thing in the room. She's not being dramatic. She's not just pregnant. She's paying for a life with her own body. And the least we can do is notice the bill.
caption: Pregnancy isn’t the waiting bit.  She builds the baby out of her own body…bones, blood, even part of her brain.  Then pays again in her career, her safety, her ease. And gets told to glow about it. Of course it’s beautiful. Both things are true. But the heaviest cost you can add is being a man who isn’t really there. Ask how SHE’S doing. Not just the baby.  #shesnotcrazy #cycleawareness #marriage #understandingwomen #relationships

author: georgiana.popa16
title: The two-glasses technique for teaching perspective
summary: A mother demonstrates a simple role-playing game using two pairs of glasses to help children reframe negative situations. By switching between 'black glasses' (negative) and 'coloured glasses' (positive), children learn to identify and choose their own perspective.
key_points: Use two pairs of glasses: black for negative thoughts, coloured for positive ones.
Model the negative and positive responses for the child initially.
Help the child understand they are the 'boss of their thoughts'.
Keep the positive glasses 'in your pocket' as a reminder that you can choose your perspective.
scripts: It's just a stain, I can rewrite the homework.
It's just a test, I have a thousand tests.
Maybe they had a bad day. Anyway, I am not how they said I am.
Maybe at the next birthday they will invite me.

title: Toddler defiance hack: ask 'are you big/brave enough to…?'
summary: A creator explains that toddlers (around 2-4) suddenly discover autonomy and resist instructions with 'no', tantrums, hitting or biting. Her hack is to stop asking them to do things and instead ask if they think they are old, strong, smart, brave or big enough to do it, tapping into their desire to prove themselves.
key_points: Toddler defiance often reflects a new drive for autonomy, typically emerging between ages 2 and 4.
Instead of 'Will you…?', ask 'Do you think you're big/strong/smart/brave enough to…?'
Works for tasks like tying shoes, brushing teeth, putting a dish in the sink, tidying toys.
Pick any superlative that fits the task and let them proudly show you.
scripts: Do you think you're old enough to do this?
Are you strong enough to do this?
Are you smart enough to do this?
Are you brave enough to do this?
dedupe: toddler defiance hack ask if they are big enough
transcript: did your cuddly cute baby turn into a defiant monster of a toddler seemingly overnight well i have a hack for that see toddlers hit a phase whether it's at two or three or four where all of a sudden they realize they're a whole ass person and they have autonomy and any attempt at taking some of that autonomy from them will be met with uh tantrums screaming no hitting biting yada yada so here's the hack um I never ask a defiant toddler if they would do something I ask them if they think they're old enough to do something I ask them if they're strong enough to do something I ask them if they're smart enough to do something I ask them if they're brave enough to do something and guess what they're desperate to prove that they are they're desperate to show me that they are smart enough to tie their own shoes that they are old enough to brush their own teeth that they are tall enough to put their own dish in the sink that they are strong enough to put their toys away okay so don't ask your toddler to do something ask them if they are brave enough smart enough old enough big enough whatever or pick your own superlative and watch your toddler do that thing and do it excitedly, okay?
onscreen: I never ask a defiant toddler if they would do something

author: connectedbeginnings
title: Toddler hitting, biting, pushing: a 4-step gentle response
summary: A licensed therapist explains that toddlers (around 2) hit, bite and push because they lack words for big emotions and are in a fight-flight-freeze state. Shaming or punishing increases the behaviour and doesn't teach alternatives. She gives four steps: anticipate and block, validate the emotion, set the boundary, and teach what to do instead.
key_points: Hitting/biting/pushing is very common around age 2: children express emotions through their bodies because they lack words.
When activated, kids are in fight-flight-freeze mode; many 'fight'.
Don't shame or punish; it tends to increase the behaviour and doesn't teach an alternative.
Step 1 - Anticipate: watch for cues/triggers and block the hand before the hit; remove them from overwhelming situations.
Step 2 - Validate the emotion (e.g., angry about a diaper change).
Step 3 - Set the boundary calmly: "I won't let you hit."
Step 4 - Teach what to do instead: gentle touches, hit the floor or scream into a pillow when angry.

caption:
Toddlers often resort to hitting, kicking, biting, or pushing as a means of communication when they are unable to express their emotions effectively. It’s important to approach these situations with empathy and understanding, using gentle parenting techniques to guide their behavior.

Here is a four step process that can be highly effective in addressing these behaviors:

1. Anticipate the action: By observing your toddler’s cues and recognizing their triggers, you can proactively intervene before the hitting, kicking, biting, or pushing occurs. This might involve removing them from a situation that is overwhelming or providing alternative activities to redirect their attention.

2. Validate the emotion: When a toddler becomes upset and resorts to physical behavior, it’s crucial to acknowledge and validate their emotions. By saying things like, “I can see that you’re feeling frustrated,” or “It looks like you’re upset,” you help them understand that their feelings are valid and heard.

3. Set the boundary: Clearly and calmly communicate that this behavior is not acceptable. For example, you can say, “I won’t let you hit. Hitting hurts others.” This sends a clear message while maintaining a respectful and gentle tone.

4. Teach alternatives: After setting the boundary, it’s important to guide your toddler towards more appropriate behaviors. You can say, “hands are for gentle touches.”If you’re frustrated we can hit a pillow.” “Let’s practice pretend biting please.” This helps them understand that there are alternative ways to express themselves and get their needs met.

title: Toddlers under 3 don't understand 'no' and 'not' — say what TO do
summary: A speech therapist demonstrates with her daughter that toddlers under three often misinterpret negative sentences ('which one has no sticker?'). Citing research, she explains toddlers may hear 'no climbing on the stairs' as 'climbing on the stairs', so parents should phrase directions positively. For safety, use a simple 'no' or 'stop' while physically moving the child, then say what they can do.
key_points: Research (Austin et al. 2014; Feiman et al. 2017; Nordmeyer & Frank 2014) suggests children under ~3 often process negative sentences as affirmatives.
Instead of 'no jumping on the couch', say what to do: 'The couch is for sitting' or 'Let's sit on the couch'.
In safety situations, say a simple 'No!' or 'Stop!' and physically move the child so they learn the word's meaning, then tell them what they can do.
Test it at home: hold two items your toddler knows well and ask 'Show me which one is NOT the ___'.
Lack of understanding is only one reason toddlers don't obey; impulse control and boundary-testing also play a role.
scripts: The couch is for sitting.
Let's sit on the couch.
Show me which one is not the apple.

title: Transitioning children to the 'Santa' spirit
summary: A guide on how to handle the moment a child starts doubting Santa Claus by transitioning them into 'becoming a Santa' themselves. This involves teaching them the joy of anonymous, empathetic giving rather than just receiving.

author: ileana.justine
title: Treat girls' interest in hair and outfits as real skills
summary: A mum shares insights from educator Beck Goodman on how to parent daughters who are interested in beauty. Instead of shaming them as vain, acknowledge their interest and ask process-oriented questions to validate the skill and practice involved. This approach helps avoid gendered double standards and encourages valuing 'feminine' skills.
key_points: Affirm a child's interest in their appearance by asking about the skill behind it.
Ask process questions like 'How did you match those colours?' or 'You must have practised that braid for a long time'.
Avoid the double standard of teaching girls that beauty is an ideal and then shaming them for caring about it.
Value traditionally 'feminine' skills like styling hair or outfits as much as 'masculine' skills like running or building.
Be intentional about teaching children that effort and practice are what make skills valuable.
scripts: How did you match those colours together?
What was your inspiration for the outfit?
How do you think mom learned to do your braids like that? She must've practised for so long.
transcript: As the mom of a little girl and a former little girl myself, this video changed my brain chemistry. This video didn't go viral, but I legitimately think about it every single day, so I need to show it to you. Something that I see all the time with my preschool age girls is that unlike the boys who will come into session and say things like, look how fast I can run, look how high I can jump, the girls will often come into session and say, look how pretty my dress is, do you like my hair? And I really want to instill in these girls that doing your outfit and your hair are skills. They're practiced and gained skills. So now what I do when they say things like that, after being like, yeah, that is beautiful. I'll ask some questions like, how did you match those colors together? What was your inspiration for the outfit? How do you think mom learned to do your braids like that? She must've practiced for so long. And something really cool happened this morning. I walked into a session and this girl who's very into all things being pretty said your hair looks really pretty today and i said okay thank you and she said how did you do that did it take a long time you must have had to practice so that was really cool to see this video shifted the way that i think about all of the skills that we deem like feminine because we teach girls from the time they're born that beauty is an ideal they should strive for we show them princesses we put them in dresses we put bows on their heads and we teach them that beauty is so important. And then when they care about beauty, we shame them for it. When toddlers come into class and say like, isn't my dress so pretty? We tell them instead, well, you should be caring about other things like the things that boys care about. You should care about running fast and jumping high and building tall towers. But we've taught them their entire lives that what they should care about is beauty. So why aren't we teaching them to appreciate and value those skills alongside the actual aesthetic. Learning to braid your hair is a skill. Learning which colors to wear is a skill. Learning how to put together an outfit that's aesthetically pleasing to yourself and others is a skill. It shows a lot of emotional intelligence. There are so many things that go into beauty. I don't think we realize sometimes how hierarchical we are with how we value skills and which skills we deem important, and this really shifted my mindset about the way that I'm going to teach my daughter and the way that I'm reteaching myself. Because our world teaches children that little girls should strive to be beautiful and they should care about their appearance, and then when they do, we call them vain. And this double standard doesn't exist for boys in the same way. So when we want to raise children to live in a more equitable and equal world, we need to also teach boys that when they care about their outfits, that's great. So anyway, that's a video that completely altered my brain, and it has changed the way that I'm going to parent. It has changed the way that I think about valuable skills, and I think it's a good reminder to be intentional with what we're teaching our kids.

author: elythia.nastere
title: Understanding Postpartum Bleeding (Lochia)
summary: A midwife explains that postpartum bleeding (lochia) is normal after any birth and typically lasts up to six weeks. She provides guidance on how to distinguish normal recovery from a potential postpartum hemorrhage, emphasizing the need for medical attention if bleeding is excessive.
key_points: Lochia occurs after both vaginal births and C-sections.
Bleeding is heaviest in the first 1-2 days and should gradually decrease.
Color transitions from bright red to brownish over the first week.
Hemorrhage warning: soaking a large maternity pad in under 1-2 hours or passing very large clots.
Excessive physical effort can cause bleeding to increase again.
Lochia should not have an unpleasant odor; foul smell may indicate infection.

title: Understanding temperament: Orchids vs. Dandelions
summary: This video explains why siblings in the same family can have different emotional needs using the 'orchid vs. dandelion' metaphor. It emphasizes that temperament is innate and that sensitive children (orchids) require different environmental support to thrive compared to more resilient children (dandelions).
key_points: Children are born with different temperaments: 'dandelions' are hardy, 'orchids' are highly sensitive.
Sensitive children feel emotions more intensely and take longer to return to baseline.
Parenting the same way for all children may not meet every child's individual needs.
Sensitivity is not a weakness; with the right environment, it leads to empathy and creativity.
Focus on what each specific child needs rather than assuming parenting is the sole cause of emotional struggles.

transcript: Ever wondered why one sibling can struggle with intense emotions while the other one seems completely fine, even though they grew up in the same family? I'm a clinical psychologist who specializes in borderline personality disorder, so let me explain. Think of some kids as born an orchid and some are born as a dandelion. Dandelions are naturally hardy, right? They literally grow in the cracks of a sidewalk. But an orchid needs a little bit more TLC, the right light, the right method of watering just the roots. If you care for both flowers the same, like just pouring some water into them every day, the dandelion might be fine, but the orchid might not thrive. It's the same with kids who are born with different temperaments. One child might be naturally more emotionally sensitive. They feel things more intensely and have a harder time calming down. While the other child might just be naturally less reactive. And if you parent the two kids the same, telling them both just to calm down when they cry, the dandelion kid might be able to calm down more easily but the orchid may not. Two siblings can grow up in the same household with the same parents and experience that family completely differently. The same family doesn't meet everyone's needs perfectly. Keep in mind that when orchids do get what they need they bloom into something beautiful. Both orchid kids and dandelion kids are special in their own ways.

caption:
Same family- one kid has BPD and one doesn't. Why?

Because BPD isn’t simply caused by parenting or childhood experiences. It develops through a complex interaction between nature and nurture.

Some children are born with more emotionally sensitive temperaments. They feel emotions more intensely, react more strongly, and may take longer to return to baseline.

Think of it like **orchids and dandelions.** 🌸🌼

A dandelion can thrive in lots of different environments. An orchid may be more sensitive to its environment and need different conditions to thrive.

So even when parents treat two children similarly, those children may experience the same parenting very differently.

Trauma, abuse, neglect, invalidation, and other environmental experiences can make these differences more extreme but temperament and genetics matter too. And importantly, being highly sensitive isn't inherently a weakness.

Under the right conditions, that sensitivity can come with incredible strengths: empathy, emotional depth, creativity, passion, and connection.

The question isn't always: “What went wrong in this family?” Sometimes a better question is: “What did this particular child need?”

caption:
Discipline can feel so complicated sometimes, but it comes down to being firm AND kind. I consider myself very strict because I am extremely consistent in my discipline, but I NEVER withdraw my love, support, and attention as part of that. Withdrawing your love communicates rejection and shame, as well as taking away the tools your child has to truly regulate: a calm & connected adult. I want my lesson to land every time I discipline my child instead of their focus shifting to their anger toward me, their intense feelings of rejection/shame, or rage toward the person they hurt for “getting them in trouble.” 

Instead of “time outs”, I give “time ins” where I stay WITH my kids to help them calm down and process. The problem with that is that if I’m on my own, my kids who didn’t do anything wrong have to be left alone. So in those instances, they get to watch a show (we’re a very low screens family btw) while I go in the other room with whoever needs a “time in.” This has been especially effective for my middle because she has to deal with the consequence of not getting to watch a show on top of being separated from her siblings. We have also instituted “earning” one show at the end of the day if she doesn’t hit or kick at al and I’ve seen a huge decline in this behavior once we started this consequence (the video is a month old) and she has only hit once since then. 

My middle (seen here) has always struggled to speak when she is overly emotional, which is why she hits & kicks when she’s overwhelmed. To be clear, she only hits her older sibling (never her younger her one) and she has NEVER hit me, my husband, or other children. Sibling hitting is extremely normal and peaks around 2-3 years old, then drops significantly between 3-4 years old, and should stop around 5 years old with consistent discipline & once a child has better language access under stress & better impulse control.

title: When your son repeats 'manosphere' ideas: get curious, don't shame

Respond with curiosity: ask where the idea came from and what he thinks.

Play the long game: if he can bring these conversations to you, you're more influential than any algorithm.

If your son repeats something misogynistic or extreme that he’s heard online, take a deep breath.

This isn’t the moment to shame him.

It’s the moment to get curious.

When children feel judged, they stop talking.

When they stop talking, the internet becomes their teacher.

Instead of rushing to correct him, ask where the idea came from.

Ask what he thinks.

Ask how it makes him feel.

Very often, underneath statements about girls, masculinity or relationships is something much more vulnerable:

Fear of rejection.
Fear of not being enough.
Fear of failing.
Fear of not knowing where they fit.

When we respond to the feeling first, children become much more open to challenging the belief itself.

Remember, you’re playing the long game.

You’re not trying to win one argument.

You’re trying to raise a young man who knows how to think critically, question confidently and stay connected to the people who love him.

author: drlindsayemmerson
title: When your toddler hits another child: attend to the hurt child first
summary: A parenting doctor explains that children aged 2 to about 7 are still developing perspective-taking, so hitting is developmental rather than defiance. She critiques four common reactions (public shaming, immediate extraction, over-apologizing, ignoring) and recommends going to the hurt child first, stating the rule once, and inviting the child to make a repair instead of forcing a 'sorry'.
key_points: Ages 2-7 (Piaget's preoperational stage): the ability to register another person's pain is still forming.
Avoid loud public correction (shame shuts down learning), instantly removing the child, over-apologizing to the other parent, or ignoring it.
Step 1: go to the child who was hit first, crouch down and check on them; your toddler learns most by watching this.
Step 2: calmly, once: 'We don't hit. Hitting hurts.' and name the other child's feeling.
Step 3: offer a repair action (e.g. checking on the other child) rather than a forced apology.
If they hit again, give a choice ('play gently or we'll take a break') and follow through every time.
If your child refuses to repair, that's okay; the modelling already happened. Learning builds over many repetitions.
To the other parent, a brief 'I'm sorry that happened, we're working on it' is enough.

We don't hit. Hitting hurts. Marcus is sad right now.
Can you go check on Marcus?
You can play gently or we'll take a break.
I'm sorry that happened, we're working on it.

transcript: When your toddler hits another child, the most critical thing you do isn't what you say to your toddler. Most parents never realize this. I know the pressure of that moment. You're managing three relationships at once, your child, the child who got hit, and every adult in the room watching you handle it. And the instinct is to react fast. But here's what I see in my practice. The parents who handle this best aren't the ones who react fastest. They're the ones who know what to do before it happens. So here's the developmental piece that changes everything. Children age two through about six, seven, are in what Piaget called the pre-operational stage, a period when the brain is still building the capacity for perspective taking. Asking a toddler to fully register that another child is in pain is like asking someone to describe a color that they've never seen. The concept isn't fully formed yet. This isn't defiance, it's development, an emerging skill that needs guidance. Now, the four responses most parents reach for all miss the moment. The public shame response, a loud, audible correction for the room to hear, delivers shame, not instruction. Shame shuts down learning. The other adults feel reassured. Your toddler does not feel taught. The immediate extraction, scooping your child away from the situation, keeps everyone safe, but removes them from the exact teaching moment that was right there. The over-apology, turning to the other parent and immediately managing the relationship, models adult social management instead of child accountability. your toddler watches you handle the fallout for them. The ignore a gentle be gentle and let it pass leaves your child who cannot yet take another person's perspective without any guidance at all here's the response that works and the step that most parents never think to take go to the child who was hit first not your child not the other parent the child on the ground crouch down are you okay that looked like it hurt your toddler watches you attend to the consequence of what they did. That is the most powerful modeling moment in the entire interaction. More powerful than anything you say directly to them. Then calmly to your toddler. We don't hit. Hitting hurts. Marcus is sad right now. Short once. Then the step most parents skip. Give your child the chance to repair. Can you go check on Marcus? Not a forced sorry. Something physical that begins to wire the link between their action and someone else's experience. If they hit again, you can play gently or we'll take a break. Then follow through every time. Your toddler may refuse to go and check in on the other child, and that's okay. The most important part already happened. You modeled it. They watched you go to the child on the ground first. The repair doesn't have to land perfectly in this moment for the learning to happen. It happens across dozens of imperfect try again moments. And when the other parent is watching, a brief, warm, I'm sorry that happened, we're working on it. It's enough. What they need to see is you handling it well. That is it.

caption:
You’re at a playdate. Everything is fine — and then it isn’t. Your toddler hits the other child, and you have about 30 seconds to either teach something or miss the moment entirely.

Here’s what most parents don’t know: children ages 2–7 are still developing the brain capacity for perspective-taking — the ability to genuinely register that another person is in pain (Piaget & Inhelder, 1969). The hit isn’t defiance. It’s development. And your child needs a guide through this moment, not just a consequence.

The four most common responses — the public correction, the extraction, the over-apology, the ignore — all miss the teaching opportunity for different reasons.

The response that works starts with a counterintuitive step:
Go to the child who was hit first. Crouch down. “Are you okay? That looked like it hurt.” Your toddler watches you attend to what they caused — and that’s the most powerful modelling moment in the whole interaction.

Then, calmly, once: “We don’t hit. Hitting hurts.” Then give them the chance to repair.

Not a forced sorry. Something to do.

Save this for before the next playdate. 💛

title: Why Ignoring Negative Behavior and Rewarding Positive Requests Matters
summary: This video explains that children often learn to yell or whine because those behaviors get an immediate, animated response from parents. To change this, parents should prioritize acknowledging and rewarding polite requests while not reinforcing negative attention-seeking behaviors.
