caption:
My brother was kind enough to let me share this video, and I want to start by saying how much I love him and my niece. He is an incredible dad, and she is an incredible child.

This moment was not unusual or “bad parenting.” It was simply such a clear example of something happening in homes every single day.

Our children often ask for what they want in ways we would rather they didn’t. They interrupt, whine, yell, or ask repeatedly. And many parents wonder: Why does this keep happening despite everything I’m doing?

Here is one reason we often miss.

When children engage in behavior we want to stop, they usually get a very immediate response. We look at them. We acknowledge them. We begin explaining, correcting, negotiating, or reminding. Even when we do not give them what they asked for, that behavior often produces a large amount of attention—and usually a much more animated version of us.

But when they ask appropriately, wait patiently, or accept that something is not available, those moments can pass with far less acknowledgment.
That is exactly what this video captures.

Charlie asked for something appropriately. My brother did respond, but he said, “in a minute,” without looking up. But a few seconds earlier, she was yelling and repeatedly asking, and received a much bigger and more immediate response.

So what might she learn?

Asking appropriately does not work nearly as well as getting louder and asking again.

This doesn’t mean we must immediately give our children everything they request. It means that when they use the behavior we want to see more often, our response to it needs to matter.

When your child asks appropriately, notice it. Look at them. Respond as quickly as you reasonably can.

And when they cannot have it immediately but wait patiently or handle the answer well, point that out too:

“Thank you for waiting so patiently.”
“I noticed how flexible you were.”
“I really liked the way you asked me.”

Children can only do more of what we want when they know exactly what worked. And every response teaches them which version of asking works best.

Drowning is the number one cause of non-illness-related death in children between the ages of one and four. So how are you teaching your child to drown? Just this afternoon, I drove by my neighborhood pool, and I could have easily counted 10 to 15 kids running around in puddle jumpers and life jackets. Children in this target age range between one and four. Every second, your preschool and toddler age child spins in a flotation device. They are learning to drown and the reason is twofold. First, let's talk about muscle memory. Life jackets, puddle jumpers, arm floaties, those donut rings that you put around your waist, all of them position a child to be in the drowning position. Take a look at the screen here. This is what the drowning position is. The drowning position is vertical, head up, feet on the bottom. And because you start putting your child in this from the time that they're about a year old, maybe even earlier, you are literally teaching every muscle fiber in their body to stay in this position. The drowning position is vertical. The swimming and life-saving position is horizontal. Infants, toddlers, and preschoolers' bodies are growing and developing at such a rapid pace. And muscle memory is a vitally important part of human development. It's how we learn to do normal basic human functions. It's how we learn to crawl and then walk and then run. It's how we learn to hold a pencil and write. It's how we learn to feed ourselves. And it's how we learn to do more complex actions like riding a bike and swimming. So the way that your child stays positioned and learns to move at this age is crucially important when it comes to swimming. You don't want a toddler and a preschooler to be spending all of their time in the water in the vertical drowning position. But unfortunately, that's how all of these flotation devices position them. And when they spend all of their time like this, how are they supposed to learn any other way? How are they supposed to gain muscle memory to be in the horizontal swimming and life-saving position? This leads into the second part of how you're teaching your child to drown, And that is by instilling a false sense of security in them. You see, the thing is, a child needs to know what they weigh in the water. They need to know what their own buoyancy is without being in a float. It is vitally important that a child gets to know their own buoyancy. What does their body feel like in the water? This is what keeps a child from jumping back in the pool during non-swim times. More than 70% of childhood drownings happen during non-swim times. Maybe you're at the public pool and everybody's drying off. Mom's attention is on a couple of other kids. And the two-year-old, because they don't know what they really feel like in the water because all they've ever known is the security of a float, runs and jumps back in the water when nobody's looking. Drowning is quick. Drowning is silent. Or perhaps it's a backyard pool and the child slips out unattended. Because despite what critics believe, even the best parents turn their back for just a second. And because that child doesn't spend any time outside of their puddle jumper or their floaties or their life vest, and because they believe that that's what they really weigh and feel like in the water, they jump back in and they drown. By the time somebody finds them, it's too late. It takes that long. My son drowned during non-swim time. So what can you do to fix this? Get your child out of the floats. But my child needs the float because he can't swim. Then get in the water and work with them on these swim skills. Get your child in life-saving swim classes. In the drowning community, we have this saying, skills before thrills. What that means is your child should have a healthy fear of the water. Recreational water activity should be presented to your child from the earliest age as yes this is something that we love and enjoy but this is also something that can hurt you. It can kill you. Your child should be instilled with a healthy fear of the thing that has the greatest potential to claim their life. Stop putting your child in a puddle jumper and then encouraging them to jump into the water and then making videos and posting them on social media calling your child fearless. I don't want you to be me. I don't want you to be in my situation. I don't want you to be in the situation of thousands and millions of other parents who have gone through it. title: Why labeling a child's protest as a 'tantrum' causes shame
summary: A therapist explains that labeling a child's healthy protest as a 'tantrum' invalidates their needs and adds shame to their big emotions. This pattern can lead children to suppress their feelings to maintain connection, potentially resulting in anxiety and depression later in life.

Labeling a protest as a tantrum adds shame on top of the original feeling.
Repeated invalidation teaches children that their emotions are 'too much'.
Children may become 'good girls' to stay connected to parents, while feeling alone with their emotions.
Acknowledge the feeling and the need behind the protest instead of shaming.

Anyone with a cold sore should not kiss the baby or share utensils with them.
Seek urgent care early: early treatment matters, but prevention is the best protection.
One study found 63% of parents felt too embarrassed to ask relatives not to kiss their baby — set the rule in advance.

HSV-1, commonly known for causing cold sores, can be very dangerous for newborns if they become infected. Newborns have undeveloped immune systems, which makes it hard for their bodies to fight off infections. When a baby contracts HSV-1, typically through close contact with someone who has an active cold sore, the virus can spread quickly throughout their body, including to the brain and other vital organs.

Early treatment is crucial, but the best protection is preventing exposure to HSV-1. author: drchelsey_parenting
title: Why traditional consequences fail neurodivergent children
summary: A parenting coach explains that punitive consequences are ineffective for neurodivergent children during meltdowns because their learning brain is offline. She recommends focusing on connection, regulation, and supportive structures like movement breaks and sensory tools instead of punishment.
key_points: Consequences delivered during a meltdown do not teach because the child is in fight-or-flight mode.
Learning happens in the prefrontal cortex, which goes offline during dysregulation.
Use a 'regulation station' with sensory tools to help children calm down.
Break tasks into 3-5 minute chunks with movement breaks.
Validate the child's feelings before attempting to problem-solve.
Effective discipline requires heavy positive support and connection first.

author: abbyeckel
title: "You can use my eyes, not my brain": teaching boys to own mental load
summary: A mom of boys shares the phrase "You can use my eyes, but not my brain": she will point to something she can see, but will not think through a task for her son when he already knows how to do it. She argues that boys have historically been under-expected and allowed to outsource cognitive and care work to women, and that raising them to carry their own mental load takes deliberate, repeated effort.
key_points: Help with physical things (pointing to a lost item you can see) but don't narrate steps of tasks the child has already been taught and can do.
Stepping in is faster in the moment but teaches that hard thinking can be outsourced to someone else, usually a woman.
Name the reluctance and still expect the effort: acknowledge they don't want to think it through, then require them to do it.
Show them how repeatedly instead of doing it for them; this takes time and intentionality.
Involve boys in care work and talk openly about the invisible labor of running a home.
Drop "for me" from chore requests ("Can you put that in the dishwasher?") so chores are framed as shared responsibility, not favours to mom.

I am not going to narrate the steps of something we've been through many times before. I'm not going to think through it out loud for him. I mean, it sure as hell isn't the easier path, but it's simply the right one. author: mindandhearttherapist
title: 'Is it unfair or unjust?' — a question to help kids sort conflicts
summary: A licensed therapist teaches her kids to ask whether a situation is unjust or just unfair. Unjust means someone is hurt or bleeding, using really inappropriate language, or you feel very unsafe — go get an adult. Unfair means hurt feelings, which are valid but call for coping and communication skills rather than adult rescue.
key_points: Unjust = someone is hurt/bleeding, very inappropriate language, or your alarm bells are going off → get an adult.
Unfair = feelings hurt, disappointment, not getting your way → valid, but work through it with coping and communication skills.
Helping kids tolerate 'unfair' builds resilience; not every hard feeling means something is wrong.
Parents can ask themselves the same question when a child pushes their buttons.
scripts: Is it unfair or is it unjust?

That is unjust and that is when you should come get an adult. If it is unfair, your feels got hurt, completely valid, but we need to figure out a way to manage that. Is this unjust or is it just unfair/uncomfortable?

It’s a question I ask my kids all the time because not every hard feeling means something is wrong. Sometimes it’s just disappointment, frustration, or not getting their way.

summary: A mom tells how her 4-year-old was crushed when work stopped her from doing a promised-feeling pickup. Only use the word 'promise' for things you will definitely do
Kids adopt the language and become more flexible when plans change

Resist the parental urge to problem-solve; being a safe listener builds trust and openness.

What if the best way to connect with your child was to stop talking to them?

author: kelsewhatelse
title: 'The talk' for new dads: keep comforting the baby even when they want mom
summary: A mother explains the advice she gives every soon-to-be dad: newborns often seem to want only mom when upset (she can breastfeed/rock them), and dads must keep learning to comfort the baby anyway. Her husband took a few minutes longer using the 5 S's, but persisting built his bond and confidence, gave her breathing room and prevented resentment.
key_points: It is common for an upset newborn to calm faster with mom (e.g. via breastfeeding); this is not personal and the phase passes.
Dads should keep comforting the crying baby themselves instead of handing them to mom every time.
A dad's soothing will look different and be more physical: use the 5 S's (swaddling, side/stomach position while holding, shushing, swinging, sucking).
It may take 5-10 minutes longer at first, but the baby learns to calm with dad faster over time.
Persisting builds the father-baby bond and dad's confidence, and gives the mother rest and freedom.
Defaulting to mom 24/7 can lead to the partner feeling resentful.

caption:
Summary of the Talk:

* Clarification* : baby will probably only " want Mom" when they are upset and need comforted. I don't mean all the time. 

1. It’s Okay if Your Baby Prefers Mom Initially:
 It’s normal for a baby to seem more attached to Mom at first. This has nothing to do with you personally. Babies don’t form opinions to hurt your feelings, and this phase won’t last forever. Over time, you will develop a bond. (And this isn't every baby and every set of parents! I'm speaking directly to the parents for whom this applies to)

2. Comforting Your Baby is Harder, But Do It Anyway:
 Even if it feels more challenging for you to comfort your baby compared to Mom, keep trying. 

3. Your Comforting Style Will Be Different:
 Don’t expect to soothe your baby the same way Mom does. Your approach may be more physical—learn techniques like the Five S’s (swaddling, swinging, shushing, sucking, side-lying). 

4. Avoid Defaulting to Mom for Comfort 24/7:
 It might seem easier to hand the baby over to Mom since she calms them down faster, but remember, crying is how babies communicate. Actively comfort your baby yourself. The more you do it, the easier it will become, and the more confident you’ll feel as you bond with your child. 

Why This Matters:
Many dads feel unwanted during the newborn phase, so they distance themselves or focus on other tasks. This often leaves moms feeling overwhelmed and resentful while dads feel unneeded. Stick with it—it’s okay that it’s hard, and it’s completely normal. You’ve got this! 

Put in the effort from the beginning to be an active, comforting parent. If you don’t, down the road—whether it’s in a month, a year, or three years—you’ll find yourself needing to reevaluate your role as a 50/50 partner in parenting. That conversation will be much harder than simply starting off right from the beginning. It’s better for everyone in the long run.

title: 10 tips for bathing a newborn
summary: A second-time mom lists her top tips for newborn baths in the caption, illustrated with clips of bathing a baby in an infant tub. Tips cover never leaving baby unattended, timing around feeds, preparation, water temperature, bath length, gentle products and drying skin folds.
key_points: Never leave the baby unattended in the bath, even for a few seconds; take baby with you.
Don't bathe a hungry baby; feed about 10-15 minutes before so they are calm but not too full.
Have everything ready beforehand: a basket of bath essentials and clothes laid out.

Keep baths short, 5-10 minutes, to avoid drying sensitive skin.
Always keep one hand on the baby; an infant tub or support seat helps.
Use gentle fragrance-free products sparingly; plain water is enough for most of the body.
Wash top to bottom: face with water only first, diaper area last; clean neck rolls, underarms, behind ears and thigh creases, then pat (don't rub) dry, especially in creases.

onscreen: 10 things I wish I knew before bathing a newborn
caption:
My top 10 tips for bathing a newborn as a second-time mom 🛁👶✨

1. Always take baby with you even if you’re just going a few feet away or need something quickly. NEVER leave them unattended. 

2. Don’t bathe a hungry baby. Try feeding about 10–15 minutes before bath time so they’re calm (but not too full).

3. Have EVERYTHING ready before you start. Keeping a basket with bath essentials next to you and their clothes laid out really helps.

4. Check the water temperature. Warm, not hot (around 98–100°F).

5. Keep baths short. 5–10 minutes is plenty. Longer baths can dry out baby’s sensitive skin.

6. Always keep one hand on baby. Babies are slippery! A baby tub like the one I’m using or a support seat really helps.

7. Use gentle, fragrance-free products. Less is more. Plain water is often enough for most of the body.

8. Wash from top to bottom. Start with the face (just water), then work your way down. Save the diaper area for last.

9. Don’t forget the little folds. Neck rolls, underarms, behind ears, and thighs (milk and lint love to hide there). A soft washcloth helps a lot.

10. Dry thoroughly. Pat dry (don’t rub) and make sure all creases are dry to prevent irritation.

✨ Bonus tip: Stick to sponge baths until the umbilical cord stump falls off (usually 1–2 weeks).

author: irennegourmet
title: 11 pieces of advice that changed us as parents
summary: A Romanian-language carousel of parenting reminders focused on patience, connection and self-esteem. It includes remembering how small your child's hands are when you're annoyed, often telling children how lucky you are to be their parents, and praising them to others within earshot. Other slides suggest using 'after' instead of 'if', being a safe space for every emotion, and remembering that your voice becomes their inner voice.
key_points: When you're irritated, look at how small their hands are: they're just beginning life and need help.
Tell them often how lucky you are to be their parents.
Children slow everything down, and that's the point.
If you only have 5% today, giving 5% is still 100% of what you have.
Criticism won't make them stop loving you; it will make them stop loving themselves.
Your job is to teach them to live without you, and to be beside them through pain rather than shield them from it.
Praise them to other people, toys or pets while they can hear, as if they're not listening.
Replace 'if' with 'after' ('After you do X, you can Y').
The voice you use with them becomes their inner voice. Be a safe space for every emotion, without criticism or judgment.

summary: A Montessori teacher with 20 years' experience gives three tantrum strategies: regulate yourself first because children mirror your emotions, name and validate the feeling instead of saying 'stop crying', and offer a choice to restore a sense of control.
key_points: Regulate yourself first; your calm presence signals safety, while frustration escalates the tantrum.
Name and validate the feeling instead of 'stop crying'.
Offer limited choices during a tantrum to give back some control (hug or space; deep breaths or squeezing hands).

transcript: This is why when handling your child's tantrum, nothing is working. After 20 years as a Montessori teacher dealing with hundreds of children, I've seen that most parents handle tantrums the wrong way without even realizing it and discovered that there are many hacks that no one tells you about to help any child calm their tantrums. Here are three of the best ones. One, stay calm and regulate yourself. Your child's brain mirrors your emotions. If you react with frustration, their tantrums will be worse. Your calm presence signals safety, which helps them calm down. Two, name the feeling. Instead of saying, stop crying, try validating their emotions like this. That scare you? That's okay. When kids feel understood, they stop fighting back. Three, offer a choice. When a child is having a tantrum, it's like they don't have control. So by giving them some choices, it helps them regain some power. Try asking, would you like a hug or some space? Would you like to take some deep breaths or squeeze some hands? this helps them focus and calm down faster. Would you like me to share more ways to help you handle your child's tantrum? Comment parenting and I will make a video series out of this.

3 Tips I Got to Reduce Jealousy when Introducing Toddler to Baby

author: dr.connerbor
title: 5 newborn care tips for first-time dads
summary: A pediatric chiropractor and new dad shares five practical newborn tips: reading the diaper wetness indicator line, lowering a baby feet-first to avoid triggering the Moro (startle) reflex, holding the baby tummy-down along your forearm, burping with the back straight and head neutral, and using the rooting reflex (stroking the cheek) to spot hunger.
key_points: Many disposable diapers have a wetness indicator line: yellow when dry, turns blue when wet.
Lower a baby into the crib feet first, head last; lowering head-first can trigger the Moro (startle) reflex and wake them.
Holding the baby tummy-down along your forearm ('wrapped around your arm') takes pressure off the tummy and engages head/neck muscles.
For burping after a bottle, keep the baby's back straight and head neutral and wait - patting isn't always needed.
Stroke the baby's cheek: if they turn and try to latch on your finger (rooting), they are likely hungry - feed them.
credentials: chiropractor (DC, DACNB), owner of a pediatric therapy clinic

products.name: disposable diapers
products.type: wetness indicator line helps track diaper changes

caution: Creator is a chiropractor, not a pediatrician; the claimed benefits of the forearm hold for neck strength are his opinion. Always place the baby on the back to sleep.

ill.caption: Diaper wetness indicator: the line is yellow when the diaper is clean and turns blue when wet.
Forearm hold: baby lies tummy-down along the parent's arm, which can ease tummy discomfort.
Burping position: keep the baby's back straight and head neutral until the burp comes.

transcript: Here's five things that I wish I knew as a first-time dad. When a diaper's clean, these lines are yellow. When the diaper's dirty, lines turn blue. Lying a baby down, what you don't want to do is put them down with their head going down first. That's going to trigger something called your moral reflex, which is your startle reflex, especially at night as they're going down from bed. What you want to do is when you bring them down, you want to bring them down feet first, head second. When you're holding a baby, it's much better to hold them wrapped around your arm like this. It's going to take pressure off their tummy. It's going to help with their head and neck strength, and it puts them in a much, much better position. You're burping a baby after a bottle. A lot of people, they have them. They're patting their chest until they start burping. What I found is when you keep them in a straight line, so you keep their back nice and straight, you keep their head neutral, and if you hang here long enough, they're going to give you a good burp. Last one here, if your baby is fussy, they're screaming, if you just stroke their cheek, right now he's not going to do it, but if you stroke your cheek and they turn and they try to latch onto your finger, means they're probably hungry. You want to get them a bottle. You want to make sure they feed.

caption:
5 things I wish I knew. I’m getting there 🏃‍♂️ 

If we haven’t met 👋 I’m Dr. Conner Bor. I own NeuroActive, a pediatric therapy clinic where we’ve worked with kids and families from 40+ states and 16 countries around the world.

I spend pretty much every day thinking about one thing: how can we give a developing brain and body the best opportunity possible?

Our approach is proactive, integrated, and definitely not always conventional. We look at childhood neurodevelopment through four main pillars:

🧠 ACTIVATE the brain and body with the right sensory and neurological input
🥩 NOURISH the body with what it needs to grow, develop, and function
💪 CHALLENGE kids appropriately so their brain and body are constantly adapting
🛡️ PROTECT them by reducing unnecessary things that may interfere with healthy development

I’ve spent years working with kids with everything from developmental delays and autism to brain injuries, and now I’m also getting to apply a lot of what I’ve learned to raising my own son.

This page is basically where those two worlds collide.

I’m going to share what we do in the clinic, what I’m doing at home, what the research says, what I agree with, what I disagree with, and probably a few things that will make some people upset along the way 😂

If you’re nodding your head right now, you’ll love what’s coming. Follow along for more!

author: drdianasharp
title: 5 parenting competencies linked to good child outcomes (Epstein study)
summary: A research psychologist summarises five of Robert Epstein's 'Parents' Ten' competencies from a 2010 survey of about 2,000 parents. Love and affection ranked first, and surprisingly the parent's own stress management ranked second in predicting children's happiness and success. She notes the study's limits: parents self-rated both their skills and their children's outcomes.
key_points: Showing love and affection (warmth, acceptance, one-on-one time) was the top predictor of happier, more successful children.
Managing your own stress was the #2 predictor, higher than experts expected; use healthy calming strategies so stress doesn't run the household.
Maintain healthy adult relationships (partner, co-parent, relatives, friends); kids learn from how you treat adults, especially under stress.
Respect and teach independence: help children become capable rather than doing everything for them.
Value education and learning by modelling curiosity and enjoyment of learning, not necessarily degrees.
Caveat: data were self-reported by parents, so don't treat it as a 'should I become a parent' checklist.
caution: Based on a single self-report survey; correlations, not proof of cause.

caption:
5 signs you would be a good parent, according to Robert Epstein’s 2010 analysis of parenting competencies.

Important caveat: this was not a perfect study. Parents rated their own parenting and also reported on their children’s outcomes, including happiness, health, school/work success, and the parent-child relationship.

So please don’t use this as a “Should I become a parent?” checklist.

But I do think the findings are useful, especially because some of the strongest predictors were not the most obvious ones.

Epstein called the ten competencies “The Parents’ Ten.” Here are 5 signs from that list:

1. You would show love and affection.
You would support and accept your child, show warmth, and make time for one-on-one connection.

2. You would work on managing your own stress.
You would try to reduce stress for yourself and your child, use healthy calming strategies, and avoid letting stress run the household.

3. You would build healthy adult relationships.
You would try to maintain healthy relationships with a spouse, partner, co-parent, relatives, friends, or other important adults, and model respectful relationship skills.

4. You would respect and teach independence.
You would treat your child with respect and help them become self-sufficient and capable over time.

5. You would value education and learning.
You would promote learning, model curiosity, and look for ways to give your child rich learning opportunities.

The hopeful takeaway: good parenting is not about being perfect. Many of the skills that support children can be learned and strengthened over time.

Source: Robert Epstein, “What Makes a Good Parent?” Scientific American Mind, Nov/Dec 2010. The article summarizes a study conducted with Shannon L. Fox that ranked parenting competencies linked with children’s happiness, health, success, and parent-child relationship quality.

author: the_play_edit_
author_name: The Play Edit - Easy Play Ideas
title: 7 independent-play mistakes with a 1-year-old and how to fix them
summary: A play-ideas creator lists seven mistakes she made trying to get her one-year-old to play independently, each with a fix. Key ideas: model play first, offer fewer toys, stop interrupting with praise, allow settling time, create a small calm play corner, connect before stepping away, and accept that independent play still means you're nearby.
key_points: Don't expect them to know how: sit beside them and model play, then gradually step back.
Offer one simple setup at a time - less is more at age one.
Don't interrupt: watch quietly rather than saying 'yay, well done!' every 30 seconds.
Give it a few minutes; real play can take time to start.
Create a small, calm play corner with familiar toys instead of a big, distracting space.
Connect first (cuddles, play, chat), then encourage solo play - don't sneak off the moment they're busy.
Independent play isn't all-or-nothing; they may still need you nearby.
onscreen: Mistakes I made with independent play, and how I fixed them...
caption:
I made every mistake with independent play so you don’t have to 🤦‍♀️ here’s 7 mistakes I made, and how I fixed them: 

❌ I expected her to just know how to play
🛠️ I sat beside her and modelled it first. Played together, then slowly stepped back.

❌ I gave her too much stuff
🛠️ Now I offer one simple setup at a time. Less is more when you’re one.

❌ I kept interrupting
🛠️ I stay quiet and watch. No more “yay well done!” every 30 seconds.

❌ I gave up too quickly
🛠️ I give her time to settle in. It can take a few minutes before real play starts.

❌ The space was too big and distracting
🛠️ We made a calm little play corner with familiar toys and minimal chaos.

❌ I snuck off the second she was busy
🛠️ Now I connect with her first. Cuddles, playing together, chat - then encourage solo play.

❌ I thought independent play meant doing it all alone
🛠️ She still needs me nearby sometimes. That’s okay. It’s not all or nothing.

If you’re struggling with independent play, you’re not doing it wrong. Learning through play isn’t just for babies, we’re all here figuring it out.

author: bilingualcoco
title: A bilingual child won't automatically become a bilingual adult
summary: A creator with a PhD in cognitive psychology who researches bilingualism warns that raising a bilingual child doesn't guarantee a bilingual teen or adult: without continuous use of both languages, children lose one (attrition) or become receptive-only bilinguals. In the caption she adds that kids often reject the minority language as 'uncool' and shares her plan to build a positive emotional connection to French for her 2.5-year-old.
key_points: 'Use it or lose it': a child must keep actively using both languages, or one may be lost (language attrition).
Without enough use, children can become receptive bilinguals - they understand but can't speak the language well.
Expect a phase (childhood, pre-teen or teen years) when kids reject the minority language as uncool because peers don't speak it.
Build enjoyment and connection with the minority language early, e.g. favourite TV shows and books in that language (her examples: Trotro, T'choupi in French).
There must also be a real need/demand to use the language, not just exposure.
Maintaining bilingualism takes sustained effort for many years, not just in early childhood.

I call, I show up, I'm the "bad guy." He gets to leave safely without losing face with his friends. Every kid deserves that safety net.
caption:
In our house, those four words have nothing to do with being polite. It’s the secret signal I established with my boys years ago. 

It means: I’m in a situation I don’t like. I want to come home.. but I don’t want to be the “tattletale” or the “uncool” one. 

When I see that text, I don’t ask questions. I call him immediately, I sound “annoyed” and tell him he has to come home right now because of a family emergency or a chore he forgot. 

I get to be the “mean mom” and he gets to stay safe. 

I’ve used this with my 22 year old when he was younger, I’m using it with my 15 year old now and I’ll be using it for my 7 year old when he gets older. In a world with so much pressure, I want my kids to know I will always be their “out”.

title: Age-appropriate chores: a family's list from age 4 to 16
summary: A mother cites a 'Harvard 75-year study' linking childhood chores to later success, happiness and self-esteem, and in the caption lists the chores her children do at each age. She argues that being trusted with tasks gives children ownership, purpose and teamwork.
key_points: Age 4-5: sorting socks, placing napkins on the table.
Age 10: sorting/folding laundry, vacuuming, cleaning counters, polishing shoes, setting the table, stacking wood, putting out bins.
Age 13: making the bed, cleaning own room, making packed lunches, walking the dog, baking a cake.
Age 14: grocery shopping, picking up a sibling from school, helping with homework/reading, cleaning the bathroom, making dinner.
Age 16: cleaning the kitchen, collecting siblings, babysitting, running errands like the post office.
Being trusted with real tasks gives kids ownership and a sense of their place in the family.

caption:
Our parents instinctively must have known this. Wisdom passed down through generations perhaps only confirmed by more recent studies.

Our children have been doing chores from a very young age. When they were 4 or 5 years old, it was sorting socks or placing napkins on the dinner table. Now, a bit more grown up, here are some of the tasks they are trusted with:

10 year old:
Sorting and folding laundry 
Vacuuming
Cleaning countertops
Polishing shoes
Setting the table 
Stacking the wood
Putting out the bins

13 year old: 
Making her bed, tidying & cleaning her room
Making packed lunches when necessary
Walking the dog 
Baking a cake
Helping me paint (More recently)

14 year old:
Grocery shopping
Picking up her brother from school
Helping him with homework/reading
Cleaning the bathroom
Making dinner 

16 year old:
Cleaning the kitchen
Collecting siblings from school
Babysitting 
Going to the post office for mum

Our children are a bit older now so they tend to be able to do most things but whatever their age, children take pride in being trusted with tasks. This gives them a sense of ownership and marks their purpose and place within the family structure. It encourages teamwork and gives them appreciation also for all those less visible things we do for them. A win win in my eyes really, not only do we get a little extra help but they too, will gain so much more, in the long run. 

So despite the groaning and moaning, just remember, you’re doing it for their own good. And if you can put your feet up knowing something is being taken care of for you, well that’s even better….

title: Baby movement 'library' before 9 months
summary: The creator explains the neuronal group selection theory, describing how babies explore varied movements from birth to 9 months to build a 'library' of motor skills. He emphasizes the importance of providing varied movement experiences like tummy time to support later development.
key_points: Babies explore varied movements from birth to 9 months, building a 'library' of motor skills.
Around 9 months, babies shift to selecting and refining movements that work.
Varied movement experiences like tummy time are essential for building this library.
Research shows babies with less tummy time may reach crawling milestones later.

transcript: There's a window in your baby's brain development that closes at around nine months and what happens before it closes shapes everything that comes after. So there's this Nobel Prize winning neuroscientist named Gerald Edelman who developed something called the neuronal group selection theory and what he discovered is that your baby's brain learns in two distinct phases. Phase one is what I called the library phase and this happens roughly from birth to about nine months and during this phase your baby is basically trying everything flailing their arms kicking their legs moving up down sideways fast slow and whatever weird combinations you can think of your baby is systematically exploring every possible way that they can move their body and why are they doing this well because their brain is building a library a catalog of here's what my body can do and the more varied the movements the richer the library meaning the more options your baby has to draw from later. And research shows that babies actually make something like 31,000 leg movements per day in the early months. And that's just the legs. And every single one of those movements is adding another entry to that library. Then at around nine months, they graduate to phase two. And this is the selection phase. So your baby stops trying everything and starts figuring out what actually works. So they've built their library and now they're learning to use it. Then through trial and error they discover which scrolling pattern gets them across the room, which reach actually gets their hand on the toy, and which way of pulling leads to standing. Their brain isn't simply collecting anymore, it's curating, selecting the movements that work and strengthening in those neural pathways. And here's what's really important. Your baby's brain can only select from movements that it has practiced. So if your baby never experienced a certain movement pattern during phase one, it won't be available for selection in phase two, because that neural pathway simply won't exist. And there's actually research showing that babies who spent less time on their tummy had later onset of crawling milestones, and not because tummy time is magic, but because it's one of the many varied position that adds entries to the library. So that means that phase one has a window, and what you do during that window shapes the foundation for everything that comes after because you cannot just go back and add to the library later and this is exactly why i built baby acrobatics short research-backed movement routines that give your baby the varied movement experiences that their brain actually needs and this program is reviewed by child development professionals and it's based on the actual neuroscience of how babies learn to move so if you want to start giving your baby more purposeful movement experiences and you want to make sure that they're building the richest movement library possible, then just check out the baby acrobatics blueprint on my profile.

Michele A Lobo et al. Child Dev. 2012 Jul-Aug.

Behaviors emerge, in part, from the interplay of infant abilities and caregiver-infant interactions. Cross-cultural and longitudinal studies suggest that caregiver handling and positioning influence infant development. In this prospective, longitudinal study, the effects of 3 weeks of enhanced handling and positioning were provided to 14 infants versus control infants provided to 14 infants at 2 months of age. The infants were assessed with follow-up through 15 months of age. Prone behaviors in prone were immediately observed. Short-term advancements occurred in prone behaviors, including prone, head lifting behaviors. Longer term advancements occurred in months after the experience of prone transfer, crawling and walking. This suggests broad and long-lasting effects of a brief periods of change in behaviors.

author: abanaturally
title: Behavior analyst: a sibling's voluntary generosity isn't spoiling
summary: A BCBA responds to a viral video where an older sister gave her disappointed younger sister the toy she had hoped for. She argues that a child freely choosing kindness is a learned pro-social skill, different from forced sharing, and that one genuine act of kindness doesn't create entitlement; giving in to repeated demands to stop whining does. She explains how she models and names generosity at home.
key_points: Kindness, generosity, sharing and noticing others' disappointment are skills that grow through modelling, practice and reinforcement.
Model out loud: 'It looks like you need another block, would you like one of mine?'
Name generosity when it happens so the child connects behaviour and effect.
Forced sharing can breed resentment; freely chosen sharing is the goal.
Distinguish rare, novel, genuinely disappointing moments from routine demands; entitlement comes from giving in demand after demand to stop tantrums.

Would you like to share my cookie? I'll give you half of it.
I really appreciate you sharing with me.

transcript: I absolutely love this video and I know that the comment section has some strong opinions about what should have happened but I am leaning a little bit in a different direction and I'm going to tell you why my name is Jenna Mozilla and I'm a word certified behavior analyst teacher and mom of two girls let's get into it number one nobody told the sister you need to give that to her nobody said, you are older, so you must share. From what we can see, she looked at her younger sister, noticed that she was disappointed, and chose to do something incredibly kind. And that is a beautiful pro-social behavior to have. And as somebody who's actively trying to raise kind and generous kids who make the world a better place, that is a behavior that I am constantly modeling in front of them. If we're playing together, and I can see that somebody needs another block, I will say out loud, it looks like you need another block. Would you like one of mine? Or if I have a cookie, I might say, would you like to share my cookie? I'll give you half of it. And when they are generous with me, I make sure to name that out loud as well because I want to connect their behavior with what just happened. For example, I really appreciate you sharing with me. Or Grace, you are one of the most generous three-year-olds I have ever met. Believe it or not, those are skills. Kindness is a skill. Generosity is a skill. Sharing is a skill. Noticing when somebody is disappointed is a skill and when those skills are modeled by the people in their home and practice and reinforced over time with our kids they then become things that feel good in itself doing not because somebody forced you to do it but because there is joy in bringing joy and happiness to somebody else's life additionally I do want to point out that the younger sister was simply disappointed she wasn't demanding she didn't grab it out of her older sister's hand. She didn't say, you need to give that to me. She was genuinely sad. And as somebody who feels very strongly about not reinforcing children's misbehavior, I do, however, differentiate between moments that are novel, confusing, or high stakes. And to me, this was one of those. This is not a random Tuesday afternoon where an adult is turning off the TV and the child is melting down and now the adult is giving it back. This was a little girl who was looking forward to opening something special and was disappointed when it wasn't the one she was hoping for and that is completely normal. I think that this is where people are making a huge leap. One genuine act of kindness is not going to create a spoiled child. What creates an entitled child is an adult giving in to demand after demand because they want to get the crying, the whining, and the tantrums to stop. That is not what happened here. This is a moment where an older sibling recognizes that their younger sibling is disappointed and sad and chooses to step in and share something special and to me that is not spoiling a child that is modeling what generosity and kindness look like in the home
onscreen: Behavior analyst responds: when one child gets the toy the other child wanted
caption:
We say we want to raise kind, generous kids, but then when a child chooses generosity on her own, people immediately panic that someone is being spoiled.
That is the part I think we need to look at.

There is a big difference between a child being forced to give something up and a child freely choosing to share something special. One can create resentment. The other is a sign that kindness has been modeled, practiced, and reinforced enough that it showed up naturally, and that is the goal.

Not a child who gives everything away because she feels responsible for everyone else’s feelings. Not a child who believes every disappointed feeling means someone has to fix it for her. But children who have seen enough generosity that they know how to offer it, receive it, and eventually return it.

We don’t build that by lecturing kids to “be kind” in the hard moments.

We build it in the tiny everyday moments. When we share with them. When we notice their generosity. When we name thoughtfulness out loud. When they see that people in their home care about each other without keeping score every single time.

That is not spoiling.

That is a beautiful little glimpse into the culture being built in that home

P.S: If this were her friend instead of her little sister, nobody would be calling it spoiling. They’d probably just call it kindness.

author: abanaturally
title: Behavior analyst: teaching kids to put equipment away after an accident
summary: A BCBA reacts to a viral clip of a dad calmly addressing kids after someone was hurt by a skateboard left out. She builds on it with an evidence-based approach: practise the skill outside the heated moment, state expectations and have the child repeat them, agree consequences in advance, show exactly where things go, and reinforce the child when they do it right.
key_points: Teach the skill outside the moment: state the expectation, model it, have the child show you, then give feedback or praise.
Have the child say the expectation back; wait for the answer rather than getting pulled into back-and-forth.
Set the consequence in advance (e.g. lose access to the skateboard for a set number of days) so it is fair and you don't need to yell or lecture.
Be specific about where things go ('the skateboard goes in the garage, against the wall'), not just 'put it away'; let kids help choose the spot.
Open with something positive (you love watching them ride) before raising the concern.
Notice and praise ordinary moments of following through; attention mostly given for misbehavior increases misbehavior.
If praise isn't enough, use a tally/point system exchanged for a reward the child cares about; expect it to take a few tries.
scripts: Kids, when you're finished playing with your toys, I expect you to put them away. What do I expect you to do when you're finished playing?
That's right. When you put your toys away, you keep your privileges, like using your skateboard. If you don't, you lose the skateboard for [X] days.

caption:
1. This might take a few tries. Stick with it. It is worth it.

2. Lead with something positive before you set the expectation. Tell them you know how much they love riding their skateboard and that you love watching them enjoy it. Then go into the concern. That one shift in how you open the conversation changes everything.

3. Be specific about where things go. “Put it away” is not an instruction, it is a wish. You can even let them help pick the spot. Kids follow through better when they feel like they had a say.

4. When they mess up, let the consequence do the work. You already set this up ahead of time, which means you do not need to yell, lecture, or repeat yourself. Just follow through calmly and consistently.

5. If the behavior is really important and praise alone is not moving the needle, a point system can help. Every time they put their equipment away, they earn a tally. When they hit the goal, they cash it in for something they actually care about: extra screen time, staying up later, having a friend over, a pick from a grab bag. The reward will depend on your child. Two things to know before you start: the skill has to be taught first or the system will not work, and the system has to be faded out properly over time. It is a tool, not a permanent fixture.

P.S. If we haven’t met yet—hi! I’m Jenna. I’m a behavior analyst, teacher, and mom.

I started this account to help parents and educators with practical, evidence-based strategies that actually work, so you can enjoy more peaceful days without constant power struggles.

So if you’re looking for real-life, easy-to-follow tips (without the fluff), you’re in the right place!

author: thrivingmindsmontessori
title: Better questions than 'How was your day at school?'
summary: A Montessori teacher of 20+ years explains that 'How was your day?' is too vague for young children, who live in the present and usually answer 'good' or 'nothing'. She suggests three concrete questions that trigger memories through movement, social interactions and demonstration.
key_points: Avoid vague questions like 'How was your day?'; young kids find summarising a whole day overwhelming.
Ask 'What did your hands do today?' – kids remember through movement (painting, writing, playing).
Ask 'Who was kind to you today?' – helps them recall positive social moments.
Ask 'Show me something you learned today' – demonstrating is easier than describing.

author: mihaela.maris
title: Body safety talks start early: a mother's wake-up call
summary: A Romanian mother found her 2y9m daughter hidden in a changing cubicle with a 6-year-old boy who had his trousers down, at an airfield where all families know each other. She removed her daughter calmly, told the boy to dress, and informed his mother. Afterwards she learned that such situations happen most often among acquaintances and in relaxed settings, and that age-appropriate sex education should start in the first years.
key_points: Such incidents happen most often among people you know: at home, at parties, while adults are in another room.
Supervision can slip precisely in 'safe', familiar places — stay alert there too.
Age-appropriate, teach: the correct names of private parts; that they are private; who may see or touch them and in which situations; that the child can say 'no'.
If you discover an incident: calmly remove your child, don't shame the other child, and inform the other child's parent.
Body, boundaries and safety conversations should be repeated, not a one-off talk.

author: christina_pax_
title: Body safety: 'In our family we don't keep secrets, only surprises'
summary: A mom calmly teaches her young daughter the difference between secrets and surprises. Secrets aren't safe, so the family doesn't keep them; surprises (like a gift or drawing) are fine because they will be revealed. If anyone asks the child to keep a secret, she should say she always tells mommy and daddy.
key_points: Establish a family rule: we don't keep secrets, because secrets can be unsafe.
Distinguish surprises (happy, temporary, e.g., a birthday gift or a drawing for dad) from secrets.
Give the child a ready response if an adult or anyone asks them to keep a secret.
Keep the tone light and practise with a real surprise (e.g., draw a surprise picture for daddy).

author: thatmomkathryn
title: Book for kids' negative thinking: Captain Snout and the Superpower Questions
summary: A teacher, registered social worker and mom of two boys recommends Daniel G. Amen's children's book 'Captain Snout and the Superpower Questions' for kids stuck in 'always/never' thinking. The book explains automatic negative thoughts as 'ANTs' (e.g. the all-or-nothing ANT) in kid-friendly CBT terms and teaches 'superpower questions' like 'Is that true? Are you 100% sure it's true?'. After repeated reading, her 7-year-old can name his ANT and challenge it himself.
key_points: 'Always/never/nobody' statements are normal cognitive distortions (thinking traps) in young kids.
The book frames them as ANTs - automatic negative thoughts - with types such as the all-or-nothing ANT.
It teaches 'superpower questions' to challenge thoughts, e.g. 'Is that true? Are you 100% sure it's true?'.
Read it repeatedly; then in the moment ask your child which ANT they're having and what the superpower question is.
Even a 4-year-old could follow the concepts; useful for all kids, not only anxious ones.

Do you remember what the superpower question is?
Is that true? Are you 100% sure it's true?

Sometimes I get so caught up sharing the funny, chaotic side of motherhood that I forget I also have an educational background in teaching and children’s mental health and development. ❤️

One thing I want to do more of is share the resources that have genuinely helped the kids I work with—and my own kids too.

📖 Captain Snout and the Superpower Questions by Daniel G. Amen @doc_amen is one of those books.

It helps children recognize that not every thought they have is true. Instead of automatically believing negative thoughts, it teaches them to ask “superpower questions” that challenge those thoughts in a way that’s simple, empowering, and age-appropriate.

author: ellistonpediatrics
title: Breath-holding spells in babies and toddlers: pediatrician explains
summary: A pediatric practice shows a real breath-holding spell and a pediatrician explains that these episodes are common and usually harmless. A child gets so upset they hold their breath, may turn red or blue, and can briefly pass out, after which the brainstem restarts breathing automatically. The priority is keeping the child safe and letting it pass, and involving the pediatrician to confirm the diagnosis.
key_points: Breath-holding spells typically start between 6 and 18 months (can be as early as 6 months) and most children outgrow them by age 4-6.
They are triggered by big emotions: frustration, pain or being startled; the face turns red and lips may turn blue.
If the child faints, the breathing reflex takes over automatically; children cannot hold their breath long enough to harm themselves.
During an episode: stay calm, lay the child flat on their back somewhere safe, and let it pass.
Do NOT shake the child or put anything in their mouth.
Tell your pediatrician, especially if episodes are frequent, happen without crying, or the child is not quickly back to normal.
caution: Get a first episode assessed by a doctor to rule out seizures or heart problems.

Breath-holding spells can be one of the most frightening things a parent witnesses — but the good news is that they are very common and usually harmless. These episodes typically start between 6–18 months, often happen during big toddler emotions (frustration, pain, or being startled), and most children outgrow them by age 4–6. What to remember: • Stay calm and keep your child safe • Lay them flat on their back • Do NOT shake or put anything in their mouth • Recovery is usually quick and complete Always loop in your pediatrician so they can confirm the diagnosis and rule out anything else — especially if episodes are frequent, happen without crying, or your child is not back to normal quickly afterward. title: Building lifelong trust: keep your child's confidences private
summary: A creator asked a friend who is best friends with her mom what her mom did to earn that trust. The answer was that when she shared something big or personal as a child, her mom kept it between them and never brought it up at dinner, with relatives or on the phone with friends. Kids notice and remember this, and it shapes the relationship later in life.
key_points: When your child confides something personal, keep it private; don't retell it at the dinner table, to relatives or to friends.
Children notice when their confidences are honoured or shared, even if they don't say anything.
These early experiences build the trust that makes a close adult relationship possible.
Exception (not stated in the video): safety concerns may need to be shared with appropriate adults.

author: doctormyro
title: Chewing gum after a C-section to restart the bowels
summary: An anesthesiologist explains why her gastroenterologist husband gave her gum right after her C-section. Abdominal surgery temporarily slows the bowels, causing nausea, bloating and constipation; chewing gum ('sham feeding') signals the gut to restart, and studies link it to earlier hospital discharge and fewer complications.
key_points: A C-section is major abdominal surgery and temporarily 'puts the bowels to sleep' (postoperative ileus).
This can cause nausea, bloating and constipation after surgery.
Chewing gum stimulates saliva and digestive signals that help wake the bowels.
Studies associate post-op gum chewing with faster return of bowel function and earlier discharge.
Consider packing gum in your hospital bag if a C-section is planned or possible; check with your care team.

title: Chore 'zones' instead of chore charts to teach initiative
summary: A mental-load educator replaced chore charts, which kept her as the manager, with a Danish-inspired 'zones' system: each child owns one shared space (living room, mudroom, car, breakfast clean-up) and must check it, notice what's out of place and fix it without a list. The goal is kids who see what needs doing, not just follow instructions.
key_points: Give each child one shared zone (e.g. living room, mudroom, car, breakfast clean-up) to be responsible for.
No list or instructions: the child must look, notice what the space needs and act.
Zones are deliberately shared spaces, teaching kids to tidy things that aren't only theirs, as part of a family team.
The parent's only prompt: 'Have you checked your zone?' This removes the parent's job of managing a chart.
Builds noticing and initiative, an early lesson in the mental load.
scripts: Have you checked your zone?

transcript: If you want to teach your kids about the mental load, I have a really good hack for you. This hack will teach them how to observe what's going on in the space, to take initiative on their own, and to adopt a mentality that these are shared spaces, and we're a family team, and we all work together. You don't just pick up your own stuff. You can pick up other people's, and it's totally okay. This hack didn't come from me. It came from my friend who is from Denmark, and here it is. you give your kid a zone of the house to be in charge of. For example, our daughter is in charge of the living room. It's her job to regularly check it out, observe what's out of place, and put it back together. Each of our kids has a shared space that belongs to them and it's their zone. And it has helped so much in their initiative taking and then being a family team player. Let me know if you try it and what you think.

caption:
I tried the chore chart. Multiple times. Cute laminated version. Magnetic one on the fridge. The whole production.

And every time, I ended up being the manager of the chart.

So we started doing zones instead.

A zone is one shared space your kid is responsible for. Living room. 

Mudroom. Car. Breakfast cleanup. The key word is shared. Because part of what we’re teaching them is that we clean up things that aren’t only ours. We put away laundry that isn’t only ours. We notice messes that aren’t only ours. That’s how a family works.

There’s no list. There’s no instruction sheet. 

They have to walk in, look around, see what the space needs, and take action. That’s the whole point. It’s training the muscle of noticing. Of initiating. Of using your own eyes instead of waiting to be told.

And the bonus for me is I’m not generating a list. I’m not running the chart. I’m not the manager of the chore chart anymore.

My only prompt: have you checked your zone?

Because the goal isn’t kids who do what they’re told. It’s kids who see what needs doing.

The full age-by-age breakdown is inside my free Summer guide.

author: cristinaiancuu
title: Clingy baby? It's separation anxiety — what to answer relatives
summary: A Romanian mom offers a reply to relatives who say a clingy baby under one year will become a 'mama's child': it's a normal developmental stage called separation anxiety. Her baby's brain has developed enough to realise mom exists even when out of sight, so she misses her for the first time. The caption explains timing (often starting 6-9 months, most common 10-18 months, may last to 2-3 years), signs, and responding with patience plus peek-a-boo to teach object permanence.
key_points: Separation anxiety is a normal sign of neurological development, not spoiling.
It often appears around 6-9 months (can be earlier or later), is most common at 10-18 months, and can last until 2-3 years.
Signs: crying, irritability or insistently seeking the parent when separated from the main caregiver.
Respond with patience and understanding rather than pushing independence.
Play peek-a-boo to teach object permanence — that you come back even when out of sight.
Children supported through this phase build secure attachment.
scripts: Yes, she's stuck to me and I'm very happy about it. I talked to the pediatrician — she's going through a developmental stage called separation anxiety.
Her brain has developed so much that she realises I exist even when she can't see me. She's missing me for the first time, and I'm going to tell her I miss her too and want to be with her.

caption:
💡 Anxietatea de separare este sennul că bebelușul tău se dezvoltă neurologic. 

Când apare anxietatea de separare?

✅ între vârsta de 6 și 9 luni, dar poate apărea și mai devreme sau mai târziu, în funcție de fiecare copil; cel mai frecvent observată între 10 și 18 luni și poate persista până la vârsta de 2-3 ani.

Ce este anxietatea de separare la bebeluși?

📖Anxietatea de separare este o etapă normală în dezvoltarea bebelușilor în care aceștia încep să recunoască persoanele apropiate și să dezvolte un atașament față de acestea. 

Cum ne dăm seama că bebelușul are ancietate de separare? 

👶🏽 În această perioadă, bebelușii pot deveni anxioși sau agitați când sunt separați de părinții sau îngrijitorii lor principali, manifestându-se prin plâns, iritabilitate sau căutarea insistentă a părintelui.

Ce faci când bebelușul are anxietate de separare?

❤️ Când bebelușul manifestă anxietate de separare, este important să răspunzi cu răbdare și înțelegere. 

🧸	Jocul de-a „cucu-bau” (peek-a-boo): Este un mod distractiv de a învăța conceptul de permanență a obiectului și de a-l asigura că, deși uneori nu ești vizibil, te vei întoarce.

🧍‍♀️ Copilul care primește sprijin și înțelegere în perioadele de anxietate de separare este mai predispus să dezvolte încredere în sine și în ceilalți. Această încredere construită în primii ani de viață poate fi fundamentală pentru relațiile pe care le va avea mai târziu.

title: Co-regulation: why comforting a melting-down child isn't coddling
summary: A parent coach explains that traditional parenting labelled children good or bad by behaviour and saw comforting a tantrum as coddling. She says research shows a dysregulated child in fight/flight/freeze/fawn needs co-regulation - a calm adult who stays with them so they can 'borrow' that calm - since self-regulation abilities only begin developing around age 7. Parents still need to teach healthier ways to express big emotions.
key_points: Behaviour has something underneath it; kids aren't simply 'good' or 'bad'.
Comforting a child during a meltdown is not rewarding the behaviour.
Co-regulation: stay calm and present with a dysregulated child so they can borrow your calm until their nervous system settles.
Children's brains start developing independent self-regulation around age 7, so young kids need adult help.
After co-regulating, still teach healthier ways to express big emotions.
Your own regulation is the foundation; children mimic what is modelled.
caution: The specific 'around age 7' figure is a simplification; self-regulation develops gradually through childhood. Post also promotes a paid workshop.
transcript: you were raised with traditional parenting, you were taught that children are either bad or good based on bad or good behavior. You weren't taught that there's anything underneath behavior because your parents didn't know that there was anything underneath behavior. And on top of that, you were taught that to comfort a child in a moment that they are tantruming or melting down is coddling them and telling them that it's absolutely okay to behave that way. Thankfully, we now have decades of research on the emotional, psychological, and developmental needs of children. And we know that what children need in a moment where their brains are severely dysregulated and their nervous system is in fight, flight, freeze, or fawn is co-regulation, which is where a calm, emotionally regulated adult is able to sit with a severely emotionally dysregulated child in their dysregulation and let that child borrow from the adult's calm in that moment until their nervous system is able to regulate. A child's brain is not going to start to develop the abilities to do that on their own until they're around seven years old. However, we don't stop there. We still have to teach our children how to have their big emotions and to express them in healthier ways.

author: amy_demos
title: Coach, don't rescue: dad talks a baby out of being 'stuck'
summary: A father finds his baby daughter stuck in a basket and, instead of lifting her out, coaches her step by step (roll over, push up) until she gets herself out, ending with a proud baby who wants to try again. The parents, former public-school teachers, explain they try to avoid 'rescuing' and instead coach kids through problems, citing the advice 'don't do anything for a child they can do for themselves.'
key_points: When a child is stuck on a solvable problem, pause before rescuing and coach them through it.
Give small concrete steps (e.g., 'roll this way', 'push up') rather than doing it for them.
Use encouraging language that reframes the situation ('you're not stuck').
Principle: don't do anything for a child that they can do for themselves.
The parents observed as teachers that 4th–5th graders who were often rescued learned less than those allowed to fail.
Stepping in is faster, but letting them solve it builds confidence and resilience.
scripts: I think you can do it.
We're going to roll over. Roll this way. Now get yourself out.
You're not stuck. You're brave and strong. You can do it.
credentials: parents; former public school teachers (4 years)
caution: Coaching works for safe, low-risk struggles; step in when there is any safety risk.

caption:
The patience level of this man 👏🏻

Jordan turned the corner to find Ellie “stuck” in a problem that felt too big (to her) to solve on her own. But with a little coaching, instead of being rescued, she got to rescue herself 👌🏻

I have to admit, it’s hard for me to be patient enough to resist just stepping in and “fixing” it. If I was the one who turned the corner, I might’ve just pulled her out. Stepping in is faster. It’s easier. And it’s usually less annoying in the moment 😅 

But we both really do believe giving them the time and space to solve their own problems leads to the most long-term growth, so I’m proud of Jordan for being more patient than me. We’re really doing our best to avoid “rescuing” our kids and instead are aiming to coach them though their problems, big or small. 

Some parenting advice we heard early on really stuck with us: “Don’t do anything for a child they can do for themselves.” 

We both spent four years teaching in public school, and we observed that the fourth and fifth graders who got “rescued” by their parents weren’t learning nearly as much as the ones who had a chance to fail. 

We know our kids’ “problems” won’t always be as easy or simple as getting out of a basket a few inches high 🤣 but I’m pretty sure no matter how big the problem gets, the temptation is still always going to be there for us to step in and fix it. 

Leaving this video here as a reminder that whenever I’m tempted to step in for one of my kids, nothing beats that look on their face when they solve something they didn’t think could 💛

author: cameliacrisanofficial
title: Common physical changes during pregnancy
summary: A pregnant woman shares a list of common, often underestimated physical and emotional changes during pregnancy to normalize the experience for others. She covers symptoms ranging from fatigue and nausea to body changes like skin breakouts, joint pain, and postpartum recovery expectations.
key_points: Nausea can occur throughout the entire day, not just in the morning.
Extreme fatigue in the first trimester is normal and common.
Breast soreness and growth can happen very early in pregnancy.
Hormonal changes often cause constipation and bloating.
Skin and hair may not always 'glow'; breakouts are common.
Physical changes like urine leaks, darker areolas, and wider feet are normal.
Postpartum recovery takes time; the body does not bounce back instantly.
caution: While the creator shares common experiences, any persistent or concerning symptoms should be discussed with a healthcare provider.

caption:
Co-regulation = the Game-Changer in parenting!

So many people still believe kids need “toughening up” and that emotions should be suppressed.

But neuroscience tells us otherwise!

When a child is overwhelmed, their nervous system is in distress. 

Meeting them with calm, connection, and co-regulation isn’t “giving in” or “coddling”—it’s being responsive. 

It forms the foundation of how they learn to regulate themselves in the future.

Co-regulation is not weakness. 

It’s a powerful, evidence-based way to help kids develop resilience, emotional intelligence, and self-control.

Respect, empathy, and emotional safety aren’t extras in parenting. They’re essential 🫶🏻

caption:
The most persistent and cascading effect of my childhood is my anger and reactivity. My home had big love in it for sure but reactivity was ever present in my home when I was young. Things that required only a 2 or 3 in intensity, often became 8’s, 9’s, and 10’s. The environment was often unpredictable, ordinary mornings with brooding auras, meals seething, and the snap of leather belts.

I spent nights in the kitchen, in the aisles of grocery stores, and on morning commutes trying to make jokes, searching for ways to bring levity and reduce the tension. Sometimes I was successful, but many times I was not.

At times… it felt like the smartest and safest thing to do was to stay as small as possible. Perhaps I would avoid the incoming anger or wrath. I actually got half decent at it… a mixture of a clown and a mime… tragically when you shrink one part of yourself, you also shrink the others.

It took much of my twenties and thirties to process and heal those parts. 

Now a dad, I have made strides, and I have not repeated many of the same things. But with anger… the progress has been slow, and the victories are rarer than I’d like to admit. 

Books, therapy, and honest communication with him about these failures I engage in regularly. I don’t enjoy being so vulnerable, nor showing my worst moments. However, I know it is precisely my capacity to do that, that gives me any chance of becoming something more, something better. Huck I think needs to see me this way at times, trying, failing, and being honest about it. Now I have improved, but there is a lot of work left, still many storms ahead. 

It’s funny though… we often talk about bison… haha he’s a huge fan. The thing he likes most about them, is that they’re the only animals in the world, when a storm comes, they run directly towards it.

And when you’re a father, if you want to be a good one, that’s exactly what you have to do. At least, that’s what I’m trying to do.

Love you. - J. 

#Parenting #EmotionalGrowth #Anger #Reactivity #Fatherhood

title: Dermatologist: sunscreen rules by age for babies and toddlers
summary: Responding to a tip about applying sunscreen with a makeup brush, a dermatologist summarises sun protection by age. Under 6 months: no sunscreen, use UV clothing, wide-brimmed hats and shade. 6 months to 2 years: zinc oxide (mineral) sunscreen because of the immature skin barrier. Over 2: any mineral or chemical sunscreen the child tolerates — any sunscreen is better than none.
key_points: 0-6 months: avoid sunscreen; use UV-protective clothing, wide-brimmed hats and shade.
6 months-2 years: use a zinc oxide (mineral) sunscreen.
2 years+: mineral or chemical, any format the child tolerates (spray, gel, lotion, cream).
Cumulative sun exposure, not just sunburns, raises lifetime skin-cancer risk.
Tip from the stitched video: apply sunscreen with a makeup brush if a child resists.

They’re counting on ALL of us—not just moms! All parents, grandparents, guardians, caretakers, babysitters, aunts/uncles can be empowered using evidence-based guidelines. Knowing when and what to apply is a great first step. Babies and toddlers (6 months to 2 years old) have an undeveloped skin barrier, so using zinc oxide–based sunscreens enhances tolerability and avoids systemic absorption. From 2 years and above—I meant what I said, “whatever you can get them to tolerate!” Spray, gel, lotion, cream—get it on there! Don’t let perfect be the enemy of great. Positional asphyxia: weak neck muscles let the head drop forward and close the airway.
Commonly cited limit: about 2 hours at a time for under-2s, around 30 minutes for newborns.

Children under the age of 2 should only be kept in car seats for limited periods—ideally no more than 2 hours at a time for those under 2 years old and 30 minutes for newborns. This is because extended time in a car seat can place strain on their developing spine and restrict their ability to move freely, which is vital for healthy growth. For newborns, the position of the car seat can also compress their chest and reduce oxygen levels, increasing the risk of breathing difficulties.

While car seats are essential for safety during travel, they are not designed for prolonged use outside of the car. To protect a child’s health and development, parents should take breaks during long journeys, allowing the child to stretch, move, and change position. Always use car seats according to safety guidelines and be mindful of the time spent in them to ensure optimal well-being.

title: Dr. Becky's lightning-round parenting answers (with Hasan Minhaj)
summary: Comedian Hasan Minhaj asks Dr. Becky quick-fire parenting questions. Her answers: you can't force vegetables (parents offer, kids decide whether and how much); occasional bribes are fine when truly necessary; name it when you need your phone. key_points: Food: you can't force vegetables. Your job is to offer; the child's job is to decide whether and how much to eat.
Bribes (candy, money) are acceptable once in a while when something truly has to happen and there's no danger.
If you must check your phone during play, say so and keep it brief.
Don't threaten a bully's parents.
Santa: let children enjoy the fantasy play that involves you; if they ask directly, they're probably ready for the truth.
When you catch a lie, address what made truth-telling hard rather than punishing the lie.
Explain death simply and concretely: the body stops working.

author: elenaamatei
title: Falling asleep with a bottle led to tooth demineralization: a mom's lesson
summary: A Romanian mom shares her 'biggest mistake': letting her older daughter fall asleep with a bottle of milk in her mouth. After the pacifier was removed around 17 months, the child transferred her sleep association to the bottle nipple, waking 4-5 times a night needing milk, and the milk left on her teeth overnight caused rapidly progressing enamel demineralization. She urges parents to avoid sleep associations with bottle sucking and to consult a doctor and pediatric dentist.
key_points: Don't let a baby or toddler fall asleep with a bottle of milk in the mouth - milk pooling on teeth overnight can cause demineralization/decay.
Sucking can become the only way a child links sleep cycles, causing frequent night wakings (4-5 times a night in her case) even when not hungry.
When removing a pacifier, watch that the child doesn't transfer the sucking association to the bottle.
Her daughter accepted the pacifier being thrown away in two days with no crying - removal can be easier than expected.
Demineralization can also be linked to deficiencies; get it assessed by your doctor and a pediatric dentist - baby teeth matter.

author: natestone84
title: Family rule: if you think something kind, say it out loud
summary: A dad shares a family rule that started when his 4-year-old daughter admired a stranger's pink hair and he encouraged her to tell the girl. The compliment visibly lifted the stranger, who had been drawing them. The family now practises voicing kind thoughts, and over time the kids' compliments shifted from appearance to character.
key_points: Family rule: when you think something kind about someone, say it out loud - 'kind thoughts belong to the people we think them about'.
Started at age 4; young kids first notice appearance (shirt, hat, hair), which is fine.
With practice, compliments evolve to character ('I love the way you laugh', 'You made everyone feel included').
Accept that sometimes people won't react; the goal is practice, not perfection.
Builds confidence, observation, and courage, including with strangers (with a parent nearby).

I love your hair.
I love the way you laugh.
You made everyone feel included.

transcript: What is one of our big family rules? The first time we did this, I was on a date with my oldest. She was four at the time. And there was this girl over to the side of us with bright pink hair. And she said, Daddy, I love her hair. And so I said, well, you know the rule, kiddo. So she walked over there a little nervous and tapped the girl on the knee. And the girl looked up and she said, I love your hair. And this girl's disposition just changed immediately. And then a few minutes later, she brought this picture over to us. And she's like, actually, I was drawing this picture of you guys. And so we as a family decided that when we think something kind that we would say it out loud that our kind thoughts not belong to us, but to the people that we think them about.

caption:
One of our family rules is:

If you think something kind, say it out loud.

We started practicing this when our oldest daughter was four years old. At first, it was little things:

“I like your shirt.” 
“I like your hat.” 
“I like your hair.”

Because that’s what kids naturally notice first.

But over time, as they’ve practiced it more, their compliments have changed too.

Now they notice things like:
“I love the way you laugh.”
Or:
“You made everyone feel included.”

I think that only happens because they’ve practiced noticing people.

It’s vulnerable sometimes. Especially with strangers.

There have been moments where our kids worked up the courage to say something kind and the person barely heard them or didn’t react much at all. And honestly, that’s okay too.

The goal isn’t perfection. 
The goal is practice.

Because practice doesn’t make perfect — it makes permanent.

And over time, we’ve watched our kids become more confident, observant, thoughtful, and brave in the way they move through the world.

What makes this story even sweeter is that the girl had actually already been quietly drawing us before my daughter ever walked over to compliment her.

The last line in this reel is something we say often in our family:

“Our kind thoughts don’t belong to us. They belong to the people we think them about.”

So say the nice thing out loud. 
The world needs it.
