Dacă vorbim de o anestezie inventată acum 100 de ani, nu ieri, nu alalt ieri, nu acum 5 ani. Vorbim de epidurala care este inventată acum 100 de ani. Trebuie să ai cunoștințe, să vorbești cu medicul cu anestezistul, să ți-o cumperi singur de la farmacie, să vii cu ea în plăsuță. Nu-mi place deloc sistemul ăsta și mi se pare foarte complicat și practic face orice ca să naști natural 100% sau să te bagi în cezariană. Iar faptul că te măsoară ei și îți zic la cât centimetri poți să pui epidurala, mi-e mi se pare foarte... Deci, înțelesa cu care te măsoară și le bagi în tine, nu poți să estimezi exact. E ca o ruletă internă, să zic așa, dar nu e o ruletă cu centimetri. Și sincer, nici nu cred că nașterea Iisus la o sută despre știință, ci și despre cum se simte femeia în acel moment. Câtă încrederea, câtă sarcină este, câtă susținere primește. Așa se liberează oxidăcina. Și, de ce să mint, pot să nași natural fără ea, doar că doare. Și dacă tot s-a inventat acum 100 de ani epidurala, de ce să stau să nu o primesc dacă vreau să profit de ea? La ambele sarcini, vă zic sincer, nu am simțit aproape deloc durere, chiar dacă una a fost 30 de ore și una a fost 2 ore, travaliu. Și după a doua naștere, de fapt, după fiecare naștere, m-am ridicat în jumătate de oră și m-am spus pe cap și mi-am făcut duș și am filmat, chiar dacă practic nu ai voie să faci asta, dar nu am avut nicio reacție adversă, fiindcă n-am avut o doză mare, mi-am simțit picioarele. În fine, cam astea sunt fricile mele, să zic așa. Și am avut două nașteri extraordinare, neașteptat de bune, dar tocmai de aceea nu mi se pare corect că nu pot avea și asta cumva în orașul meu și trebuie să călătoresc 600 km de distanță sau cât îi, fiindcă sistemul medical în România, din păcate, nu e atât de bine pregătit să oferă o experiență empatică, firească, împreună cu partenerul, dacă îți dorești sau nu, sau cu prietena, mama, pentru mai multe femei, chiar și la stat. Fiindcă pentru multe nașterea asta este o traumă și nu e de mirare că în România suntem pe locul 3, parcă, cu cele mai mari rate de cezareane din Europa, este peste 44%. Femeile se simtă tot mai în siguranță la programare, într-o operație controlată decât într-un medic chaotic, ceea ce este normal în care nimeni nu le ascultă și nu le bagă în seamă și nu au timp să discute cu ele. Fiindcă totul este pe hai repede că nu avem timp și vine următoarea. Și asta cumva nu este bine neapărat a medicilor și e a sistemului în general, că nu sunt pregătiți. Eu prima oară când am avut travalul 30 de ore și am avut epidurală chiar dacă nu m-a dorut și am dormit, nu cred că ar fi a stat cineva la stat după mine să zică hai, lească, avem timp, oi, e ok. Cred că fiecare femeie merită răbdare și respect. Și nu vă zic că cezăriana e o chestie rea, fiindcă foarte multe femei alegă asta și e perfect pentru ele, dar trebuie să fie alegerea ta, nu a medicului și să-ți împună el. De exemplu, o prieteni a spus, eu plec în vacanță și eu poți te ajut să naști doar cu două zile mai repede. Vrei așa sau nu? Adică e cel mai intim moment din viața ta în care ești cea mai vulnerabilă și cea mai frumoasă experiență în care îi naști și poate o să ai asta doar o dată sau de două ori în viață. Ai dreptul să trăiești chestia asta așa cum îți dorești. Adică, la mine acum bebe e sănătos, eu sunt sănătoasă, m-am simt bine în toate sarcinile, dar emoția tot rămâne acolo, fiindcă știu că mai am două luni și un pic și e normal, fiindcă e o treabă serioasă, e o treabă care se întâmplă de câteva ori în viață și cumva îmi place foarte mult să vorbesc despre femei, despre subiectul acesta, fiindcă știu cât de mult contează și pentru ele să aibă această experiență exact așa cum și-o doresc și să aibă puterea de să-și exprime dorințele față de medic. Eu am fost, de exemplu, la cinci medici și niciunul nu mă rog să se nasc natural, că e prea mare, că avea 3,8 kg, că îs îngustă în bazin, că vrăjele de genul ăsta, ca până la urmă să-i nasc pe amândoi și să nu fie o problemă. Adică dacă vă doriți neapărat un lucru, și la cezareană există ora magică, ora aceea tu schim, tu schim, să nu ți-l ia pe bebe, să-l lași, să-l albutezi imediat. Și există un plan de naștere. Știu că nu se practică la toată lumea, știu că poate multă lume nu știe de ele, dar cred că cu cât mai mult femeile sunt informați despre treaba aceasta și află informațiile și discută cu partenerul și cu medicul despre asta o dată de două ori, de trei ori, cu atâta și ei la rândul lor o să încerce să modifice lucrurile și să se întâmple lucrurile așa încât mediul pentru femei în viitor să fie unul de tot mai plăcut, fiindcă știm că mamele noastre nu au născut deloc într-un mediu plăcut, cu țipete, cu urlete, cu așa ți-a plăcut, așa e și acum și cu un pins pe burtă, ceea ce știm clar că acum este mai bine, dar eu cred că totuși am putea să fie mai bine în viitor, la fel cum momentan în anumite țări din Europa se întâmplă lucrurile mult mai firesc și mai ușor și frumos și într-o armonie pentru și pentru femei, mai ales pentru mamă și pentru copil dar și pentru partener dacă vrea să fie acolo sau prietenă ca să creeze tot acest mediu mult mai plăcut pentru ea și o amintire frumoasă.

summary: A single mother shares her experience of financial hardship and loss of independence after having a child. She emphasizes the importance of discussing financial arrangements, such as bill splitting and asset ownership, before the baby arrives to avoid financial dependence and control.

Adjust contributions to reflect reduced income and unpaid childcare duties.
Ensure the lower-earning parent retains personal money and autonomy.
Protect individual assets like car insurance no-claims bonuses.
Recognize signs of financial dependence or control early.

author: stefaniaelenam
title: Fixing toddler sleep with a consistent schedule
summary: A mother shares how returning to a strict, age-appropriate sleep schedule helped resolve her toddler's bedtime struggles. By waking the child at a set time and respecting specific wake windows, they reduced bedtime duration and reclaimed their evening time.
key_points: Consistent wake-up times are essential for a stable sleep schedule.
Respecting wake windows (e.g., 5 hours and 5.5-6 hours) helps prevent overtiredness.
If a nap ends early, move bedtime earlier to compensate.
An earlier bedtime does not necessarily cause an earlier wake-up time.
Consistency is key; improvements may take at least seven days to manifest.

title: Flower lesson: teaching a son it's okay not to be picked

Some people are only in your life for a while, and that's okay.

author: _karlaadriana_
title: Former kindergarten teacher: private vs state kindergarten pros and cons
summary: A woman who worked two years in a private and one year in a state kindergarten (Romania) shares what parents should consider. Private kindergartens are more modern, better resourced and provide all meals, but she warns that daily activity photos are often staged, sick children are often kept in the group because 'the client is king', there is rarely a daily medical triage, and staff are not required to be qualified teachers.
key_points: Private kindergartens: usually more modern approach (no shaming punishments like 'black dots' or the 'naughty chair'), more materials, and all meals provided.
Don't choose a kindergarten based on daily activity photos – children are often sat down just for the photo and many activities don't really happen.
Ask whether a doctor/nurse does a daily morning health check; in many private kindergartens a doctor comes once a week or not at all.
Sick children are often kept in the group in private settings because paying parents' wishes prevail – a reason children catch illnesses often.
Private kindergartens aren't required to employ qualified teachers; ask about staff training and qualifications.
The creator herself started as a private kindergarten teacher with no training in the field (previously a toy-store sales assistant).
caution: The creator's experience is anecdotal and specific to the Romanian private/state system; individual schools vary significantly.

Sau în plus, mi se pare să servească toate mesele oferite de grădiniță, adică micul dejun, gustările și prânzul. Cred că se mai iau greutate de pe umerii părinților și totodată toți servesc aceeași masă. Și acum vorbim de minusuri. Cel mai mare minus pentru mine este faptul că părinții sunt aburiți cu pozele pe care le primesc în fiecare zi. Acum o să vă spun eu realitatea care am lucrat și la creșă, și la grupă mijlocie, și la grupă mare, mai ales la creșă, dacă voi chiar credeți că copiii ăia au atâta răbdare și concentrare să facă toate activitățile pe care le vedeți voi în poza aia, spun cu siguranță că vă înșelați amarnic. Siguranță există și excepții, dar în mare parte, chiar și la grupei mai mari, copiii sunt așezați pe scaun, chiar dacă nu vor să facă, chiar dacă nu știu să facă, cât să apară în poză și după pleacă mai departe și n-au făcut activitatea aia niciodată. Copiii sunt mai stresați cu pozele alea decât de activitate în sine, pentru că ei înainte să se așeze pe scaunul alea activitate îi cauți de haine mordare, ude, de muci, de bale pe la guriță, de orice să fie în regulă pentru poza aia. Nu contează că în restul zilei copilului cu măci până în gură, la poza aia pe care o vede părintele, trebuie să fie țiplă. Deci, da, data viitoare, când alegeți o grădiniță, pentru că, wow, ce activități frumoase au, să știți că de multe ori activitățile alea nu se întâmplă și sunt doar de poze. Eți vorba aia, clientul nostru, stăpânul nostru, păi așa este acolo, pentru că fără banii părinților, grădinița nu ar funcționea. Și atunci, ce se întâmplă când un părinte își aduce copilul bolnav la grădiniță? Credeți că este trimis acasă așa cum ar trebui sau că rămâne în colectiv? În primul rând, la grădinița privată, de obicei, nu este în fiecare zi un medic acolo ca să facă triajul în fiecare dimineață și poate vine o dată pe săptămână, dacă vine și atunci. Și de cele mai multe ori, dacă ești copilul cui trebuie, o să rămâi în colectiv și dacă ești bolnav. Pentru că banii vorbesc acolo. Și uite așa, dacă vă întrebați de ce vă rățește nouă stop copilul la o grădiniță privată, ăsta este motivul. Un alt minus la grădinița privată este faptul că nu sunt obligați să aibă cadru didactic calificat, adică se poate angaja oricine ca și educatoare acolo. De exemplu, eu când am început să lucrez la grădinița privată, nu aveam nici un studiu în domeniu și chiar ultimul meu job fusese la Teddy ca și vânzătoare. Deci da, astăzi pot să lucrez la Teddy și mâine pot să merg să fiu educatoarea copilului tău la o grădiniță privată. Nu spun că asta este rău, din contră consider că am fost mult mai implicată și mai atentă decât alte persoane care aveau studii în domeniu. În ceea ce privește grădinița de stat, cu siguranță aș menționa prezența medicului zilnic și face triajul în fiecare dimineață. Părintele nu pleacă de acolo până când copilul nu este verificat Ca să știe dacă îl ia înapoi acasă sau rămâne în colectiv Bineînțeles, tot personalul de acolo are o anumită pregătire în domeniu Și i-a dat un examen pentru a ocupa postul Sau cel puțin, așa ar trebui Din experiența mea la stat, copiii au fost mult mai mult scoși în curte Afară, la aer curat, în pauze sau oricând aveau timp Și la finalul zilei, până veneau părinții, copiii se distrau în curte și mi se pare că acolo cadrele didactice pot pune accentul pe copil să învețe ceva și nu accentul pe poze ca să atragă un client nou la grădiniță. Ca și minusuri, pentru că există și ele aici, bineînțeles. Cred că este bugetul mic acordat acestor instituții, cauza căruia nu se pot renova clădirile, nu se poate cumpăra mobilier nou, poate mai multe jucării, clar sistemul învechit de învățământ, care mi se pare că este același decât eram eu la grădiniță acum 20 de ani. Și faptul că la stat posturile încă sunt ocupate de persoane foarte în vârstă, care din păcate nu mai au răbdarea necesară pentru copii. Și odată cu ei rămân și metodele astea de a pune copilul pe scaunul roșinii, de a da buline negre, de a cipa la ei pentru că nu știu cum altcumva să își impună autoritatea. Încă un minus, dar poate nu pentru toată lumea, este faptul că la micul dejun, la unele grădinițe de stat, trebuie să îi pui pachetelul de acasă și atunci mi se pare și pentru părinți că trebuie să se gândească în fiecare zi ce se pună, dar și pentru copii, pentru că fiecare vine cu altceva și atunci vrea și de la ăla, vrea și de la ăla, ăla poate nu vrea să-i dea și atunci vă dați seama ce iese la masă. Da, în concluzie, eu consider că este și mai benefic și mai ieftin să duceți copilul la o grădință de stat, dacă prindeți loc, bineînțeles. Dacă nu, cu siguranță există și grădinițe private care chiar își iau treaba în serios și sunt oameni incapabili și devătați meseriei.

author: thrivingmindsmontessori
title: Four questions not to ask your child and what to say instead
summary: A Montessori preschool explains four common questions that backfire: offering a fake choice ('Would you like to brush your teeth?'), forcing apologies, threatening with 'Do you want a consequence?', and checking comprehension with 'Do you understand?'. Each comes with an alternative phrasing.
key_points: Don't phrase non-negotiables as questions - it implies a choice and sets up a power struggle; state it.
Forced 'say sorry' teaches performance over empathy; instead ask how the other child felt.
'Do you want a consequence?' is a disguised threat that triggers fear rather than learning.
'Do you understand?' often gets a false yes from embarrassment or fear of disappointing you; ask them to show you instead.
scripts: It's time to brush your teeth.
How do you think your friend felt when you did that?
Could you show me how you do it?
dedupe: questions never to ask your child
transcript: Would you like to brush your teeth? Never ask that. That actually creates confusion in the child. It sounds like you're giving them an option. So if you want them to brush their teeth, you just set yourself up for a power struggle. Instead, say, it's time to brush your teeth. Can you say sorry? Sorry. Never ask that. Force apologies teach performance over empathy. A child might say sorry just to please you, not understanding why their actions have hurt someone. Instead, ask, how do you think your friend felt when you did that? Do you want a consequence? Never ask that. It's a disguise threat. Children often hear, I'm about to get punished, which activates fear, not learning. Do you understand? Never ask that. Many kids will nod yes, even if they don't, because it is embarrassing to admit confusion or because they're afraid to disappoint you. Instead, ask, could you show me how you do it?
onscreen: NEVER ASK THESE QUESTIONS TO YOUR CHILD!
it sounds like you're giving them an option!
How do you think your friend?
caption: Today I want to share with you some questions you should never ask your child and why 😄#parentingtips #parentinghacks #parenting

author: mom.outofoffice
title: Gently correcting adults who label your child 'shy'
summary: A parenting-tips creator describes a neighbour calling her daughter shy in front of her, and seeing the child look down as if wondering whether it was true. She calmly reframed it aloud. She argues kids absorb labels, so parents should describe behaviour instead of labelling it and be willing to correct other adults kindly.
key_points: Children absorb labels like 'shy' or 'difficult' as part of their identity.
Gently correct the label in front of the child so they hear the alternative.
Describe the behaviour rather than labelling the child.
Example reframes: 'learning to manage big emotions', 'likes to observe before joining in', 'trying something new takes courage'.
scripts: She's not shy, she just likes to take her time before joining in.
He's learning to manage big emotions.
She likes to observe before she joins in.
He's trying something new, and that takes courage.
onscreen: I know it might sound rude, but I started gently correcting adults when they label my kids.
And here's why you should too.
caption:
I didn’t think I’d be that mom… 
the one who gently steps in to correct a stranger. 
But then it happened.

We were in the elevator when a neighbor smiled and said to me (loud enough for my daughter to hear):
 “She’s so shy. Doesn’t really like people, huh?”

I froze for a second. Not because of what she said but because I saw my little one look down like she was wondering if it was true.

And that’s when it hit me. Kids don’t question labels they absorb them.

In that moment, I realized I had a choice. So I calmly said, right in front of her: 
“She’s not shy, she just likes to take her time before joining in.”

It may seem like a small thing, but our kids are shaping their identity right now. And if we’re not careful, someone else’s quick comment can stick harder than we realize.

That’s why I’ve learned to stop labeling and start describing. 
❌Instead of saying “He’s difficult” or “She’s shy,” 
I try something like:
✔️ “He’s learning to manage big emotions.” ✔️ “She likes to observe before she joins in.” ✔️ “He’s trying something new and that takes courage.”
 Because kids are learning, growing..they are human. 

And I’ll always be the voice that reminds her of who she really is.

Has someone ever labeled your child in a way that didn’t sit right with you? 👇

📌 SAVE this for the next time someone tries to define your child in front of them.

And tap ❤️ if this gives you a little relief knowing you can speak up (with love and no guilt)

author: drlorashahine
title: Green breast milk: why milk color changes and when to call a doctor
summary: A reproductive-health MD explains that breast milk naturally varies in color: colostrum is thick and yellowish, mature milk is white, and milk can look bluish at the start of a feed and creamier at the end. Green milk is usually caused by something the mother ate or took (spinach, kale, seaweed, green drinks, food dyes, iron supplements, spirulina, some medications) and is still safe for the baby. She lists symptoms that warrant contacting a provider, such as signs of mastitis.
key_points: Colostrum (first milk) is usually thick and yellow/orange; mature milk is typically white.
Milk can look thin and bluish at the start of a feed and turn creamier toward the end.
Green milk is usually from foods (spinach, kale, seaweed, green smoothies, food dyes) or supplements/medications (iron, spirulina); color normalizes within a day or two.
Green milk is still nutritious and does not need to be dumped if it was stored safely.
Contact your provider or a lactation consultant if milk is pink, red or black, or the color changed after a new medication.
Breast pain, swelling, redness or fever with no food explanation may signal mastitis - call your doctor.

ill.caption: Mastitis: inflammation of the breast tissue, often linked to Staphylococcus and Streptococcus bacteria - a reason to call the doctor if milk changes come with pain, redness or fever.

transcript: POV, you look down after pumping and your breast milk is literally green. Oh my god, isn't it great? Green breast milk, is that safe? I'm Dr. Laura Shaheen, let me explain. Breast milk changes color more often than people realize. Cholestrum, or the first breast milk, is usually thick and yellowish, and more mature milk is typically white. But breast milk can actually change color even during the same feeding. It can start off with a bluish tint and then turn a little creamier or white towards the end. So why green? most of the time it's something that the mom ate or drank. Spinach, kale, seaweed, green drinks, even food dyes can turn breast milk a different color. Once it's out of your system in a day or two, the color is back to your normal. That green milk is still full of nutrients and antibodies wonderful for the baby. You don't need to dump it as long as it's been stored safely. But if there's no food explanation and you have other symptoms of breast pain, swelling, redness, or a fever, call your doctor. This could be a breast infection called mastitis. Most of the time though, it's just the smoothie. Share this with a friend, stay curious about your body, and follow me for more.
onscreen: POV: you look down after pumping and your breast milk is literally GREEN...
caption:
Green breast milk is not a reason to panic. 

Breast milk isn’t always white, and the color can change from one feed to the next. 
Early milk can look thin and bluish, colostrum is often yellow or orange, and a green tint is usually traced to something you took, like an iron supplement, spirulina, or certain medications and possibly something you ate. 

In most cases your milk is still doing exactly what it should for your baby. 

Check in with your provider or a lactation consultant if your milk is pink, red, or black, if the color changed after starting a new medication, or if you have breast pain, redness, or fever.

Make your face light up every time your older child walks into the room.
The first second of greeting your child matters more than 10 minutes of structured alone time.
Accept help from your partner to manage the newborn so you can focus on the older child.

transcript: Day two of telling you things that I wish I would have known before I went from one to two kids. I paid a therapist 200 bucks an hour for this tip and now I'm going to give it to you for free. And if you missed day one, go back. Today we're talking about something that saved me hours of mom guilt. Although I still found things to feel guilty about, let's be honest. So you know the advice that everyone gives you when you have your second baby? They always say that no matter what, once the baby is here, make sure that you are finding time to have one-on-one time with your firstborn so that you can remind them how special they are and how much they mean to you. In theory, great advice. In reality, borderline impossible with a newborn. And don't get me wrong, my husband is fabulous. He could take the baby so that I could focus on time with my older kid. But when it comes down to the day-to-day and you are in those trenches and that survival mode, one, remembering to set that time aside. Number two, finding a way to do it where you can actually be present and not stress out even more feels like a giant weight on your shoulders. Anyone who has said that they have pulled that off seamlessly is either A, lying to you, or B, has more help than they're letting on. My therapist told me what actually matters is your face which looks a little ratchet postpartum okay but that's not the point. I made sure that my face lit up every time my older kid walked into the room. The way you greet your kid in that first second matters way more than the 10 minutes of alone time that you couldn't get. For me personally that was just an added weight of mom guilt and pressure and a daily check mark that I was trying to live up to and I was just setting myself up for failure. author: tiwtchy.witch
title: Grieving your pre-motherhood identity
summary: A pregnant creator discusses the emotional transition to motherhood, arguing that society often ignores the grief associated with losing one's pre-motherhood identity. She suggests using rituals to honor this transition and validate the complex emotions of matrescence.
key_points: Matrescence involves a significant identity shift that can include grief.
It is normal to feel a loss of your former self during pregnancy.
Modern culture often dismisses this grief by focusing only on the 'glow'.
Ancient cultures used rituals to mark the transition to motherhood.
Creating personal rituals, like writing letters or sculpting, can help process this change.

gifts.name: Letter to former self
gifts.how: Write a letter to your pre-motherhood self to acknowledge the transition.

gifts.name: Figurine ritual
gifts.how: Sculpt a figurine representing your former self and bury or break it.

caution: This is a reflection on emotional well-being; if you are struggling with severe depression or anxiety, please seek professional support.
transcript: Having my ideal body was one of my goals this year, but little did I know that my ideal body was literally a pregnant body. I have gained a little bit over 20 kilos during this pregnancy. I haven't even completed the eighth month yet. And what's funny is that every time I tell somebody this, they're always like, oh my god, it's okay, don't worry, you'll get your body back. And in my mind i'm like oh that's sweet but like what body bag like there's no way that these boobs are gonna reform into what they were i might be skinny again but i won't have my old body not the way that it was about midway through this pregnancy i had a little bit of a crisis with this idea and i wrote about it a little bit on my sub stack which you can check out if you'd like because i realized that not only was I not going to get my body back, I wasn't going to get myself back. The days of the maiden are over for me. The maiden is quite literally dead. I'm becoming a mother now. And while that transformation is beautiful and magical and beyond anything I could have ever imagined, there's also so much grief in it. And our modern societies don't get that. They don't want us to accept the death of our former selves. They don't know that we need to grieve who we were. So I ended up doing what I do best, which was some research about how people in ancient cultures dealt with this. Was there this acknowledgement of the grief of losing your past self, of losing the maiden that you once were? Turns out that yeah, of course there was. Like with the festival of matrinalia in ancient Rome, where women would gather to celebrate fertility, but also mourn the freedoms and identity of their pre-maternal selves, with rituals like unbinding their hair and removing knots from their clothing, all of these symbolic ways to release their former selves. And then you had like ancient Egyptian women who understood birth and pregnancy as this liminal spiritual space. So they would create these pregnancy chambers called birth bowers, where expected mothers would retreat during their final months. Like they deeply understood that we get really hermity in the third trimester. And they would do things like sculpt figurines of their former selves and then break them or bury them. or they would write letters to the gods expressing their fears about identity loss and there are so many of these acknowledgements and rituals in the ancient world and it's just so striking how disconnected we are today today we're just bent on getting our body back be grateful for now enjoy it you're glowing style the bum like the capital consumerist grip on our minds is deep to the point where we've just collectively forgotten how big of a transition this is this is by far one of the greatest expansions that a person could experience in their lifetime. I'm literally carrying another fully-fledged human inside of me right now. Like, what? How is this not on the front page of every newspaper every day? And even though we remember it for other things, like when we're transitioning from high school to college, or from college to get a job, or even from single life to married life, we've collectively forgotten that this major transition comes with a loss. Loss as big as the transition itself deserves as great a morning. There is a self that I have known and grown with for 33 years that is dying as this new person evolves inside of me. And though we're different every day and every year and 33 isn't like 32 and your 30s aren't like your 20s and I think that the river, the gulf between maidenhood and motherhood is so much wider, greater, and deeper than any little veil or valley along the journey of maidenhood, if that makes sense. Anyway, if you're pregnant and you've gained weight and you're feeling insecure about your body, just know that it's okay. Do a little ritual. Write a letter to who you were. Make a little sculpture that represents the maiden that you once embodied and break it or bury it. And if you're a mother, if you've been in and out and down and through and up this deepest and most difficult of valleys that I've ever experienced, I have so much respect for you. You are what makes the world go round. You are the backbone of all of life. So just know that you're a goddess. I love you.

author: sensible_amber
title: Guiding children through moral dilemmas
summary: A parent describes using a pedagogical approach when her children found a bully's failing assignment. Instead of intervening, she asked them to play out their plan to humiliate him, helping them realize the emotional consequences and ultimately choose a kinder path themselves.
key_points: Use moral dilemmas as opportunities for children to learn empathy.
Ask questions to help children visualize the consequences of their actions.

title: Hand your son the invisible work: 7 mental-load tasks for kids
summary: A parenting educator explains that instead of only visible chores, she gives her 9-year-old son 'invisible' cognitive tasks so he learns that running a household doesn't happen by itself. She lists seven, with what each teaches, arguing this is how he won't be a 25-year-old blind to his partner's mental load. Ends with a promo for her guide.
key_points: Make the grocery list himself: check the pantry and fridge and write what's running low.
Track his own weekly schedule: check the calendar on Sunday and write it on a whiteboard; no reminders from mum.
Notice when consumables (toothpaste, shampoo, snacks, batteries) run out and add them to the list; if he forgets, he runs out.
Check his own clothes are clean before they're needed (e.g. Thursday night for Friday's uniform) and start a load or ask for help.
Coordinate plans directly with friends and tell the parent what he needs.
Plan his own transitions using the clock (at 9 he doesn't need 'shoes on in 10 minutes').
Notice when family members need something and offer help.
Mental load is learned by doing it, not by lectures.
caution: Ends with a promotion for the creator's paid guide.
dedupe: teach kids invisible mental load tasks

ill.caption: Invisible task #1: the child makes the grocery list by checking the pantry and fridge himself.
What the seven tasks share: they are cognitive labour, not chores.

onscreen: I stopped asking my son to help.
I started asking him to do the invisible things.
The ones he never knew were happening.
The visible chores are easy to hand off. Take out the trash. Feed the dog. Fold his clothes.
He does those. He notices doing them. Sometimes he complains. That's the wrong list.
The list that actually changes him is the invisible one. The mental work. The planning work. The remembering work.
Here are the 7 I hand him. Every one reveals something he never knew was happening.
1. Making the grocery list before shopping.
Not just "add milk to the list." Actually making the list.
He walks through the kitchen. Opens the pantry. Checks the fridge. Notices what we're running low on. Writes it down.
What he learns: the shopping trip is the tip of the iceberg. The invisible planning is 80% of the actual work.
2. Tracking his own schedule for the week.
I do not remind him about practice, tutoring, or the birthday party on Saturday.
He looks at the calendar every Sunday night.
Writes his week on a small whiteboard in his room.
What he learns: his life is his own to track.
Which was always true. He just never had to notice.
3. Remembering when things run out and adding them to the list.
Toothpaste is almost empty. Shampoo. His favorite snack. Batteries for his flashlight.
I do not track his consumables anymore. He checks. He adds to the list. If he forgets, he runs out.
What he learns: someone was tracking every consumable in the house. Constantly. In their head. That someone was me.
4. Checking whether his clothes are clean before the morning.
Not "did mom wash my soccer uniform." Actually looking.
Thursday night, he checks his uniform for Friday's game. If it needs washing, he starts a load. Or asks me for help with the machine.
What he learns: nobody was silently running a laundry system in the background. That system was a person. That person had a name.
5. Coordinating with his own friends for plans.
Not "mom, can you ask his mom." He asks his friend. He confirms the time. He tells me what he needs from me.
I do not manage his social calendar for him.
What he learns: social plans involve coordination. Multiple people. Multiple confirmations. Multiple details. Which mom was doing invisibly for years.
6. Deciding what needs to happen next in his own day.
He is 9. He does not need me to say "put your shoes on, we're leaving in 10 minutes." He can look at the clock.
He plans his own transitions. Homework then dinner then shower. In that order or not. His decision.
What he learns: executive function is a job. Not a personality trait. Not something adults magically have. A specific job someone was doing for him.
7. Noticing when someone in the family needs something.
Dad had a hard day. Mom is tired. His younger cousin is bored at the family gathering.
He notices. He offers something. Not because I told him to. Because he saw.
What he learns: emotional attunement to other humans is a practice. Which mom was doing constantly, invisibly, for the whole family. And which he is now expected to also do.
Notice what all 7 have in common.
None of them are chores. All of them are cognitive labor.
He was never being asked to do them. Which meant he never knew they were being done. Which meant he thought running a household happened by itself.
He is starting to see. Which is the whole intervention.
He will not be the 25-year-old who cannot see what his partner is carrying.
Not because I lectured him about mental load.
Because I made him do it. For years. In his own life first.
Which is the only way it ever installs.

title: Handling Santa Claus without lying: 'some people believe'
summary: A parent explains how, from about age 2, they presented Santa as something some people believe in and some don't, sharing movies and books but letting the child decide. This avoided the ethical dilemma of lying and the risk of the child 'spoiling' it for classmates. When the daughter later asked directly, the mom told her she is Santa and that grown-ups get to be Santa too, which delighted her.
key_points: Share Santa stories, movies and books, but don't insist he is literally real.
Tell children that some people believe in Santa and some don't, and that it's okay to have different beliefs.
Ask open questions instead of declaring the answer: how do you feel about it, do you think he's real?
This approach helps kids respect classmates who believe differently and avoids them 'ruining it' for others.
When the child asks directly, answer honestly and frame it as joining the magic: parents are Santa and they can be Santa when they grow up.

author: ABA Naturally
title: Handling Unsafe Toddler Behavior and Following Instructions
summary: A board-certified behavior analyst explains how to get toddlers to follow instructions by being clear, consistent, and proactive. She advises against arguing or repeating commands multiple times, suggesting instead that parents state expectations clearly and follow through immediately with physical prompts if necessary.
key_points: Avoid vague commands like 'don't fall'; use specific instructions like 'walk off the structure'.
Do not engage in back-and-forth arguments, as this reinforces the behavior.
State expectations in a calm, neutral tone and follow through immediately.
Proactively review expectations and use role-play to practice desired behaviors.
Acknowledge and reinforce everyday positive behaviors to build cooperation.
scripts: Back up.
Come to me.
Walk off the structure.
Johnny, come down the stairs.
credentials: board-certified behavior analyst, teacher, and mom
caution: The advice to use 'physical prompts' (physically moving the child) should be applied gently and with awareness of the child's autonomy and potential for dysregulation.
transcript: No, Mateo, you're going to fall. No. You're going to fall. Look out. You're going to fall. No. Yeah. No. Yeah. No. But I'm going to let you fall. Your child's doing something unsafe, or you need them to follow instructions, and you just told them to do something, and they blatantly didn't. My name is Jenna Mazzillo, and I'm a board-certified behavior analyst, teacher, and mom of two girls, and today we're going to talk about what we can do the next time so our kids follow instructions the first time. First things first, if we want our kids to follow instructions, we need to make it really easy for them. That means being crystal clear and explicit. So instead of saying something like, you're going to fall, which doesn't tell our child what to do, and not even saying, don't do that, or don't swing on the structure, which doesn't tell our child what to do either, tell them exactly what you'd like them to do. So saying something like, back up, come to me, or walk off the structure. And the thing we want to avoid doing is engaging in a back and forth with our child when they're not listening to us. Because one, it just delays them from following through. They get to stay within that activity longer. Another thing is we're engaging in the very behavior that we don't want our kids to engage in. So we're showing them that persistence in arguing pays off. When you argue, I'll argue back with you. And when you say something, I'll say it back. We're also showing them that arguing is an acceptable way to solve problems and just giving them a ton of attention for engaging in a behavior that we don't want them to. Instead, what we want to do next time is clearly state our expectation in a calm, neutral tone of voice and we're going to immediately follow through. It teaches our kids that instructions are followed right after I say it. When you repeat yourself five times and then you wait to take action, our kids learn, oh, I don't have to do anything until my mom asks me the fifth time. And in the long run, they end up struggling more because they're never really sure where the boundary is. So in this case, I would have said, Johnny, come down the stairs. Let's say Johnny didn't. I would have repeated it. Johnny, come down the stairs and immediately provided him with a physical prompt. I would have gone to go get him. Now, if not following instructions is a common occurrence, something that you can do is review your expectations proactively and roleplay them. Another thing we want to do is find out what are some of Johnny's favorite things. So we might say, Johnny, what are some of the things that you love to do in our house or you love to play with our activities? And Johnny's going to let us know, I really love my iPad. I love watching TV. Excellent. So when you follow instructions, the first time I ask, you get to continue using those privileges. You get to stay on your iPad. You get to use the TV this many times a week, whatever the rules are in your house. Now, we're also going to let Johnny know what happens if he does not follow our expectations or instructions the first time. And when you don't follow my instructions, Johnny, then we lose access to the iPad for however many days you said or whatever the limit is. But the biggest piece to this is that we reinforce our kids when they meet our expectations and they follow our instructions. Our kids get a ton of attention when they don't follow our directions. You see that back and forth that that child got? That was a lot of good attention for him. So what we want to do is those everyday behaviors that make our life easier that we wouldn't think to acknowledge because we think our kids should just be doing them. We want to acknowledge them because that is so valuable for our kids and they're going to learn over time what behaviors get mom's attention and which do not.

caption:
When our kids get hurt because they were being unsafe or not following instructions, it’s tempting to use that moment as a teaching opportunity. “I told you that would happen!” But here’s the truth: in that moment, nothing is sinking in.

Think about it. If you cut your finger while chopping and your partner rushed over with, “How many times have I told you not to cut like that?” — would you think, “Oh, right! Silly me.” Of course not. You’d want them to check if you’re okay. Same goes for laughing it off. When kids are hurt, the best thing we can do is comfort them. Save the lesson for later, when they’re calm and ready.

Now here’s where role-play comes in — and this works for ANY age.

Step 1: Instruction

Parent: “Sophia, when you get home from school, bring your backpack upstairs and put your water bottle in the sink. What should you do when you get home from school?”

Sophia: “Bring my backpack upstairs and put my water bottle in the sink.”

Step 2: Model the behavior

Parent: “Exactly! Let me show you what that looks like.”

Step 3: Practice

Parent: “Now you show me what to do with your bag and bottle when you get home.”

If your child gets it right, reinforce (step 4)! If they need help, give feedback and practice together.

This simple, evidence-based method takes just a few minutes,  but it saves hours of frustration later when directions aren’t followed.

P.S. If we haven’t met yet—hi! I’m Jenna. I’m a behavior analyst, teacher, and mom.

I started this account to help parents and educators with practical, evidence-based strategies that actually work, so you can enjoy more peaceful days without constant power struggles.

So if you’re looking for real-life, easy-to-follow tips (without the fluff), you’re in the right place!

title: Handling a TV tantrum without giving in or punishing

key_points: Regulate yourself first and make a plan before responding.

Keep re-offering a hug so the child knows it's available, and respect it if they refuse affection.
Use playful, sensory calming the child likes (e.g. blowing on their hair) and invite deep breaths.
Tell a story of your own childhood tantrums so the child feels understood and not alone.
Explain the reason for the boundary only once the child is calm.
Praise the child for naming feelings, then let them talk; move on and reconnect with something fun.
Avoid yelling, shaming, punishing or distracting to stop the tantrum.

title: Handling a bilingual toddler refusing to speak the minority language
summary: A bilingual parent shares her approach when her 3.5-year-old daughter refuses to speak the minority language. Instead of forcing the child, she waits for calm, explains the value of bilingualism, and uses a 'recasting' technique where she repeats the child's English response back in the target language.
key_points: It is normal for bilingual toddlers to assert independence by refusing to speak a specific language.
Avoid forcing the child to speak; wait until they are calm before discussing language choices.
Explain the benefits of bilingualism in a way that highlights it as a special skill.
Accept the child's response in the majority language and 'recast' it by repeating it in the target language.
Maintain consistent use of the minority language without making a big deal out of the child's mixed responses.
Small, repeated conversations about language value are more effective than single interactions.

Name feelings and breathe together before problem-solving.

Families do recover from the transition.

title: Helping children process big emotions after holidays
summary: A mother explains that tantrums following exciting events like holidays are common because young children struggle to process intense, overwhelming emotions. key_points: Tantrums after exciting events like holidays are normal and not a sign of failure.
Young children cannot yet articulate feeling overwhelmed and express it through crying or hitting.
Holiday magic can be confusing for toddlers, leading to cognitive overload.
Get down to the child's level and name their emotions to help them regulate.
Plan a slower pace during holidays to reduce stress for both parents and children.

author: keylimelanna
title: How Early Socialisation Causes Autistic Girls to Mask
summary: An autistic creator analyzes a video experiment where five-year-old children taste salty jelly. While boys openly voice their disgust, girls hide their feelings to remain polite and avoid offending the adult. The creator explains that societal pressure for girls to people-please and internalize discomfort leads to masking, which contributes to autism going undiagnosed in girls.
key_points: By age five, girls are often socialised to prioritise politeness and people-pleasing over their honest feelings.
Masking natural responses and suppressing discomfort causes autistic traits in girls to be overlooked or misunderstood.
Autistic girls are frequently criticized as rude or bossy when being direct, reinforcing intense masking behaviors.
Parents should encourage children to express genuine feelings and discomfort rather than enforcing politeness at all costs.

author: nurturedfirst
title: How grandparents handled a toddler's pink-cup meltdown perfectly
summary: A parenting educator describes her toddler melting down at her parents' house because her sister had the pink cup. The grandmother validated the feeling, the grandfather offered to look for another cup, and when there was none they held the boundary and comforted her without teasing until she finished crying and negotiated a turn herself. The point: kids don't need us to fix disappointment, they need to be taken seriously while they feel it.
key_points: Name the feeling and the situation: acknowledge the disappointment without fixing it
Offering an alternative is fine, but it is OK if it doesn't work; hold the boundary (don't take the cup from the sibling)
Comfort the child physically and let them cry it out; don't tease or tell them to stop crying
Small problems to adults feel big to a toddler's brain; take them seriously
Once the feelings pass, children often find their own solution (she asked her sister for a turn afterwards)
scripts: You really love having the pink cup, and your sister has it tonight. That's tough.
It's hard when your sister has your cup. I wonder what other colours we have? Should we go look?
credentials: parenting educator (Nurtured First, runs a parenting course)

media.name: Parenting Little Kids course
media.why: Teaches how to respond to tantrums effectively.

ill.caption: It's OK for a child to be disappointed; we don't need to fix it, just give them the chance to cry while holding the boundary.

onscreen: I was at my parents for dinner tonight, when my toddler started having a huge meltdown. She wanted the pink cup. Her sister had it.
My mom was the first to speak...
You really love having the pink cup, and your sister has it tonight. That's tough.
It's hard when your sister has your cup. I wonder what other colours we have? Should we go look?
She held his hand and went to the cupboard with him.
They looked through all the other sippy cups.
She fell into her Papa's arms.
He looked at us with a smile, but never teased her. She cried a bit more.
Once she had cried all her tears over being disappointed, she came back to the table.
She asked her sister if she could have the pink cup once she was done with it. Her sister agreed.
She carried on with her meal.
After the meal was over and my toddler had left the table, I talked with my parents.
Jess, what do you usually reccomend people do when kids cry over things like having a pink cup?
I smiled: "I teach parents to do exactly what you just did."
It was ok for her to be disappointed about not having the pink cup. We didn't need to fix it. We just needed to give her a chance to cry about how disappointed she felt.
I told them how it was ok to hold this boundary...
And then I said... "At a deeper level my favourite part of the interaction was how you took her seriously. You didn’t tease her. You didn’t tell her to stop crying.

She was allowed to be sad about the pink cup. It seems like a small deal to us, but to her brain, it matters. You tried to help her find a solution, and you gave her a hug when she didn’t feel better."
This entire interaction reminded me of the importance of seeing our tantruming kids as whole humans who are having a hard time.
How powerful would it be if every parent and grandparent could show up this way during a tantrum?
How would the world change if we taught kids it’s ok to be disappointed - and when they are disappointed they can cry in our warm safe arms.

title: How one mom told her daughter the truth about Santa
summary: A mom of quadruplets shares her script for when a child asks if Santa is real. First she asks if the child is sure she wants to know. Then she explains that Santa isn't a man in a red suit but the spirit of giving without needing thanks, and that she bought the presents herself. The child is then 'passed the baton' to help keep the magic for younger siblings and others.
key_points: Before answering, check: "Are you sure you want to know? Once you know, you can't unknow it."
Explain Santa as an idea/spirit of giving rather than a person; reveal that parents bought the gifts.
Link it to giving: e.g. a family Secret Santa where kids choose, wrap and anonymously deliver gifts.
Ask the child not to spoil it for others and give them a role (hiding the elf, wrapping gifts for siblings).
Frames the end of the 'magic' as the start of a new phase.

Yes, there really is a Santa Claus, but he's not an old man with a beard and a red suit.
Santa Claus is the idea of giving for the sake of giving, without acknowledgement and without a thank you.
Now the baton is passed to you – it's your turn to play Santa.

author: greatcompanypodcast
title: How parenthood changes your brain
summary: Developmental psychologist Dr. Aliza Pressman explains that the transition to parenthood is a major period of brain development. She reframes 'mom brain' or 'dad brain' as the brain reallocating resources to prioritize keeping a human alive, rather than a sign of cognitive decline.
key_points: Parenthood is the third biggest period of brain development in a person's life.
This brain growth occurs in both biological and adoptive parents.
Parenthood often motivates healthier habits like quitting smoking or drinking.
Forgetfulness in new parents is the brain reallocating resources to prioritize the baby.
caution: The claim that this is the 'third biggest' brain development period is a simplification of complex neurobiological research.

caption:
Here's what I mean by " speaks their language"⬇️ (Hosted)

I don't mean book any tour that speaks the native language of your child. I mean book a tour that has been designed for childrens' brains. 

And when you're in Rome, you have to book @mariaclaudiatours . Her tours are built specifically for families. 

She kept our kids' attention for 2 hours making the learning a fun game, having them use their imaginations to role-play Gladiators, etc And the work she did getting our kids interested in Italy, paid off for the entire rest of the trip. 

Children do not think, perceive, and learn the same way adults do. So when we take our children on tours built for adults, yes they can learn, but they're not going to learn nearly as much or be nearly as invested if you were taking them on a tour that is designed for children.

When we are in museums with our small children (Who are visibly very invested in the museum), we have people ask us " how did you get your kids so into museums?!" 

And our answer is that when we take them to the museums, we make sure that we are speaking their language. We book a child-friendly tour when we can, and if we can't, we are making our own scavenger hunts, and we are at their level explaining things to them the entire time. 

Kids can LOVE history. They can LOVE art. We just have to give them a chance to love it in a language that they understand.  And when they are invested, when they are in love, they are more likely to "behave". 

And don't get me wrong, kids are still going to be kids . They need movement for their bodies, they're going to make squeaky noises and we have to have grace for that and meet their needs . 

And yes, we have other museum behavior expectations that we practice all the time: Quiet voices. Walking feet. Look with your eyes, not with your hands. Wait your turn.

 But if you want your kids to be truly invested, our biggest rule Is for ourselves, as parents, is give them an experience that they can actually understand.

author: Playful Heart Parenting
title: How to be a playful parent when you are exhausted
summary: This video explains that being a playful parent does not require high energy or big physical involvement. The creator suggests that small, silly actions can provide a dopamine boost that actually increases alertness and energy levels.
key_points: Playfulness does not require big physical effort.
Simple acts like making silly faces or wearing items on your head count as play.
Engaging in play can provide a dopamine boost that makes you feel more awake.
It is okay to skip play if you are truly unable to access that energy.
transcript: You
onscreen: The #1 question I get asked about being playful as a parent:
How do you have the energy?
caption:
The thing about energy:

(Well it’s a few things)

1- I do NOT always have the energy for the kind of playfulness you see here. Playfulness doesn’t require big physical involvement - it can be as simple as wearing underwear on your head or making a silly face or sound. 

2- it never actually takes as much energy as I *think* it’s going to take

3- being playful and hearing the belly laughs and happy squeals as a result INSTANTLY re-energizes me and gives me a boost of dopamine that usually makes me actually more awake and alert than I felt before

Of course, we’ve got to read the room, tune into our kiddos and into ourselves and it’s always okay to not be playful if we are not feeling it or able to access it in any given moment. 

But if you’re thinking, “I’d love to be more silly and playful but I’m just too exhausted,” I invite you to try just a little something and see how it makes you feel!

title: How to clean a newborn's mouth and gums
summary: A Romanian doctor demonstrates cleaning a newborn's mouth after the bath: wash hands, wrap a sterile gauze pad around a finger, moisten it with plain water or saline, and gently wipe the upper and lower gums, inner cheeks and tongue in circular motions without pressing or going deep. Wrap a sterile gauze pad around your finger and moisten it with plain water or saline solution.
Gently wipe the upper gum, the inner cheeks and the lower gum in small circles - don't press, scrub or go deep into the mouth.
Also wipe the tongue, where milk residue builds up.
For a newborn without teeth this is all the oral care needed; tooth care changes once teeth erupt.

author: natashafigueroa1021
title: How to do perineal massage to reduce tearing
summary: Using hand gestures, a clinician (presented as 'my doctor') explains antenatal perineal massage: hook fingers just inside the vagina, feel the band of muscle at the bottom, and pull down toward 5, 6 and 7 o'clock for 10-20 seconds each. It should feel like an uncomfortable stretch, not tearing. The aim is a more stretchy perineum at delivery.
key_points: Insert fingers just inside the vaginal opening and hook onto the band of tissue at the bottom (toward the anus).
Press/pull downward at the 5, 6 and 7 o'clock positions.
Hold each stretch 10-20 seconds.
It should feel uncomfortable/stretchy but not painful.
Goal: tissue stretches more easily during birth, reducing the chance of tearing.
caution: Evidence shows antenatal perineal massage (usually from ~34-35 weeks) modestly reduces episiotomy and severe tears, mainly in first births; it does not guarantee no tearing as implied. title: How to handle a child hitting you: calm block, space, repair later
summary: A role-play shows a parent calmly stopping a child from hitting ('I will not let you hit me because you're angry'), stepping away to fold laundry and inviting the child to come when ready. Later, when the child is calm and asks for a snack, the parent revisits the incident, restates the limit, offers acceptable ways to express anger, and reconnects. The caption suggests ending with a hug.
key_points: Stay calm and in control of yourself; physically stop the hit.
Give the child a chance to calm down on their own while you stay available nearby.
Talk about what happened once the child is calm, not in the moment.
Restate the limit clearly: you don't hurt other people's bodies because you're angry.
Offer alternatives: stomp, scream into a pillow, growl.
End with reconnection (e.g. a hug); repeat the same process each time until the behaviour stops.

I love you. I do not like being hit. Let's go get you a snack.
caution: Leaving a very young or highly dysregulated toddler alone may not suit every child; stay within earshot.

title: How to respond when kids ask you to buy them something
summary: A couple explains that since their kids were about 3, they answer toy requests with enthusiasm plus the question 'How are you going to get that?'. Children research prices, figure out how to earn the money and save up, while parents coach but never rescue them by buying it.
key_points: Start from around age 3 with small store requests.
Respond positively ('That looks really cool!') instead of a flat no, then ask how the child could get it.
Explain that a credit card is not magic: it is the parent's money and the child needs their own.
Ask 'What would have to be true for you to have this?' and break the goal into steps.
Step one is research: let the child price-compare (e.g. a $45 LEGO set) and calculate how much they need.
Offer ideas for earning money and coach through the process, but expect some tears.
Never crush the dream or say it's impossible, and never rescue them by buying it for them.

title: Ideal child development routine vs. average school day
summary: A developmental psychology student uses AI to generate an 'ideal' daily routine for child development, which prioritizes unstructured play, connection, and chores over academic instruction. The video contrasts this with the average school-aged child's day, arguing that children are structurally over-schooled and lack sufficient time for free play and regulation.
key_points: The ideal day includes 2-4 hours of unstructured outdoor play.
Focused skill-building (school/academics) should only take 30-90 minutes daily.
Children need 1-2 hours of social play with peers without adult intervention.
Meaningful contribution (chores) and boredom are essential for development.
The average school day provides too much academic time and too little free play.

prompts.prompt: Give me the ideal day for a child to develop into a healthy adult.
prompts.purpose: To design a developmentally appropriate daily routine for a child.

caution: The 'ideal' routine is a theoretical model and may not be practical for all families or school systems.

ill.caption: 'Ideal routine' for a child: regulation and connection, 2-4 hours outdoor free play, 1-2 hours social play, 30-90 min skill building, chores, boredom, movement, connection and story.
Average school-age day for comparison: school 6-7 hours, extracurriculars, homework, little free play.

author: bekah
title: Independent play is a skill you can train from about 18 months
summary: A mum argues parents don't need to constantly entertain kids with sensory bins and activity stations; independent play is a learned skill. From around 18 months, when she has a task (dishes, cooking), she tells the child she's busy and finishes the task, starting with about 10 minutes and extending. She stresses staying present and validating feelings rather than abandoning the child.
key_points: Independent play is a skill, not just a personality trait; it takes practice.
Start around 18 months during a real task like washing dishes or cooking.
Begin with short chunks (~10 minutes) and gradually increase.
Commit to finishing the task without stopping, even for a snack request; the child can wait a few minutes.
Expect tears at first; you are doing something different, not something bad.
Stay nearby and acknowledge their feelings; it's not cry-it-out because you are not leaving them alone.
scripts: I'm sorry, Mommy's doing this activity right now. You're going to have to wait.
It's okay to feel sad or frustrated that I'm busy. I'm here, and I'll be done soon.
caution: Personal approach; ensure the child is safe and in sight while you finish the task.

Stop feeling like you need to entertain your kid. Stop with the sensory bins, the activity stations, you don't need to do all that. Playing independently is not a personality trait. It's not just an inherent quality a child is born with or not born with. Yeah, different personalities can contribute to making it easier, but ultimately this is something that I train my kids to do. author: authornikkidestina
title: Instead of forcing an apology, apologise for your child and reconnect
summary: A parenting-class instructor explains that forcing a toddler who hit someone to say sorry produces an empty apology that comforts no one. Instead, the parent apologises to the hurt child on their own child's behalf, then takes their child aside to reconnect. This models empathy, since kids learn by watching, and the connection builds the confidence to be kind.
key_points: Hitting/pushing is a predictable part of toddler development, usually from impatience or big emotions.
Forced apologies are not sincere, don't help the hurt child, and can breed resentment and shame.
Apologise to the hurt child yourself, acknowledging their pain.
Then take your child aside to calm and reconnect before teaching better choices.
Kids learn more from what you model than from what you tell them.
scripts: I'm so sorry that Johnny hit you. I know that hurt.
Johnny, you need to sit with mom.

Johnny, you need to sit with mom before I know what it is. get it you apologize on behalf of your child what is that doing it's modeling modeling kids learn through watching you not what you tell them
onscreen: Here’s what to do instead of forcing your children to apologize.
Stop Forcing Your Child to Share Apologize
caption:
In these sessions, I guide parents on responding when their toddler inflicts harm on others - a predictable part of child development.

Apologizing on behalf of your child, then reconnecting with them, is a more effective approach than forced apologies.

Children typically misbehave due to difficulties managing emotions and feeling disconnected from their caregivers.

At the playground, a child might push another child on the slide because they're impatient.
Forced apologies and shame can foster resentment in children, rather than encouraging empathy.

Apologize on behalf of your child and move into reconnecting with your child so that you can help them make SMART choices even when they experience negative emotions. The connection they build with you will create the self confidence they need to then be kind to other people.

title: Intentional parenting habits from childhood
summary: The creator shares intentional parenting practices from her upbringing, including 'dad camp' for practical skills, involving children in hosting dinner parties, a bedtime 'campfire' circle for connection, and supervised volunteering to build gratitude.
key_points: Dad camp: Teach children how household items work by showing them the mechanics.
Involve children in hosting: Let them help set the table, choose music, and light candles.
Bedtime campfire: Create a ritual with stuffed animals, stories, and a recap of the day.
Supervised volunteering: Expose children to different walks of life to build gratitude and awareness of privilege.

author: luciebfink
title: Introducing a newborn sibling to a toddler to reduce jealousy
summary: A mom shows the hospital meeting between her toddler son and new baby sister and shares the deliberate steps they took to make him feel included. Several of the '8 things' are visible on screen: photos of him in the baby's bassinet, letting him hold her only when he asks, and never blaming the baby for making him wait.
key_points: Have the toddler arrive when mom is ready and greet him first, without the baby in arms, then invite him onto the bed to see the baby.
Put photos of the older sibling in the baby's bassinet so he feels special and included.
Hand the baby over calmly and only when he's ready and asks to hold her.
At home, let him hold the baby whenever he asks, but don't pressure him or keep asking.
Don't blame the baby when he has to wait; say 'Daddy's just finishing up!' or 'Mommy will be right there.'
Expect ups and downs after the new arrival even if the start goes well.

author: drspf
title: Introducing the newborn: greet your older child first, baby not in arms
summary: A doctor shares the best advice he got for his second child: when the toddler first meets the newborn in hospital, don't be holding the baby when the older child walks in. Greet the older child first with eye contact, hugs and cuddles, then introduce the baby together, reinforcing that they are still safe and a priority.
key_points: Don't be in bed holding the newborn when your older child first walks into the hospital room.
Greet the older child first: eye contact, hug, cuddle – baby not in your arms.
Then introduce the baby together, so the baby is welcomed rather than seen as a threat.
The first impression can shape how the older child feels about the new baby.
credentials: doctor (Dr. Daniel Sugai; speaks of his patients)
caution: Says it's backed by attachment and sibling-transition research but cites none.

transcript: watch this closely because it's actually done on purpose our second child was born we were told something very specific when you have your first child meet the newborn the biggest tip is don't be hanging out on the hospital bed holding the newborn when your older child walks in because for a toddler that moment can feel like a shock you're suddenly seeing your parent already focused on someone else and that first impression can shape how they feel about the baby so instead you greet them first when they walk into the room. No baby in hand. You make eye contact, you hug, you cuddle, and then you introduce the baby. This is actually backed by child psychology and it's based on attachment and sibling transition research. You're reinforcing, you're still safe, and you're still my priority. It turns the baby from a threat into something where you're welcoming the baby into your family together. I tell my patients and my friends who are having a second baby to do this because this was probably the best advice I got when having my second child. Hope this helps. Peace.

author: libbyzflanagan
title: Introduction to elimination communication
summary: The creator explains a simple elimination communication (EC) technique: holding a baby over a potty during diaper changes to catch urine or stool. This leverages the baby's natural instinct to hold waste until the diaper is removed, helping to keep the baby dry and save on diapers.
key_points: Hold the baby over a potty for about a minute after opening the diaper.
Babies often have an instinct to pee or poop immediately after the diaper is removed.
This method is not formal potty training but a way to respond to baby's needs.
It helps keep the baby's skin and clothes dry and reduces diaper usage.

author: sandra_n_yusuke
title: Japanese kindergarten 'good poop' calendar teaches gut health
summary: A mom raising kids in Japan shows the summer calendar her kindergartners receive. It illustrates poop types with characters (hard balls, banana, mushy, watery), asks which is a healthy poop, and gives a parent info sheet with constipation-friendly foods. It lists 5 promises for good poops, and kids log their poop type with stickers for 30 days to earn a prize.
key_points: Teach kids that poop type is a signal from the body; 'banana' poop is the healthy one.
5 promises for good poop: eat meals well; go to bed early and wake up early; play actively outside; drink plenty of water; don't hold poop in.
Track poop type daily (e.g. 30-day sticker chart) to build body awareness.
Includes a list of foods that help with constipation for parents.
Make the topic fun and shame-free with characters and rewards.

author: lucycandella
title: Kids can handle your big feelings, just not blame for them
summary: A mom explains that children can sense a parent's emotions even when hidden, and without guidance they may internalise them and feel responsible. The fix isn't never being dysregulated but naming your feelings out loud, telling children it's not their fault and not their job to manage, and reassuring them they're safe and cared for.
key_points: You can't fully hide stress, anger or grief from young children; they pick up on it.
Young children tend to assume they caused a parent's feelings unless told otherwise.
Name your emotion out loud and explicitly say it's not their fault.
Tell them they don't have to handle it for you and that you're still going to take care of them.
The goal is repair and reassurance, not being a perfect, never-dysregulated parent.
scripts: These are my feelings. They are not your fault. You did not cause them.
I can handle them. You don't have to handle them for me.
You're going to be okay. I'm still going to take care of you. I'm going to show up for you. You are safe.

If you don't have the ability to regulate yourself and put language to what you're feeling and like quite literally say out loud, these are my experiences. They are not your fault. You did not cause them. I can handle them. You don't have to handle them for me and you're going to be okay. I'm still going to take care of you. I'm going to show up for you. You are safe. It's about being able to sit with yourself, name your emotions, name them for your children and let them know that they're going to be safe and cared for regardless of how you feel that day.

Things I learned in my studies before having kids - the bad news: you actually can’t hide your emotions or dysregulated nervous system from your children as well as you think you can and without guidance they easily internalize your emotions.

As long as they know they are not to blame, responsible for managing your behavior, or going to receive less love and/or nurturing, children don’t tend to shy away from strong emotions the way we have been taught to do as adults.

author: joycethedentist
author_name: Dr. Joyce Kahng | Cosmetic Dentist OC Veneers
title: Kissing baby on the lips and cavity-causing bacteria
summary: A dentist explains that babies are born without cavity-causing bacteria and acquire them from caregivers, especially between ages 1 and 3 when the oral microbiome is most impressionable. Kissing doesn't cause cavities directly, but saliva sharing (kisses, straws, utensils, bites of food) transfers the bacteria. The goal is reducing, not eliminating, transfer; she admits it's an imperfect effort as a mom.
key_points: Babies are not born with cavity-causing bacteria; they are mostly passed on from caregivers' saliva.
The window of greatest risk is roughly ages 1-3.
Reduce saliva exchange: avoid mouth kisses, sharing straws, utensils and bites of food.
Complete avoidance isn't realistic; the aim is to lower the amount transferred.
Caregivers with high cavity-bacteria levels (frequent cavities) pass on more risk; caring for your own teeth helps.
caution: Consistent with mainstream dental guidance on reducing transmission, but presented as one dentist's view; discuss with your child's dentist.

It only transfers cavity causing bacteria. Also, even if mom is taking great measures not to kiss the baby or share utensils, that baby will most likely get some amount of bacteria transferred from somewhere. The goal is simply to reduce the amount of cavity causing bacteria that is transferred to the baby. So now let's think about this. Every baby has a different amount of cavity causing bacteria in their mouths. Which ones do you think are more you're likely to get cavities.

caption:
👄 Kissing your baby on the lips? Yay or nay? 

From an oral health perspective, it’s best to minimize saliva exchange with baby as much as possible. It’s not because we are afraid of bacteria 🦠. Bacteria is normal. 

However, we do want to minimize the transfer of certain strains that express disease. It’s all a balance. ⚖️

💗I’m going to say that from a mom perspective, it’s not always that easy. 

I’ve actively shielded Preston from mouth kisses…

But then while I’m not looking he grabs my water bottle and drinks from the straw. 🤦‍♀️ Wants a bite of my food. Or sometimes even ice cream. Yes, saliva can exchange even while sharing utensils. And who knows what else he is doing when I’m not looking lol. 

At first I used to freak about it. But I think the key is just being aware of the dynamic. 

📌For most people, this will be an imperfect effort. It has been for me, but hopefully my collective efforts will help minimize future dental decay. 

🧫 I also think this may be eye opening for people because ALL OF US have a different bacterial makeup in our mouths which can account for such variation when it comes to caries risk (despite good oral hygiene efforts). The oral microbiome is a part of the equation that we don’t talk about enough but as you can imagine, an important one.

author: nurse_sydney
title: L&D nurse explains colostrum: small amounts are normal
summary: A labour & delivery and postpartum nurse explains colostrum as the 'learning milk': the first, nutrient- and antibody-rich milk, which can start during pregnancy. The tiny volume suits the newborn's very small stomach, helps stimulate the first bowel movements (lowering jaundice risk), and hand-expressing 0-5 ml is normal; milk 'comes in' around day 2-5.
key_points: Colostrum can begin to be produced during pregnancy and is the baby's first milk.
Small volumes are intentional: the newborn stomach is tiny and the baby is 'learning' to handle milk.
Colostrum stimulates the baby's first bowel movements, which helps reduce the risk of jaundice.
Getting 0-5 ml when hand-expressing is normal; a suckling baby usually gets more than you can express.
Mature milk usually 'comes in' around day 2-5 postpartum, often with breast fullness/engorgement.

It's also known as liquid gold because it's packed with all kinds of amazing nutrients and antibodies and all kinds of things that baby really needs in that first few days of life. author: hackyourhr
title: Letting kids 'appeal' a no and interrupt politely
summary: A new mom from a family of six describes two practices her parents used. Children could ask to 'appeal' a decision and add reasons, and parents would explain their final answer or change their mind, teaching respectful disagreement and self-advocacy. To interrupt adult conversations, kids put a hand on the parent's arm and waited to be acknowledged.
key_points: From around age 7, allow children to say 'May I please appeal?' after a no.
In the appeal, the child adds reasons or context that might change the parent's mind.
Parents then give feedback: either the reason for the no (e.g. family dinner) or agree to change their mind.
This builds psychological safety to disagree calmly and teaches self-advocacy.
Polite interruption rule: child places a hand on the parent's shoulder/arm and waits to be acknowledged instead of talking over adults.
Goal: children can be heard, as long as they are respectful.
scripts: May I please appeal?
Thank you for telling me that extra context. I can make that work.
dedupe: child appeal parent decision interrupt hand on arm
transcript: I'm one of six kids and I just had a baby and there's something that my parents did with me that I'm going to do with my little boy. I have memories from as early as like seven years old being able to appeal my parents' decision if I disagreed with them. And what this did was they were teaching me in real time how to communicate more effectively and then open the door for me to advocate for myself. So this could look like me saying, hey, can I go to Sally's house? They would say no. And I would say, may I please appeal? Yes. I would say, well, later today we're going in this direction. We're going to pass her house. So you could just drop me off. And then her parents could take me home. In my initial ask, I just asked if I could go. And then in my appeal, I added reasons why they might change their mind. And then there would be feedback given. No, you cannot go to their house because we're having family dinner tonight. Or thank you for telling me that extra context. They're not using these words with little seven-year-olds. I can make that work. I will change my mind. What that did in me instilled in me a psychological safety to disagree with my parents in a pretty neutral way. People will ask what it was like to grow up in a big family. And it's those types of things that really stuck out to me. Another one was if my parents were talking and instead of just speaking over them and interrupting them, we would put our hand on their shoulder or on their arm and wait for them to acknowledge us. So they're in an adult conversation. One of their six children comes up and calmly puts our hand on their arm and then waits for them to acknowledge us. It kept it pretty calm and peaceful in social situations because we weren't all just running around acting crazy, like assuming that we could talk over any adult talking to my parents. So instead of children should be seen and not heard, children could be heard. You just had to be respectful about it.
