author: drpeckpelvicpt
title: Levator ani avulsion: the little-known childbirth injury
summary: A pelvic floor physical therapist explains levator ani muscle (LAM) avulsion, where part of the pelvic floor muscle tears off the pubic bone during vaginal birth. It affects about 20% of people who give birth and about 50% with forceps deliveries, is rarely diagnosed (best seen on 3D/4D ultrasound) and has no well-studied surgical fix. About half have no lasting symptoms, but it strongly increases the risk of pelvic organ prolapse.
key_points: LAM avulsion: the levator ani (pelvic floor) muscle partially or fully detaches from the pubic bone on one or both sides during birth.
Occurs in roughly 20% of vaginal births and about 50% of forceps deliveries.
Most women don't know they have it; it's best diagnosed with 3D/4D pelvic floor ultrasound, palpation is unreliable.
There is no well-established surgical repair.
About half of affected women have full resolution of symptoms, but it is strongly associated with later pelvic organ prolapse.
Knowing you have it can inform your prolapse risk; ask about pelvic floor PT if you have symptoms postpartum.

ill.caption: Pelvis model showing where the levator ani pelvic floor muscles attach to the pubic bone.

transcript: So here's a fun fact. There's an injury that can happen during childbirth that I actually didn't even know about until a year or two after I started being a pelvic PT. And the large majority of my patients, even my postpartum patients, have never ever heard of this injury. It actually affects around 20% of people who have given birth, which is kind of crazy. That's like one in five people and nobody has any idea that this injury exists. And this injury is called a levator ani muscle avulsion or LAM avulsion for short. And basically what happens is we're talking about the levator ani muscles, which are the muscles at the bottom of your pelvis or your pelvic floor here. And we refer to them all together as the levator ani. Something that can happen during childbirth is that as that muscle stretches and as we have that baby, part of that muscle can actually tear off of the pubic bone. There are different levels of severity. Like it can tear just a little bit. It can tear fully on one side. It can tear a little bit on both sides. It can tear fully on both sides. Even though it's 20% in the general population, it's actually 50% in people who have a forceps delivery. The thing is, most women have no idea that this has happened to them. There's a few reasons for this. Number one, it's kind of a pain to diagnose. You can sometimes palpate it by actually feeling like, is there a muscle attachment there? Results are kind of iffy. Best way to diagnose it is actually with 3D, 4D ultrasound, which is a little bit more specialized and you're not just gonna generally get that after you give birth. The other reason we don't really bother diagnosing it is because we don't really have a fix for it. We have no surgical options to kind of reattach that muscle to that bone, at least nothing that has been well-studied, well-documented, and has good results. There's a good number, about half of women who have this, and may have a full resolution of any pelvic floor symptoms, but there is a very strong correlation with levator anti-muscle avulsion and development of pelvic organ prolapse. You are much more likely to develop a pelvic organ prolapse if you have a levator avulsion. So the unfortunate truth is, even if you have one, there's not a lot you can do about it, but it can give you information about your risk factor for developing prolapse and potentially some other pelvic floor dysfunction.

Most described nonsurgical treatments for LA in the literature are pelvic floor muscle exercises and pessary. Long-term benefits of conservative treatments in women with major LA are not clear. author: openmindwithdrmonica
title: Looking beneath 'bad behaviour': curiosity about skills and needs
summary: A school occupational therapist describes a student sent out of class for talking, running around and not working. Instead of anger, she got curious about what was happening in his body, emotions, unmet needs and skill gaps: he felt restless high energy, craved connection, and was embarrassed because he couldn't read the directions, believing he should draw a picture. Her point: much 'noncompliance' is really missing skills and unmet needs.
key_points: Approach difficult behaviour with curiosity rather than anger: ask what's driving it.
Check in on body sensations (racing heart, high energy, need to move), emotions, unmet needs and skill deficits.
Children may act out (clowning, running around) to hide that they are struggling, e.g., with reading.
Go through the task with the child: highlighting unknown words revealed he didn't understand the instructions at all.
Children with dyslexia, language impairment or ADHD often 'can't' rather than 'won't' meet expectations without support.
scripts: Help me understand the directions.
dedupe: behavior unmet needs skill deficits curiosity

ill.caption: Body-sensation check-in chart (fast heartbeat, sweaty, high energy, tense, shaky, hot, low energy…) used to help a child notice what is happening in their body before behaviour escalates.

transcript: Today one of my students was kicked out of class for talking, running around, and not doing his work, so I brought him to the therapy room to check in. I wasn't angry about his behaviors. I was curious about the factors driving them. What was going on in his body, his emotions, what unmet needs and skill deficits were barriers to his ability to be engaged and meet expectations. He felt overwhelming energy, a racing heart, a burning need to move. He felt silly and playful, craving connection, but also embarrassed and confused because he struggles to read. When we read the directions for the assignment he didn't do, he highlighted all the words he didn't know. He thought he was supposed to be drawing a picture. This wasn't a case of noncompliance. author: cynthiaarscott
title: Low-energy ways to stay connected with little kids
summary: A mom shares low-effort ways to stay present with her young son when she has no energy: whispering, using body language instead of words, short open-ended prompts, and explaining energy as a car's fuel tank that sometimes needs refilling. At bedtime she plays calm audio stories instead of reading aloud. The tips are in the caption; the audio is unrelated.
key_points: Whisper your answers and questions; it takes less energy and signals calm (kids often whisper back).
Respond with your body instead of words: excited eye blinks, thumbs up/down, a hand squeeze, a back rub.
Use short, genuine open-ended prompts like 'I wonder?' or 'What do you think?' and let the child run with it.
Explain that bodies are like cars needing gas; some days the tank is low and you need rest, and you love them the same either way.
At bedtime, play non-stimulating kids' audio stories instead of doing all the reading yourself.
scripts: I wonder?
What do you think?
Our bodies are like cars that need gas. Today my tank is low and I need rest and quiet to fill it up. I love you exactly the same when my tank is empty or full.

caption:
I’ve mastered this!!👇

1. I whisper my answers or questions. Whispering takes SO much less energy than speaking out loud and it actually signals calm to my nervous system and theirs at the same time. Sometimes my son will even match me and whisper back.

2. I use my body to speak instead of words where I can. Eyes blinking for excitement in what he’s saying, thumbs up or down, a squeeze of the hand, a rub of the back. It takes way less output than talking but still shows him I’m present and paying attention.

3. Sometimes I answer with short open ended prompts like “I wonder?” or “what do you think?” Said genuinely, not dismissively! He almost always runs with it himself, which is honestly the best case scenario on a low energy day.

4. I explain that our bodies are like cars that need gas to go! Some days the tank is full and I have lots of energy. Other days it’s low and I need rest and quiet to fill it back up. I tell him I love him the exact same when my tank is empty or full! He’s started checking in and asking if my tank needs gas, which is the sweetest thing.

5. At bedtime, I queue up non-stimulating kids audio stories instead of doing all the reading myself. I don’t make a big deal of it and he still gets excited to pick his audio stories. He’s also always asleep by the end of them so it’s a win-win because I get my alone time faster. (Comment “stories” below and I’ll send you the link to my app where these live)

It’s obviously not realistic to be 100% everyday and I want them to know that! So instead, I let myself be a human and practice these which honestly keeps me calmer, more patient and way less ragey!!

author: uncommon_kait
title: Low-pressure habits that get kids eating vegetables
summary: A nutritional therapy practitioner shares simple habits that normalise vegetables (in the caption): serve veg as an ordinary part of every dinner without pressure, eat them yourself first without comment, offer dips and sauces, and stop cooking separate meals. Her point is that repeated exposure without pressure builds acceptance.
key_points: Make vegetables a normal, unremarkable part of every dinner, not the star or a punishment.
No negotiating or 'three more bites' rules; just keep presenting them, for years.
Eat your vegetables first and without comment; kids copy what you do more than what you say.
Offer dips and sauces (ranch, hummus, tahini); the goal is exposure, not purity.
Stop making separate meals for the kids.

onscreen: Boring shit I do to make my kids think vegetables are part of every meal and they typically eat them first
caption:
My kids are growing up in a completely different normal than I did, and I did not do it through rules or lectures.

I did it through repetition and a few stupidly simple strategies.

1.	VEGETABLES ARE JUST PART OF DINNER. NOT THE POINT OF DINNER.
They are not the star. They are not the punishment. They are just there.
Broccoli next to the chicken. Carrots in the stir fry. Cucumber slices on the plate.
No fanfare. No negotiation. No “you have to eat three bites.”
Just present. Repeatedly. For years.
Research consistently shows that repeated exposure without pressure is what builds acceptance in kids. Not forcing. Just normalizing.

2. I EAT THEM FIRST AND WITHOUT COMMENT
Kids watch everything. When they see me eat the vegetables without making it a whole thing it registers as normal adult behavior.
That is the most powerful nutrition intervention I have. Not what I say. What I do.

3.	SAUCE MAKES EVERYTHING EDIBLE
My kids will eat almost any vegetable if there is something to dip it in.
Ranch, hummus, tahini, whatever. I do not care. The vegetable is still getting eaten.
The goal is exposure not purity.

4.	I STOPPED MAKING SEPARATE MEALS
This was the hardest shift and the most important one.
One dinner. Modifications allowed. Separate meals not an option.

The healthy lifestyle worth passing down is not a curriculum. It is a live demonstration. 
Repeated, imperfect, consistent.

If screaming starts, pick the child up and leave immediately without warning or explanation.

title: Mindset shift for pregnancy exhaustion
summary: A pregnant mother shares a perspective shift to help manage feelings of inadequacy during pregnancy. She explains that her body is performing the equivalent of round-the-clock NICU-level care, which justifies her reduced capacity for daily chores.
key_points: Pregnancy requires significant metabolic energy.

title: Narrate household 'noticing' out loud so kids learn it
summary: A home-systems creator says noticing what needs doing isn't innate; kids catch it from hearing someone do it. She narrates ordinary observations out loud (full trash, running out of milk, what 'done' really means) and also when she's choosing a minimal reset because she's tired. key_points: Say observations out loud casually: 'The trash is getting full, I should take it out before it overflows.'
Narrate restocking: 'We're almost out of milk, I'm adding it to the list.'
Narrate the standard: the difference between 'done' and 'done done' (e.g. closet still needs a reset).
Model flexibility: 'I'm tired tonight, so I'm doing the bare-minimum reset, and that's okay.'
It's not a lecture; kids gradually absorb the habit of noticing and start echoing it.

caption:
“The trash can is getting full, I should take it out before it overflows.”
Said out loud, every time, even though nobody asked. Because noticing isn’t a skill kids are born with. It’s a skill they catch from watching someone else do it constantly.

“We’re almost out of milk, I’m adding it to the list.”
Not a big announcement. Just a normal sentence, said in passing, every single time it happens. So eventually they start noticing the milk too.

“This room looks pretty good, but the closet still needs to get reset before it’s actually done.”
I narrate the difference between done and done done out loud constantly, even when I’m just talking to myself basically. It plants the standard without ever having to sit them down and explain it.

“I’m tired tonight so I’m doing the bare minimum reset, and that’s okay.”
Because they also need to hear that the standard flexes sometimes, and that’s not a failure, that’s just being a real person.

None of this is a lesson. I’m not teaching anything in these moments. I’m just thinking out loud instead of keeping it all in my head like I used to.

But here’s what happens over time. They start saying the same things. “The trash is getting full.” “We’re out of milk.” Word for word, because they’ve heard me notice it a hundred times.

Noticing isn’t instinct. It’s something they catch from someone else doing it first.

So I just keep doing it, out loud, even when it feels boring or unnecessary. Because eventually, it sticks. 🖤

author: annaleegrace15
title: New sibling: don't overuse the 'big sister/big brother' label
summary: A mother shares advice from her therapist about avoiding the constant use of 'big sister' or 'big brother' labels for a firstborn child. She explains that tying a child's identity too closely to a helper role can lead to meltdowns and feelings of insecurity, and suggests balancing this with affirmations of the child's individual worth.
key_points: Avoid constantly referring to an older child only as 'big sister' or 'big brother'.
Tying a child's identity to a helper role can make them feel their value depends on it.
Remind the older child they are loved and capable just as they are.
Balance the excitement of a new sibling with affirmations that the child does not need to change.
scripts: You are still you, our family is just growing.
transcript: Day one of telling you things that I wish I would have known going from one kid to two. I paid a therapist $200 an hour for this information and now I'm going to hand it over to you. The very first thing that this therapist told me was to stop constantly referring to my older child as the big sister. Now that went against literally every fiber in my being. I wanted to congratulate her on her new title and make her feel special and excited. And I'm not saying you can never call your kid big sister, big brother and make them feel excited about that. but I think that we were doing it a little too much. But when you tie your kid's identity to a role, they might begin to feel like their value depends on it. Big sister began to make her feel like she only mattered in our family dynamic because she helped, because she protected her baby sister. So instead, our therapist recommended also throwing in phrases like, you are still you, our family is just growing. And please, for the love of whatever cosmic force is in charge here, do not start mentally smacking yourself upside the head every time you say big sister, big brother. because it is so exciting and deserves to be celebrated. I personally just wish that I would have had the forethought to remind my firstborn way more often how perfect and capable she was just by being herself and that she didn't need to change anything just because a new baby was coming. Come back for day two and I'll tell you the tips that my therapist told me that saved me eons of mom guilt.

onscreen: HOW TO KEEP YOUR BABY ALIVE
caption:
The first month is basically “survival mode, but make it newborn.”
Here’s the stuff no one warned me about — but absolutely should have:

1️⃣ Feed them more often than you think
Newborn stomachs are tiny. Every 2–3 hours (or more often if they cue) keeps them fed, hydrated, and growing. Yes, even at 3 a.m.

2️⃣ Watch diapers like a detective
6–8 wet diapers a day means they’re getting enough milk. Dry diapers, dark pee, or no poop for days = call your pediatrician.

3️⃣ Keep their sleep space boring and safe
No pillows, no toys, no cute blankets. Firm mattress + fitted sheet.
It looks “too simple” — that’s the point.

4️⃣ Hold them upright after feeds
20–30 minutes upright reduces reflux and helps prevent choking. It’s boring. It works.

5️⃣ Don’t overheat them
One more layer than you’re wearing — not five. Overheating is a real risk in the newborn stage.

6️⃣ Always burp mid-feed
Newborns swallow air like it’s their hobby. Burping halfway through reduces gas, crying, and spit-up drama.

7️⃣ Know the real red flags
Blue skin, fever over 38°C, weak cry, difficulty breathing, refusing feeds — these are “go now” signs. Everything else? Usually normal newborn chaos.

💛 You don’t need to be perfect in the first month — you just need to be aware, responsive, and rested enough to notice what your baby needs.

transcript: On average, when you set up a new TikTok account in the name of a teenage boy, it takes just 30 minutes before the first piece of extreme misogynistic content will be promoted to that account. We are witnessing a kind of algorithmically facilitated mass radicalisation on a scale that we've never seen before. And that can be really scary and overwhelming, particularly for parents and for educators. And especially when we have a generation of non-digital natives who are parenting and educating a generation of digital natives. There's really no such thing as online harm. We think that there is this kind of artificial barrier between the online and the offline world, but increasingly that simply isn't the case. Where we see forms of intimate image abuse, for example, with technological tools used to facilitate them, the offline harms are immense. Very often in school settings, for example, we see online abuse and offline bullying go absolutely hand in hand. But there are so many things that we can do. We can make sure that we are giving children the tools that they need to tackle these challenges when they come across them. A big part of the solution is around tech regulation, but there's also lots that individual parents and educators can do. Starting with familiarising themselves with the online landscape that young people come into contact with, and then progressing to safe, non-judgmental conversations with them. The more that we talk to young people about these issues, the more opportunities there are to intervene, and to provide them with some of the tools that might help them when they're facing these kinds of challenges.

caption: “My Milk Looks Bad” #dump Colostrum is the first form of breast milk produced by the mother during pregnancy and immediately after birth. It is thick, yellowish, and packed with essential nutrients, antibodies, and growth factors that play a crucial role in a newborn's early development and health. What Colostrum Contains: Antibodies and Immune Cells: Colostrum is rich in immunoglobulins, particularly IgA, which coats the baby’s digestive tract to protect against infections. Proteins: Colostrum contains high levels of easily digestible proteins that support tissue growth and development. author_name: Dr. Kibby McMahon | Clinical psychologist | DBT & CBT expert
title: Orchid and dandelion kids: why siblings experience the same family differently
summary: A clinical psychologist specialising in borderline personality disorder explains that children are born with different temperaments: 'dandelions' are hardy, 'orchids' are emotionally sensitive and need more tailored care. Parenting two children identically (e.g. telling both to calm down) may work for one but not the other. BPD arises from temperament/genetics interacting with environment, and sensitive kids can thrive with the right support.
key_points: Temperament differs from birth: some children feel emotions more intensely and take longer to calm down.
Same parenting can be experienced very differently by two siblings.
'Just calm down' may work for a less reactive child but not for a highly sensitive one; adjust support to the child.
BPD is not simply caused by parenting; it results from nature-nurture interaction (trauma, invalidation can amplify).
Sensitivity is not a weakness; with the right conditions it brings empathy, creativity and depth.
Better question than 'what went wrong?': 'what did this particular child need?'
transcript: Ever wondered why one sibling can struggle with intense emotions while the other one seems completely fine, even though they grew up in the same family? I'm a clinical psychologist who specializes in borderline personality disorder, so let me explain. Think of some kids as born an orchid and some are born as a dandelion. Dandelions are naturally hardy, right? They literally grow in the cracks of a sidewalk. But an orchid needs a little bit more TLC, the right light, the right method of watering just the roots. If you care for both flowers the same, like just pouring some water into them every day, the dandelion might be fine, but the orchid might not thrive. It's the same with kids who are born with different temperaments. One child might be naturally more emotionally sensitive. They feel things more intensely and have a harder time calming down. While the other child might just be naturally less reactive. And if you parent the two kids the same, telling them both just to calm down when they cry, the dandelion kid might be able to calm down more easily but the orchid may not. Two siblings can grow up in the same household with the same parents and experience that family completely differently. The same family doesn't meet everyone's needs perfectly. Keep in mind that when orchids do get what they need they bloom into something beautiful. Both orchid kids and dandelion kids are special in their own ways.
onscreen: One kid has BPD. One doesn’t.
might be able to calm down more easily
orchids do get what they need
caption:
"Why does one of my children have BPD while the others don't?"

Because BPD isn’t simply caused by parenting or childhood experiences. It develops through a complex interaction between nature and nurture.

Some children are born with more emotionally sensitive temperaments. They feel emotions more intensely, react more strongly, and may take longer to return to baseline.

Think of it like **orchids and dandelions.** 🌸🌼

A dandelion can thrive in lots of different environments. An orchid may be more sensitive to its environment and need different conditions to thrive.

So even when parents treat two children similarly, those children may experience the same parenting very differently.

Trauma, abuse, neglect, invalidation, and other environmental experiences can make these differences more extreme but temperament and genetics matter too. And importantly, being highly sensitive isn't inherently a weakness.

Under the right conditions, that sensitivity can come with incredible strengths: empathy, emotional depth, creativity, passion, and connection.

The question isn't always: “What went wrong in this family?” Sometimes a better question is: “What did this particular child need?”

title: Pelvic floor PT: strengthen your body before getting pregnant
summary: A pelvic floor physical therapist explains that many women experience severe back, pelvic, and sciatic pain during pregnancy due to the exacerbation of pre-existing injuries by hormonal changes and increased physical load. She recommends using the 6-12 months before conception to correct asymmetries, strengthen stabilizing muscles, and release tight muscles to ensure a more comfortable pregnancy.
key_points: Pregnancy hormones and changing physical load can flare old back, hip, or knee injuries.
Ideally, start preparing 6-12 months before trying to conceive.
Focus on fixing asymmetries, strengthening stabilizing core muscles, and reducing excess muscle tightness.
A stronger body may lead to less pain and a more comfortable pregnancy experience.

They can barely walk, their backs hurt so bad, their pelvis is like shooting pains into their body, they have sciatica, so many different things going on with these women. And I'm able to help them a little bit in these moments, but the biggest thing that I just see over and over and over and think all the time is, oh my gosh, if only I could meet these women at the beginning of their pregnancy. author: elenamuntean_
title: Phrases to help a shy child join other kids' play
summary: A mom of a nearly 7-year-old son explains why she stopped telling him to 'just ask if you can play'. That question is easy to refuse, and one 'no' can stop a shy child trying. Instead they rehearse joining phrases at home that assume he is already welcome.
key_points: 'Can I play with you?' invites an easy 'no'; a single refusal can make a shy child stop trying.
Teach joining phrases that assume inclusion rather than asking permission.
Rehearse the phrases at home repeatedly so they come out automatically when the child is nervous.
On very shy days, let the child stand close and ease in by asking how the game works.
scripts: What are you guys playing?
Can I be on a team?
I like that game, can I try?
Need another player?
That looks fun, how do you play?
onscreen: When my son wants to play with other kids but feels too shy to join, I don't say: "just go and ask if you can play". Here's what I teach him to say
When my son wants to play with other kids but feels too shy to join, I don't say: "just go and ask if you can play".
Here's what I teach him to say
caption:
Five minutes into the playground or birthday party, and my almost 7-year-old son drifts to the edge. He wants in. He just can't make himself walk over.

Later he'll tell me the same thing every time: "I felt too shy."

I used to say "just go ask if you can play." 
Then I actually watched what happens when a kid does that. "Can I play with you?" is an easy thing to say no to — not out of meanness, just because it's a question with an obvious exit. And for a kid who's already nervous, one "no" can be enough to make him stop trying altogether.

So we ditched the ask-permission approach. Instead, we practice phrases that assume he's already welcome:
🔹 "What are you guys playing?" — treats him as already part of the moment, not someone requesting entry
🔹 "Can I be on a team?" — no single kid has to be the one who says yes or no
🔹 "I like that game — can I try?" — leads with curiosity, not a request
🔹 "Need another player?" — he shows up as helpful, not as an outsider
🔹 "That looks fun, how do you play?" — for the shyest days, when he just needs to stand close and ease in slowly 

We rehearse these at home, over and over, so they come out without him having to think.

He still freezes sometimes. That part hasn't gone away. But now he has an opening line ready instead of just standing there hoping someone waves him in.

author: the_meaningful_mama
title: Play 'Where's Mama?' instead of peek-a-boo to build language
summary: A child development specialist who worked 7 years with language-delayed kids plays a peek-a-boo variant using 'Where's Mama? ... Mama!' instead of 'boo'. She explains that repeating a functional word like a family member's name helps babies learn who you are and eventually say it. Siblings and grandparents can use their own names too. She stresses peek-a-boo itself isn't bad.
key_points: Replace 'boo' with a meaningful word: 'Where's Mama?' / 'Where's Dada?' then reveal with 'Mama!'.
Repetition is key; she states babies need to hear words around 1,000 times before saying them.
Siblings and grandparents can substitute their own names.
Supports both receptive (understanding) and expressive (speaking) language.
Traditional peek-a-boo is not harmful; this is just a more functional tweak.
scripts: Where's Mama? Where's Mama? ... Mama!
credentials: child development specialist; 7 years working with language-delayed children
caution: The '1,000 times' figure is a rough popular estimate, not a precise research finding.
transcript: Hey, where's mama? Look, where's mama? Mama! Ready? Mama, where's mama? Where's mama? Mama!
onscreen: Reasons why we don’t play peek-a-boo at our house as a Child Development Specialist
caption:
Sure, in this video, I’m playing a version of peek-a-boo, but notice the changes I make to the game! I’m not saying that peek-a-boo is wrong or bad! I’m just saying, as someone who worked with severely language delayed kids for 7 years this little switch up made the world of difference when it came to language development. So much so I play this version with my own kids! 

We play “Where’s Mama?” or “Where’s Dada?” This is a great way to start introducing your name to your baby. It helps them learn who you are and, eventually, will aid them in saying your name too! Why is this important? Repetition! Babies need to hear words 1,000 times before they even start to say them. That’s a lot! While “boo” is a fun word to say, I prefer using more functional words in this game. That’s why we don’t just play peek-a-boo with “boo.”
Personalized Play: This game is also a fantastic way for everyone to engage with your baby. Siblings or grandparents can substitute their names too, which helps with both receptive and expressive communication. Plus, it makes the game even more special for the person playing with the baby when they hear their name instead of the usual “boo.”
Encouraging Social Engagement: Notice how I don’t move my hand until there’s social interaction? This encourages play and social interaction while also teaching cause-and-effect. For example, when I touch Mom, she uncovers her face! Cause-and-effect skills are important precursors to language development.
Incorporating these small adjustments into playtime can make a big difference in your baby’s communication skills and social development. It’s not just about having fun—it’s about laying the foundation for essential language skills that will benefit them for years to come! Make sure you Follow @the_meaningful_mama

author: mama_nurse_tina
title: Polyhydramnios (too much amniotic fluid) explained by an L&D nurse
summary: A labor and delivery nurse explains polyhydramnios: excess amniotic fluid affecting about 1% of pregnancies. She covers causes, when it occurs, symptoms, how providers suspect and diagnose it, and the risks to baby and mother.
key_points: Affects about 1% of pregnancies; usually in the second half, but can appear from 16 weeks.
Causes include gestational diabetes, a baby who can't swallow amniotic fluid efficiently, and rarer causes.
Severe cases cause pressure symptoms: heartburn, shortness of breath, frequent urination, swollen vulva, constipation.
Suspected when the uterus measures large, weight gain is higher than expected, or baby's position/heartbeat is hard to find.
Diagnosed by ultrasound (same as low fluid).
Risks for baby: preterm labor and umbilical cord prolapse when waters break.
Risks for mother: placental abruption and postpartum hemorrhage.
transcript: Okay, now you want to know about the other one, don't you? Too much amniotic fluid. That's known as polyhydramnios. It affects around 1% of pregnancies. Some causes can be gestational diabetes or issues with baby that doesn't allow them to efficiently swallow that amniotic fluid or some other more rare causes. Polyhydramnios usually occurs in the second half of pregnancy, but it can occur as early as 16 weeks. Not everyone with this has symptoms, but if you have a more severe case, then that growing uterus with all that fluid is going to put pressure on the surrounding organs so you could have symptoms like heartburn and shortness of breath and peeing more often and a swollen vulva and constipation all of those goodies. If you have no symptoms then why would your provider ever suspect this? Well at your appointments if your uterus is measuring larger than expected or you're putting on more weight than you would anticipate or they're having a hard time palpating the fetal position in utero or they're having a hard time finding that fetal heartbeat with all that fluid then they may suspect it. Polyhydramnios is diagnosed the exact same way that not enough fluid is diagnosed and that's by ultrasound. Polyhydramnios can be a risk for baby because some of the complications include premature labor and an umbilical cord prolapse or that umbilical cord coming down in front of baby's head with all of that water if your water breaks but it can also be a risk for the person carrying the baby because severe polyhydramnios can cause you to be at risk of something called placental abruption when the placenta comes away from the wall before the baby's ready to be born and it can also increase your risk of having a postpartum hemorrhage.

title: Postpartum Visitor Rules and Newborn Boundaries for Twin Boys
summary: A Romanian mother of twin boys shares the boundaries she set after birth to protect her newborns from infections and reduce postpartum stress. Her rules included no visitors for two weeks, strict hand hygiene, no mouth kissing, no sick guests, and sleeping in separate cribs.
key_points: Enforce a two-week visitor-free period after birth to rest and adapt.
Require all visitors to wash or sanitize hands before touching newborns.
Prohibit anyone with cold symptoms or cold sores from visiting.
Never kiss newborns on the mouth to protect them from herpes and viral infections.
Place newborns in their own cribs from day one to avoid exhaustion-related co-sleeping accidents.
Rely on medical professionals rather than unsolicited advice for infant feeding.

title: Postpartum perineal care routine after a vaginal birth
summary: Filmed less than a day after giving birth, a mom shows the steps she goes through every time she pees postpartum, a part of recovery she says no one prepared her for. She layers a pad with an ice pack, witch hazel cooling pads and perineal foam, uses a peri bottle to rinse, a numbing spray, and wears disposable postpartum underwear. She also notes heavy bleeding and that the belly still looks pregnant.
key_points: Expect heavy postpartum bleeding and a belly that still looks pregnant for a while after birth.
Prepare a 'padsicle' stack in advance: pad + ice pack for swelling + about 3 witch hazel cooling pads + perineal relief foam on top.
After urinating, rinse with warm water from a peri bottle instead of wiping.
Then spray a numbing/cooling pain-relief spray (e.g. Dermoplast) before pulling up the pad.
Disposable postpartum underwear holds the whole stack in place.
Each bathroom trip takes time in the first days; keep supplies by the toilet.

author: jessicakroll
title: Postpartum reality: fundal checks and recovery
summary: The creator shares her personal experience with the immediate postpartum period, highlighting the intensity of fundal checks, the physical weakness experienced the day after birth, and the challenges of postpartum bathroom recovery. She emphasizes the importance of being prepared for these realities.
key_points: Fundal checks are performed frequently after birth to monitor uterine contraction and bleeding.
Fundal checks can be painful; request that nurses perform them gently.
Extreme physical weakness is common in the first 24 hours after birth.
Recovery of mobility happens relatively quickly within the first day.
Stool softeners can assist with the first postpartum bowel movements.
Postpartum bathroom hygiene can be time-consuming and frustrating.

After those two hours are done, they move to every four hours to eight hours to 12 hours, something like that. So like it's really just those first two hours that are pretty intense. author: chaoswithcara
title: Praise kids 'behind their backs' within earshot
summary: A mom of three explains that she and her husband intentionally talk to each other about their kids' good behavior when the kids are nearby but not part of the conversation. Overheard praise (e.g. about telling the truth) feels more genuine to children and reinforces the behaviors parents want to see.
key_points: When kids are within earshot but not directly addressed, tell your partner about something good they did.
Be specific about the behavior (e.g. telling the truth when asked about eating Play-Doh).
Overheard praise feels authentic because the child knows you're not saying it just to them.
Works well for preschoolers (she uses it with her 3- and 5-year-olds); a small, intentional way to reinforce behavior.
scripts: I asked him if he was eating the Play-Doh, and instead of lying he told me the truth. I'm so grateful he trusted me, and I'm so proud of him for telling the truth.

transcript: So my husband and I talk behind our kids' backs all the time. It's not what you think. We have a five-year-old, a three-year-old, and a one-year-old. And for our five-year-old and our three-year-old, whenever we know that they are close and within earshot, but we're not directly having a conversation with them, my husband and I will talk to each other and tell each other things that we want to positively reinforce in our kids. So it may sound like, oh my gosh, today Hudson, man, I asked him if he was eating the Play-Doh and instead of lying to me and telling me he wasn't, he told me the truth. And I am just so grateful that he trusted me to tell me the truth. And I'm so proud of him for telling me the truth. And we will talk to each other about our children's behaviors behind their back, but within earshot for them to hear. This is such a powerful way of reinforcing that positive behavior. It's just something about when you know that they're not talking to you, like they're not faking it. They really think this about me. It's just a fun, intentional, small way that we can go out of our way to positively reinforce the behaviors that we want to see in our kids and in a way that is impactful for them.

author: harmonious_nest
title: Praise vs. encouragement: what to say instead of 'good job'
summary: A conscious-parenting creator contrasts evaluative praise ('You're such a good helper', 'I'm so proud of you', 'You're an amazing artist') with encouragement that describes what the child did, how it feels, and invites reflection. The caption tells how her 3.5-year-old son refused to try writing after a mistake ('I'm no good at this'), which led her to research suggesting labelling praise can create pressure and fear of failure.
key_points: Describe what the child did instead of labelling them ('All the toys are put away' vs 'You're a good helper').
Point to the child's own feelings ('You must feel so proud of yourself') rather than your approval ('I'm so proud of you').
Show gratitude for help: 'Thank you, I really appreciate your help'.
For art, notice enjoyment and ask questions instead of judging ('What's this part of your picture?').
Labels, even positive ones, can make some children afraid to try things they might fail at.
scripts: Wow, this room is so clean. It feels so good. All the toys are put away. Thank you so much, I really appreciate your help.
You went pee-pee in the potty. You must feel so proud of yourself.
It looks like you really enjoy doing art. What's this part of your picture?
caution: 'Research shows praise harms your child' is overstated: studies mainly warn against person-focused or inflated praise; specific, sincere praise of effort is generally considered fine.

I really appreciate your help. Baby, you went pee-pee in the potty. I am so proud of you. Baby, you went pee-pee in the potty. You must feel so proud of yourself. Wow, sweetie. You are such an amazing artist. It looks like you really enjoy doing art. What's this part of your picture?

caption:
I thought everything was going perfectly with my first until he was about 3.5 and rufused to try writing.

✨I share the most important lessons and tips I've learned as a mom working with my own kids. Follow @harmonious_nest you don't have to make them same mistakes 🔥

The first time we were going to try tracing letters he was soooo excited. We each had our own paper, he had a huge grin on his face, he started at the top of the "A" and slowly traced down.

About halfway down the line his pen wiggled out of line and his face broke. Almost in tears he said "I can't do it! I'm no good at this!"

And that was the last time he was willing to try.

I was in shock, I'd never talked to him like that and work so hard to remain calm whenever mistakes were made.

I wanted to help him overcome this so bad but had no idea what to do nor why this had even come up.

He's a really talented kid and has always tried so many things.

I went into a hyper fixated fury of research looking through all of the worlds top child psychologists and development specialists work to see if I could find what happened.. And I did.

I found out that praising your child (defined here as labeling them - even positively - like you are so smart, you are so talented AND/OR as congratulating them based on their accomplishments) develops a ❗FIXED MINDSET❗in your child. They start to worry more about maintaining the belief that they are smart tham about learning, so if they try something new that seems like they might not get it they will avoid it.

If been telling my kid he was so smart his whole life, and now I was seeing the fruits of a fixed mindset.

I started focusing on only encouragement - you must feel so proud, wow you worked so hard, look at how you're practicing etc.

And I was beyond words relieved when a month later he started being willing to practice writing without that same fear of failure.

Don't get me wrong I still let my kid know I'm proud of them, I just say it in moments like I would I love you (not tied to specific thing they've done.

I've put some of the most pertinent research in the comments for you.

title: Praise your partner in front of your child to model appreciation
summary: A child psychologist's carousel recommends openly bragging about your partner in front of your child. Children who hear parents appreciating each other learn to notice others' efforts and voice appreciation themselves, while children who hear criticism learn to focus on mistakes.
key_points: Regularly and specifically praise your partner out loud where your child can hear it.
Name concrete efforts (fixing things at home, being thoughtful) rather than generic praise.
Children copy what they hear: appreciation teaches them to notice small efforts and say thanks.
Criticising or focusing on a partner's mistakes in front of children teaches them to do the same.
Model kindness and appreciation at home and children will follow the example.

author: dragosbuzzi
title: Prevent school violence by listening to kids so they'll tell you things
summary: Responding to school attacks in Romania (Bistrița, Pitești), a Romanian father argues that metal detectors and social-media bans can't catch the warning signs peers see online. He cites US Secret Service research showing that in most school attacks other children knew beforehand, and that averted plots were stopped because a child told an adult. His conclusion: children only confide in adults who listen, so parents must listen attentively from the early years, even to talk about superheroes, if they want teens to tell them what they hear in the hallways.
key_points: US Secret Service Safe School Initiative (2002): in 81% of school attacks at least one person (usually a peer) knew of the plan beforehand.
A later analysis of 67 averted plots found most were stopped because a child who noticed something told an adult.
Metal detectors can find a knife but not a worrying post or 'close friends' story - only kids see those.
Taking away phones and yelling teaches children to stop telling you things.
Listen fully to your young child's small stories now so they trust you with serious things as teens.

THE FINAL REPORT AND FINDINGS OF THE SAFE SCHOOL INITIATIVE:
IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PREVENTION OF SCHOOL ATTACKS IN THE UNITED STATES
UNITED STATES SECRET SERVICE AND UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION
U.S. Secret Service • Safe School Initiative • 2002

In most cases, other people knew about the attack before it took place. In over three-quarters of the incidents, at least one person had information that the attacker was thinking about or planning the school attack (81 percent, n=30). In nearly two-thirds of the incidents, more than one person had information about the attack before it occurred (59 percent, n=22). In nearly all of these cases, the person who knew was a peer-a friend, schoolmate, or sibling (93 percent, n=28/30). Some peers knew exactly what the attacker planned to do; others knew something "big" or "bad" was going to happen, and in several cases knew the time and date it was to occur. An adult had information about the idea or plan in only two cases.

Peers: In nearly two-thirds (n = 41, 61%) of the cases, the plotters' friends, classmates, or peers observed the communication or behavior firsthand. In 22 of these cases, they reported the information to a school administrator or teacher. They also told their own parent (n = 7), an SRO (n = 6), or outside law enforcement (n = 5). In one case, the classmates told a private substance abuse counselor. These findings emphasize the importance of schools establishing and maintaining a safe school climate where students are empowered to speak up if they see a friend or classmate in distress. Building rapport with students and taking the initiative to ensure each student has a positive connection to a member of the staff, not only helps students academically and emotionally, but also fosters trust. As a result, when students have concerns about someone, they are comfortable coming forward with this information.

author: Emmers
title: Preventing Entitlement by Building Frustration Tolerance
summary: This video discusses how to prevent entitlement in children by allowing them to experience boredom and disappointment. It encourages parents to support their children through these feelings rather than immediately fixing them.
key_points: Entitlement is prevented by allowing children to practice handling disappointment and boredom.
When a child asks for attention while you are busy, set a clear boundary.
Encourage independent problem-solving by asking, 'What will you come up with in the meantime?'
Avoid rushing to fix every uncomfortable feeling, as this prevents the development of frustration tolerance.
scripts: I know you want to play. I'm finishing dinner, then I can join you.
Do you really want me to play with you? I'm finishing dinner and I can join you in a bit. What will you come up with in the meantime?
transcript: How to not raise an entitled kid? Start by giving them practice with everyday disappointment and frustration and let them be bored. I'm the founder of Emerus. Follow Emerus HQ for everyday ways to help kids build emotional skills. We need to help kids build frustration tolerance, which means being able to handle things not going your way even when you don't like it. So here's one thing to practice today. When your kid says, I'm bored, play with me, and you're making dinner, try saying, do you really want me to play with you? I'm finishing dinner and I can join you in a bit. what will you come up with in the meantime? They might protest, might throw a fit. You can understand their frustration and still finish dinner. Practicing handling the weight and disappointments. When we rush to fix the disappointment, they aren't able to build the skill to handle it on their own. And that is a key thing that's needed to prevent entitlement. Follow Emmer's HQ for playful ways to help kids handle big feelings and build confidence.
caption:
Helping prevent entitlement starts with small, everyday moments—like letting our kids wait, feel disappointed, or be bored. 💛
That doesn’t mean ignoring their needs. It means offering support without rushing to fix every uncomfortable feeling.

“I know you want to play. I’m finishing dinner, then I can join you.”

We’re giving them practice learning: “I can want something, wait for it, and handle how that feels.”

Which is hardest in your house: waiting, boredom, or hearing “no”?

Follow @EmmersHQ for playful ways to help kids handle big feelings and build confidence.

author: andraeudrea
title: Prioritise family outings over household chores
summary: A mother reflects on her children's perception of their parents, noting that they associate their father with exciting 'firsts' and outings, while she is associated with daily routines. She resolves to delegate or postpone chores to be more present for memorable family experiences.
key_points: Children often have selective memories, valuing novel 'firsts' and outings over daily care.
The parent who performs the majority of daily chores may be under-credited in their children's memories.
It is important to occasionally postpone cleaning or cooking to join family outings.
Ask children about their favourite memories to understand what they truly value.
Delegating tasks or accepting less-than-perfect housework can free up time for connection.

Mai țin minte când tatii a făcut, nu știu ce, am fost și eu la Disney cu ei, dar erau mult prea miști să-și amintească și amintesc când au fost cu tatăl lor la Disney, iar eu n-am fost cu ei atunci. Și întotdeauna am avut un motiv pentru care nu m-am dus cu ei, dar nu întotdeauna a fost un motiv de ce nu-l trebuie cum a fost, de exemplu, ieri când s-au dus la stăniu și mi-ar fi plăcut foarte mult să merg cu ei, însă a trebuit să stau cu cea mică care a lui place zăpada și le-aș fi stricat toată distracția pentru că a mai încercat și a plâns 10 minute cât am stat în zăpada, a plâns continuu, așa că eu am preferat să-i las pe ei să se distreze și eu să rămân cu cea mică acasă. Însă, în trecut au fost și momente în care, este adevărat că am preferat să rămân acasă ori să mă odihnesc, însă de cele mai multe ori a fost un motiv de genul Mergeți voi, iar eu în acest timp fac curat, pun la spălat, pregătesc ceva de mâncare, ceva de genul, oricum. Și mă gândeam așa câte multe momente am ratat, momente frumoase în care ei s-au distratit, s-au simțit bine. Eu mă bucuram că ei au avut această experiență cu tatăl lor, cu care nu reușeau să petrece atât de mult timp pe cât petreceau cu mine, pentru că eram acasă în permanență cu ei. Însă, pentru că eu făceam cu ei acasă lucruri repetitive, nu știu, desenam, cântam, coloram, Asta le făceam în fiecare zi. Bineînțeles că în memoria lor au rămas momentele astea mai faine, în care au mers nu știu unde, au făcut pentru prima oară anumite lucruri și își amintesc mult mai puțin celelalte lucruri. Nu m-am supărat, însă a fost o lovitură, dar m-a scuduit așa puțin, pentru că, într-adevăr, avem memorie selectivă, însă vor trece ceva ani până când ei ori să-și dea seama care au fost motivele pentru care eu am rămas acasă Și uite că de multe ori nu au fost neapărat niște motive atât de relevante pentru copilăria lor, ce au fost mai mult pentru că era necesar, într-adevăr, era necesar să fac curățenie, mai ales în momentele în care locuiam în Franța și nu aveam niciun fel de sprijin de nicăieri. și aveam nevoie să rămân să fac mâncare, curățenie, dar nu era ceva ce nu aș fi putut să amân și să fi petrecut timpul ăla cu ei. Și bineînțeles că îmi pare rău că am lipsit de la multe distracții de ale lor, pe care le-au avut doar cu tatăl lor Și nu sunt nici invidioasă pe el, nici geloasă. Mă bucur că au avut experiența asta cu tatăl lor, dar îmi pare rău că nu am avut-o și cu mine și că nu am fost acel gen de mamă care să lasă toate lucrurile, să spun ok, poate să aștepte, dar eu mă duc să mă distrez cu copiii. Și asta este ceva ce vreau să fac pe viitor, mi-am propus să fac pe viitor, să fac mai multe lucruri pentru prima dată cu ei, să fiu și eu prezentă, nu doar tatăl lor și să poate să mai deleg, poate să îmi iau mai mult ajutor, poate să vă îndemn și pe voi să vă gândiți la lucrul ăsta, pentru că știu că sunt foarte multe mame în situația mea și foarte multe mame care își dedică mult, mult timp casei, curățenii, ceea ce este normal, este absolut normal, însă ratăm de multe ori momente faine.

author_name: Miruna Ioani 🦷 Și Blondele Gândesc 👱‍♀| Dentist
title: Private cord-blood stem cell banking: a dentist's critique
summary: A Romanian dentist and mother argues that private umbilical cord blood banks profit from parents' hopes. She says the chance of using a child's own stored cells is about 0.04%, because in conditions like leukaemia the child's own cells may carry the defect and donor cells are preferred, so public banks are far more useful. She chose delayed cord clamping instead.
key_points: The probability that privately stored cord-blood cells are used for that child is cited as ~0.04%.
For genetic conditions/leukaemia, the child's own cells may carry the defect; healthy donor cells are usually needed, which is why public banks are valuable.
Collecting cord blood takes a significant amount of blood from the baby; she opted for delayed cord clamping.
Stored cells are only enough for a child up to roughly 20-25 kg body weight.
Cost cited: about $1,350-2,350 upfront plus $100-175 per year; usually not covered by insurance.
Read private-bank contracts carefully: stopping storage can be expensive; private banks are banned in France and Belgium, and many European countries offer free public donation.
caution: Figures quoted from a dentist rather than a haematologist; broadly consistent with AAP/ACOG positions favouring public donation, but verify current numbers and local options with your obstetrician.

author: midwife.ellie
title: Protect the golden hour: weighing the baby can wait
summary: A UK midwife explains the 'golden hour': 60-90 minutes of uninterrupted skin-to-skin after birth, during which the baby goes through nine instinctive stages and adapts to the outside world. It benefits both breastfed and formula-fed babies, helps breastfeeding, calms the baby and supports bonding. Unless mother or baby is medically unwell, routine weighing and measuring can wait; if staff want to interrupt, ask why.
key_points: Golden hour = 60-90 minutes of protected skin-to-skin straight after birth; the timeline varies by baby.
During it the baby goes through nine instinctive stages, which makes breastfeeding easier and gives a calmer baby.
It matters for formula-fed babies too (adaptation and bonding).
Weighing and measuring are not a valid reason to interrupt; they can be done afterwards.
If asked to stop skin-to-skin, ask 'why?'; medical reasons are valid, paperwork is not.
Add the golden hour to your birth plan.

author: aliziapsych
title: Psychology PhD student: things I won't do with my child (part 2)
summary: A psychology PhD candidate and toddler mum lists parenting choices she makes, citing studies on screen: she won't compare her child to others, won't make screens the default entertainment or emotion-regulation tool, won't say no 'just because I'm the adult', won't underestimate play, and won't rescue her child from every frustration. She says it is not clinical advice.
key_points: Don't compare your child with others; comparison is linked to lower self-esteem. Make the reference point their own growth.
Don't make screens the default entertainment or the go-to way to calm a child; research links using devices for calming at 3-5 years with poorer emotional regulation.
Children used to constant screen stimulation may struggle to sustain attention at school (relationship is nuanced).
Explain reasons rather than saying no 'because I'm the adult'; blind obedience can be dangerous.
Play is how children learn and is their training ground for the real world.
Allow developmentally appropriate frustration, waiting and boredom; coping with them builds confidence.
credentials: psychology PhD candidate (not paediatric psychology; not clinical advice)
caution: The creator stresses this is her personal choice, not a clinical opinion.

She's had the Rolls-Royce of all screens from being at Times Square, but she doesn't watch TV. I think part of the reason as well that we're seeing so many complaints by teachers of children not able to sustain attention in school is because if they're handed an iPad or screen time constantly, consistently at home, then school is not going to match that level of stimulation that they have become accustomed to. I also like to encourage my child's curiosity for why things are the way that they are and not just to blindly follow what someone says just because they're the adult because that can be very dangerous. But most of all, from a psychological perspective, it is your child's training ground for the real world. author: drchelsey_parenting
title: Raising a media-literate child instead of banning screens
summary: Dr. Chelsey Hauge-Zavaleta argues that total screen bans can hinder a child's ability to develop media literacy. She suggests that instead of passive viewing, parents should encourage creative, active screen use where children act as 'makers' rather than 'takers'.
key_points: A Finnish study suggests a link between screen time and cognitive processing, but it is a correlation, not causation.
Total screen bans may leave children unprepared to navigate digital tools independently as teenagers.
The goal is to raise a 'media-literate maker' rather than a passive viewer.
Encourage creative screen activities like stop-motion animation or photography.
Discuss with children how digital content is created and how their brain reacts to screens.
scripts: Make me something and show me when it's done: a set of images, a stop motion animation, a Wikipedia entry or edit.

people.name: University of Jyväskylä
people.role: researchers behind the 8-year Finnish study on screen time

caution: The creator's interpretation of the study as a 'link' is nuanced, but parents should be aware that screen time recommendations vary by age and individual child needs.

ill.caption: Whiteboard sketch: the goal is a media-literate 'maker', not a passive viewer.

transcript: Your no screens policy is building a passive kid. There was just an eight year study out of Finland that tracked kids until they were 18 and kids who had more screen time actually scored better on cognitive processing tests, not worse. Now more screen time does not cause better cognitive processing. It's a link, not a cause. What they do on a screen matters. They may be thinking, they may be connecting, they may be building. What I see is that families with zero screens or extremely tight screen time boundaries raise a kid who turns 14, gets a laptop for the very first time, and they're this kid. They literally cannot stop watching. This child has had no on-ramp, no media literacy. They haven't learned how to text their friends. They haven't learned how to turn a TV off. They haven't learned how to tell if a news article is from a reputable source. They haven't learned how their particular brain and nervous system interacts with screens. Your goal should not be no screens ever. Honestly, that kind of fear-based parenting does no one good. Your goal should be to raise a media literate maker, not a passive viewing taker. So instead of saying you can have 20 minutes on the weekend only, I want you to say, let's make a stop motion animation together. Let's take 10 pictures of something you love. Let's find one person online who's telling a story that you think is interesting. If they make something, look at it, talk about it. If they find something, take it apart together. Zero screens is not the flex that you think it is. It's building a media literate maker that you want to aim for.
onscreen: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years — the screen time result was unexpected
Source: University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto

Summary: An eight-year Finnish study found that children who spent more time on screens tended to show better cognitive processing as teenagers, challenging common assumptions about screen use. Researchers say the key may be balancing physical activity with screen activities that encourage learning, creativity, and active thinking.

The findings suggest that the type of screen activity may be important. Digital activities that involve learning, creativity, problem-solving, or other forms of active mental engagement could potentially help explain the association observed in the study.
caption: Zero screens isn’t the flex you think it is. I know why you did it. You read the articles, you watched your kid go glassy-eyed on the couch, and you pulled the plug. That was a real decision made for real reasons and I’m not here to shame it. But an eight-year study out of Finland followed kids into adolescence and found the ones with more screen time showed better cognitive processing, not worse. The researchers were careful about why…. it’s a link, not a cause, and what mattered was what the kids were doing.  Thinking, building, solving, creating. That’s the variable. Not the number on the timer. So all my dear no screen families, please know while valiant, you can’t really “protect” a kid from technology. No screens is protecting them from ever learning to manage screens. And then they’re fourteen, a laptop lands in their hands for a group project, and every other kid is editing and building while yours can only watch. You need a media literacy on ramp.  The goal was never less screens or no screens. The goal is raising a maker instead of taker. So here’s your one move this week. Stop saying “you can have twenty minutes.” Start saying “make me something and show me when it’s done- a set of images, a stop motion animation, a wikipedia entry or edit. It changes the whole job of the screen, bc now your kid is participating. Now you can have conversations about how things are made, who made it, what AI is… all of it. Imagine your kid closing the laptop on their own because the thing they were building is done. Not because you set a timer and braced for the fight. Your child needs to learn this.  I’ll show you how to onboard your kid to screens so it’s not alllll consumption when they get their first phone- please start at age 8, and if your kid is older than that and you haven’t started, NOW is the time. author: itsalexandrakenyon
title: Raising children with a healthy body image
summary: The creator explains how her parents fostered a healthy relationship with food and body image by focusing on strength and character rather than appearance. They modeled balanced eating without diet culture and emphasized that a child's worth is independent of their physical form.
key_points: Talk about bodies in terms of strength and performance, not size or weight.
Compliment children on their character and actions rather than their physical appearance.
Avoid using 'skinny' as a compliment for anyone.
Model a balanced approach to food by eating healthy whole foods while enjoying treats in moderation.
Avoid diet talk and food guilt at home.
Children learn by mirroring their parents' active lifestyle and enjoyment of food.
caution: The creator mentions her Christian faith as a personal source of self-worth, which may not resonate with all parents.
transcript: My parents did a fantastic job at creating an environment growing up that was super healthy when it came to like food and self-image, etc. In fact, I never even thought about body image until I went to college and was surrounded by girls in the dorm who were. So let's talk about how I made it that far and the things that my parents did. The first thing that comes to mind that I think was the biggest is that my parents never talked about the importance of a physical appearance and they never talked about my body unless it was about like sports and performance and strength and like talking about a track meet or something and having the strength to do something. That's the only time we talked about like do I need to get stronger with this or that but it was never about like do I need to get skinnier or anything like that. It was always stronger. As parents of course they're going to compliment their kids on their physical appearance but I will say that the majority of the compliments that I received from my parents had to do with my character or my actions and so they would say things like you were so patient with so and so we're so proud of you or things like that. I just always knew that my heart was the best thing about me and I knew that from a young age honestly and maybe they said that a lot. I don't remember that part but I just always knew that my heart was way more important than the outside. The word skinny was like never used in my family but if it was it wasn't used in a positive way like oh they're so skinny i want to be like them so i growing up i vividly remember if someone had called me skinny i was like so frustrated because i was like i do not want to be skinny i want to be strong it was never used as a word that was positive kind of on the heels of the skinny comment my mom if she ever talked about like another woman of like oh my gosh she looks amazing it was like never she looks so amazing she's so skinny it was always she looks so amazing she's so strong look at her quads like it's always about like she looks strong i think i've said that a few times but like she really and my dad really instilled in me that being strong was really beautiful my mom is the strongest person i know physically and mentally honestly but she's very physically muscular and so a lot of my friends growing up would be like what is the secret what does your mom do what's her diet or like even still people ask that and that makes me laugh because she doesn't have one she just eats in moderation and growing up she and my dad are both a great example of this like they ate really well most of the time like very healthy whole foods but they would have the oreos at night they would have snacks dessert we all have a really really bad sweet tooth and that's fine that was never something that was looked down upon and so that like created a really healthy relationship with food for me she's definitely not an almond mom um burgers the whole thing sheets at all. I think what went the furthest is their example, like they just really made an effort in their life to be active, to eat well, and I think I saw that and wanted to mirror that. Obviously kids, that's just what they naturally do. They want to be like their parents and so I would see them be active and then also enjoy and have fun and so that's kind of the life that I started to embody and something that I value. Lastly and most important, of course, I grew up in a Christian household, I am a Christian, and they always told me that I was made in the image of God and that nothing that I could physically do could make me more or less worthy. And so I think that always was helpful. I just knew that really none of this matters and just your heart matters. Those are all the things that I could think of. Honestly, I am so aware that social media has made this a whole new beast and that people have far too much accessibility into seeing people's habits for the good or the bad and just being able to constantly compare themselves. But I will say I grew up in the age of like YouTube, Tumblr, Alexis Ren, that whole thing. And I still swear that the way that my parents made the example at home had way more of an impact on the way that I saw myself and my honestly lack thereof thinking about self-image than anything the internet could have done. So that is my encouragement to you. Do your best at home. That's all you can do and your kids will be very appreciative.

title: Reflections on a lonely state-hospital birth in Romania
summary: A mother reflects on her experience giving birth in a Romanian state hospital, highlighting the importance of having a birth companion for emotional support and advocacy. She discusses the newly approved law that mandates hospitals to allow a chosen birth companion, noting how this could have improved her own experience.
key_points: Romania has passed a law requiring hospitals to allow a birth companion of the mother's choice.
A birth companion can provide essential emotional support and advocate for the mother's needs.
Lack of support can lead to feelings of neglect, anxiety, and difficulty getting basic care.
Staff manners and respectful communication should be integrated into medical care.
Patients have the right to be informed and involved in their own medical procedures.

title: Repairing with a 3-year-old after ignoring her while on the phone
summary: A mom's 3-year-old tells her she felt ignored. The mom apologizes, explains she was distracted writing something on her phone, validates that the child deserves her full attention, and offers a concrete plan: next time, tap me and say 'Mommy, I'm trying to talk to you'. Shows a model repair conversation and welcoming kids' feedback.
key_points: When your child says they felt ignored, listen and apologize without defensiveness.
Briefly explain what happened (distracted, on phone) without making excuses.
Name their feeling and affirm they deserve your full attention.
Give the child a concrete strategy for next time (tap and say 'Mommy, I'm trying to talk to you').
Thank them for telling you — it teaches that speaking up is safe.
scripts: I'm sorry that I made you feel not heard.

Next time, if I'm not responding when you're trying to get my attention, could you tap me and say, 'Mommy, I'm trying to talk to you,' so I can put down what I'm doing and give you my full attention? Because you do deserve my full attention.
Thank you for being able to talk to me about this.

He literally did not care that I had spent 30 minutes mixing that to the perfect consistency. 

He didn't ask about what I was doing next.

What would it be like to have our time seen as valueless? Our efforts ignored?

I'm not saying we should bend to our children's whims but i'm saying we should offer them respect as humans.

author: andreeamonica06
title: Respecting a toddler's boundaries at the park
summary: A mother discusses the importance of respecting a toddler's boundaries regarding their personal belongings at the park. She argues that forcing a child to share against their will teaches them that their needs are unimportant and that their 'no' does not count. The video advocates for teaching children to respect others' limits while also allowing them to practice setting their own.
key_points: Bringing a toy to the park does not mean a child is obligated to share it.
Forcing a child to give up their toy can teach them that their feelings and boundaries do not matter.
Allowing a child to say 'no' helps them understand the concept of consent.
Teach children to ask for permission before touching another child's belongings.
The only expectation when bringing toys to a public space is that they might get lost or broken.

Am avut astăzi o altercație cu doamnă în parc și știu că o să deschid cutia Pandorei, dar trebuie să vă spun și părirea mea cu privire la acest aspect, pentru că nu este vorba despre jucării, este vorba despre limite. Am ieșit cu Noua afară de dimineață, am luat cu noi și tricicleta, am mers într-un parc, moment în care el s-a pus în leagăn și a parcat, a parcat, bicicleta lângă leagăn. La scurt timp vine un băiețel și ia tricicleta lui Noua. N-o a văzut, a început să mărie, a început să cârie, s-a agitat, chiar a întins mâna spre tricicletă, moment în care băiatul ăla, nu știu, i-a făcut cu mâna așa, gen, hai, dă-te la o parte. Era și casca pusă pe ghidon și nu a apucat să plece cu ea, m-am așezat lângă el și am spus, uite, știi, el acum este într-o perioadă în care nu vrea să împartă, astăzi nu poate să-ți dea tricicleta, dar cu siguranță o să-ți o dea data viitoare. Îl ia de pe tricicletă și îmi spune Da, și trebuie să stau eu acum să-i spun că nu vrea el să-i odea 3 secunde am rămas blocată, dar doar 3 Pentru că se întoarce la mine și spune Doamnă, vii cu jucării în parc, îți asumi? Și am spus să-mi asumi ce? Dacă vin cu jucării în parc, nu înseamnă că sunt și obligată să le împart, corect? Nu! Pentru că noi suntem adulți și știm ce înseamnă limitele. Ca adulți este foarte sănătos din partea noastră să-i învățăm și pe cei mici, oricât ar fi ei de mici, să-i învățăm ce înseamnă limitele. Singurul lucru pe care eu trebuie să-mi l-asum atunci când vin în parc cu un lucru este că acel lucru se poate strica sau se poate pierde. Tu ai pretenția și ai așteptarea ca eu să-i explic copilului meu că trebuie să-i dea copilului tău tricicleta lui în condițiile în care tu nu vrei să-ți asumi că trebuie să-i explici copilului tău că nu are voie cu tricicleta respectivă în acel moment. I-am dat un exemplu cât se poate de clar ca să o fac să înțeleagă de fapt ce contează pentru mine. Și i-am spus, dacă copilul dumneavoastră în momentul să are o jucărie în mână și al meu o vrea, dumneavoastră îi luați jucăria copilului din mână ca să-i o dați copilului meu? Nu cred. Și îmi zice, păi da, dar el n-a vrea tricicleta în mână. Da, dar era lucrul lui care era lângă el, pus de el. Hai să ne gândim puțin ce înseamnă pentru un copil atât de mic să iei lucrul lui și să-i dai altui copil. Asta ce înseamnă? Voi vă gândiți un pic ce se întâmplă în creierașele lor? El ce o să perceapă? Că el nu este important? Că i s-a luat jucăria? Că celălalt copil e mai important decât el? Pentru că i-a luat jucăria? Și pentru că tot a circulat în ultima vreme teaba asta cu nu înseamnă nu, dacă tu ai pretenția ca al tău copil să asculte de tine când îi spui nu, lasă-l și pe el să spună nu la rândul lui și să înțeleagă ce înseamnă nu. Poate o să vi se pară o prostie, poate o să mă considerați nebună, poate o să fiți de acord cu mine, nu asta este ideea, dar Noua are aproape un an și nouă luni și eu încerc, pe cât se poate, în limitele bunului simți, să-i respect deciziile. Îl las mereu să aleagă, îl ajut și-l îndrum spre a înțelege ce-și dorește cu adevărat, iar dacă el într-un moment simte să spună nu, pentru mine va fi nu. Și acum ca să vă dau și câteva detalii extra, Noua este un copil extrem de înțelegător, extrem de afectuos cu ceilalți copii și dornic să împartă mereu. Noi ieșim cu jucării în parc și, din contră, el este dornic să găsească copii cu care să se joace. De cele mai multe ori, noi însirăm ajunsile în parc și când ceilalți copii vin să se joace, noua singur, fără să-i spună nimeni, se duce cu mașinuța și îi dă copilului în mână mașinuța, doar, doar să se joace împreună. Noua, în parte și mâncare, în parte și jucări, este extrem de atent la ceilalți copii. Tocmai de-aia și eu, la rândul meu ca mamă, încerc să îl respect pentru că văd ce tip de comportament are și știu ce educație vreau să-i ofer și ce valori vreau să îi dau. Când i-am adus aceste argumente, doamnei, mi-am spus, da, dar și el mi l-a stat jos de pe bicicletă. Și am stat un pic să mă gânesc, am zis, doamne, zic, eu nu mi-aduc aminte să o mai fi văzut pe femeia asta vreodată. Și apoi, după discuție, când am stat, să rumbe, de fapt, povestea, mi-am dat seama că ieri, când să plecăm spre casă, băiețelor respectiv nici n-am băgat de seama o secundă că e același copil, nici măcar o secundă, Mă rugații, uite, și noi trebuie să plecăm acasă și, uite, el își vrea bicicleta, că e a lui, hai te rog frumos să o dai, nu știu ce. Târguiala asta a fost preț de aproape 5 minute. Moment în care au venit două doamne, de aia zic că n-am interacțiunea cu doamna de astăzi, au venit două doamne să-i spună, știi, uite, te strigă mama ta, hai să mergem, nu știu ce, l-au luat pe sus sau plecat cu el. A, păi și eu te întreb pe tine, e corect să-mi reproșesc că ți-am dat copilul jos de pe tricicleta mea și e corect să stau să mă târguiesc pe lucru meu și să mă milăgesc și să cer voie, practic cer voie să-mi iau lucru înapoi? Băi, nu știu, hai să ne respectăm un pic și să respectăm nevoile altora. Da, am plecat cu o stare foarte proastă din parc pentru că toată discuția s-a efectuat țipându-se la mine. Fiecare alege cum decide să se comporte, dar vreau să vă zic că nu aveți idee de câte ori nu a plecat din parc fără să beneficieze de o jucărie pe care și-o dorea. Și-am stat și ne-am târguit și am explicat, mami, știu, uite așa și așa și pe dincolo și am explicat, rupându-mi se sufletul în mine de dezamăgirea lui. Da, nu știu, suntem mame, suntem oameni, suntem păriți, dar hai un pic să ne trezim.

author: safetostruggle
title: Responding to 'you NEVER / he ALWAYS' without arguing or caving
summary: A parent educator uses a Peter Pan metaphor for children's 'always/never' exaggerations during big emotions. Don't argue about whether it's true (Mr. Darling) and don't take every word literally and cave (Lost Boys). Be Wendy: acknowledge the feeling and steer back to reality by talking about what you can do today.
key_points: 'Always/never' statements come from big emotions; kids stretch reality to show how serious they feel.
Don't argue the facts ('you went swimming three times this week').
Don't cave or over-apologise in response to the exaggeration.
Acknowledge the feeling, then focus on what's possible today.
scripts: It does feel disappointing. Swimming with you is fun. Today we can...
I know it feels that way sometimes. Here's what we can do right now.
