You're not going to go full Mr. Darling and try and yank him out of Neverland. You're not going to argue with all of their always and nevers like it's your life mission to end Peter Pan. Oh, you never get to go first. Your brother always gets what he wants and he never gets in trouble. yeah right give me a break you are not going to mr darling this but you're also not going to go full lost boys here either you're not gonna like drink the peter pan kool-aid and take full value of everything your child says be like oh baby i didn't realize that this was so hard i'm so sorry you can go first the next time you do not have to get all the way into neverland to help your child always a never talk comes out when your child feels a big emotion and so they stretch the story of reality to make more sense of that feeling and show you how serious they feel so that you take them seriously. But you get to be Wendy. You get to be the character that sees Neverland and also knows when it's time to head home. So you're not going to play into the always and nevers you're going to talk about today. Hey, I know it feels that way sometimes. Here's what we can do right now.
onscreen: Don't get lost in the argument about whether NeverLand is real
Don't be a YesMan to Peter Pan's every idea
Kids go to Neverland to make sense of big feelings and to try to get you to take them seriously.
Be Wendy. Meet Peter Pan in neverland. Guide them away from always and never, back into reality, by talking about what we can do *today*
caption:
It’s a TRAP! ⬇️ 

Peter Pan showed up in my house today when I said we couldn’t go swimming. Peter Pan said “you NEVER take us swimming!” (I take them a few times each week). 

But I’m smart enough to leave the ticking time bombs to Captain Hook. So all I said was, “it does feel disappointing. Swimming with you is fun. Today we can xyz.” 

Be Wendy and help Peter Pan out of his misguided journey 😉 Your more rational child is waiting for you on the other side.

author: mikaross.therapist
title: Responding to teen criticism: 'drag them into their need'
summary: A therapist recounts her 16-year-old daughter slamming the fridge and saying 'there's never any food here'. Instead of defending herself or listing what's in the fridge, she named the underlying need ('I hear you need help figuring out what to eat for lunch'). This defused the attack-defence cycle, and weeks later her daughter phrased it as a need herself.
key_points: Meeting criticism with defensiveness starts an attack-defend cycle.
Underneath anger, frustration or irritation is a want, need, hurt or fear - respond to that.
Avoid lecturing about rudeness or 'compiling evidence' against the complaint.
Naming the need defuses the moment and teaches the teen to state needs directly next time.
Works in other relationships too (partners).
scripts: I hear you need help figuring out what to eat for lunch.
dedupe: respond to criticism by naming the need
transcript: A few months ago, my 16-year-old shut the refrigerator door angrily and said, there's never any food around here. It was clearly an attack on the person who had just spent $450 at the grocery store. Instead of responding to her criticism with defense or letting her know how rude and disrespectful she was being, or even compiling evidence by letting her know all of the things that were in the refrigerator that she could eat, I instead said, I hear you need help figuring out what to eat for lunch. I did this because I'm know. Meeting criticism with defensiveness just enters us into the attack-defense cycle. Instead of defensiveness, I chose to drag her into her need. Underneath all anger, frustration, and irritation is a want, a need, a hurt, or a fear, or some combo of those things. And in that moment, she was like, oh, which to me was an admission that I was right and that she recognized that what she was doing was not okay. The next time she had the same feeling, she looked at me, it was a couple weeks later and said, I need help figuring out what to eat for breakfast. So by dragging people into their needs, you're not only diffusing the situation, but teaching them how to treat you next time. So I was teaching her the next time that she's frustrated, reach for a need and she'll elicit less defensiveness in the listener.

title: Risks of Purple Pushing and Back-Lying Birth Positions
summary: A certified birth doula critiques the practice of 'purple pushing' (breath-held pushing) and delivering on one's back. She explains that these methods work against gravity, narrow the pelvic outlet, and increase the risk of severe perineal tearing and other complications.
key_points: Purple pushing involves holding your breath and bearing down for 10 seconds.
Purple pushing can cause burst blood vessels in eyes, hemorrhoids, and perineal tears.
Lying on your back works against gravity and narrows the pelvic opening.
Upright, mobile positions allow for better pelvic movement and descent.
Discuss pushing positions with your healthcare provider well before labor.
caution: This content challenges common hospital practices; discuss your birth plan and preferences with your OBGYN or midwife.

Gives toddlers a concrete sense of time and reduces 'are we there yet?'

title: Romania: employer can pay up to 1,500 RON/month for nursery tax-free
summary: A Romanian legal explainer carousel: since January 2024 employers may pay up to 1,500 RON per month per child for crèche or kindergarten, free of income tax and social contributions. The benefit is optional for the company, applies to state or private accredited units, and requires supporting documents.
key_points: Up to 1,500 RON/month per child for crèche or kindergarten fees, exempt from income tax, CAS and CASS.
Eligibility: employee with an employment contract (CIM); child aged 0-6; enrolled in an accredited/authorised crèche or kindergarten.
Amount must not exceed 33% of your gross salary (per the carousel).
Only one parent can claim it, and only from one employer.
Payment: company pays the kindergarten directly, or you pay and get reimbursed - invoices/receipts are needed either way.
Works for state or private units, as long as you actually pay something (monthly fee, after-school programme, meals).
Micro-enterprises can grant it but cannot deduct it, so it is their choice.
It is not a state subsidy and not automatic - ask HR to include it in benefits. Legal basis: OUG 115/2023, Law 239/2020, Fiscal Code (Law 227/2015).

title: Romanian dermatologist's SPF picks for babies and kids
summary: A Romanian dermatologist lists sunscreen recommendations by age: no direct sun under 6 months, mineral SPF from 6 months, chemical-filter SPF allowed from 2 years, with specific pharmacy brands for each. Extra tips cover limiting sun time, hats, sunglasses, UPF clothing and frequent reapplication.
key_points: Under 6 months: do not expose the baby directly to the sun.
After 6 months: mineral SPF (e.g. Uriage mineral cream, Heliocare 360 Pediatrics mineral fluid, Bioderma Photoderm Pediatrics mineral cream, Avene mineral fluid).
After 2 years: chemical-filter SPF can be used (e.g. Avene kids spray, La Roche-Posay Anthelios Dermo-Pediatrics invisible fluid, A-Derma Protect kids spray, Dermedic Sunbrella milk spray).
Don't keep babies in the sun long even with SPF; add hats, sunglasses and UPF clothing.
Brand matters less than broad spectrum, ease of application, and reapplying every 2 hours (and after water).

author: nurseinthemakingkristine
title: SIDS prevention summary from a nursing-student study card
summary: A nursing content creator walks through a SIDS study card: definition, risk factors and prevention. The prevention steps are back sleeping, a firm mattress with nothing in the crib, no smoking or vaping, no overbundling, no bed-sharing, pacifier use, a room temperature of 68-72°F, and stopping swaddling once the baby shows signs of rolling. She sums it up with the ABCs: Alone, on their Back, in a Crib. The video ends with a plug for a nursing study bundle.
key_points: SIDS is the sudden unexplained death of a healthy infant under 1 year; risk is highest from birth to 6 months.
Risk factors include prematurity, sleep position, a sibling who died of SIDS, nicotine exposure and socioeconomic status.
Always place baby on their back (supine), never on the tummy or side.
Use a firm mattress with no toys, blankets, pillows or stuffed animals.
Avoid smoking or vaping during and after pregnancy, including second-hand smoke.
Don't overbundle; keep the room at a normal temperature of 68-72°F (20-22°C).
Baby should sleep on a separate sleep surface, not in the parents' bed.
Offering a pacifier may reduce SIDS risk.
Stop swaddling once baby shows signs of rolling over.
ABCs of safe sleep: Alone, on their Back, in a Crib.

transcript: Let's talk about Sudden Infant Death Syndrome, also called SIDS. Let's look at ways to prevent this. The first one is to avoid overbundling or overdressing the infant. Next is to avoid smoking and vaping during and after pregnancy. Secondhand smoke can absolutely increase the risk for SIDS. Let's look at the newborn's bed. Now, the bed should be a firm mattress, and you definitely don't want them sleeping with toys, blankets, pillows, or stuffed animals. These can cause suffocation. The next one is no co-sleeping. Now, I know many parents do this, but according to the National Institution of Health, this increases the risk for SIDS. So, infants should sleep separate from their parents. Next is how they sleep. Now you want to have the baby sleep in a supine position, meaning on their backs. You don't want to have the baby sleep on their bellies or on their sides. Next is pacifier use. Now the NCLEX likes to ask about this. It actually is encouraged for them to use the pacifier because a pacifier might decrease the risk for SIDS. Let's look at the room temperature for sleeping. Now you want a normal room temperature. Ideal temp is 68 to 72 degrees Fahrenheit because overheating may increase the risk for SIDS. And lastly, you need to stop swaddling once the baby shows signs of rolling over because swaddling when a baby rolls over can increase the risk for SIDS and suffocation. So for SIDS, remember the ABCs of sleeping alone, on their back, and in a crib. If you need more help in your pediatrics or mother-baby class, you can grab the Complete Nursing School Bundle. Happy studying, future nurses.

title: Safe Skincare Ingredients in Pregnancy and Breastfeeding
summary: A skin specialist explains which skincare ingredients are safe to use during pregnancy and lactation, such as hyaluronic acid, vitamin C, niacinamide, controlled AHA/BHA concentrations, peptides, ceramides, and mineral sunscreen. She also warns against using retinoids, high-concentration salicylic acid, and benzoyl peroxide.
key_points: Avoid retinoids (retinol, retinal, tretinoin) entirely during pregnancy.
Limit AHA and BHA concentrations: glycolic up to 5%, lactic up to 10%, salicylic up to 2%.
Vitamin C helps prevent pregnancy melasma and brightens skin.
Hyaluronic acid stays in superficial skin layers, making it safe for daily use.
Opt for mineral (physical) sunscreens to shield skin from UVA and UVB rays safely.

author: your.babywearing.bestie
title: Safe babywearing: always be able to see baby's whole face
summary: A babywearing consultant shows that fabric covering a baby's face or holding the head down in a carrier is unsafe, especially for newborns. The rule: you should always be able to glance down and see your baby's entire face so you can check their nose and mouth and that the chin is off the chest.
key_points: Never let carrier fabric cover the baby's face or press the head down, even to make them feel cozy or help them sleep.
A chin resting on the chest can restrict the airway, especially in newborns.
You should be able to glance down and see the baby's whole face (nose and mouth) at all times, in every carrier style.
A carrier that is too big, wide or tall for a newborn can cause this problem; choose one that fits.

ill.caption: Babywearing safety rule: if you can't see your baby's face, it isn't safe.

onscreen: If you can't see your baby's face, it isn't safe.
caption:
I know why it happens... you’re trying to help baby feel more secure, less floppy, better supported and cozy so they can sleep. Or maybe you bought a carrier that you thought would support your newborn but it's just too big, too wide, too tall. 

Or maybe you’ve seen others do it and thought, “That must be how it’s supposed to look or be worn." So naturally, you give it a whirl.

(You’re definitely not alone in doing any of those, so no judgement whatsoever- i mean it!)

The issue is simple though.. when fabric covers their face or holds their head down, it quietly creates risk {{especially for newborns}}.

You can’t see their nose and mouth. Their chin can rest on their chest restricting or limiting airflow. 

You should always be able to glance down and see their entire face. 

This is pretty much the foundation of safe babywearing.. so let's normalize this: seeing baby's entire face in every style and all types of baby carriers. ♡

author: psihoterapeutcatrinel
title: Setting boundaries with grandparents about sweets
summary: A psychotherapist acts out a common scene where a grandmother gives a child biscuits against the parent's wishes and dismisses the parent. She shows the boundary version: calmly stating who decides, allowing one biscuit now, announcing the consequence (the package will be thrown away next time) and then actually following through.
key_points: Grandparents often ignore or minimise parents' rules ('What's the harm? He wants it').
Boundaries are set through what you do, not just what you say — a boundary is your consequence for the other person's behaviour.
State calmly that you make the decisions about the child's sweets, without arguing.
Announce the consequence in advance (next package will be thrown away), and follow through when it happens again.
If the child is caught in the middle: prepare them by making clear what will happen.
Don't speak badly about the family member in front of the child.
scripts: Grandma, I don't want to argue with you. I told you I make the decisions about the child's sweets. I'll let him have one biscuit now, but next time, if you give him a package, I'll have to throw it away.

ill.caption: When a child is in the middle of a family boundary: 1) make visible to the child what will happen, 2) don't speak badly of the family member.

author: itsokayamy
title: Shift sleeping: how two parents each got 6 hours with a newborn
summary: A first-time mom explains that she and her husband slept in shifts once their baby was exclusively formula-fed (from about one month). She slept 7pm-1am while he did all feeds, then he slept 1am-7am, and she napped in the morning. Each parent got about six uninterrupted hours.
key_points: Split the night into two shifts so each parent gets ~6 hours of uninterrupted sleep (e.g. 7pm-1am and 1am-7am).
The on-duty parent handles all feeds and care while the other sleeps undisturbed; try not to wake each other.
This worked for them because the baby was exclusively formula-fed from about one month (anyone could feed).
The baby slept in her own crib; try a few schedules to find one that works for both parents.
The off-shift parent can add a short nap the next morning.

title: Speaking kindly about your own body shapes your kids' body image
summary: A mother of several children shares how, since her first child's birth 16 years ago, she deliberately stopped negative body talk, dieting talk and constant weighing in front of her kids - even faking it at first. Her teenager recently thanked her for never hearing her criticize her body, and her 7-year-old lovingly praised her 'big, fat, squishy belly'. Her message: how you talk about your body becomes how your children see theirs.
key_points: Children learn how to see their bodies from how they hear you talk about yours.
Avoid negative self-talk, diet talk and constant weighing in front of kids.
Describe your body by what it does (made babies, runs, hikes, gardens, snuggles) rather than how it looks.
If you don't believe it yet, 'fake it' - it is a daily conscious effort, but it pays off and can improve your own self-image.
When your teen wants to talk, drop everything and listen.

I took a moment, took a breath, let the shame roll over me, and thought about what my teenager said to me about two weeks ago. They had just gotten back from school. I was working in my room at my desk, and they said, Mom, can I talk to you for a minute? And of course, I threw everything to the side and said anything. When your teen wants to talk, you shut everything down real quick. We snuggled up on my bed, and they said mom i was thinking about it today and i have never heard you say anything bad about your body i've never heard you talk about losing weight dieting how you don't like certain parts of yourself you've only ever talked about your body being good being strong being beautiful or just kind of being indifferent to it and i think that that has impacted me hugely thank you thank you so much mom so i finished taking that deep breath and i looked at my seven-year-old and i said, I know. Isn't it great? Do you know what this big, fat, squishy belly has done? It made you. It made your siblings. It runs. It hikes. It gardens. It creates arts and crafts and food and fun and silliness and the best snuggles. And she said, I know. That's why I like it so much. And listen, loving my body has not been easy. But the moment my child was born 16 years ago, I told myself the way that my child sees their body is going to be the way that they think I see mine. This negative self-talk, this weighing myself constantly, it ends now. Even if I don't believe it, I'm gonna fake it like I do. And every single day, it's been a struggle. Every single day, it has been conscious effort to be nice about my body. And up until a week ago, I didn't know if it even mattered. Guess what? It matters. title: Speech therapist tip: verbal routines instead of 'say car'
summary: A speech-language pathologist shows that instead of prompting a child to 'say car', you can turn everyday phrases into repeated sing-song verbal routines ('We're going in the car... let's go!'). key_points: Avoid demanding 'say ___'; instead repeat the same phrase the same way each time (a 'verbal routine').

Pause before the last word to give the child a chance to fill it in.
Children learn gestures, sounds and words through imitation once they anticipate what comes next.
Other verbal routines: 'Ready, set, go!', 'Peek-a-boo!', 'Uh oh' when something falls, '1-2-3, go!', 'How big is ___?', any song or rhyme.

title: Starting solids: 4 main rules and a month-by-month guide (Romanian)
summary: A Romanian food-diversification creator jokes that first-time parents worry about strict food lists, then gives four main restrictions: no salt until about age 2, no sweeteners and absolutely no honey before 1, cooking method matters (no fried, smoked or raw food), and minimise choking risk through how food is served. The caption adds a month-by-month plan: allergens one per week from 6 months, nuts/peanuts by 7 months, smaller pincer-sized pieces at 8 months, and expect first food refusal at 9 months.
key_points: No salt until close to 2 years — a good chance for the whole family to cut salt.
No sweeteners, and absolutely no honey before 12 months.
Serve cooked food: no fried, smoked or raw foods.
Reduce choking risk through food shape and texture.
6 months: seasonal fruit and vegetables, iron-rich foods, and 4 common allergens introduced one per week (suggests egg and milk) if no allergy risk factors; with risk factors, see an allergist first.
7 months: add cereals/pseudocereals and continue allergens, including nuts and peanuts.
Up to 8 months, offer soft finger-length sticks (about two fingers thick, never round); from 8 months, smaller soft pieces for the pincer grasp.
Around 9 months, expect the first food refusal: lean on favourite recipes but keep exposing to seasonal produce.
caution: Partly stricter than mainstream guidance: WHO/NHS advise no added salt before 1 and limited salt afterwards, and many soft raw fruits are fine. Nuts and peanuts should only be given as smooth butter or powder, never whole. Confirm allergen introduction with your pediatrician.

author: genzanxietytherapist
author_name: Jeannie Elbing, Anxiety & OCD Therapist in CA
title: Stop nagging a procrastinating teen: let them own the deadline
summary: An anxiety therapist explains that procrastination is an internal argument in the teen (one part knows they should start, another wants to scroll or game). When parents nag, they take one side of that argument, letting the teen fight the parent instead of sitting with their own discomfort. She suggests staying quiet and, when the late-night crunch comes, calmly naming it and going to bed, signalling the deadline and consequences are the teen's.
key_points: Notice the reminder loop ('Have you started yet? It's getting late') — it comes from love but often backfires.
Nagging externalises the teen's inner conflict so the tension is between you instead of inside them.
Growth comes from learning to tolerate one's own discomfort; carrying it for them removes that chance.
Instead of reminding, wait. When the 11 pm crisis hits, stay calm, don't rescue, and go to bed.
The message: the deadline is yours, the consequences are yours, and I trust you to handle both.
scripts: Looks like you're going to have a late night. I have an early morning, so I'm heading to bed. Maybe next time you'll start a little earlier.
transcript: After dinner do homework okay? Do you have a lot of homework today? Yeah I have a lot of homework. Can you stop asking me? I'm literally just trying to eat. Now I don't have any appetite. Mama. Is it a lot of homework? Okay okay okay okay. Okay here's what you're going to say when your teen procrastinates and turns you into the knack. If you're new here I'm Jeannie and I help parents understand the psychology behind their teen's behavior. First I want you to notice the loop you're in. Have you started yet? You should really get started. It's getting late. It all comes from a place of love and it's doing the opposite of what you think. Because procrastination is really just routine arguing with themselves. When half of them knows they need to start, the other half would rather scroll or play video games or do literally anything else. And the second you start nagging, you take over one side of that argument for them. So they get to drop it. Now the fight is with you, which is a lot more comfortable than the fight with themselves. Growth happens when people learn to tolerate their own discomfort. When we keep carrying that discomfort for our kids, we're also carrying away the opportunity for them to build that skill. So instead of nagging, just wait. And when the crisis hits at 11 o'clock, calmly say, looks like you're gonna have a late night. I have an early morning, so I'm heading to bed. Maybe next time you'll start a little earlier. That's it. You're saying the deadline is yours. The consequences are yours. And I believe you're capable of handling both.
caption:
The reminders keep coming out of your mouth and somehow you became the bad guy...

You hear yourself doing it. “Have you started yet? It’s getting late. You should really get going.” It all comes straight from love, and it’s quietly backfiring.

Here’s what’s really going on. Procrastination is your teen stuck in an argument with herself, one half knowing she needs to start and the other half wanting to scroll or game or do anything else.

The moment you start nagging, you pick up one side of that argument for her, so she gets to set it down. Now the tension is between the two of you, which is a whole lot more comfortable for her than sitting in the struggle inside her own head.

The catch is that growth lives in learning to sit with that discomfort. Every time you carry it for her, you’re also carrying off the chance for her to build the muscle.

So instead of reminding, let it be quiet. And when the eleven o’clock crunch hits, stay easy and say, “Looks like a late night ahead. I’ve got an early morning, so I’m heading to bed. Maybe next time you start a little sooner.”

That’s the whole thing. You’re telling her the deadline is hers, the outcome is hers, and you trust her to handle both.

Save this for the next time you feel the nagging start. Share it with a parent stuck in the loop.

author: poredecisions.md
title: Stretch marks in pregnancy: what the evidence actually supports
summary: A dermatology resident explains that no topical product is proven to prevent pregnancy stretch marks; genetics, number of babies and weight gain matter most. If you want a belly routine anyway, she suggests centella asiatica, hyaluronic acid and a thick moisturizer, always combined with 5-10 minutes of nightly belly massage, which studies suggest may be the part that matters.
key_points: No cream or oil has been proven to prevent stretch marks; anyone promising that is overselling.
Biggest risk factors: genetics, carrying multiples, and how much weight is gained in pregnancy.
Centella asiatica (cica products) stimulates collagen and is the most frequently cited topical.
Hyaluronic acid acts as a humectant to draw moisture into the skin and support elasticity.
Seal with a thick, greasy moisturizer such as Vaseline, Aquaphor or CeraVe Healing Ointment.
Massage the belly for 5-10 minutes nightly; some studies found topical benefits disappeared without massage.
Check any routine with your OB/dermatologist; stretch marks are normal and can later be treated with in-office procedures or prescription topicals.

In fact, anyone telling you, use this product, you won't get stretch marks in pregnancy, is lying to your face. Genetics, how many babies you're pregnant with, and how much weight you gain during that pregnancy probably play the biggest roles. But I completely understand wanting to do everything you can to mitigate that risk. So let's break it down based on what topicals have the best evidence. Centella Asiatica is frequently cited. It does stimulate collagen synthesis, therefore theoretically allowing the skin to withstand those stretching and shearing forces that happen in late pregnancy. You can find it in over-the-counter serums, creams, a lot of those cica-containing products, and I do think it is worth adding to your pregnancy belly routine. Hyaluronic acid is also another must. This is going to be a molecule that's found naturally in the body that you can apply as a topical humectant to help further draw in moisture to keep the skin as hydrated as possible. It also helps support skin elasticity, again preparing it to withstand those stretching and shearing forces, and there's lots of over-the-counter options to choose from. But the most important thing is to incorporate all these topicals with belly massage. In fact, some studies even found that improvement seen with some topicals tested was lost when you compared it to patients who didn't incorporate belly massage. Whether it's the actual ingredients doing the magic or the act of rubbing and massaging the skin for five to ten minutes nightly, or maybe the combination of both, a belly routine without the belly massage is futile. title: Surviving the 0–2 years 'big test' as a couple: three tips
summary: A Romanian mother of two says a child's first two years are the biggest test for a relationship and shares three tips beyond basic communication: set boundaries with friends/family you confide in, divide work by priorities rather than strict 50/50, and value actions over words. The caption adds that couples who last are often those who went through hard times together.
key_points: Talk to each other first—venting to friends/family is pointless if you don't talk as a couple.
If you confide in friends or family, require them to respond respectfully about your partner; set limits if they don't, and solve problems between yourselves.
Teamwork isn't 50/50: agree which things matter in your home and make sure they get done 100%—some days one does 20% and the other 80%, without questions or eye-rolling.
Watch what people do, not what they say: hold hands, hug when you wake up.
Instead of asking what needs doing, pick one task, however small, and just do it.
Hard periods are normal; couples who rebuild together after them tend to last.

caption:
I was just recording myself cleaning the kitchen when Ocean came in, visibly upset. Willy had told her she was annoying—all because she wanted to read his owl books with him.

So we paused everything. Not because he was “in trouble,” but because these little moments? They’re everything. Especially when it comes to teaching emotional intelligence and nurturing connection between siblings.

I told him: you’re allowed to feel annoyed. But you’re not allowed to call someone annoying. That’s not who she is—that’s how you felt. And your feelings? They’re yours to name and manage, not hers to carry.

We’re working on teaching the difference between labeling someone else and expressing how you feel. Because when kids learn to do that—especially with their siblings—they build the foundation for safer, healthier relationships in every part of their life.

If I had been taught this kind of emotional responsibility as a kid, I would’ve had better relationships with my siblings… and with friends. I would’ve known how to speak from my feelings without hurting others. I’m not just trying to raise kind kids—I’m trying to raise connected ones.

We also talk a lot about respecting Willy’s space and his books. It’s okay to say, “I feel frustrated when you touch my things.” It’s not okay to push people away with shame or harsh words.

This is what it looks like to break cycles, to teach communication, to raise emotionally intelligent humans—one messy, real-life moment at a time.

I got a lot of head bob and firmness to me- it’s because I’m passionate. I want to be what they need when they want it and also when they don’t.

title: Teach teens to recognise manipulation: six red-flag phrases
summary: A Brazilian couple lists phrases teenagers should learn to recognise as manipulation, explains why each is a red flag, and gives teens simple phrases to protect themselves. They argue that manipulation loses power once a teen can name it, and these conversations should happen before someone teaches the lesson the hard way.
key_points: 'Decide now' is a warning sign: people who respect you give you time to think.
'If you liked me, you'd do this' is guilt used to control, not love.
'Don't tell anyone': a secret that causes fear, shame or tightness in the chest is a signal to ask for help.
'Everyone does it': your limit doesn't need the group's approval.
'You're exaggerating' after someone hurts you is also manipulation (making you doubt your feelings).
'Prove you trust me': trust is never proven with passwords, intimate photos, lies, your body or risk-taking.
Keep ongoing dialogue with teens; naming manipulation weakens it.

caption:
Not my usual content but a very important message. Raising boys into good men isn’t about making them ‘tough’, it’s about making them respectful. We need to teach them that consent isn’t awkward, it isn’t optional, and it definitely isn’t confusing. It’s simple - if it’s not a clear, enthusiastic yes… it’s a no.

I didn’t grow up with these conversations. No one really sat us down and explained what respect should feel like, what boundaries look like, or that our voice actually mattered. And because of that, so many of us learnt the hard way.

We can teach them emotional intelligence, support them in advocating or problem solving to meet their needs, and help them develop grit.

We OVERLOAD our kids when we encourage and let them ruminate in circles with no way forward. That is a lot of stress for new brain. We have to be leaders and show them how to process.

A lot of people get stuck on validating the feeling part (because there was a lack of this in our childhood) and forget we have TEACH them how to move forward. We can encourage emotional intelligence and hold boundaries at the same time because Boundaries and consistency make kids feel safe.

Little kids (And even teenagers and young adults to a certain extent) have Bummer Blindness.

To them, EVERY bummer (big or small) truly feels like a BIG important crisis. This is why we take them seriously and why we validate BUT ➡️

We have to actively TEACH and CALIBRATE their new brains to differentiate between BIG bummers and LITTLE bummers.

We are NOT “moving on.” We ARE “moving forward.”

And we COMMUNICATE to our children that how they feel is important and we’re going to move forward. And we can revisit and problem solve as needed.

Most of the time they do not even feel the need to revisit the little bummers. They just needed to feel heard in the moment and then shown a pathway forward.

And of course the tone is important here. We are not using this to be sarcastic or punish them. It is a loving and motivating “you can do it, you can do this” tone. The delivery is important, and we have to regulate ourselves so that we are in a mental space to be kind, motivational, and firm in our delivery.

And of course there will always be extremes. We use our discerning adult brains to apply this according to the situation and to the individual child. I could give the parenting tip “we need to teach our kids to be kind to people” and someone would say “well not to people who will hurt them.” Well yes, of course. That is why we use our adult discernment. So apply accordingly.

title: Teaching Self-Control Through Parental Example
summary: A mother shares a personal story about how her husband taught their son self-control by modeling it himself during a moment of anger. The core message is that parents should demonstrate the behavior they want to see rather than just telling their children what to do.
key_points: Parents should model the behavior they expect from their children.
Self-control involves acknowledging feelings like anger while choosing how to respond.
Taking a deep breath is a practical tool for practicing self-control.
Actions and examples are more effective teaching tools than verbal instructions.

author: openmindwithdrmonica
title: Teaching a meaningful apology: 4 steps and an apology letter
summary: A school therapist describes a student who snapped at his teacher, then, given time and space, identified his type of anger and wrote an apology letter. She outlines four parts of a real apology and argues that reasons are explanations, not excuses, and that forced or rushed apologies are less meaningful.
key_points: Give the child time and space to calm down and process before expecting an apology.
Help them identify the kind of anger (e.g., tired/hungry, didn't get their way, unfairness, hurt by someone).
A meaningful apology has 4 parts: 1) take ownership of the action, 2) explain the reason, 3) acknowledge the hurt and say sorry, 4) state strategies for next time.
Apology letter template: 'Dear ___, I am sorry that I ___. You felt ___. I was feeling ___. Right now I would like to ___. In the future I will try to ___.'
Reasons for behavior are explanations, not excuses; knowing them helps fix the problem.
Accountability plus compassion can teach more than punishment or suspension.
scripts: I am sorry that I ___. You felt ___. I was feeling ___. Now I want to ___. Next time I will try to ___.
credentials: therapist working with children in schools (Dr., 10+ years)

author: growing.with.taylor
title: Teaching toddlers to wait with 'waiting hands' behind the back
summary: Instead of just saying 'wait', the creator teaches her toddler a physical position: hands behind the back, body still, a short pause, then release. She expects only about 2 seconds at first, because a long wait loses a young toddler and turns into a battle. Modelling it every time gives the child a concrete idea of what waiting looks like.
key_points: Toddler impulse control (especially under 18 months) is still emerging; 'wait' alone is too abstract.
Model 'waiting hands': hands behind back, body still, short pause, then release.
Start with less than 2 seconds; asking for 10 seconds early on leads to a power struggle.
Expect to model it every time at first; over time the body learns what waiting means.
Use it everywhere: doors, parking lots, snacks, around pets.
scripts: Waiting hands.
Hands behind back... and release.
caution: A taught 'wait' skill is not a substitute for holding hands/physical control near traffic or other real dangers.

ill.caption: 'Waiting hands' demonstration: the toddler holds hands behind the back for a short pause before being released.

onscreen: If I make him wait 10 seconds, I lose him.
Waiting hands is a micro skill.
Toddler impulse control under 18m is still emerging.
caption:
Start here.

If your toddler hears “wait” and instantly escalates, it’s not a listening problem. It’s a “they don’t know what to do with their body yet” problem.

This is what I do instead.
“Waiting hands”but behind the back.

Model hands go behind the back. Body still. Then we wait together. Less than 2 seconds is perfectly acceptable.

It gives them a clear, repeatable position instead of just a word floating in the air. At first you’ll have to model it every single time. Like, a lot. That’s normal.

But over time, their body starts to recognize “oh, this is what waiting looks like.” Less yelling “wait.” More teaching what wait actually is.

Try it in your next real-life moment and tell me how it goes 🩷

author: always.upper.elementary
title: The '30-second rule': only point out what someone can change in 30 seconds
summary: An elementary teacher explains a kindness rule to her class: if someone can't change something about themselves in 30 seconds or less, don't mention it. Untied shoes, lint or an open zipper can be pointed out privately; hair, body or appearance comments cannot be fixed and words can't be fully taken back. The lesson also covers responsibility for words, apologizing and 'filling buckets'.
key_points: Rule: only comment on something a person can fix in 30 seconds or less (untied shoe, lint on a shirt, unzipped pants).
Say such things privately so the person isn't embarrassed.
Never comment on hair color/texture/style or body—things people can't change quickly.
Hurtful words can't be completely taken back; apologizing helps but doesn't fully undo the harm.
We choose what we put into the world—spread kindness and 'fill other people's buckets'.
Easy to adapt at home for school-age kids, and for adults modelling it.
scripts: Hey, your shoe's untied. I wanted to tell you privately because I didn't want you to feel embarrassed, but it happens to all of us.
If somebody can't change something about themselves in 30 seconds or less, then you shouldn't be mentioning it to them.

products.type: Quickly removes lint from clothing.

transcript: If somebody can't change something about themselves in 30 seconds or less, then you shouldn't be mentioning it to them. If you say, hey, your shoe's untied, or hey, you have a little fuzzy on your shirt there, or if you say, hey, your pants are unzipped. I wanted to tell you privately because I didn't want you to feel embarrassed, but it happens to all of us. If you tell someone something like that, they can change those things in 30 seconds or less. But if you comment on someone's hair color or hair texture or hairstyle or body, they cannot change that in 30 seconds or less about themselves. Your words have power. If you say something that someone can't change in 30 seconds or less, you say those things. Try to fix it. You try to apologize. You try to take the words back. Take it back. Take it back. Take it back. And you try to undo what you said, undo what you did, but it's something they couldn't change about themselves, and so it's very messy. You can't totally take those words back. You can't totally fix it. Your words have power, and your words matter. If you walk out of this room spreading kindness to the people around you, spreading love to the people around you, that is what truly makes a difference.
onscreen: SECONDS OR LESS, THEN YOU SHOULDN'T BE MENTIONING IT TO THEM.
caption:
Students being rude? Try this! 

In this lesson, we discussed how….

- we are responsible for our words & actions
- we need to spread kindness and love
- we choose what to put out into the world 
- our words & actions have power and an impact on others
- once our words & actions are out in the world, we cannot erase them or fully take them back
- we can choose to fill other people’s “buckets” or do the opposite 
- apologizing is an important part of making things right after we make a mistake

I reminded my students that we did this lesson on the last day of school because I want them to remember this concept for the rest of their lives!

Of course there are small, random exceptions to this 30 second rule, but making this concept concrete for my students has been incredibly helpful!

SAVE this reel as a reminder to try this in your classroom too—it is SO worth it! 🙌🏼

title: The 'Do Good Jar': rewarding kids caught doing good
summary: A mother raised by two psychologists shares a reward system she now uses: a 'do good jar' filled with cheap small surprises. When a child does something good unprompted, she names the specific behaviour and lets them pick from the jar. The point is to catch children doing things right instead of only correcting mistakes.
key_points: Use any container (e.g. a mason jar) filled with cheap surprises: wrapped small toy animals, temporary tattoos.
Reward only good things done beyond what is expected or without being asked.
Name the specific behaviour: 'I noticed you helped your brother get his shoes on today without me asking.'
Rewards don't need to be big; young kids are excited by any small surprise.
'Catching them being good' encourages repetition of positive behaviour.

author: play_spark
title: The 'bye-bye game' to teach a baby to call you by name
summary: A speech/play-focused creator demonstrates a game to help a baby learn to say 'mama' (or 'dada'): say bye-bye, step away briefly, say your own name and run back excitedly. Over time you pause slightly longer so the child fills in your name. The caption adds guidance for AAC users and for babies who don't enjoy it.
key_points: Say "bye-bye", walk away for about 1-2 seconds, say your own name (e.g. "Mama!") and run back excitedly.
Repeat so it becomes a predictable verbal routine with no pressure to talk.
Gradually pause a little longer before saying your name so the child can say it first.
Never wait longer than about 5 seconds – it becomes stressful or a demand.
If the child is an AAC user, have a partner sit with them and model on the device while you model verbally.
If baby isn't interested or seems distressed by you walking away, stop and try another time or another game.

Mama!

transcript: Teaching your baby to request you by name, play the bye-bye game. You say bye-bye, then you call your own name and come running back excitedly. It becomes a verbal routine and it doesn't put any pressure on them. Watch. Bye-bye! Then you slowly wait a little bit longer while they wait to say your name, and eventually they just start requesting you. Bye!
onscreen: You say bye bye then you call
Did I hear someone say mama?

caption:
Two years ago 😭😭

Watch the entire video to see the technique work. Right now, Rudy calls me Da. 

KEY TAKEAWAYS: 

Say bye bye, walk away for approximately 1-2 seconds, say your own name, and excitedly run back. 

If your child is an AAC user, having a partner play this game is key so they can sit with them and model on the device while you model verbally. 

If baby isn’t interested, don’t push it. Try again another time. If baby seems distressed with you walking away (even playfully), this is not the game for them at this time. 

And finally, try not to extend wait time to longer than 5 full Mississippi seconds. Any longer and it starts to feel like a requirement for them to request to play the game.

author: maternal.mastermind
title: The 'glass apple': a safe signal for kids to tell you hard truths
summary: A homeschooling mom keeps a glass apple with a written promise: 'If you're scared to tell me something, bring this apple as a reminder that I'm here to help and support you. I won't get mad. I love you.' When a child brings it, she knows to stay calm, and she says it has made her kids more honest.
key_points: Choose an object (hers: a dollar-store glass apple) and write a promise on it in permanent marker.
Kids bring the object when they're scared to confess something.
It warns the parent to keep calm before hearing the news.
Keep the promise: no anger, help and support – this builds trust and reduces lying.
scripts: If you're scared to tell me something, just bring this apple to me as a reminder that I'm here to help and support you. I won't get mad. I love you.

products.type: Acts as a safe signal for honest communication.

transcript: My kids don't lie to me. It's because of this apple. Let me tell you how. So I've had this apple probably 10 years. It's just from the dollar store. Nothing fancy. It's a glass apple, but you can see how it's like worn off. I put in permanent marker. I'm going to read what it says. If you're scared to tell me something, just bring this apple to me as a reminder that I'm here to help and support you. I won't get mad. I love you. And that's what it does. And I can tell you, my kids abuse this apple hundreds of times, but the cool thing about it is when they bring this apple to me, it gives me a heads up not to lose my cool that I'm like, Oh my gosh, they're scared. They're scared to tell me something. They don't want to lie about something. Um, and it's awesome. It's like this olive branch thing. So if you're struggling with kids not telling you the truth or hiding things, this is a fantastic bridge. So if you're scared of kids not telling you the truth, I suggest trying this out. My name is Lauren. I'm a mom. I've been homeschooling for a long time and I'm here to help you to follow along for more tips and also smash that like button and share this with a friend or someone that is struggling with their kids right now because this has turned my kids into truth tellers. If you’re looking for a gentle way to build trust with your kids, try this! What’s something that helps YOUR kids feel safe opening up? author: nurture.infused.parenting
author_name: Jodie Jones- Parent Coach and Behaviour Consultant
title: The 'lion enclosure' visual to stop yelling during meltdowns
summary: A parent coach explains that when parents shout during a child's explosive behavior, both are in a fight response. Her visual: imagine your screaming, insulting child is trapped in a lion enclosure – you'd ignore the insults and get them to safety. The job during a meltdown is to help the child feel safe, not to punish the words.
key_points: Yelling at a challenging child is your own fight response to conflict; awareness helps you choose differently.
A child kicking, biting or shouting is also in a fight response – it's not personal.
Don't take dysregulated insults personally.
Picture the child in a lion enclosure: your only job is to make them feel safe.
If you keep losing your cool, it's a sign your own nervous system needs calming too.
transcript: Parents, if you get more loud and shouty when your children are challenging, then this visual tip is gonna stop you in your tracks so you don't turn into the trunchbull. You need to know three things for this visual to work. One, when you flip your lid at your child and we should have that chokey installed, you're actually having a fight response to conflict. Your body's trying to keep you safe. Two, you can't choose how your nervous system responds to conflict, but when you're aware of it, magical things can happen. And three, when your child is kicking, biting, shouting, or whatever it is that makes you want to throw them out of the window, they are also having a fight response. So it's not actually personal. Please, Lord, if you want to survive parenthood, do not take your child's dysregulated insults personally. So here's the visual tip. Picture this. Your explosive child has been placed into a lion enclosure. They're kicking, screaming, lashing out. Get me out of here, you stupid idiot. Do you, A, shout back. Don't call me an idiot. Say sorry now or you're staying in that lion enclosure. If you picked A, carry on scrolling, or B, you'd see that they were scared, ignore their insults and scoop them up to safety. Here's the thing, there's not actually a lion in the enclosure, but their body doesn't know that. So the next time they're kicking off, picture them in a lion enclosure, where your only job is to get them feeling safe. And remember, if you keep losing your cool, it's a sign your body needs to know, the lion's not really there.

could stop shouting at your kids
once and for all, this visual tip
GET ME OUT OF HERE YOU STUPID
OR B, YOU'D SEE THAT THEY WERE SCARED, IGNORE THEIR INSULTS
caption: Reposting this viral video as I still have people telling me now how they use this analogy in their personal and professional lives to help shift mindset around explosive behaviours. #consciousparenting #parentingtips #parenttips #parenting #emotionalintelligence

author: meganhilljensen
title: The 'service gingerbread man': a December kindness tradition
summary: A no-prep December tradition: a family member secretly does an act of service for someone else and leaves a gingerbread-man ornament in its place. The recipient then has 24 hours to serve another family member and pass the ornament on, continuing until Christmas. Demonstrated with a mom making her son's bed and the son tidying his sister's toys.
key_points: Pick someone in the family and do any act of service for them (make their bed, hang their shirts, tidy their toys).
Leave the gingerbread ornament where the service was done; add a note if it's unclear who it was for.
The recipient has 24 hours to do a service for someone else and pass the gingerbread on.
Continue the cycle every day through December until Christmas.
Help younger children choose and carry out their act of service.
Needs no prep; the ornament can be homemade (e.g., cardboard, markers, peppermint 'buttons').

gifts.name: Service gingerbread man
gifts.how: Pass a gingerbread ornament between family members as a token for completing acts of service.

dedupe: service gingerbread man christmas kindness tradition
transcript: Introducing the service gingerbread man. Throughout December, he gets passed around our family doing service. So today, my son forgot to make his bed, and for my active service, I'm going to make his bed for him. And then I'll leave the gingerbread sitting on his freshly made bed. Later, when he finds him, he now gets to pick someone else in our family to provide an active service for. In this case, my daughter dumped out all of these toys and didn't clean them up. so he's going to take a few minutes and clean them up for her then when he's done you guessed it he'll leave the gingerbread man sitting in its place we'll then help her do some service for someone else in the family and it'll continue in a cycle of family-focused service every day until Christmas
onscreen: A December tradition that doesn't add more stress or work...
AND THEN I'LL LEAVE THE GINGERBREAD SITTING
IN THIS CASE MY DAUGHTER DUMPED OUT ALL
WE'LL THEN HELP HER DO SOME SERVICE FOR SOMEONE
caption:
This is actually a tradition from my childhood! So all credit goes to my parents for the idea! The service gingerbread was a part of December for as long as I can remember. It’s so simple, and there isn’t any prep work, plus it spreads love and service in your home. Win win. :) 

Here’s how it works:

Whoever is starting out, selects somebody in the family to do an act of service for. It can be anything! Then, they leave the gingerbread man in place of whatever they did. (On a made bed, or in their closet if they hung shirts, etc.) if it’s unclear who the service was for, they can always leave a note! Then the recipient of the service act now has 24 hours to do an act of service for someone else in their family. And of course they then leave the gingerbread ornament for the next person to find and pass on. The gingerbread gets passed from family member to family member until Christmas! title: The 4 bare-minimum essentials to bring your baby home
summary: A new mom cuts through registry overwhelm by listing just four things you need to take a baby home safely: a properly installed car seat, a safe sleep space, a way to feed the baby, and going-home clothes. key_points: 1) Car seat: the hospital may check that the base is installed and the baby is strapped in correctly before discharge; car seats expire - check the date of manufacture.

In hospital the baby can just wear a diaper and swaddle - easy for skin-to-skin; add swaddles for warmth.

author: tilscience
title: The biological cause of hyperemesis gravidarum (HG)
summary: A pharmacist explains the research of geneticist Dr. Marlena Fejzo, who identified that the hormone GDF15 is the primary driver of hyperemesis gravidarum (HG). The video explains that the placenta produces high levels of GDF15, and women with lower pre-pregnancy levels are more sensitive to the spike, causing severe nausea.
key_points: Hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) is a biological condition, not a psychological one.
GDF15 is a hormone produced by the placenta that triggers severe nausea.
Women with low GDF15 levels before pregnancy are more susceptible to HG symptoms.
Research into desensitizing treatments is ongoing but currently lacks NIH funding.
If experiencing severe nausea, advocate for yourself with medical providers.
caution: The video discusses experimental treatment concepts; always consult your OB-GYN or healthcare provider for HG management.
transcript: For decades, doctors have treated morning sickness as either a mystery or dismissed it as psychological. But we've actually understood the primary cause since 2016, thanks to one researcher who got tired of being told her severe pregnancy nausea was all in her head. Dr. Marlena Fezjo, a geneticist at UCLA, experienced hyperemesis gravidarum, an extreme form of nausea affecting about 2% of pregnancies. She was so sick that she needed a feeding tube and around-the-clock care. When she reached out to her doctor for help, he told her that women with her condition were just seeking attention and acting, quote, infantile. Yep. This was in 1999, and Marlena was bedridden with a feeding tube. So naturally, she did what any great scientist would do. She got mad and decided to figure this out for herself. Starting with zero funding and a 30-page survey she posted on her brother's website, Marlena began collecting data from women with severe pregnancy nausea. The NIH rejected her funding request multiple times, so she got creative. She partnered with 23andMe to collect genetic data and eventually identified the culprit, a gene called GDF15 that produces what she calls the vomiting hormone. Here's what she discovered. Everyone has this hormone and it normally helps you avoid poisonous foods or tells your body to rest when stressed. But during pregnancy, your placenta pumps out massive amounts of this. Women who get really sick have low levels before pregnancy. So when these levels suddenly spike, their bodies basically freak out. The wildest part? Marlena has a potential treatment based on desensitizing people to the hormone beforehand, kind of like an allergy test. But guess what? The NIH keeps denying her funding, even though they funded a similar-sized study on erectile dysfunction genetics. Shocker. So women are now trying her approach on their own with their doctors. After years of pregnancy nausea being dismissed or misunderstood, we now have a clear biological explanation. It's likely an evolutionary mechanism that's no longer necessary in our modern environment, similar to other vestigial biological processes. The breakthrough came not from some large institutional research center, but from one determined scientist who refused to accept it's all in your head to prove it. transcript: As a therapist and a mom to two young boys, there are some phrases in our house that we no longer say. And we've replaced them with other phrases that tend to work better for our family. This doesn't mean that this is the right fit for everybody, but this is what works for us. In our house, we no longer say practice makes perfect. In my opinion, perfect does not exist. It's an unrealistic expectation to strive for. But what we do say is practice makes progress. Because if you want to get better at something, you can practice at it and get better. To strive for perfection is not realistic. If one of our children falls and starts crying, we don't say, get up, shake it off, you're okay. Children are allowed to feel their feelings. And most of the time what I'll say is, are you hurt or are you scared? A lot of times my children will say, I was scared. It was a scary thing to fall down. I thought maybe I was hurt, but I was just scared. I'm not going to invalidate the way that they're feeling We also don't say were you good or bad or be good, be a good boy We say people make good decisions and sometimes people make bad decisions That doesn't make them a good or bad person

title: Third-time mum's essential items for the maternity hospital bag
summary: A Romanian mum expecting her third baby lists the items that made her hospital stays easier, based on two previous births. Her highlights are a lidocaine or cooling spray for the perineum, extra-large maternity pads, prunes or fibre snacks against post-birth constipation, energy snacks, disposable bed pads, a large bottle with a straw, unsweetened coconut water, and comfortable wire-free bralettes. She also suggests a tripod for photos.
key_points: A local anaesthetic (lidocaine) or soothing spray for the perineum reduces burning; ask your doctor whether it needs a prescription.
Extra-large maternity pads, which can be chilled, plus a cooling gel: bleeding is much heavier than a period.
Pack prunes, fruit pouches or other fibre foods: constipation after pushing is common and the area is sore.
Pack plenty of snacks and protein bars for energy during labor and after.
Disposable bed pads (underpads) for hygiene and comfort, for you and for the baby.
Bring a large bottle or cup with a straw so you can drink while lying with the baby, and stay hydrated.
Unsweetened coconut water provides electrolytes during and after labor.
Soft, wire-free bralettes that don't constrict, which also help with breastfeeding.
Optional: a tripod or selfie stick for photos and videos with the baby.

Say hi and bye to characters to practise gestures and greetings.
Pause to let them fill in the blank: 'Close! And… open!'
Model two-word combos: 'next page', 'more open', 'turn page'.

title: Toddler throwing food: 3 responses that work better than ignoring
summary: A parent coach explains that toddler food throwing is communication (full, frustrated, overwhelmed), not defiance, and that ignoring it can escalate throwing. Drawing on a pediatric SLP's demo, she recommends pausing and resetting, having the child help pick up thrown food, and giving unwanted food a designated spot off the plate.
key_points: Food throwing is usually a signal (full, done, frustrated, overwhelmed) from a child without the words to say it.
1. Pause and reset: remove the plate, offer water, try again in a few minutes.
2. Have them help right away: food thrown means food gets picked up (a natural, age-appropriate consequence).
3. Give them a place for unwanted food (a bowl or napkin), off the plate but not on the floor.
Model words like 'all done' so the child can say it instead of throwing.
Ignoring throwing may increase it because the underlying need isn't met.
scripts: Oh, you're telling me you're all done.
Pick it up. Thank you.
All done if you don't want it. Put it right here.
credentials: certified parent coach (demo credited to a pediatric SLP)

You don't want orange. All done, orange. Okay, stop. Before you say no throwing one more time, your toddler is not being defiant. They're trying to tell you something that their brain just doesn't have the words for yet. Most parents are responding to the throw, but the throw is not the problem. It's the signal. Think about the last time that you were frustrated and couldn't find the words. Your body probably did something too. Maybe you slammed a door, threw your hands up, or even walked away. Your toddler's version of that is throwing food. Same nervous system, same overwhelm, just a much smaller body with fewer tools. Toddler language is still in its earliest stages of development. When they're overwhelmed, hungry, full, or frustrated at the table, they don't have the words or neurological capacity to express what's happening. So their body does it for them. The food throw is just the message. It's saying something isn't working right for me right now. And I don't know how to tell you. And here's what most parents don't realize. Ignoring throwing food can actually make it worse. When a toddler throws food and nothing happens, their brain learns that didn't work. I need to try harder. So they throw more with more force because the underlying communication need still has not been met. What this pediatric SLP shows is that the most effective response meets the communication need that's underneath. Pause and reset gives the nervous system a moment to recalibrate. Cleaning up connects the action to a consequence in a developmentally appropriate way, and giving unwanted food a place off the plate gives the toddler a way to say, hey, I don't want this without having to throw it. When a toddler learns that their needs get met without throwing, the throwing stops. Not because they were punished out of it, but because they found a better way to be heard. And that is the difference between managing behavior and actually meeting the need that's driving it. Offer a limited choice of two appropriate outfits so the child keeps some control.
Helping the child feel the decision was their idea reduces the power struggle.

title: Umbilical cord care: leave it alone and fold the diaper down

Only clean it if it is visibly dirty.
Fold the front of the diaper down so it doesn't cover or rub the stump; keep it dry and clean.
Some diapers have a cut-out for the cord; not all brands do.
The stump usually falls off in 7-14 days.

author: crybabykatelynn
title: Understanding AuDHD Overstimulation and Crying

key_points: Crying in neurodivergent children can be a sign of extreme overstimulation, not a demand for attention.
Accumulated stress from sensory input, hunger, or broken expectations can lead to a 'cherry on top' moment of dysregulation.
Labelling emotional responses as 'spoiled' or 'bratty' can cause long-term shame.
Masking and trying to keep up with neurotypical standards can lead to severe burnout.
caution: The creator's perspective is personal; while valid, it should be balanced with professional guidance on emotional regulation.

author: avocatnatalia
title: Understanding GDPR consent forms for your child
summary: A lawyer explains why parents should be cautious when signing photo consent forms for their children's activities. She highlights that consent must be specific, voluntary, and revocable, and that parents have the right to refuse or request clarifications.
key_points: You are not obligated to sign broad photo consent forms for your child's activities.
Consent must be specific to each purpose (e.g., website, brochures) rather than a blanket agreement.
You have the right to withdraw consent at any time without consequences.
Children's data requires enhanced legal protection under GDPR.
Always ask for clarification on how, where, and for how long images will be used before signing.
caution: This is legal information based on Romanian/EU law; specific requirements may vary by jurisdiction.

Așadar, când primiți un formular GDPR pentru copilul vostru, trebuie să știți câteva lucruri importante. 1. Nu sunteți obligați să semnați. Consimțământul trebuie să fie întotdeauna liber. Nimeni nu poate să vă forceze sau să condiționeze participarea copilului la un anumit curs, de exemplu, de semnarea formularului. 2. Aveți dreptul să spuneți nu. title: Understanding Matrescence: The Brain Changes of Motherhood
summary: The creator explains the concept of 'matrescence,' the neurological transformation that occurs during pregnancy and motherhood. She highlights that this process happens with both first and subsequent pregnancies, rewiring the brain for new tasks like motor control and multi-child awareness.
key_points: Matrescence is the brain's transformation during motherhood, similar to adolescence.
First pregnancies rewire the brain for social awareness and reading expressions.
Second pregnancies rewire regions related to motor control and environmental awareness.
The brain does not return to its pre-pregnancy state between children.
Mothers deserve grace and patience during the transition to multiple children.
caution: The creator presents scientific concepts; while interesting, individual experiences of motherhood vary.

If you missed day one through three, go back, but today we're going to be talking about matrescence. Matrescence was coined in 1973, and it's a word that describes the transformation that your brain goes through when you become a mom. Think adolescence, but for moms. A study was published in Nature Communications just this year, and it was the first to directly compare the changes in the brain that happens during a first pregnancy compared to a second pregnancy. title: Understanding severe croup in children
summary: A mother shares her experience of her four-year-old daughter's sudden, severe case of croup that required emergency hospital care. She highlights that croup can escalate rapidly at night without prior symptoms and emphasizes the importance of recognizing breathing difficulties.
key_points: Croup can escalate quickly at night, even after a normal day.
Warning signs include a barking cough and difficulty speaking or breathing.
Severe croup requires immediate medical attention at an emergency room.
Hospital treatment may include nebulised breathing masks and medication.
Parents should monitor children closely if they exhibit respiratory distress.

author: drjoe_md
title: Understanding synesthesia in children
summary: A doctor explains the neurological condition of synesthesia, where one sense triggers another, using a viral video of a toddler reacting to an ultrasound photo as an example. He emphasizes that this is a rare but real phenomenon, often harmless in children, and advises parents to take their child's sensory descriptions seriously.
key_points: Synesthesia is a condition where one sense automatically triggers another.
Cross-modal processing is the brain's normal way of blending senses like sight and sound.
Synesthesia is rare but real and more common in children.
It is generally harmless and often outgrown or adapted to as the brain matures.
Take a child's unusual sensory descriptions seriously rather than dismissing them.
caution: The creator presents synesthesia as a potential explanation for the child's behavior, but this is a clinical diagnosis that should be confirmed by a professional if a parent has concerns.
transcript: You'll never guess what this kid tells his mom after seeing the ultrasound pictures. Take a look. What's too loud? What? This is too loud? Yeah. This? Yeah. Here. Yeah. Put it away. Put it away? Yeah. So this kid looks at a black and white ultrasound photo and starts crying that it's too loud. Not weird, not scary, too loud. Let me explain. At first you might think, oh this kid's just being dramatic, but actually there's some neuroscience behind it. Our brains naturally use cross-modal processing to blend senses, such as blending sounds and sight to understand speech. But in rare cases those wires get too crossed, and this is called synesthesia, where one sense automatically triggers another. So someone might see colors when they hear music, or in this case hear a sound when they see an image. To us it's just a photo, but to him, it's a speaker on full blast. This sort of sensory crossover is rare but real and especially more common in children whose senses are still developing. So when a toddler says a picture is too loud, believe him.

caption: A toddler looked at a black-and-white ultrasound photo and said it was too loud. While it sounds bizarre, this could be a form of synesthesia—a neurological condition where one sense triggers another, like seeing images and hearing sound. It’s rare, but not harmful. Most kids with this kind of sensory crossover don’t need treatment, and many either adapt to it or outgrow it as their brains mature. summary: A mother discusses the hormonal process of labor, emphasizing the role of oxytocin and the 'cascade of interventions' where one medical intervention can increase the likelihood of others. She advocates for informed decision-making and support for those who have experienced birth trauma.
key_points: Oxytocin is the primary hormone that primes the uterus and drives labor.
The 'cascade of interventions' occurs when one medical intervention increases the likelihood of further interventions.
Synthetic oxytocin for induction may not function the same as natural oxytocin.
Medically necessary interventions save lives, but voluntary ones should be chosen with full information.
Postpartum counseling is recommended for those feeling traumatized by their birth experience.
caution: This content reflects the creator's personal perspective on birth; always discuss birth plans and medical interventions with your obstetrician or midwife.

author: goodenoughpsychiatrist
author_name: Good Enough Psychiatrist | Soe Thein, MD
title: Unpredictable caregiving as an adverse childhood experience
summary: A psychiatrist explains research suggesting that unpredictable care - not less care - is an adverse childhood experience. In rat studies, stressed mothers with limited resources gave the same amount of care but in fragmented, unpredictable patterns, and their pups had higher stress and worse outcomes; similar patterns were seen in human mother-infant play, and a large study linked unpredictable childhoods to higher depression risk. He stresses that stressed parents are not neglectful and that supporting parents supports children's development.
key_points: Unpredictability of caregiving (not amount of time or care) is being recognized as an adverse childhood experience.
In rat studies, mothers deprived of nesting material gave the same amount of care but in a fragmented, unpredictable pattern; their pups showed higher cortisol and worse behavior and cognition.
Similar patterns were observed when scoring human mothers playing with infants.
A large epidemiological study (about 30,000 children) linked unpredictable childhood to a much higher depression risk (cited as ~12-fold).
Stressed parents are not neglectful; consistent routines and predictable responses help, and parents need support to provide them.

Unpredictability is a childhood adversity that contributes to mental health problems
Laura M. Glynn, Sabrina R. Liu, Charles Golden, Michael Weiss, Candice Taylor Lucas, Dan M. Cooper, Louis Ehwerhemuepha, Hal S. Stern & Tallie Z. Baram

Although adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) increase risk for mental illness at the population level, existing ACEs screens are less helpful in forecasting individual outcomes, suggesting they may not capture significant elements of childhood adversity. We have previously identified unpredictable parental and household experiences as an ACE that pertains poorer cognitive and mental health. However, the contribution of predictability to established ACEs in real-world settings is unknown. Here, using existing ACEs screening in California, we added the five-item Screen on Unpredictability in Childhood (QUIC-S) in 19 pediatric clinics serving broad sociodemographic constituencies and compared children the link of each screen with mental health diagnoses. Whether the ACEs or QUIC-S associated with probabilities of externalizing symptoms, sleep disorders, anxiety and somatic. Each screen provided unique contributions and combining them doubled the strength of associations. For depression and sleep the QUIC-S identified vulnerable individuals missed by ACEs improving risk detection and facilitating future interventions.
caption:
Unpredictable childhood is associated with negative mental health outcomes in children. It is now beginning to be discussed as a new adverse childhood experience. 

I want to highlight the distinction that stressed parents are NOT neglectful parents. They provide care but their care becomes fragmented and inconsistent. This is seen in both animals and humans. Scientists can mimic unpredictable care in rat models by limiting resources for rat moms. What the data collectively show is is that if we want healthy children, we will need to do a much better job at supporting parents. A lot of the times, parents are doing their best to be consistent and reliable but socio-economical forces can get in the way of creating a predictable environment for children.

author: thejuliebarry
title: Use fewer words to help a late-talking toddler
summary: A side-by-side demo contrasts typical long parent questions with simplified speech-therapist phrasing for children having difficulty acquiring language. Saying less and focusing on core words makes key words easier to pick up; grammar should still be correct.
key_points: For toddlers struggling with language, shorten sentences and emphasise core words.
Instead of 'Are you ready to leave the playground to go eat?' say 'Playground all done. Bye-bye playground. Time to eat.'
Instead of 'Should we go home to see Daddy?' say 'Daddy home. We go see Daddy.'
Instead of 'Do you want the ball?' say 'Ball?'
Keep grammar correct where possible (e.g. 'Let's go eat') while saying less.
scripts: Go bye-bye car, see grandma.
Playground all done. Bye-bye playground. Time to eat.
Daddy home. We go see Daddy.
Ball?

onscreen: What does it look like to use "less words" to promote language?
caption:
Using fewer words / less language for children who are experiencing difficulties acquiring language is a strategy we suggest to parents at this crossroad.

✅ Try “Time to go bye bye. Let’s go eat.”

✅ Daddy home. We go see Daddy.

✅ Ball?

author: married.as.huish
title: Using a Family Handbook for Consistent Consequences
summary: The creator discusses using a 'family handbook' that outlines specific, predetermined consequences for rule-breaking. This approach aims to reduce parental stress and empower children to make their own decisions by understanding the outcomes of their actions.
key_points: Create a family handbook with pre-defined rules and consequences.
Predetermined consequences remove the need for reactive, emotional discipline.
Allowing children to choose their actions knowing the consequence fosters decision-making skills.
The goal is to maintain a positive relationship with children while providing clear structure.
caution: The effectiveness of this method depends on the age-appropriateness of the consequences; ensure they are fair and not shaming.
transcript: My parents gave us consequences that other parents definitely would not approve of. So let's talk about it today. My parents created a family handbook that was a bit unhinged and had a whole bunch of rules with consequences written inside of the handbook. Every single rule had a specific, already predetermined consequence for that rule. This was actually brilliant. My parents didn't have to have the daily stress of coming up with consequences on the fly. This was also an interesting thing for us kids because we could know exactly what was going to happen if we broke a rule. And we could choose if the consequence was worth breaking the rule. And sometimes we did. Sometimes we decided, I'll take that consequence, so I'm going to go ahead and break that rule. And you know what? That was totally fine with my parents. That's how they built this whole system. If ever we got into big fights and we were slamming doors and yelling at each other, we would have consequences like having to wash the windows, one of us inside and one of us outside the window, washing the same window at the exact same time, having to stare at each other for hours and hours until the chore was complete. As a parent of now teenagers, I realized how amazing this concept is. Everything was just predetermined. I could just look up the consequence. It was done. I still had a relationship with my parents and no one was the bad guy. I'm genuinely curious to all of you parents out there would you make a family handbook and then have set consequences and be brave enough to let your children choose to make their own decisions knowing that they're choosing their consequence good or bad please follow along because I'm going to find that handbook and I'm going to share with you guys all of the rules that my parents wrote as unhinged as they are because some of them are so good and you are not going to want to miss out Thank you.

Getting on the same page as a couple and leading with foresight changes everything in a home. Rules and consequences should never just be about control or reacting in the heat of the moment. When parents are intentional, structure actually empowers kids to make better decisions on their own and gives them ✨real confidence✨ in who they are!!

author: jenlatch
title: What I wish I knew before having kids: practical life lessons
summary: A mother lists lessons she wishes she'd known: don't play the 'how long until someone picks it up' game, make it safe for teens to tell you the truth, talk about substances early, expect about six months of illness when kids start preschool, offer nutritious food without stressing, take care of yourself without guilt, treat kids as you'd want to be treated, and admit mistakes.

Talk about substance use much earlier than you think you need to.
When a child starts preschool, expect about 6 months of frequent illness as their immune system adjusts; it evens out.
Offer nutritious food, but don't stress if they don't eat it.
Caring for yourself mentally, spiritually and physically makes you a better mom—no guilt.
Filter the noise of parenting advice: treat your children how you'd want to be treated.
Don't cling anxiously to the little years—there's a long future together; when you mess up, admit it.
