author: mytherapycorner
author_name: Anna Aslanian, LMFT, CGT, AF-EMDR-C /Parenting, Couples & Trauma
title: What a couples therapist tells couples before they have kids
summary: A marriage and family therapist warns that a baby reorganises a relationship: partners can start to feel like logistics coordinators, resentment can grow quietly, and fights become frequent small ones about chores and bedtime. Couples who do well expect this, keep talking, stay curious, repair, and ask for help (including couples therapy) before it becomes a crisis.
key_points: A baby reorganises your life completely; you'll both meet new versions of each other.
Expect to feel more like logistics coordinators than partners at times.
Resentment grows quietly when exhausted partners stop actively choosing each other.
Arguments tend to be frequent and about small things (dishwasher, whose turn for bedtime).
She describes the first three years after a child as the hardest for couples.
Protective habits: talk it through in advance, stay curious about each other, keep repairing, seek help or couples therapy early.
transcript: This is what I tell the couples I work with before they have kids. Your relationship will be tested in ways you cannot prepare for. Not because something is wrong with you as a couple, but because baby doesn't just add to your life. It reorganizes it completely. The version of your partner you know now, well, you're both about to meet new versions of each other. Some of it will be beautiful. In fact, a lot of it is so beautiful, transforming. But some of it will be very, very hard. And nobody tells you that you will stop feeling like partners and start feeling like logistics coordinators. And people don't tell you enough that the resentment can grow quietly between the two of you because you're exhausted and you love each other, but you have stopped choosing each other. And that arguments won't really be about the big things, but the small things, and they'll be frequent, right? Like who unloaded the dishwasher and who is going to put the baby to sleep next and what all of that means. So I'm not saying this to scare you. I'm really not. I'm saying this because couples who do well are the ones who prepare for all of this and talk through it and reconnect and often do couples therapy and they go through this coming out even stronger. And what helps is knowing that this is what's coming. The first three years after having a child are the hardest. They stay curious about each other. They keep repairing. They ask for help before it becomes a crisis. Having a baby is one of the most profound things you will ever do together. It's beautiful. It truly is. But it will also ask more of your relationship than almost anything else you've ever experienced. So go in with your eyes open and go in as a team and know that there is help available.

The transition to parenthood is one of the most under-prepared-for experiences in a relationship.

author: twinklsend
title: What is hyperlexia? Early reading and its link to autism
summary: A special-education (SEN) teacher from Twinkl explains hyperlexia: reading or language skills well above age expectations. It is not an official diagnosis, but she cites a ~14% likelihood among autistic learners and says it may be a missed sign of autism in girls, who get labelled 'gifted' instead. A key feature is strong expressive language and decoding with weaker comprehension.
key_points: Hyperlexia = reading/language skills above what's expected for age; not a formal diagnosis.
Cited figure: about 14% of autistic learners show hyperlexia.
May be an overlooked sign of autism in girls, who get labelled 'gifted and talented'.
Signs: intense interest in letters and numbers, long attention for reading, strong visual memory, reading without being taught.
Also: love of repetition, musical ability, reciting the alphabet early.
Speech may sound mature, but understanding (receptive language, implied meaning, instructions) can lag; may parrot phrases (echolalia).
caution: Hyperlexia alone does not mean autism; consult a pediatrician or developmental specialist if early reading comes with weaker comprehension or social-communication differences.

title: What to Say Instead of '5 More Minutes' When Leaving the Park
summary: A developmental therapist explains that warnings like 'we're leaving in 5 minutes' are good in principle but toddlers don't understand time. Offer a choice for the last activity: slide or swing.
Make the end concrete: 'You can go down 3 more times, then we go.'
Make the transition itself fun: e.g. bunny-hop to the car.

De asemenea, n-am avut nevoie nici măcar de pijama pentru că am avut constant pijama de alăptare sau post-operație de la ei. Nimic nu-ți trebuie. Poate singurul lucru pe care te-aș încuraja să-l iei este un cablu mai lung de încărcat telefonul sau tableta în cazul în care, nu știu, se întâmplă să fie un pic mai departe priza. Eu mi-am luat la mine, dar m-aș fi descurcat și cu unul normal fără nicio problemă. Dar altfel toate doamnele, infirmiere, medici, neonatologi, nu știu, toată lumea care m-a vizitat în alea trei zile cât am stat în spital au fost extrem de drăguțe și au făcut ca experiența mea dureroasă de altfel să fie mult îmbunătățită față de cum ar fi fost probabil dacă nu aș fi avut parte de acest tratament. Eu știu că dacă aș fi avut parte de o experiență traumatizantă, nu cred că m-aș mai fi gândit în veci la al doilea copil. Dar acum, uitându-mă un pic în spate, uitându-mă la felul în care am fost tratată acolo, iau în considerare treaba asta și tot acolo m-aș duce să nasc, pentru că realmente mi s-a părut că am primit tot sprijinul de care am avut nevoie. Am avut inclusiv un psiholog care a venit, am avut un consultant în alătare. Aș putea spune că la consultantul alăptare, deși mi-am dat informații necesare și valoroase pe care le pun în practică acasă, acolo parcă am simțit un pic mai puțină, nu aș zice nici lipsă de empatie, nici deschidere și nici disponibilitate, dar era o doamnă un pic mai în vârstă și mi s-a părut mie că, nu știu, parcă n-avea așa foarte mult chef în ziua respectivă, poate am prins-o și eu mai plictisit într-o zi, habar n-am dat. De altfel, informațiile pe care mi le-a dat au fost foarte ok și cred că mă și obișnuisem cu toate persoanele care intrau la mine în rezervă, erau extrem de zâmbitoare și așa mai departe. Eu am stat singură în cameră pentru că mi-am luat pachet de rezervă dublă, după care mi-am luat pachetul de stem și am avut upgrade pentru rezervă single. Nu știu cum e să mai stai cu încă cineva în cameră. Eu știu că mi-a plăcut să fiu singură, am fost mulțumită de treaba asta, pentru că am putut mă vibe în pace și în liniște, am putut să aprim lumina când am avut eu chef. Mi-am chemat copilul, adică mi-am chemat copilul, au zis că a venit singur. Am cerut de la neonatologie să-mi primesc copila și nu în cameră și a văzut să facă câtă gălăgie a vrut ea, fără să mă simt prost că poate trezesc pe altcineva, nici pe mine nu m-a trezit la rândul meu altcineva. Am avut și vizitatori și nu am simțit că, ok, vizitatorii vor deranja pe persoana care e cu mine. Nu știu, eu m-am simțit foarte bine și la fel aș alege și a doua oară. Nu mai știu dacă v-am zis, dar nu este niciun fel de parteneriat plătit cu Regina Maria, pur și simplu a fost experiența mea, una foarte, foarte bună la ei și medicul meu, nu mai zic, o să mă laud că este medicul meu, dar a fost minunată. Dacă urmează să nașteți natural sau prin cezariană la maternitatea Regina Maria din București și poate vă e frică sau aveți capul plin de gânduri, că sunt sigură că este și asta o situație, eu vă încurajez să vă duceți cu toată crederea acolo pentru că a fost foarte bine. În seara de dinaintea externării eu am început să plâng în cameră și îi spuneam soțului meu că eu nu vreau să mă externez, că mie mi-e frică să mă duc acasă și singură cu copilul, mă rog, singură, să mergem noi doi singuri acasă cu copilul, dacă nu o să știm ce să-i facem, unul la mână și doi la mână, ce să o fac eu acasă cu toate durerile astea pe care le am. Dar felul în care au decurs lucrurile, mi-au arătat că eram pregătită să plec acasă și acum la 11 zile de la naștere, deci 8 zile de la externare. Mă simt foarte bine și, deși mai menajez în continuare operația și în continuare mai am câteva săptămâni bune de repaus, mă simt bine. Deci, în urmare că am văzut atât, deci, dacă urmează să nașteți acolo, să știți că cel puțin asta este garantat, Oamenii vor avea grijă de voi și vă doresc mult succes și să aveți parte de o naștere ușoară și de o recuperare în zicit mai ușoară.

title: What your toddler's behaviour actually means (and what to say)
summary: A Montessori preschool teacher reframes four common toddler behaviours: throwing food (cause-and-effect or 'I'm done'), saying no to everything (learning autonomy), hitting/biting (lack of words for big feelings), and dumping toys (learning space and movement). key_points: Throwing food = exploring cause and effect, gravity, or signalling 'I'm done'; stay calm and involve them in cleanup.
Saying 'no' to everything = practising making choices; offer two acceptable options.
Hitting/biting = big feelings without words; don't yell, state the limit and give them words to use.
Dumping toys = learning how space and movement work; clean up together as part of play, not punishment.

title: When your 5-year-old asks 'Does yelling make me bad?'
summary: An occupational therapist filmed affirmations with her 5-year-old daughter, who unexpectedly revealed she thought getting mad made her bad. The mother reframed it by admitting she also yells sometimes and asking whether that makes her a bad mommy. The caption lists the emotional lessons she teaches at this age.
key_points: Children can quietly internalise that their big feelings or behaviours make them 'bad'.
Share your own imperfections ('Mommy yells too, I shouldn't, but I do') to show behaviour doesn't define a person.
Teach: everyone makes mistakes and mistakes are fixable.
Teach: you can feel several feelings at once.
Teach: there's more than one way to repair a relationship, not just saying sorry.
Teach: parents have emotions, and even when mad they still love the child.

caption:
I can’t believe this was 3 and a half years ago! 

I remember feeling caught off guard that she shared such a vulnerable thought for a 5 year old. 

Being an occupational therapist, millennial mom doing all the cycle breaking work, talking about anxiety and how our nervous systems respond to emotions and sensory input was just a casual Tuesday conversation—- but I didn’t know she had been internalizing this thought.

It was an important moment for me to help her reframe this narrative and show her my own faults. 

I wanted her to know that our behaviors don’t define us; I wanted her to know that even adults are still figuring out this whole “emotional regulation” thing.

Other important lessons I taught her at this age: 
➡️ everyone makes mistakes, and mistakes are fixable 
➡️ you can have multiple feelings at once

author: mybodypositivehome
author_name: Zoë Bisbing | Body Image Therapist | Speaker | Mom of 3
title: When your child calls someone 'ugly': get curious, don't shut it down
summary: A body-image therapist advises against replying 'everyone is beautiful' when a child calls someone ugly, because it ends the conversation. Instead, start with curiosity, help the child clarify what they mean, listen fully, and gently ask whether they said it to the person - using the moment to teach how powerful words about bodies are.
key_points: Avoid 'everyone is beautiful' - it shuts the conversation down.
Start with curiosity, not correction; thank them for telling you.
Help them clarify: is 'ugly' about appearance, behaviour, a feeling, something overheard, or a new word they're testing?
Listen fully and gather information before any moral lesson - a 'magic window' into their thinking.
Gently ask about impact: did they say it to the person or only to you?
scripts: Thanks for bringing this to me.
Wow... 'ugly' is a really powerful word. Tell me what you mean.
Did you say that word to them? Or only to me?
dedupe: child says someone is ugly response
onscreen: If your kid tells you they think someone is ugly, don't tell them everyone is beautiful...
caption:
✨If your kid says someone is “ugly,” don’t say “Everyone is beautiful.”

That’s a conversation ender…we want openers! 

✨Kids don’t come to us because they’ve fully formed a belief — they come because they’re trying to figure one out. And when we meet their curiosity with a shutdown, we lose the chance to teach them how powerful words about bodies really are.

Here’s how to think about this instead ⬇️

1️⃣ Start with curiosity, not correction. Thanks for bringing this to me. “Wow… ‘ugly’ is a really powerful word. Tell me what you mean.” Kids often use “ugly” before they even know what it means — this keeps the door open.

2️⃣ Help them clarify their meaning. Is “ugly” about appearance? What specifically? Can they name it? A behavior? A feeling they have around the person? Something they overheard? A new word they’re experimenting with?
You cannot teach them anything until you understand what they mean.

3️⃣ Stay open and listen fully. Your job here is to gather information, not jump in with a moral lesson. This is a Magic Window moment: they’re letting you into their thinking.

4️⃣ Gently ask about impact. “Did you say that word to them? Or only to me?” This matters. A lot. A child talking honestly to a parent is very different from using that word toward another person.

5️⃣ Offer the harm lesson without shutting them down. “I’m really glad you told me. You can always talk to me about anything — even big, strong words like that.” “But in our family we don’t use the word ‘ugly’ to someone. It’s a word that can really hurt someone, even if we didn’t mean to. Our words have power. That said, you can always speak freely with me.”

Thinking someone or something is ugly is just part of human nature… it’s not evidence of something wrong with your kid or you. AND we do have to teach kids the difference between having a private thought or opinion and being considerate of others. 

If you’re new, hello! I’m Zoë Bisbing. I’m a body image/ED therapist and mom of 3 here to help you nurture body image resilience for the whole family. Follow for more!

#bodypositiveparenting #bodyimagelessons #bodyimageforparents #lifeskills #resilientkids

author: jenniemonness
title: When your child says "you look stupid": respond to the meaning, not the word
summary: A mother's daughter told her "you look stupid" as she dressed up to go out. Instead of scolding, she assumed the child meant "you look different" or "I don't want you to leave", named that, asked for a better word, and turned it into a playful conversation before talking about how hard goodbyes are. The caption also discusses how to handle words children pick up from friends without labelling those friends as bad.
key_points: Look for the feeling behind a hurtful word: "stupid" may really mean "you look different" or "I don't want you to leave".
Name the likely feeling first, then tell the child the word doesn't fit and ask for a different one.
Make it light: brainstorm alternative words together (her child suggested "like a vampire!") and laugh before addressing the real issue.
Once the mood is light, talk about the underlying difficulty (here, saying goodbye for the night).
Scolding at an already emotional moment (a goodbye) tends to be less effective than curiosity.
With more time, ask where they heard the word, with curiosity rather than judgement.
As kids socialise they will hear words you dislike; avoid framing other children who use them as 'bad'.
scripts: Maybe you're not used to seeing me like this! But you can use a different word to tell me that.
The word stupid doesn't sound like the right word. What other word can we use?
Where did you hear that word? It's an interesting word you chose!
dedupe: child says rude word respond to feeling behind it
onscreen: I had a close friends birthday party last night...
When my daughter saw me, she said....
I wanted to tell her it wasn’t nice.
But read the caption for what I said instead.
caption:
There’s 2 things at hand here: knowing what’s 𝘣𝘦𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘥 the language and also the 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭 language being used. ⁣
⁣
First, let’s just acknowledge that I knew my child didn’t 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 mean stupid and probably meant:⁣
“You look different!” or “I don’t want you to leave.”⁣
⁣
So I said “Maybe you’re not used to seeing me like this! but you can use a different word to tell me that. The word stupid doesn’t sound like the right word.” What other word can we use? We laughed at all the different words they said “like a vampire!” Then, once it felt light, we talked about how it’s hard to say bye for the night. ⁣
⁣
Imagine how much more effective this is instead of scolding, esp at a time when it was already gonna be tough to say bye.⁣
⁣
If I had more time, I’d have extended the conversation even more. “Where did you hear that word? It’s an interesting word you chose!”⁣
Because as our children socialize more and are exposed to all different families and people, there will inevitably be exposure to things that don’t sit well with us. ⁣How do we handle this? ⁣
How do we tell our children that the word “stupid” is bad when they may hear their friend use this word all the time? So is their friend bad because he said that word?⁣⁣
⁣
I find that the best way to handle this is to talk to our children, even at a young age:⁣⁣
“You know I heard your friend use the word stupid today. I know that we talked about how that isn’t a good word to use. Every family has their own rules and things that are important. In our family it’s important to use words that won’t hurt people. Stupid can be a hurtful word. What are some other words that your friend can use?”⁣⁣
⁣
Children begin to comprehend the concept of their own family’s values and feel confident in creating their own, even when it’s different from those around them.

author: dragosbuzzi
title: When your child says 'nobody likes me': not every kid will like them
summary: A Romanian dad reflects that he taught his 6-year-old son, newly started at school, to be polite and pleasant but not how to cope when other kids don't like him. He cites peer-rating research showing about 11% of children in a class are popular, 13% rejected and about 60% liked by some and disliked by others - meaning being disliked by some kids is normal. In the caption he summarizes advice from clinical psychologist Eileen Kennedy-Moore on what to do and not do when a child says 'nobody likes me'.
key_points: In classroom peer-rating studies, roughly 11% of kids are popular, 13% rejected and about 60% are liked by some and not by others - that's normal.
Teach children not only how to be pleasant, but also how to cope when someone doesn't like them.
Don't contradict ('Of course people like you!') - kids usually insist harder.
Don't lecture or criticize when they're already down, and don't panic yourself - your reaction makes the problem bigger.
Don't call the other child's parents unless your child is in danger or it's serious bullying.
Lead with empathy; remember friendships shift quickly; if it keeps happening, talk to the teacher to learn more.

Știu ce zici și eu credeam la fel, dar totuși aș vrea să vorbim despre un studiu făcut cu mii de copii care contrazice un pic treaba asta. Metoda e simplu, au luat copiii într-o clasă și i-au fost urcate să spună pe cine plac și pe cine nu. Mii de copii au răspuns, da? Și rezultatele au fost cam așa. Într-o clasă, 11% dintre copii sunt populari, adică toată lumea îi vrea. 13% este respins, adică aproape nimeni nu îi vrea. Și 60% sunt la mijloc, adică sunt plăcuți de unii și neplăcuți de alții. 60% dintr-o clasă de 20 de copii, spre exemplu, înseamnă 12. 12 copii, ăștia nu sunt copii cu probleme. Ăștia sunt literalmente definiția copilului normal. E copilul meu și cel mai probabil e și copilul tău. Nu știu dacă e greu sau ușor de acceptat, dar copilul tău pur și simplu nu este plăcut de unii copii. Și trebuie să învățăm noi ca părinți să-l ajutăm să treacă și prin asta și vă las un pic mai multe detalii despre asta în descriere ca să nu fie clipul prea lung. Vă pup!

caption:
Am promis in clip ca las informatia aici. Uite-o, cu surse.
O am de la De. Eileen Kennedy Moore, psiholog clinician din Princeton, care scrie de ani buni despre prieteniile copiilor. Carti: “Growing Friendships” (pentru copii) si “Kid Confidence” (pentru parinti). Ce urmeaza e din articolul ei “When Your Child Says, Nobody Likes Me!”.
CE SA NU FACI
1. Nu-l contrazice. Reflexul e “ba te place lumea, uite, Andrei te place!”. Ea zice ca de obicei copilul insista si mai tare ca n-are prieteni.
2. Nu-i tine predica. Lectia 1001 nu ajuta mai mult decat cea cu 1000. Iar critica, cand e deja la pamant, aduce lacrimi sau furie.
3. Nu te panica tu. Daca te vede ravasit, problema devine mai mare in capul lui. Si ori nu-ti mai spune data viitoare, ori iti raporteaza fiecare fleac.
4. Nu suna la parintii celuilalt copil. Doar daca al tau e in pericol sau e bullying serios.
CE SA FACI
1. Intai empatie. “Suna ca si cum ai avut o zi grea.” Sau “te-a durut cand ti-a zis asta”. Si “vrei o imbratisare?”. Uneori atat e tot.
2. Tine minte ca trece. Cel pe care azi zice ca-l uraste poate fi prietenul lui de saptamana viitoare.
3. Daca se repeta, afla mai mult. Vorbeste cu invatatoarea, care il vede zi de zi printre ceilalti. Unui copil ii e greu sa-si vada partea lui.
4. Antreneaza-l inainte, nu dupa. Exersati cum saluti, cum raspunzi calm cand te tachineaza cineva.
5. Arata-i cine e deschis spre el. Ea scrie negru pe alb: nu toata lumea o sa-ti placa copilul, asta e natura umana. Sa alerge dupa cel popular, care nu-l vrea, e reteta de suferinta.
6. Fa-i ocazii. Copiii se imprietenesc facand lucruri impreuna: o activitate dupa scoala, o joaca unu-la-unu.
7. Cand ceri ajutor. Daca e hartuit sau amenintat: invatatoare si conducere. Daca tine saptamani sau luni: psiholog.

author: annalieseerinparentcoach
title: When your child steals money: no interrogation, no rant — consequence and amends
summary: A parent coach explains how to respond when a child takes money (e.g. $50 from your purse) to buy something forbidden. Don't ask whether they did it when the evidence is clear, and don't rant. Calmly state what happened, give the consequence (return the item even if you don't get the money back) and require amends (earning the money back), which also teaches them to earn money honestly.
key_points: Don't question whether they did it if the evidence is obvious — that invites lying.
Don't rant: a defensive child won't listen.
Calmly state the fact, the consequence and the amends.
Consequence: return the item purchased with the taken money, even if you don't get a refund — they don't keep things gained deceitfully.
Amends: the child earns back the money (chores, baking and selling cakes, etc.).
This teaches accountability and shows them how to earn money instead of taking it.

author: lalida_pov
title: Why 'share' doesn't work for toddlers: say 'take turns' instead
summary: A child-development creator explains that toddlers have discovered ownership but have no sense of time, so 'share' sounds like losing a toy forever. She suggests saying 'take turns', using a sand timer so the clock rather than the parent sets the rule, and giving each child their own play space to prevent conflicts.
key_points: Toddlers don't resist sharing out of selfishness; they understand ownership but not time.
To a toddler, 'share' sounds like giving the toy up forever; 'you'll get it back in 2 minutes' means nothing.
Say 'let's take turns' instead of 'share', which signals the toy comes back.
Use a visual sand timer so the timer, not you, enforces the turn.
Prevent fights by giving each child a dedicated space (a mat, corner or low shelf) that is theirs while they play.

When all the sand hits the bottom, it's her turn.

Here's what's actually happening, and the one language shift that actually makes taking turns click for toddlers. I'm Lolita. I study toddlers the way that UX researchers study users. When a toddler screams, and just won't let go, that's not selfishness. That's a brain that's discovered ownership, and just has no concept of time. here's what that means when you ask a toddler to share what they actually hear is give this up forever they have no framework for you'll get it back in two minutes because two minutes doesn't exist yet for them sharing feels like a permanent loss to a toddler and that's a time perception problem so sharing isn't the actual goal right now taking turns is here's what might work instead first stop saying share and instead say let's take turns same concept totally different signal to the toddler's brain. Take turns implies that the toy actually comes back and that one language shift alone reduces resistance. Second, use a visual timer. A sand timer works perfectly. You can say when all the sand hits the bottom, it's her turn. Now the rule isn't you, it's the timer. You're not the bad guy, the timer is. Third, before the fight happens, design the environment. caption:
Back this week with another thing I've learned doesn't work with young children: asking them to "share" 

When a toddler won't share, it's less about defiance and more about time perception. Without a sense of time, "you'll get it back" means nothing, and sharing just sounds like losing it forever.

Saying "take turns" instead of “share” signals the toy will come back. Pair it with a visual sand timer so the rule isn't you, it's the clock. Giving each kid a dedicated play space before the conflict starts also helps.

title: Why children misbehave only with their mother
summary: A Romanian psychologist (in training) explains why a child who is well-behaved at kindergarten, with grandparents or with dad falls apart with mum. She argues it is not disrespect but safety: the child drops the 'mask of control' with the most secure attachment figure and discharges accumulated tension, tiredness and sensory overload there.
key_points: Children often hold it together at kindergarten, with grandparents or in public, then release built-up tension at home with mum.
Meltdowns, whining and refusal with mum are a sign of trust and safety, not lack of respect or deliberate manipulation.
The child unconsciously knows 'mum won't leave me, mum loves me anyway', so all emotions (joy, anger, tiredness, disappointment) come out with her.
Mum carries the biggest emotional load: the child offloads fears, anxiety, fatigue and sensory overstimulation onto her.
Reframe 'he does it on purpose' thoughts before reacting; the caption goes on to describe how to respond (truncated in the saved text).

caption:
Ați observat vreodată?
La grădiniță – copilul e de aur.
La bunica – politicos și ascultător.
Cu tata – cât de cât se controlează.

Dar cu mama – mofturi, crize, țipete, aruncat de lucruri, refuz demonstrativ la orice cuvânt.
Și ți se pare:
„Parcă face intenționat…”
„Nu mă respectă…”
„Fac totul pentru el, iar el așa îmi răspunde!”

Dar de fapt –
nu e vorba de lipsă de respect. E vorba de iubire și siguranță.

Ce se întâmplă, de fapt:
	1. Copilul își dă jos masca controlului lângă mamă.
La grădiniță și în public, se străduiește să se conformeze, să fie „cum trebuie”.
Acasă, lângă cea mai apropiată și sigură figură – mama – își eliberează în sfârșit tensiunea acumulată.
	2. Mama este acel spațiu unde copilul poate fi el însuși.
Cu toate emoțiile:
– și bucurie,
– și furie,
– și oboseală,
– și dezamăgire.

Chiar și cu cele mai „grele” trăiri.
Pentru că, la nivel inconștient, copilul știe:
„Mama nu mă va părăsi. Mama mă iubește oricum.”
	3. Mama preia cea mai mare încărcătură emoțională.
Copilul își descarcă prin ea fricile, anxietățile, oboseala și suprastimularea senzorială.
Iar deseori, asta se manifestă prin comportamente pe care mama le percepe ca „rele”.

Cum să reacționezi corect?

– Amintește-ți: nu e împotriva ta. E lângă tine.
– Oferă sprijin și pune în cuvinte emoțiile:
„Ești obosit, sunt aici.”
„Îți e greu, te ajut.”
– Nu lua totul personal.
– Îngrijește-ți resursele, ca să fii un sprijin stabil.

Un copil care își permite să-și verse emoțiile lângă tine este un copil care se simte în siguranță cu tine.

author: vanessabeca1
title: Why children play outside less: the role of urban design
summary: The creator explains that children play outdoors less today not just because of screens, but because modern urban planning has removed 'independent mobility'—the ability for a child to safely reach play spaces alone. She argues that when play depends on adult schedules and car travel, it loses its spontaneous nature, and suggests that child-friendly cities should prioritize short distances and traffic safety.
key_points: Independent mobility is the ability of a child to move around their neighbourhood without adult supervision.
Research links higher levels of independent mobility to more frequent outdoor play.
When play spaces are far away, play becomes a scheduled activity dependent on adults rather than a spontaneous one.
The presence of other children in a neighbourhood encourages more outdoor play ('play produces play').
Modern urban planning often separates homes, schools, and parks with traffic, making screens more accessible than outdoor play.
UNICEF identifies independent mobility as a key principle of child-friendly urban planning.

author: doctor.mihail
title: Why dads should do hands-on baby care from day one
summary: A Romanian doctor explains that apart from giving birth and breastfeeding, fathers can do everything mothers do. In the first ~3 months babies attach to any caregiving adult. After 3-4 months they show preferential attachment and may cry if someone other than their usual caregiver bathes or feeds them. So dads should be involved in all care from the start, even imperfectly, rather than stepping in at 4-5 months when the baby protests and mom takes over. The clip ends with an event promo.
key_points: Fathers can do all baby care except giving birth and breastfeeding.
First ~3 months: babies attach to any adult who provides care (non-discriminating attachment).
From about 3-4 months: preferential attachment – baby may cry if someone else bathes or feeds them.
Get dads involved in feeding, changing and bathing from the start so the preference isn't only for mom.
Avoid the cycle where mom takes over ('Come to mama') and dad gives up ('He doesn't want me').
Involvement may be slower and messier at first, but it models shared caregiving for the child.
credentials: doctor (Dr. Mihail Pautov, per account; specialty not stated)
caution: The attachment timeline is simplified. Babies form attachments to several caregivers, and a preference for one parent is normal and changes over time. Ends with promotion for a paid event.

But what sold me was that you made videos about how dangerous indoctrinating kids to be obedient to authority is. And we know a little something in Germany about how dangerous it is to indoctrinate kids into being unquestioningly compliant to whatever authority tells them to do. Because the German society is very hierarchical culturally. And so compliance to authority is a cultural value that's existed for hundreds of years. But these German parents were like, we need to raise kids differently. And that hit me. Because I had kind of thought about that, but no one had so clearly spelled it out for me. We are here today because we have insisted on unquestioned compliance. We were baking my grandpa who’s been in the hospital/rehab facility since before Christmas his favorite pie my grandma used to make him, and it was really emotional for me.

My toddler saw. She asked if I was sad.

Many parents want to hide their tears from their kids, and of course we do. It’s been shown that up to 90% of parents don’t know how to talk about grief with their kids, nobody has taught us how and we can barely do it with ourselves!

But crying in front of your kids is actually a positive tool to building their own emotional resilience and intelligence.

Share this post with your partner and yourself to come back to.

⭐️4 reasons I allow myself to cry in front of my toddler as a MS in grief and bereavement, and a mom:

1️⃣ It helps them better trust their intuition- when they notice your feelings and what they perceive to be happening is validated, it teaches them their instincts can be trusted and are accurate.

2️⃣ It teaches them that emotions are normal and that sadness, like any other emotions, doesn’t need to be hidden or feared.

3️⃣ It creates emotional safety. When you acknowledge your feelings, it helps your child learn it’s safe for them to do the same. It shows them they’re allowed to express themselves in the home and it deepens connection and trust.

4️⃣ It helps them build empathy. My 2 year old thought to get me her favorite snack of applesauce to “help me”, and then kept hugging me. This helps them build compassion and emotional intelligence.

title: Why making your child happy shouldn't be the goal (Dr. Becky)
summary: Dr. Becky argues that rushing to cheer a child up (e.g. when they say they're the only one in class who can't read) teaches them that painful emotions are dangerous. Kids generalize from repeated patterns which emotions are tolerable; when parents avoid distress, kids pair feelings like sadness or jealousy with parental fear. Making happiness the goal of childhood can set kids up for adult anxiety, which she defines as wanting to run away from a feeling.
key_points: Resist the urge to immediately fix or reframe a child's painful feeling (e.g. 'but you're amazing at soccer', 'everyone reads at their own pace').
Children learn from patterns of interactions, not single moments, which emotions are safe to feel.
When a parent avoids a child's distress, the child learns the emotion is threatening and must be shut off.
Helping kids tolerate and cope with distress makes those feelings take up less space; happiness emerges naturally from that.
Anxiety can be understood as the urge to run away from a feeling rather than a feeling itself.
Relevant for back-to-school moments such as drop-off meltdowns or struggling with schoolwork.
caution: The causal link between aiming for happiness and adult anxiety is presented as fact but is the creator's psychological framework, not a demonstrated research finding.

They really might be. We have the urge to say, everyone reads at their own pace. But you're amazing at soccer, but you're so good at math. I want to make them happy. All that does for my kid, because during childhood, kids are not just learning about a situation with a parent. They're taking interactions and they're making generalizations. not from one moment, but patterns about what emotions are safe? What emotions can I deal with? What can I tolerate? And what emotions, as soon as I feel them, do I need to like turn off right away? And so when we make our kid happy, what we actually say to them is, I am just as scared of this emotion you're feeling as you are. And so what a kid's circuit is, I feel, let's say it's this I feel less than or it could be I feel jealous I feel sad I feel disappointed and what gets layered next to that in the circuit is my parents fear my parents avoidance those things get put together the irony is when you make happiness a goal of childhood you actually set a kid up for an adulthood of anxiety because they have a range of emotions that they've encoded as wrong and fearful and to me anxiety actually isn't a feeling it's the experience of wanting to run away from a feeling.

and so what a kid's circuit is
caption:
Over and over I hear from parents, “I just want my kid to be happy!” or “Don’t you just want your kids to be happy?” And yet… I wouldn’t say that my goal is to make my kids happy. To be clear, it’s not to make them unhappy either.

When we make happiness our goal, we start to see our kids’ distressing feelings as a problem to fix - rather than emotions to tolerate.  And then what happens is we actually pass on our own anxiety to our kids.

When we aren’t able to sit with our kids’ difficult feelings, they learn that these feelings must be bad or threatening, and then they too start seeing distress as something to avoid, rather than something they should learn to manage.

There’s a big irony here: the more we help our kids learn to cope with distress, the less “space” those feelings end up taking up; this is what allows for the natural emergence of happiness, from a place of feeling at home with oneself, not from a place of avoiding hard things at all costs.

Why is this even more relevant during back to school? Our kids will experience hard things. There will be a moment when they’re having a meltdown at dropoff, or are struggling to figure out a math equation. The most important thing we can do for our kids, is to teach them how to deal with these hard feelings, not to run away from them.

Is your toddler fighting sleep?

If you're trying to work towards independent sleep, you must bridge the separation they feel by focusing on the next connection. 

Other ways to bridge separation: 

👉🏼 Fill their hand with kisses to last until the morning (symbolizing you're always there with them.

I could list so many, but here are a few we use. Children’s brains function best when things are fun, and they feel connected. Bedtime doesn’t need to be a battle.

author: abanaturally
title: Why turning bad behaviour into a silly moment backfires
summary: A behaviour analyst (BCBA) reacts to a dad who uses humour and tickling to stop his toddler's challenging behaviour. Parent attention is highly rewarding, so being silly right after hitting, yelling or squeezing teaches the child that the behaviour produces fun. She recommends finding the function of the behaviour, teaching a replacement skill, giving clear 'do' instructions, and saving the fun for when the child behaves appropriately.
key_points: Being silly or tickling right after challenging behaviour can reinforce it, so it comes back later.

Teach a replacement that gets the same result, e.g. "I'll hold it" / "I can do it" instead of yelling "It's my tea!"
Say what TO do ("Put your hands down"), prompt it if needed, and move your body away from face-grabbing.
The moment the child behaves appropriately, pour on the fun, silliness and play.

When they hit, cry, whine, or yell, we want to look at why are they doing this? What is it producing for them? What do they want or what do they not want? So, we would want to teach her to say instead, I'll hold it or I can do it. The other thing we want to do when our kids are engaging in challenging behavior like in the video when the girl started squeezing dad's face is instead of telling them what not to do which doesn't give them any information as to what they should be doing and simply just draws a ton of attention to the challenging behavior instead we want to tell them exactly what they should be doing instead so for example put your hands down and then either prompt her hands down if she does it and move your body away and then prompt the other appropriate response may i hold the t or i'll hold the t then here's the most important part that many people forget the second our kids begin doing anything better or start engaging in appropriate behavior, that's the moment that we want to pour on the fun, the silliness, and the play. If I engage in appropriate behavior, that's when I get what I need. That's when dad really responds to me or acts silly or is positive and energetic. caption:
First things first…this is 100% common. 

Lots of parents turn on the charm after their child does something challenging, and there’s a reason why.
All humans repeat behaviors that produce good outcomes.

✨ For kids, yelling (or another challenging behavior) might “pay off” because it makes Mom or Dad act funny. The challenging behavior is positively reinforced—something enjoyable was added to their environment.

✨ For adults, being silly seems to “work” because it stops the challenging behavior in the moment. Our behavior gets negatively reinforced—something unpleasant was removed from our environment. 

So both sides are being reinforced. Kids learn, “If I engage in challenging behavior, something fun happens.” Parents learn, “If I act silly, the challenging behavior stops.” And before you know it, you’re stuck in a cycle.

The tricky part? Telling them “no,” threatening, or being funny might stop it temporarily, but it often comes right back a few hours, or a few days later.

So what should you do instead?

Always come back to the function, the why behind the behavior.

Ask yourself:
⭐ What is the challenging behavior producing?
⭐ What behavior could replace it that meets the same need?
⭐ How can I make sure challenging behavior no longer “pays off”?

When you answer those questions, you break the cycle.

And just to be clear…I’m not the “fun police.” In fact, I encourage you to be playful, silly, and give your child loads of love and attention. Just make sure that attention doesn’t come right after the challenging behavior.

caption:
I was an anxious kid myself. My third grade teacher endearingly called me “worry wart” and my high school track coach limited me to three questions per practice.

Obviously there’s many factors that lead to anxiety, but I truly believe that slowing down is one huge way to help. 

But, we have so much to do it seems. Yes, if we’re always reaching for the next to do, or next novelty, but what if we just savor in the same routines?

This year I’m decorating the house the same exact way I’ve done the past 3 years. As I was putting the garland up, it was so easy because I’ve already done it years past.

I’m also going to focus on making a lot of the same recipes that are tried and true in the new year. Nothing new, same routine.

We’ve already talked to some relatives about exchanging kids gifts instead of gifts for everyone, and on one side of the family, we’re doing a holiday train ride as an experience together. 

I’m really leaning into less is more and slowing down, and with it, I know my anxiety is lessened which definitely reflects on my interactions with my littles.

Hope this helps at least one person, and as always I truly appreciate your likes, shares, and follows ❤️

caption:
Studiile din psihologia dezvoltării arată ceva surprinzător:
abilitățile sociale, nu IQ-ul, sunt un predictor mai puternic al fericirii și reușitei pe termen lung.
(Concluzie susținută de cercetări longitudinale în educație și dezvoltare emoțională.)

Problema?
Cei mai mulți copii nu sunt învățați cum să se conecteze.
Li se cere doar „să se descurce”.

De aceea, chiar și copiii blânzi, empatici sau încrezători pot ajunge să se simtă invizibili în grupuri.
Nu pentru că e ceva „în neregulă” cu ei — ci pentru că nimeni nu le-a arătat mecanismele simple ale conexiunii.

Iată 3 obiceiuri mici, susținute de cercetări în dezvoltarea copilului, care fac o diferență reală:

✅ Obiceiul întrebării
Învață-ți copilul că o conversație e ca un joc de aruncat mingea.
Când cineva spune ceva, răspunzi cu o întrebare.
Arată interes și creează apropiere instant.

✅ Pauza de 3 secunde
Acea mică pauză înainte de a răspunde îl ajută să observe tonul și emoția.
Copiii par mai calmi, mai siguri pe ei și mai conectați.

✅ Jocul observării
La masă, întreabă: „Ce ai observat astăzi la cineva?”
Antrenează conștientizarea socială — ingredientul invizibil al carismei naturale.

Când copiii învață aceste tipare, conectarea devine mai ușoară.
Intră în grupuri cu o încredere liniștită — nu pentru că s-au schimbat, ci pentru că înțeleg cum funcționează relațiile.

Bag Races: tape toilet rolls to the floor as obstacles; kids step into grocery bags and jump-race through the course.

author: thewallertribe
title: 5 tips to keep a marriage fun in the young-kids years
summary: A mom shares five marriage tips for the demanding early years: keep chores playful, have the husband take over dinner and bedtime so she can shift out of 'mom mode', treat emotions as indicators not dictators, keep set kids' bedtimes to protect adult time, and not let kids run the household (they practise 'first-time obedience').
key_points: Make chores playful, e.g. rock-paper-scissors for dishes and diapers.
Partner takes charge of dinner and bedtime so the other can wind down and reconnect as a couple.
'Emotions are indicators, not dictators': use words to state needs instead of taking moods out on the family.
Have a set bedtime for kids to protect adult couple time in the evening (even if co-sleeping, sneak out after they're asleep).
Protect couple time, e.g. telling kids parents need time alone to talk after dinner.
scripts: Mommy and daddy need some alone time to talk after dinner.
caution: 'First-time obedience' without explanation is the creator's parenting philosophy and conflicts with gentle/authoritative parenting approaches; the couple-time tips are the more broadly useful part.

onscreen: my tips to keep your marriage fun in the early demanding years with young kids
caption:
1. make things playful
ex: play rock paper scissors over dishes and diapers

2. it’s your husbands job to take you out of mom mode. ex: josh takes care of dinners and takes charge of bedtime with all the kiddos. that gives me the evening to wind down and slowly shift out of mom mode into wife mode.

3. as a wife/mom remember that our emotions are indicators not dictators. they indicate what we’re feeling but we can take charge of our emotions and not let them run the household.
ex: just because i’m on my period and sick doesn’t mean i can be a jackass to everyone. i have words, i can use them to voice my needs.

4. have a set bedtime for your kids. 
ex: we cosleep with 2 of our kids but have recently  found a good rhythm for putting the 2 littles down and me sneaking out. so now we have our alone adult time in the living room.

5. this is half parenting but has everything to do with your marriage: don’t let your kids run your household. ex: we practice first time obedience and we can explain later. if we say something we expect obedience. i’m not going to go back and forth with “why’s” from my kid. 
ex: mommy and daddy need some alone time to talk after dinner, you guys go to your room and play. 
this is where we expect a yes mom/dad response. not a why. 

i hope you guys found some of these tips helpful! drop any extra q’s down below! not a marriage expert by any means but we’ve been thick in the little years for 6 years straight and have kept our sex life active and consistent, kept laughing together, and actually enjoyed each others company along the way.

author: bdccarpenter
title: A New Dad's Perspective on Witnessing Childbirth
summary: Fitness author Ben Carpenter reflects on witnessing his wife's childbirth, expressing deep admiration for her strength and resilience. He highlights the intensity of the physical experience and challenges the notion that women are the weaker sex.
key_points: Childbirth involves intense, raw physical pain and significant bodily fluids.
Partners should be prepared to support the birthing mother through a long and demanding process.
The transition from labor to immediate newborn care is profound and highlights maternal strength.
Men should recognize and respect the immense physical toll of pregnancy and birth.
caution: This is a personal reflection on the intensity of birth; individual experiences vary greatly.
transcript: I don't think we worship women enough. I recently had a front row seat to my wife giving birth, and it has totally recalibrated the already high opinion I held about women. Now I have watched videos and been to multiple classes, so I knew what to expect, or so I thought. Oh no, sweet summer child, I was so ignorant and naive. Worryingly high levels of blood and numerous other bodily fluids being excreted from her body on a fairly constant basis, not just during delivery but afterwards as well. A new boss mode level of pain that I have never felt, yet I am witnessing someone go through it on and off for hours. Each contraction a scream so raw and primal that I felt speechless. If I had to endure a whole nine months of pregnancy and then finish it off by pushing a whole human out of my most sensitive orifice, I would not shut the fuck up about it. But since she did this a week ago, she has barely mentioned it. Not only that, but the very nanosecond our exquisite daughter emerged, she was ready to coddle her on her chest like she hadn't spent several hours enduring a form of torture. Mummode immediately locked in and engaged like her entire life's purpose had just come to fruition. I am not saying this to pander, and I mean it with every single fibre of my being. It was the most incredibly beautiful thing I have seen in my entire life. Technically, we both get an A star for this group class project, but my contribution was suspiciously brief, and I still get to put my name on it. I feel physically and emotionally indebted to her forever. Any man who thinks that women are the weaker sex need to be at the business end of a childbirth suite supporting someone they care about.

author: msjherisouth
title: A child's most annoying trait may be a hidden talent
summary: An ADHD coach reposts a TEDx clip by youth speaker Josh Shipp, who argues that children's talents often first appear as annoyances (persistence, constant talking, joking). He tells how teacher Mrs. Wilhite redirected his class-clown behaviour into speech and debate, launching his career. The message: be the patient caring adult who redirects and cultivates the trait rather than shutting it down.
key_points: Traits that annoy adults (persistence, talkativeness, argumentativeness, joking) can be raw talents in disguise.
Instead of only correcting the behaviour, look for a constructive outlet (e.g., a talkative class clown → speech and debate).
Every child needs at least one caring adult who is patient where others are irritated.
When a child annoys you, pause, breathe, and consider what strength might be behind it.
scripts: Hey, you should sign up for speech and debate. I think you could be a gifted communicator.
credentials: ADHD coach (reposting); speaker Josh Shipp, youth empowerment expert
transcript: We unintentionally overlook a kid's raw and unrefined talent because that very talent tends to first bubble to the surface as an annoyance. And as a dad, I'm guilty of this myself 100%. My son will be like, hey dad, do you want to play Legos? And I'm like, yeah, just a minute. And then he goes and sets a 60-second timer and like stands there staring at me the entire time. I'm glad you find his persistence amusing. I find it annoying. But here's my question. What if a kid's most annoying trait is actually their biggest talent in disguise? Meaning, what if a kid's greatest asset first presents itself as a giant pain in your asset? And if that is true, how do we not make the mistake and unintentionally overlook genius simply because it first says, hello, as an annoyance? And then there's Mrs. Wilhite. She had this kid in her class. Loud, constantly disrupting, constantly talking, making everything a joke. The class clown kid. One day, Mrs. Wilhite pulls him aside. Says, hey, you should sign up for speech and debate. I think you could be a gifted communicator. And I will never forget when Mrs. Wilhite said those words to me. And you are listening to me speak today because she did. She didn't get annoyed by me, though she had every right to be. I was incredibly immature and sophomoric. She looked past it. She redirected the annoyance. And she cultivated the talent. You see, every kid needs one caring adult, like Mrs. Wilhite, in their life. To be patient where others might be pestered. So when that kid in your life inevitably annoys you. Because they're constantly getting into stuff. Or they're argumentative. Or they're annoying. Take a deep breath and consider in that moment that you too might just have your very own genius sitting right in front of you.
onscreen: Annoying Traits Can Reveal Hidden Talents

caption:
🎙️ Ever feel like your child's quirks are just too much? The constant talking 🗣️, endless jokes 😂, or nonstop energy ⚡? It might be more than just annoying—what if it's actually a hidden talent waiting to be nurtured? 🌱

Every genius starts somewhere, and sometimes that place is labeled as 'distracting' or 'difficult.' But with a little patience and understanding, you could be the one who sees the potential beneath the surface. 

Like Mrs. Wilhite, who saw past the class clown antics 🤡 of the speaker, Youth Empowerment Expert Josh Shipp, and encouraged him to join speech and debate🎤. (True story, I flew to CA and participated in one of his speaking workshops!) That simple redirection helped unlock a gift that led him to where he is today—sharing his voice with the world 🌍.

As parents, let’s take a deep breath and look beyond the irritation. You might just be raising the next great communicator, or at least, someone who’s destined for greatness. 🌟

key_points: Mothers often feel less 'allowed' to take leisure time than fathers do; it's not a lack of interests.

onscreen: POV: you married the best man and father, and you get to listen to simple, but beautiful conversations like this one as he raises your son to be just as incredible.
caption:
I had been working, dealing with some health issues, and solo-parenting for a few months while Daniel was abroad for work. Needless to say, my social life has been pretty much non-existent. 

I had a chance to go to dinner with my boys, but also with some friends, which I hadn’t done in such a long time. 

Elliott is 4, so of course I understand that it isn’t easy for him to sit around patiently while I have conversations elsewhere for long periods of time. Regardless, these are conversations we continue to have because he still has to learn to be considerate and develop that patience. 

This conversation is one Daniel took on, and it made me feel so grateful, seen/heard, and appreciated. I am the luckiest mom and wife alive. I have the two greatest boys in my life, and Daniel is the most extraordinary father for Elliott to have as an example of what it means to be a good man and human. 

#fatherson #goodmen #boymom #familythings #feelgoodcontent

summary: A mom explains that teens still need focused parent time and a bedtime routine. Set a fixed time by which chores, showers and everything else are done.
Devices are turned off and handed in at that time.
Switch from bright overhead lights to soft lamp light.
Gather together for calm activities: crafts/hobbies, chill music, a parent reading aloud, card games or puzzles.
Building in connection time earlier stops teens from wanting long talks just as parents go to bed.

But they still need focused mom and dad time. And what was happening is that each and every night we were going to bed later and later because as soon as we were getting ready to go to sleep, that's when the teenagers all wanted to start talking for the next hour or two. transcript: This experience proved that my daughters handle spending money so differently. They don't get allowance-specific shopping trips often. Usually they use their spending money here and there when we're already at the store for something else. But this time I took them to the store just so they could spend as much or as little of their allowance as they wanted. My oldest was so strategic. She knew exactly what she wanted, calculated her after-tax total, and made sure she only used a little over half of her money. She wanted to leave the store with still some spending money in her wallet. My five-year-old, whole different mission. She wanted to spend everything and get as much as possible. She kept adding things to the basket until she hit her limit, then swapped them out for quote-unquote better things as we made our way to check out. She ended up spending all but one dollar. Now, here's why I'm not worried about her approach. My oldest used to be the exact same way when she was her age, and the more chances she had to spend her own money and feel the natural consequences, the more thoughtful of her spending she became. author: amycuddy
title: Around age 11 girls' body language shrinks—teach them to take up space
summary: Social psychologist Amy Cuddy (on the Women of Impact podcast) observes that young children of both sexes move expansively, but around age 11 / middle school girls start 'collapsing' into low-power body language—pulling sleeves over hands, touching neck and face, fiddling with jewelry. She urges parents to teach daughters it's okay to take up space, speak up and share ideas, and to stop shutting that down.

Young girls and boys are naturally loud, messy and expansive in movement.
Encourage daughters to take up space, speak up and share their ideas.
Notice and stop adult habits that shut girls down when they are loud or assertive.

All of that is low-power body language, and it increases for girls when they get to that age, that middle school age. Girls’ body language tends to shrink when they get to middle school. Because girls are learning — from countless images and channels — that they are supposed to make themselves small.

It doesn’t have to be this way. We have the power to change it. By encouraging them to expand, to speak up, to share their ideas.

Let’s remind them what they were made for — to be proud, confident, whole.

Notice and name the effort afterwards ('I noticed that you tried') to reinforce it.
Shared interests (like Roblox) are a way into an older child's world.

title: Autistic daughter self-advocates about her stim with new classmates
summary: A mother shares her autistic daughter explaining how classmates noticed her eye-crossing stim, how she told them it's just how her brain works, and how they turned it into a bonding moment. After past teasing, the parents had taught her tools to self-advocate, and the mother argues that naming differences openly removes shame.
key_points: Teach autistic children simple, matter-of-fact language to explain their stims or traits to peers
Explaining openly ('that's how my brain works') can turn curiosity into connection rather than teasing
Children may not even be aware of a stim until someone points it out; prepare them before it happens
Praise the child afterwards for advocating for herself

It's part of my brain that rarely and randomly makes me cross my eyes. but then i said that i um do not know how to cross my eyes like by myself and then um she and another girl they taught me how to um cross my eyes like on my own it took me a little while to learn but i can uh do it okay like by myself show us am i doing it yes so you told them like hey guys no big deal it's just the way my autism and my brain works yeah so they understood that and then you turned it into a bonding thing with new friends yeah amazing high five

Because she's been teased in the past, we began giving Campbell the tools to advocate for her autistic traits
So she taught them about her stims and something incredible happened...
Her self-acceptance gave others the opportunity to offer the same
Maybe the secret to belonging is just being ourselves
caption:
Campbell crosses her eyes. It’s one of her autism stims. It happens at random, usually when she’s excited, and is something she cannot control. In fact, up until she was teased at summer camp, she didn’t even know it was happening.

So we began giving her tools to self-advocate, and this week, when some new friends noticed her repetitive eye movements, she was able to do just that.

I never could’ve predicted (or prayed for) such an outcome.

This interaction shows exactly why I believe it’s easier to be who you are, than hide who you are. 

When our claim differences, we remove any shame.

I’m so proud of Campbell for advocating and educating, and I’m equally proud of her peers who asked a curious question without judgment.

This is how we normalize.

This is how we begin to belong.

In fact, early and repeated exposure is what helps the body recognize these foods as safe.
So don’t wait for the “perfect time.”
Start small. Keep offering. That’s what matters.

Many years ago, when I first became a social worker, someone told me: Every child needs someone who is happy to see them when they walk through the door. 

I chose to embody that mantra from that moment on. 

With my own kids, and with everyone else’s, I have had a smile on my face when I see them and to ensure they feel welcome and wanted. 

I started throwing SommerVillage parties for my kids to have all of their friends over in part because of this mantra. 

To be the space where kids are given permission to just be kids. To laugh, and eat together, to be seen and witnessed, to be welcomed and included. 

Because in our house, we believe that there is so much worth celebrating (or maybe that’s just the life of an extrovert).

I have developed relationships with all of my kids friends. They know me, they are comfortable with me, they trust me. And it’s worth every effort to cut up fruit into rainbow kabobs or buy a dozen bags of chips.

author: princeofcloudcity
title: Bluey 'Copycat': why kids process hard feelings through pretend play
summary: A creator reviews the Bluey episode 'Copycat', in which Bluey finds an injured bird that dies at the vet, then re-enacts the event at home and insists the bird must die in the game. Mum plays along, letting Bluey safely feel and process the loss. The creator links it to the idea (Aaron Smuts' 'The Paradox of Painful Art') that fiction and play let us experience difficult emotions safely.
key_points: Children often process frightening or sad events (like death) by acting them out in play.
Join the play on the child's terms; don't 'fix' the story into a happy ending if they need to replay what happened.
Dark themes in a child's play don't mean they want bad things to happen.
Simple language like 'it was out of our hands' can help a young child understand something they couldn't control.
Bluey episode 'Copycat' is a good example to watch.

transcript: I had a friend reach out to me and say, hey, there's an episode of Bluey you should watch. I'm not a Bluey adult. I've never seen any episodes of Bluey, but I was like, yeah, sure, why not? And it turns out that episode was a really good like micro lesson about why humans like dark fiction. The episode is called Copycat. The episode is all about the importance of children interacting with their world through fictional means in order to understand it. In the episode, Bluey is playing with her dad one morning. She's copying everything he says and does and it's like this little playful thing between them until they happen to accidentally find an injured bird. Bluey stops copying everything her dad says and instead wants to pause the game and save the bird. They scoop up the injured bird, put it in a little thing, they take it to the vet and it turns out the bird doesn't make it. The nurse delivers this news really tactfully to Bluey but obviously Bluey is a toddler and she has no idea how to process still the concept really of death. In the car she's talking with her dad and she's like I wish the bird didn't have to die and the dad's like I know but it was out of our hands. It's something we can control. Bluey seems to really sit with that. Specifically the phrasing it's out of our hands it seems to have really resonated with her. She goes home and she gets her little sibling to play out the scenario of this dead bird and she gets her mom in on it too to play the bed. the mom thinks that bluey is playing out a scenario where the bird lives so the mom walks in to do her line after bluey gives the injured bird to the vet and the mom says it's fine he's gonna make it and you're okay and bluey stops her and says no no no you're not doing it right the bird dies and the mom's like oh you want the bird to die in this scenario he's like yeah that's what happened that's what happened. It was out of our hands. And the mom plays this scenario with Bluey and she gets to feel all of those scary intense adult feelings in a safe space and fully process them and she ends the episode smiling and laughing and playing with her sibling. But she needed to process through fiction first. It doesn't mean Bluey wanted the bird to die. It doesn't mean that Bluey would have ever killed the bird herself. The show reminds us how important play is to the human psyche. How important fiction and make-believe and synthetic feelings are to the human. Time to about one of my favorite academic essays of all time, The Paradox of Painful Art. Shout out to Dr. Aaron Smuts. Human beings love dark weird fiction because it allows us to feel things that might not be safe for us to feel in real life or re-feel things in a safe way that weren't safe for us to feel than the first time it makes us more rounded more empathetic human beings and it makes us healthier with how we engage with our own emotions i don't think i've been converted into being a bluey adult but i do think that episode was a quite delightful 10 out of 10

title: Bored kids lack 4 skills, not entertainment
summary: The creator argues that a child who constantly complains of boredom isn't missing entertainment but four traits: imagination, resilience, autonomy and patience. He describes signs of each gap and one way to build each. The caption promotes his ebook on communication and discipline.
key_points: Don't hand over a screen to stop 'I'm bored'; boredom is a chance to build skills.
Lacking imagination (can't invent games, relies on fixed-function toys): encourage open-ended play.
Lacking resilience (gives up quickly, fears mistakes): praise effort over outcome.
Lacking autonomy (used to being entertained/told what to do): offer choices.
Lacking patience (wants fast, high-reward experiences): reflect on the process, not the destination.
scripts: What do you do when you're bored? You find something you want to do.
caution: Opinion framework, simplified; the caption promotes the creator's paid ebook.

If your child keeps complaining about being bored and you find this irritating and sometimes even give them a screen to shut them up, you need to realise one thing. I don't know what to do. It's not entertainment that they're missing. It's these four traits. Imagination, resilience, autonomy and patience. If they're struggling to invent games on their own, rely heavily on others or toys with fixed functions and lack curiosity to explore, and can't solve problems, they lack imagination. If they quickly give up when something isn't instantly fun or goes slightly wrong or are afraid of making mistakes, they lack resilience. If they're used to being entertained, often by screens, structured activities, or constant adult input and are always told what to do and not given any choices, they lack autonomy. title: Boys are not easier to raise: countering 'boys don't cry' messages
summary: A mother of a 4- and 6-year-old son describes how her boys pick up gender stereotypes ('girls are fragile', 'boys don't cry') from outside influences despite her teaching. She shares how she lets them cry, holds them through meltdowns, physically stops hitting while saying 'I won't let you hurt my body', then has the child clean up. She argues raising respectful boys is a collective effort.
key_points: Young boys absorb stereotypes ('girls are fragile', 'boys don't cry') from peers and media even at 4.
Ask open questions to find out where a belief comes from instead of correcting immediately.
Teach that strength comes from the same things for boys and girls: eating well, moving, sleeping.
Let boys cry freely; during a meltdown, hold them and use your own calm breathing to soothe them.
If a child hits, stop them physically and calmly, then after they cool down have them clean up the mess they made.
Keep teaching consent, respect and consequences, knowing outside influences will push back.

summary: A reposted talk teaches adults how to stop letting short-term feelings derail long-term goals by building tolerance for uncomfortable emotions. transcript: Today I'm going to teach you a skill that you should have been taught when you were a child, but probably weren't, how to stop sabotaging yourself. The number one way that people sabotage themselves is that they let a short-term feeling get in the way of their long-term goal. In order to overcome this, you need to develop a tolerance for difficult emotions to be able to sit with them. First, remember that emotions, no matter how uncomfortable they are, are brief. They don't last for very long. Think of your emotions like paying a toll on the highway. You have to pause and hand over your money, but then once you've done that, you get to zoom down this wide open road and go straight towards your destination. Second, start small. If you push yourself to do something that's too uncomfortable too quickly, it can backfire. For example, let's say that your goal is to write a book, but you're not doing anything about it because you're scared and you're overwhelmed. You're trying to do too much too soon. Instead, set a goal to write a one-page article. And finally, practice. Practice sitting with your discomfort. Life every day presents us with moments of pain, frustration, annoyance, and the like. And you can use them. So for example, when you're stuck in traffic and you're feeling really annoyed, pause and notice the feeling. Label it. Say out loud, I'm feeling annoyed right now. And then get curious about it. What's really going on for you? What's especially hard about this? Is it that you're not in control? Is it that you're going to run late and it's going to upset somebody? And whatever comes up, treat it with compassion. You can say to yourself, it's okay that I'm feeling this way. Anyone would feel annoyed right now. It's just a feeling. I'm going to sit here and I'm going to breathe until it passes. Every time that you do this, you are building up your ability to tolerate these emotions. And because of this practice, you will be able to notice those feelings that come up when you are trying to do something that really matters to you and choose to move through them, not to have them block you.

Many mothers were raised in environments where their thoughts, questions, or personality were dismissed as silly, dramatic, or even “stupid.” Over time, they may begin to believe that being taken seriously means being less expressive, less curious, or less themselves. If you’re pregnant, save these tips for labor:

🌬️ Step 1: When a contraction begins, don’t hold your breath. Breathe in through your nose and slowly exhale through your mouth.

🤍 Step 2: Consciously relax your jaw. Many midwives teach a simple rule: relaxed jaw, relaxed pelvic floor.

🌸 Step 3: Keep moving. Walking, swaying your hips, or leaning over a birth ball may help your baby descend.

✨ Step 4: Don’t focus on reaching 10 cm. Focus only on the contraction you’re experiencing right now.

💡 Step 5: Rest completely between contractions. Relax your shoulders, unclench your hands, and use every pause to restore your energy.

Because here’s something fascinating…

Your cervix goes from completely closed to approximately 10 cm dilated to allow your baby to be born. 🤍

And every contraction has a purpose: helping make that happen.

💔 The problem is that many moms interpret increasing intensity as a sign that something is wrong.

They tense up.
Clench their jaw.
Hold their breath.
Fight every contraction.

And that can make labor feel much harder than it needs to be.

author: maria_carusi
title: Children don't need to be 'good' or 'strong' - they need to be heard
summary: A Romanian practitioner says she'd write two messages on her office walls: children don't have to be well-behaved, and children don't have to be strong. Adults praised as kids for never crying or asking often had needs nobody saw. Healthy children are loud, cry and ask, which helps parents notice and meet their needs, and they should feel deeply safe and protected by adults.
key_points: Don't praise a child for being 'easy' or never needing anything; a quiet, compliant child may be hiding needs.
Crying, asking and being loud are healthy ways children signal needs so parents can see and meet them.
A child shouldn't have to be 'strong' and cope alone; they need a deep sense of safety and protection from adults.
Adults raised as 'good, strong kids' often recognise unmet needs in retrospect.

title: Children's suggestibility and who gets unsupervised access
summary: The creator describes a 1990s study in which young children, repeatedly asked about a broken arm they never had, gradually 'remembered' it in detail, and some still believed it after being shown proof. Repeated negative talk about a parent around children can alter how they see that parent.
Be selective about who is alone with your children, especially relatives who criticise you.

title: Choline in pregnancy: two studies on baby brain outcomes
summary: Glucose Goddess summarizes two studies: a Cornell trial where pregnant women taking 900 vs 480 mg choline/day had babies with 20% faster reaction times in infancy and better memory/attention at age 7, and a placebo-controlled trial of 900 mg/day from the second trimester linked to healthier infant brain patterns and better behavior at age 3. The other group got 900 milligrams of choline per day. Babies were then tested at four, seven, 10, and 13 months. The results, the high choline group had a 20% faster reaction time, a marker that is linked to higher IQ as an adult. At seven years old, the kids were also assessed. The kids from the high choline group also scored better at memory and attention tasks. This study suggests that more choline during pregnancy creates a more optimal environment for the brain to be formed in as measured years later. Now, in another clinical study, pregnant mothers were in two groups. One group received 900 milligrams of choline every day from the second trimester onwards. The other group received a placebo every day from the second trimester onwards. The results, at one and three months old, the choline group had healthier brain patterns linked to a lower risk of ADHD and schizophrenia. And in the choline group at age three years old, the parents reported that their kids had better emotional regulation and behavior. So if you haven't checked out choline yet, it's a very key nutrient that we have to make sure we get enough of during pregnancy and that 90% of pregnant women today don't get enough of.

title: Clarity before correction: tell kids the rules first
summary: A 7-year-old tells his parents he keeps 'breaking rules' he didn't know existed, because they only explain them afterwards. Praise the child for speaking up respectfully.

author: binxyphoenix
title: Coaching a 2-year-old to recover from a slip in shallow water
summary: A mum shows how she reacted when her 2-year-old son slipped in a shallow, slow stream: instead of rushing to grab him, she stayed within arm's reach and calmly coached him to take deep breaths and walk to her. She argues that safely supported struggle builds resilience, confidence and problem-solving.
key_points: When the child is safe and within reach, coach rather than rescue immediately.
Use calm encouragement and breathing: 'Take a deep breath... slowly walk towards me.'
Hold out your arms so they have a clear, short goal.
Celebrate afterwards with a hug and praise for the effort.
She was 3-4 ft away in shallow, slow-moving water, ready to grab him if needed.

caution: Toddlers can drown in very shallow water within seconds; only use this approach with an adult in the water within immediate arm's reach.

caption:
Why did I handle it this way? 

Whilst we were having a paddle in a small stream to cool off, my two year old son lost his footing and slipped. He immediately started to panic as he desperately tried to regain his balance and not slip under the water. 

Edit: I need to make it clear that I was in the water with him, I was about 3-4ft away and ready to grab him if needed. My arms were reaching out to him, all he had to do was take a few steps to get to me so he got that self confidence boost. He had a big hug and was very proud of himself after.

So why didn't I rush and grab him? 

I knew that Alfie was safe, he was within reach if he did need help and he was shallow slow moving water. 

For a child to develop resilience, high self esteem and problem solving skills it is vital that as parents we give them the space to practice. If I had simply rushed in, picked him up and 'saved' him, he wouldn't have learnt anything. 

By supporting him in getting himself out of trouble he gains a sense of pride over accomplishing something so scary. 

He didn't feel alone or abandoned and listened to the advice I gave him. Alfie took a few deep breaths to calm himself and you can so clearly see him fighting back the fear. 

As soon as he makes it to me, by himself, you can see the look of pride on his face and he immediately wants to go back in the water to see daddy. 

My aim as his mother is not to keep him dependent on me to save him. I get so much joy in seeing my son gain the skills he needs to be more independent and grow as a person. 

How would you handle this situation? 

Have you ever been in a similar situation? 

Added: MY SON WAS NOT ASKING FOR DADDY because he was scared or felt like he wasn't safe with me. Look at his face, see the big beaming smile 😁 He excitedly wanted to go and tell daddy about how well he did, when we did get back to him Alfie shouted "I did it" with the biggest grin on his face, he was so proud of himself and wanted to share it with his daddy. 

#parentingstyle #respectfulparenting #mumanddad #childbehavior #childpsychology #childrensmentalhealth #family #counseling #raisingboys

title: Conversations parents shouldn't have in front of their kids
summary: A pediatric psychologist lists conversations partners should take somewhere private for children's emotional well-being, because kids are always listening. Visible items include financial stress, arguments about parenting styles, and negative talk about family members; the rest of the caption is truncated in the saved data.
key_points: Financial stress: can make children anxious, insecure or feel responsible; instead talk with kids about healthy money habits.
