onscreen: 5 Conversations with your spouse that you should NEVER have in front of your kids (And Why They Matter More Than You Think)
caption:
Here’s a truth bomb: Some conversations, no matter how minor they seem, should never be had in front of your children. 

Why? Because even if they’re not directly involved, kids are always listening. And those little ears pick up on far more than you think. 🧠👂

Here are 5 conversations to take to a private space for the sake of your child’s emotional well-being:

1️⃣ Financial Stress & Money Troubles 💸
Discussing financial woes can create anxiety in children, making them feel insecure or like they’re responsible. Kids thrive on stability, so keep financial conversations private and frame your money talk around teaching them healthy habits instead.

2️⃣ Arguments About Parenting Styles 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦
Disagreeing on how to raise your child is normal, but debating it in front of them undermines your authority and can leave them confused or feeling like they need to “pick a side.” Find a quiet space to hash it out and present a united front when you engage with your kids.

3️⃣ Negative Talk About Family Members 🗣
Talking down about a family member (even if it’s justified) teaches children that it’s okay to disrespect or disregard loved ones. It can damage their perception of relationships and loyalty. Save those discussions for when you’re alone, and model compassion instead.

4️⃣ Blaming Each Other or Shaming Your Spouse 😡
Pointing fingers or laying blame on your spouse in front of your child creates tension and may lead to unhealthy views on conflict resolution. It teaches children to see one parent as the “bad guy,” which can affect their relationship with both of you. Remember: Calm, respectful conversations set a positive example.

5️⃣ Adult Issues or Problems 📝
Discussing subjects like work stress, intimate relationship problems, or any adult-only topic in front of kids burdens them with unnecessary emotional weight. They aren’t equipped to process adult problems, so it’s important to shield them from conversations that may cause confusion or fear.

💡 The Takeaway:
Your kids absorb everything you say, even when you think they’re not paying attention.

The approach involved extensive, Food for the Brain "personalized dietary changes, supplements, and therapies," resulting in PubMed Central (PMC).gov "lowered ATEC scores and improved, PubMed Central (PMC).gov "functional abilities".
Key details regarding the study and the surrounding controversy include:

- The Findings: The twins, diagnosed at 20 months, saw their ATEC (Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist) scores drop significantly (one from 76 to 32, the other 43 to 4) over two years, according to a study published in the Journal of Personalized Medicine.

- Interventions Used: The comprehensive, non-pharmacological approach included dietary changes (gluten/casein-free), vitamins/supplements, Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA), speech therapy, and occupational therapy.

- Controversy & Criticism: Experts and organizations like the National Autistic Society have described the study's claim of "reversing" autism as "deeply insulting" and scientifically misleading, as noted by Learning Disability Today and Reuters.

- Scientific Perspective: Experts argue that while intense intervention can help children thrive and manage symptoms, autism is a developmental condition that is not "cured" or "reversed," according to Full Fact. The results of this single case study cannot be generalized to the broader autistic population.

Eden loves to play with water and always tries to turn on the fake tap on his Ikea ducting set. I've seen so many videos of these DIY projects but couldn't find any that explain the entire process, so here's one covering my attempt. First, take measurements for the backsplash and water container cabinet, then remove all the accessories from the playset. For the backsplash, make markings on a piece of foam board and cut based on the measurements before wrapping the board in a sheet of waterproof adhesive wallpaper. Roll out any air bubbles, tape down loose material and it's time to secure the backsplash, which I did by using some 3M Velco frame strips pasted on the edges of the board and counter. Next, unscrew and remove the door below the sink to release the shelf and set it aside, along with the fake tap. To drain water, the tub already has marked draining holes in it, so I drill through them on top of a plastic bag to catch the shavings. To make sure water doesn't drain all over the place, I attach the funnel to the bottom of the tub with a hot glue gun, then assemble the tap system, which is a rechargeable electric tap with its tube feeding through the hole on the counter into a 2-liter plastic jug of clean water, while the tub drains that water into another empty 2-liter jug. Then, it's time to reattach the cabinet door and secure it with a child safety lock so Eden's busy hands can't open it and spill water everywhere. The last thing to do is secure the electric tap with hot glue and your functioning tap is complete.

author: denisasimam
title: Deciding when to announce pregnancy
summary: A pregnant woman explains her decision to wait until the second trimester to announce her pregnancy to family and friends. She emphasizes that the pregnancy belongs to the couple, who have the right to choose when and how to share the news, and discusses the importance of waiting for genetic test results.
key_points: Waiting until the second trimester (approx. 13.5 weeks) can provide peace of mind due to the commonality of early miscarriage.
Waiting for genetic test results allows parents to make private decisions if serious medical conditions are discovered.
The pregnancy news belongs to the couple; they decide the order and timing of announcements.
Announcing to the whole family at once can be a fair and inclusive way to share the news.
caution: The creator mentions the possibility of pregnancy termination based on genetic results; this is a personal choice and should be discussed with medical professionals.

transcript: Oare tu cum alegi să faci, să aștepți o perioadă înainte să-ți anunți sarcina sau anunți imediat ce ai aflat? Eu sunt sărcinată în 24 de săptămâni chiar astăzi, când filmez acest video, adică, și m-am întors la această discuție pentru că îmi propusesem să fac asta încă de când am știut că vreau să așteptăm. Am așteptat să anunțăm sarcina cam 13 săptămâni și jumătate și nu nici măcar mama mea sau mama lui nu au știut până în punctul respectiv. Am anunțat toată familia odată la un grătar. Publicul larg îl am anunțat probabil pe la 20 de săptămâni, cred, și prietenii apropiați într-adevăr au știut un pic mai devreme. Noi am aflat de sarcină destul de devreme, între 4 și 5 săptămâni sau o chestie de genul ăsta, pentru că n-a fost o sarcină surpriză, a fost o sarcină programată și atunci am știut să-mi fac testul, nu știu. Mă rog, ideea este că de când am aflat și până când ne-am hotărât să le spunem apropiațiilor noștri, am trecut prin trosee de controle. Dacă aș fi pierdut sarcina singur, cred că aș fi ales la un moment dat să le zic și apropiațiilor noștri, probabil post-eveniment, dar ne-am dorit în primul rând să vedem dacă sarcina chiar rămâne și nu cumva o pierdem. Foarte multe cupluri pierd sarcina în primul trimestru și asta este un lucru obișnuit și am încercat cumva să nu ne legăm, poate sună ciudat, nu că să nu ne legăm sufletește foarte tare de această sarcină încă de la început, dar cumva am păstrat în minte că există și posibilitatea asta și hai un pic să dăm corpului timp și lucrurilor timp ca să nu fie foarte trist dacă s-ar întâmpla lucrul ăsta. Eu consider că e o gândire sănătoasă care pentru noi a funcționat, dar în același timp știu și că nu funcționează pentru toată lumea. Mai este o treabă pe care ne-am permis să o rezervăm pentru noi și anume să așteptăm să vină testele genetice, pentru că am făcut teste genetice, voiam să avem o reasigurare că totul se întâmplă într-un mod sănătos și că bebelușul în sine de viabil și este sănătos, pentru că în cazul în care am fi descoperit la testul genetic că lucrurile prezintă risc, noi am vrut să ne rezervăm dreptul de a alege pentru că gândul de a aduce pe lume un copilaj bolnav nu ne încânta onest și nu neapărat pentru că l-am fi respins sau alte lucruri de genul ăsta, ci pentru că sunt unele probleme medicale care fac ca viața să fie un chin și pentru bebeluși și pentru părinți și noi pur și simplu am vrut să ne rezervăm acest drept. Prin urmare am zis că ok, hai să așteptăm testul genetic și să vedem, bun, a trecut și momentul respectiv. Bun, îi dăm înainte și hai să ne gândim cum ne anunțăm familia, întâi de toate. Nu am anunțat-o prima dată pe mama, cum probabil foarte multe fete ar fi făcut în locul meu. Am avut chiar și un comentariu în care cineva îmi spunea că trebuie să fi fost foarte dureros pentru ea să nu știe din primul moment și pe care l-am contracarat destul de repede pentru că, onest, eu cred că momentul în care rămâi însărcinată este al tău și al partenerului tău și nu este al familiei sau al altcuiva. Devine ulterior după ce împărtășești cu ei, dar până atunci este dreptul tău să anunți în ce ordine vrei tu, cum vrei tu și pe cine vrei tu. Ne-am decis să ne anunțăm familia împreună, așa că ne-am rugat pe cumnatul meu să ne ajute să îi strângem pe toți la un grătar, ca să nu dea de bănuit că avem ceva să le spunem, i-a adunat ei. Și la acel grătar i-am anunțat pe toți, a fost foarte drăguț, toată lumea a fost foarte drăguță, au fost și nașii noștri de cununia acolo și efectiv chiar pot să zic că am anunțat toată familia în același timp. Mi-am dorit foarte tare să fie foarte echitabilă treaba asta, pentru că atunci când ne-am anunțat căsătoria, am anunțat fiecare la casele lui și a fost drăguț și așa, nu a existat nicio supărare, nimeni nu s-a întrebat oare al câtelea om am fost care a aflat și așa mai departe, doar că aici mi s-a părut, nu știu, dacă tot se înțeleg familiile bine, hai să-i punem la o lată și să-i anunțăm așa. Pe de o parte sunt super de acord să aștepți o perioadă înainte să începi să le spui oamenilor că ești inserținată, pentru că cred onest că perioada în care nu am zis nimănui nimic a fost cea mai frumoasă și nu că oamenii s-au purtat într-un fel anume cu noi după ce am anunțat, dar pur și simplu a fost acel ceva de care știam doar noi și cumva ne-a apropiat foarte tare. Deci, din punctul ăsta de vedere, super yay că am așteptat. Apoi, dacă știi că vrei să aștepți testul genetic și știi că vrei să ai obținuie în cazul în care se întâmplă ceva din nefericire și mai știi și că oamenii care te înconjoară nu ar fi de acord cu treaba asta, la fel, cred că e o idee foarte bună să aștepți și să-ți asiguri, cel puțin câte vreme mai există, să-ți asiguri dreptul de alege. În ales că e cu siguranță foarte dificil să treci printr-o asemenea procedură de întregrupere de sarcină dacă este nevoie sau chiar și de pierdut sarcina, atât fizic și psihic, nu mai zic dacă ai așteptat foarte multe vreme copilașul ăsta, poate să fie foarte dureros și poate să fie foarte greu ca oamenii din exterior să vină către tine cu toate intențiile bune, dar uneori nu cu cele mai bune replici. Și asta a fost partea bună a faptului că am așteptat. Partea mai puțin bună, sarcina oricum vine în sine cu foarte multe schimbări corporale, dar foarte multe schimbări hormonale și psihice și de toate. Sunt femei care au o sarcină dificilă și le este foarte rău fizic, dar psihic se simt ok sau psihic era într-un alt mindset atunci când au rămas însărcinate. Femei, de exemplu ca mine, care sunt foarte ok fizic, Eu chiar am o sarcină foarte ușoară din punct de vedere fizic și o doresc sincer în felul ăsta absolut tuturor oamenilor, dar pe care le lovesc foarte tare emoțional și sunt absolut convinsă că dacă ai un fond din ăsta anxios sau depresiv sau ai avut o depresie sau așa mai departe, ar trebui să fii extra atentă la tine că e foarte ușor să alunești. Și nu-ți dai seama cum arunești pe panta asta. Și, na, poate mai sunt și femei care nu au parte nici de unarea, nici de altarea. Și atunci ăla cred că este cazul ideal. Dar, după cum spuneam, partea mai nasoală a faptului că am așteptat mai mult până să anunța a fost faptul că nu am avut atât de mult suport moral pe cât nici nu mi-am dat seama că aș fi avut nevoie. Din fericire, eram și sunt într-un proces terapeutic și m-a ajutat foarte tare treaba asta dacă am putut să mai ventilez acolo multe dintre gândurile pe care le aveam și m-a ajutat și faptul că partenerul meu este un om care a reușit să... Nu vreau să zic că să se adune, că nu era neatunat, dar care a reușit cumva să vină în întâmpinarea mea cu toate gândurile, fricile și lucrurile care au venit odată cu sarcina și poate că au fost câteva momente în care mi-aș fi dorit să pot să vorbesc cu prietenele mele mai devreme despre asta sau să pot să vorbesc cu mama mai devreme despre asta, Deși sunt foarte multe lucruri care îți trec prin minte atunci când rămâi însărcinată pe care uneori nici prietenele tale apropiate nu pot să le înțeleagă, deși ele au toată bunăvoința să fie acolo lângă tine. Mi-am apreciat foarte mult când prietena mea apropiată mi-a zis zilele trecute că ea nu înțelege singurătatea asta pe care eu o resimt în sarcină, dar înțelege faptul că poate mi-e dificil. Și adevărul este că nici eu nu înțelegeam înainte că e treaba cu singurătatea asta în sarcină, despre care tot citeam prin toate cărțile, învățam în facultate și așa mai departe. Dar mi se pare că până când nu experimentez nu e același lucru. Apropo, mascara asta de la Girovital e foarte nice prin faptul că se demachează extrem de ușor numai cu apă. Spuse, astea sunt argumentele mele pro și contra dacă să aștepți să anunți sau nu. Tu cum ai făcut sau cum ai făcut într-o situație similară?

title: Doing Chinese Postpartum Confinement (Zuo Yuezi) in Hong Kong
summary: An American mother in Hong Kong describes completing 'sitting the month' (坐月子), the Chinese postpartum confinement tradition lasting 30-100 days. A live-in confinement nanny (月嫂) cooked four warm meals a day and helped with cleaning; she did ginger foot baths, avoided cold food and mostly stayed home to rest and bond, while going out for walks with her baby in a carrier when she needed to.
key_points: Zuo yuezi ('sitting the month') is a Chinese postpartum rest period of about 30-100 days focused on recovery and feeding the baby.
A 月嫂 (confinement nanny) can live in 24/7 to cook, clean and help with the baby.
Traditional practices she followed: only warm food, four meals a day, ginger foot baths every other day.
Hardest part for her was staying home and resting; she still went out for walks with baby in a carrier.
Core idea worth borrowing: plan real help and rest for the first month.

Postpartum confinement is well-documented in China, where the custom is known as "Sitting the month": 坐月子 "Zuò yuè zi" in Mandarin or 坐月 "Co5 Jyut2" in Cantonese. [11] The period of confinement ranges from 30 to 100 days. Confinement for one month (30 days) is considered "mini confinement" while confinement for three months (100 days) is considered "full confinement". After 100 days, the Hundred Days Banquet (百日宴) is held to celebrate the baby reaching 100 days old.

The Chinese custom of postpartum confinement is documented as far back as the year 960. [12] Women are advised to stay indoors for recovery from the trauma of birth and for feeding the newborn baby. Aspects of traditional Chinese medicine are included, with a special focus on

Women are advised to stay indoors for recovery from the trauma of birth and for feeding the newborn baby. Aspects of traditional Chinese medicine are included, with a special focus on eating foods considered to be nourishing for the body and helping with the production of breastmilk.

In Guangdong and neighboring regions, new mothers are barred from visitors until the baby is 12 days old, marked by a celebration called 'Twelve mornings' (known as 十二朝). From this day onwards, Cantonese families with a new baby usually share their joy through giving away food gifts, while some families mark the occasion by paying tribute to their ancestors. author: helmut_granda
title: Don't Dismiss Kids' 'Why' Questions
summary: Clip of a man in a TV interview arguing that questions like 'why is the grass green?' or 'why is the sky blue?' are profound, and dismissing them ('don't ask dumb questions') teaches kids that using their mind is bad. Better to say it's a good question, admit you don't know, and look it up together.
key_points: Never answer a child's question with 'don't ask dumb questions' or 'who knows'.
Praise the question, admit if you don't know, and look up the answer together.
Encouraging curiosity keeps kids willing to think deeply.
scripts: That's a good question. I don't know the answer — maybe we can look it up.
Nobody knows — maybe when you grow up, you'll be the person to find out.
transcript: For example, a kid asks, Mommy, why is the grass green? And very often you get an answer like, oh, don't ask dumb questions, or who knows, when in fact it's an extremely profound question. And how much better would it be? Why is the sky blue, or anything like that? In both those cases, it goes to the fundamentals, in one case of biology, in the other, of a kind of physics. How much better it would be to say to the child, that's a good question, Johnny, I don't know the answer, maybe we can look it up. or nobody knows, maybe when you grow up, you'll be the person to find out. I think kids who are discouraged from asking those questions wind up learning the lesson that there's something bad about using the mind, and we lose resources, and we need those intellectual resources because we are in very perilous times. And I think the complex and subtle problems that we face can only have complex and subtle solutions, and we need people able to think complex and subtle thoughts. And I believe a great many children have that capability if only they're encouraged.

title: Don't assume - ask: a toddler's 'mess' was really cleaning up
summary: A dad shows a toddler throwing oats in the bin and then the sink, which looked like making a mess. By stepping back and asking questions, he discovered she was trying to clean up the whole time. key_points: Before reacting to 'misbehaviour', ask what the child is trying to do - her intention was to clean up, not make more mess.
Avoid threats like 'If you don't listen, we won't make porridge again' based on assumptions.
Too many questions and comments while a child is focused on a task fall on deaf ears.
Once you know the intention, guide it: remind them of the correct way (e.g. show how you wiped the counter before).

Stop throwing the oats in the sink. If you don't listen, we won't be making porridge again. Commonly used responses. Why did that go in the sink? The way you talk about yourself and your body in front of your kids can have a massive impact on how they see themselves. When they hear you criticize your appearance or talk negatively about your body, they pick up on that, and it can shape their own self-image. But here’s the thing—you deserve to see yourself for how amazing you truly are. Your body is just one part of you, and honestly, it’s the least interesting thing about you.

You’re kind, you’re strong, you’re capable of so much, and those are the qualities that really matter. author: wellnessandwisdom
title: Don't say 'I'm fine' when you're not: honesty keeps kids' intuition intact
summary: A podcast guest (a dad) describes his young daughter sensing he was upset and asking if he was okay. He first said 'I'm fine', then corrected himself, thanked her for noticing and admitted he was working through something. He argues denying what a child correctly senses disconnects them from their intuition, and sharing feelings honestly shows kids they don't need to be perfect.
key_points: If your child notices you're upset, don't deny it - an 'I'm fine' gives them an inaccurate reflection and teaches them to distrust their perception.
Thank them for noticing and give an honest, age-appropriate explanation without burdening them.
It's okay to correct yourself a minute later if you reflexively said 'I'm fine'.
Showing imperfection helps kids feel they can show their emotions too.

I started to do a 'shake it out' dance when I'm in a bad mood. I shake out each body part from head to toe so they see me choosing to shift my energy on purpose instead of just staying grumpy. Now my son does it with me which makes us both laugh and we practice doing it when he's grumpy too.

I explain my emotions to my kids like the weather. Feeling happy is like a sunny day, sad is like a rainy day...and just like the weather emotions aren’t bad and they always change! We feel our emotions, we let them tell us what we need and then we can let them go when we’re done with them.

I want my kids to know their emotions are always okay AND they don’t have to hold onto them forever. I want them to know that they have the power to create an incredible life with their own minds. That’s truly the greatest gift I could ever leave them with!!

caption:
As a mom of five, I’ve learned to be really intentional about what enters our home. Not because I’m anti-toys… but because I want their play to feel imaginative and open ended, and we personally thrive with less stuff. 

So a handful of years ago, I realized that asking family members for experiences over things, was a huge blessing, not just for the children, but for them as well! So when family asks what to get the kids, I gently steer the conversation toward the things that make memories—not clutter. The gifts they remember long after the wrapping paper is gone.

Here are five ideas I always share:

✨A membership or pass - the zoo, a children’s museum, a local farm, the state park. Something that gives them a whole year of adventure, and opportunities to invite that family along with us!

✨A special outing together - a movie date, lunch at their favorite café. Kids will always remember time over things.

✨A skill-building experience - pottery class, music lessons, sewing lessons, baking days. Something that nurtures their interests.

✨a subscription the child can receive in the mail each month- some we have enjoyed are National Geographic for kids, Ranger Rick, highlights, wild flower girls, and Daphne’s diary! Plus the child can share things they loved that month with the gifter! 

✨A project they can do with that family member - a birdhouse kit, a bread-baking afternoon, a craft box, a day spent learning a new hobby side by side.

✨A family trip - obviously this one is a larger gift but one that can be so fun - a trip together, making memories!

Because childhood is so short…and honestly, what they remember isn’t the toy —it’s the moments they felt loved and poured into! 

What do you all think? Do you do this too? If you have any other ideas, feel free to drop them below!

A de novo mutation is a new genetic alteration present for the first time in a family member, resulting from a variant in a parent's germ cell (egg/sperm) or occurring during early embryo development. These mutations are not inherited from either parent. They occur spontaneously during DNA replication and can cause genetic conditions, with rates increasing with parental age.
Key Aspects of De Novo Mutations
- Definition: Meaning 'new' or 'fresh' in Latin; the child has a mutation not present in the parents' blood or tissue.
- Occurrence: In the parent's germ cells (germline) or during fertilization.
- Mosaicism: A condition where a person has a genetic condition in some cells but not others, a consequence of a de novo mutation.

author: drdianasharp
title: Five parent traits linked to highly successful kids ('The Formula')
summary: A cognitive psychologist summarises research by Ronald Ferguson and Tatsha Robertson (book 'The Formula', 2019) from hundreds of interviews with highly successful adults. Common parent traits: a burning desire to parent well, making early learning playful, showing kids a world of possibilities, engaging in deep conversations about meaning, and supporting the child's own goals rather than the parent's.
key_points: Parents had an unusually strong drive to raise their child as well as they could.
Before kindergarten they taught early maths and reading in playful ways - it felt like play, not desk work.
They exposed children to many possible paths (e.g. a zookeeper who loves their work), not just prestigious careers.
They took children's big questions seriously, sometimes thinking about them for a day or two before answering.
They helped children pursue what mattered to the child, not to the parent.
The book describes eight parenting roles; all are learnable.

caption:
No one is a perfect parent.

But studies like this one can help us learn new ways to support our kids as they figure out what they care about and work toward their dreams.

Harvard economist Ronald Ferguson and journalist Tatsha Robertson asked: Are there common ways parents of happy, highly successful young adults supported them, even across families with very different income levels and cultural backgrounds?

They analyzed hundreds of interviews and published what they learned in a book: The Formula: Unlocking the Secrets to Raising Highly Successful Children (2019).

What surprised them? They found common patterns across a wide variety of families.

They called these the eight roles of parenting. My video describes four, and I’ve put all eight in the pinned comments below.

What I find especially encouraging is this: every one of these roles is learnable. You don’t have to be born knowing how to do them, and you certainly don’t have to do them perfectly.

Here’s one of the most important findings, and it fits well with what we know from the science of learning and motivation. These parents intentionally looked for ways to help their children discover their own dreams and develop the skills and confidence to pursue them.

For about half of the young adults in the book, Harvard happened to be part of that path toward their real dream. Accidentally. 😊

The takeaway? You are not the only factor in your child’s successes or struggles. But you can support them in powerful ways that no one else can.

And you can learn how to get better at it. That’s one reason I value research on the science of parenting so much.

Like all research about the wilds of parenting, this study has limitations. But it also has unusual depth and breadth.

Check out the pinned comments for all eight parenting roles, and send me any questions you have about the study or how you might apply these ideas in your own family! ❤️ #parentingtips #scienceoflearning #scienceofparenting

caption:
Gentle parenting encompasses four main elements: empathy, respect, understanding, and working with personal boundaries. Despite its name, gentle parenting also implies maintaining a certain level of discipline. The key is for the rules set by the parent to be age-appropriate and conducive to the child’s development.

The primary tool for a parent should be words, not shouts or imposing boycotts. This approach can protect the child from unnecessary anxiety, teach them to act in challengi, make decisions independently, and not fear making mistakes. Such flexibility will help them adapt easily, first in school and then in independent life.

It’s important to understand: gentle parenting by no means suggests permissiveness or the absence of discipline.

This technique requires a parent to have a great deal of patience and compassion, especially in moments when a child throws a tantrum or refuses to do what is required of them. Following the principles of gentle parenting can be particularly challenging for moms and dads in such situations.

summary: A mother describes raising her kids with the spirit of a 1990s childhood but with modern knowledge: no screens in the car, lots of colouring, outdoor play, boredom, chores and old-school games, combined with car-seat safety, nutritious food, regulated nervous systems and adults who apologise. Mostly lifestyle inspiration.
key_points: No screens in the car - let kids look out the window and let their minds wander.
Long unstructured stretches of colouring, painting, outdoor/forest play and collecting things.
Let them be bored: when she declines to play, they invent games (e.g. 'the floor is lava').
Involve kids in cleaning and chores.
Prefer simpler, slower games that don't over-guide; limit YouTube/app time.
Sweets only at parties (her rule); keep modern safety such as proper car seats.

transcript: Part 2 of how I'm giving my kids a 90s childhood without the bad bits. Like Sonny D, the body shaming, and the bit where the kids just bounce around the back of the car like fucking teddy bears. No screens in the car, just letting them look out the window so their minds can wander. Colouring and painting for hours on end. Playing the radio in the background. Stick fights in the forest. Epic. Getting them hyped about old computer games that challenge the mind, build focus and spark imagination. Games that don't overguide or overwhelm like many modern games. Collecting piles of things for no reason. Selecting a DVD to watch on a projector if it's a nighttime movie as there's far less blue light exposure. I make them help me with the cleaning and when I refuse to play with them they come up with amazing games. Look, the floor is lava! The goal is to bring them up like it's 1996 but with nutritious food, regulated nervous systems and adults who model real apologies.

caption:
90s parenting, but eh…TWEAKED 😅✨ No “angel delight” but also…no watching toy hauls on YouTube. Lots of made-up songs, playing with sticks and making bedsheet tents…less of the TV babysitter 😂

Look I AM raising my kids with some of the 2025 perks (hello, Tonibox and foldable scooters) but really trying to keep the spirit of our ’90s days alive. Think: crafting > unmonitored time on apps. Getting dirty outside and learning by doing > 4 hours a day of YouTube kids brain rot. 

Was 90s parenting perfect? No. That’s why I’m taking some and leaving the rest 😂 No “do it because I said so” and no menu of coco pops followed by Nutella crackers followed by Nutella on UPF toast. But yes to the letting us be bored! YES to the making us help with chores! YES to all the outdoors time! 

What are your modern parenting rules that would confuse your ’90s parents? 😂 Mine is “sweets are for parties only (coz colorectal cancer is on the rise wahayyyy) … sweets were their go-to bribe haha. I mean, it always worked 🤪 But my kids genuinely think dry All Bran or 85% organic dark chocolate is THE SH*T it works just as good 🤣

My first reel on this brought in thousands of new followers. HELLO! Swear I’m not AI haha I’ve been posting content (primarily on YouTube) since 2013! Xx 💋

author: inourhouseandhome
title: Habits one mom avoids so kids learn discomfort isn't an emergency
summary: A creator who has worked with kids and families for a decade lists habits she avoids to build tolerance for boredom and frustration: background TV, screens in waiting rooms and cars, snacks to stop emotions, negotiating after a decision, repeating herself many times, over-explaining during meltdowns, giving in after escalation, constant stimulation, and instantly rescuing from every uncomfortable feeling. Her claim: short-term peace can create long-term chaos.
key_points: Avoid constant background TV and noise; kids' nervous systems need quiet.
Skip screens in waiting rooms and in the car to build patience, conversation and boredom tolerance.
Don't use snacks to stop every emotion — that teaches comfort instead of coping.
Don't negotiate after you've given an answer; don't repeat yourself 14 times before following through.
During meltdowns, say less; over-explaining adds stimulation.
Don't hand back the item after a meltdown escalates — it teaches intensity works.
Don't instantly rescue from every uncomfortable feeling.
credentials: a decade working with kids and families (as stated)
caution: Firm generalisations (e.g. what each habit 'teaches the brain') are the creator's opinion; use judgement — comforting a distressed child is not the same as rescuing from all discomfort.
onscreen: Things I go without so my kids learn discomfort isn’t an emergency...
caption:
THE NON-NEGOTIABLES ⬇️

⚡️Constant background TV → teaches the brain to rely on constant input

⚡️iPads in every waiting room → removes opportunities to build patience and boredom tolerance

⚡️Endless snacks to stop every emotion → teaches comfort instead of coping

⚡️Negotiating after I already gave the answer → teaches persistence changes boundaries

⚡️Repeating myself 14 times before follow through → trains kids not to respond the first time

⚡️Using screens to avoid boredom in the car → removes creativity, conversation, and frustration tolerance

⚡️Over-explaining during meltdowns → adds stimulation to an already overwhelmed brain

⚡️Giving back the thing after the meltdown escalates → reinforces intensity as a strategy

⚡️Constant noise and stimulation all day long → keeps nervous systems dysregulated

⚡️Immediate rescue from every uncomfortable feeling → prevents resilience from developing

Because here’s what I learned after a decade working with kids and families…

Short-term peace can create long-term chaos.

Every time intensity changes the outcome, the brain logs it.
Every time discomfort gets rescued instantly, tolerance stays low.
Every time a boundary disappears because the reaction got bigger, the pattern gets stronger.

This is not about being strict or a “no funner mom”
It’s about understanding what behavior is practicing every single day.

I’m not raising kids who only function when life is convenient, stimulating, and tailored to them 24/7.

I’m raising kids who can tolerate boredom. Hear no without collapsing. Exist without constant entertainment. Regulate without needing someone else to fix every feeling immediately.

That’s the shift.

And most parents are not failing because they’re bad parents…

They’re failing because nobody ever taught them how behavior actually works.

Comment ROOT if you’re ready to stop managing moments and start changing patterns.

summary: A mum explains that her kids' after-school meltdowns were mostly hunger plus tiredness. She now hands them a snack (a smoothie in a lidded mason jar) the moment they get in the car, before any complaints, and says it brings immediate calm.

title: Having a newborn with ADHD: what was hard and what was easier
summary: A mom with ADHD, three weeks postpartum, shares what has been harder, easier and better than expected. Hard: emotional regulation with poor sleep, and sensory overstimulation while recovering and learning to breastfeed. Easier: executive function ('mom brain' figuring out routines) and people-pleasing (easier to say no). Going well: life slowing down and bonding.
key_points: Sleep deprivation can amplify ADHD-related emotional dysregulation and worry; remind yourself 'this is tired worry brain', not reality.
Expect sensory overload postpartum (pain, itching, learning to breastfeed, crying); it improves day by day.
Executive dysfunction may be less of a problem than feared as baby-care routines become automatic.
The newborn phase can make it easier to say no to people and stop people-pleasing.
Look for ADHD-specific pregnancy support: she recommends ADHD coach Dusty Chipura's support groups and workbook.

author: moniquecesd
title: Hiding vegetables in yogurt for an autistic child with severe food selectivity
summary: A Brazilian mum of an autistic son with severe food selectivity (he accepts only yogurt) shows how she gradually blends other foods into his yogurt: egg white, zucchini, beetroot, carrot, sweet potato and a cornstarch porridge made with almond milk because of a milk allergy. She started with a few drops and increased slowly.
key_points: Start by adding just a few drops of a vegetable purée (she began with beetroot and sweet potato) to the one accepted food, then increase slowly.
The child may notice the colour change; keep the taste and texture as close to the safe food as possible.
Egg white was easiest to hide because it changes neither taste nor texture.
Because of a cow's milk allergy, she makes cornstarch porridge with almond milk and adds a spoonful at a time.
Foods hidden over time: egg white, zucchini, beetroot, carrot, sweet potato, cornstarch porridge.
caution: Severe food selectivity (only one accepted food) needs assessment by a paediatrician, dietitian and feeding therapist; hiding foods is one family's workaround, not a treatment plan.

title: Hiking with toddlers: tips from a therapist mom
summary: A therapist mom started taking her daughter on short hikes as soon as she could walk to burn energy; now at two she out-hikes her mom on a one-mile loop. The caption shares tips: bring a carrying option at first, don't expect them to walk the whole way, and drop distance/time goals because toddlers hike slowly.
key_points: Start short hikes as soon as a child walks; daily outdoor time also helps the parent cope.
Bring a carrying option at first (stroller, carrier or another adult); don't expect toddlers to walk the whole way.
With practice her 2-year-old needs almost no carrying on trails under about 1.5 miles.
Don't set a distance goal, or if you do, have no time expectations; toddlers stop to dig and climb.
Rushing makes it less enjoyable; let them explore.
Teach that they can't get too far and must come back to you.

products.name: carrier
products.type: Allows carrying a toddler during longer hikes.

onscreen: When you started taking her hiking to help her burn energy, but....
Jokes on you because it just made her stronger with better endurance
caption:
When your two year old can lap you on the trails 😅. 

I started taking Lila out for short hikes as soon as she could walk. We both love being outside, and honestly as a mom getting outside every day is a huge part of my parenting strategy. 

There noise is easier to deal with. No one hates some fresh air. And initially it was an easy way to let Lila work off some energy. 

But man oh man, the joke is now firmly on me. 

Yesterday, I took her and a friend out for a one mile loop we’ve done countless times. And honestly, I could barely keep up. 😅

Thankfully, she fully understands she can’t get too far and always comes back. 

But I’m just so amazed. At her strength. Her endurance. Her abilities. All as a young toddler. 

Some tips for hiking with toddlers:
✨bring some sort of carrying option when you’re getting started. A stroller, a carrier, another adult. Haha. At this point, I know anything under about 1.5 miles will require so little carrying from me, I bring nothing. But don’t start out with the expectation that they will walk the whole time 
✨don’t have a distance goal. Or if you, have no time expectations. Toddlers hike slow. They stop to dig. They jump off rocks. Rushing makes the experience a whole lot less fun. 
✨snack - if you’ve got a toddler, I shouldn’t need to explain this 
✨embrace the mess - you’re gonna leave dirty. That’s ok. It’s good. It’s great for sensory integration and building immunity. Just look away if it really bothers you. 
✨bring friends - it’s such a game changer to feel like I can actually have a full conversation w a friend. I can’t do that at a playground. But on the trail? There’s so much more freedom. 

Getting out of the house every day is almost a non-negotiable at this point. And I loooove watching my kids get stronger and build their endurance. Plus it’s just an easy way to reduce screen time. 

Inspo: @madimscott 

Have you taken your toddler hiking yet? It’s a 10/10 experience for me.

author: nikkiivoryhealing
title: How dismissing a child's crying teaches them to suppress emotions
summary: A somatic healer acts out a parent saying 'What are you crying about? You're fine. Stop crying or go to your room' and voices the beliefs the child forms: big emotions aren't safe, expressing them risks disconnection, so they must be suppressed. She argues this can lead to adults who dissociate and struggle with regulation, depression and anxiety.
key_points: Avoid dismissive responses like 'You're fine', 'Enough', 'Stop crying or go to your room'
Children need an emotionally attuned caregiver who empathises and helps them process feelings in order to learn regulation
Repeated dismissal can teach: big feelings aren't safe, expressing them threatens connection, so suppress them
Adults raised this way may struggle to feel or express emotions
caution: Presents a deterministic chain (dismissal → chronic depression/anxiety) as fact; the general point about emotional attunement is mainstream, but outcomes are not that certain. Creator is not a licensed therapist.
transcript: What are you crying about? You're fine. Enough. I don't want to hear that. So either stop crying or go to your room. Okay, so what I'm learning is it's not safe to feel big emotions. That feeling and expressing my big emotions results in disconnection from my caregiver, which puts my survival at risk. So in order to remain in connection with my caregivers, which is necessary for my survival at this age, I must suppress my emotions. I'm essentially learning that feeling is bad and I must disconnect from the place in which I feel them, which is my body. That's for 20 years and I'll be an adult who doesn't know how to feel or express their emotions and uses dissociation or disconnection from self as a means of coping. Life will feel really dull and I will likely be chronically depressed and anxious.

caption:
If your childhood resembled this to ANY degree, you likely have trouble with emotional regulation today.

SHARE this with something who may have had a similar experience so they can feel seen and validated too 🫶🏻

Emotional attunement is a CORE NEED during childhood. We need an emotionally attuned caregiver who is able to empathize with our emotions AND help us process them, in order to learn how to regulate our emotions.

When we have an experience similar to the one in this video, we develop the following core beliefs:

‼️ It’s not safe to feel big emotions

‼️ Feeling and expressing big emotions creates disconnection from caregiver and in turn threatens survival

‼️ In order to survive I must suppress my emotions

‼️ Feeling is bad, I must disconnect from my body, the place in which I feel them

Through somatic work we have to power to learn how to feel our emotions in a way that doesn’t feel so overwhelming and unsafe.

title: How parents checked their daughter after a bad snowboard crash
summary: Parents of a young snowboarder show how they responded to one of her hardest crashes. One parent stopped other riders from dropping in while the other checked her spine and neck before moving her out of the landing, then asked about pain in specific body parts and tested movement before calmly praising her and letting her try again. The caption notes the mom is first-aid and first-responder certified and stresses knowing how to help or calm a child until help arrives.
key_points: If you see the impact, note where and how the child hit — it helps assess injuries.
Secure the scene first: stop others (e.g., riders above) from coming into the area.
Check spine and neck before moving the child; only move them if they can move safely.
Ask about pain in each area (bottom, back, head, arms), then check movement: look fully left/right, arms up, arm across the body.
Give the child time to calm down, then praise effort and let them decide whether to continue.
Parents of kids in risky sports should consider first-aid training.

caption:
This crash scared the hell out of us as her parents. No doubt is it one of the hardest crashes we have seen her take but her strength to overcome it to try again is a testament to her resilience and talent. 

Crashes are hard to watch, but the reality is that they do happen. Especially when you are trying new things. In order to let little Cashy follow her heart and fly we have to put our fear aside and let her push herself how she wants. 

With that being said, we were lucky it wasn’t worse of a slam. This sport is gnarly. In order to progress (if that is her choice) she is going to have to go bigger and faster which could result in a few bumps, bruises or breaks.

It is our job as her parents to make sure that we know how to help her or at the very least calm her down while help arrives. Whit is both first aid and first responder certified. 

What you don’t see in this shortened video is that we both saw the impact in person so we know where and how she hit. Whit stopped and held up other riders from dropping while I did a quick check on the spine and neck to make sure she could move out of the jump landing. After we got her to the side of the park and somewhat calming her down we started with injury protocol. We asked questions, and then started having her move everything in order to distract her as well as teach her how to really concentrate on if there is pain.

We sat on the side of that jump line for a good 30 minutes checking everything, taking deep breaths and then eventually laughing. Once we all, Cash included, determined that she was fine she went off to smash the rest of this long run to the lift. Not only did she get herself down to the lift, she wanted to go back and have another go at the jumps!

I know that people get mad at the crashes, hence why we don’t put many up but they truly are an important part of the process. Our hope is that this video at least helps one other parent with injury protocol and remaining calm after a heavy crash.

title: Husbands: make your wife feel seen as a woman, not only a mom
summary: A text-on-screen post (story in the caption) about asking husbands what changed most in their wives after kids. He realised he thanked her as a mother but hadn't made her feel seen as his wife, and learned to ask about her day and remind her she is still the woman he fell in love with.

onscreen: I Asked Husbands What Changed In Their Wives After Kids. Most Didn't Mention The Kids At All:
caption:
I asked a group of husbands what changed the most in their wives after they became parents.

Most of the answers were predictable.

„She worries more.“

„She’s always tired.“

„She puts the kids first.“

Then one man said something I didn’t expect.

„My wife stopped feeling like anyone noticed her.“

He explained that everyone kept asking about the baby.

How the baby was sleeping.

How the baby was growing.

Whether the baby was eating enough.

Almost nobody asked how she was doing.

Not really.

She was surrounded by people every day, but somehow felt more invisible than ever.

Then he said something that stayed with me.

„I realized I was thanking her for everything she did as a mom.“

„But I hadn’t made her feel seen as my wife in a long time.“

That hit harder than I expected.

Because becoming parents changed both of their lives.

But only one of them slowly started feeling like their entire identity had disappeared.

He told me the biggest thing he learned wasn’t to help more around the house.

It was to remind her that before she became the mother of his children, she was the woman he fell in love with.

Sometimes that meant asking about her day instead of the kids‘.

Sometimes it meant planning an evening that had nothing to do with parenting.

Sometimes it simply meant looking at her like she was more than the person holding everything together.

Kids didn’t change who she was.

They just made it easier for everyone else to forget.

title: Introducing broccoli to babies: cut, rest 30 minutes, then steam
summary: A medical chemist and mother explains why she introduced broccoli (before cauliflower) mixed with carrot during her baby's start of solids. She cuts broccoli and lets it rest about 30 minutes so the enzyme myrosinase can convert glucoraphanin into sulforaphane before heat inactivates the enzyme, then steams it lightly. Carrot is paired to make digestion gentler, as broccoli can cause gas.
key_points: Introduce broccoli before cauliflower: both can cause gas, but broccoli is usually better tolerated.
Start with a small amount mixed with an already-tolerated food like carrot.
Cut broccoli into small pieces and let it sit ~30 minutes before cooking to allow sulforaphane to form.
Then steam gently; heat inactivates the myrosinase enzyme.
Broccoli contains fermentable fibres (raffinose, fructans) and sulphur compounds that can cause gas; carrot's pectin is gentler.

title: Jesy Nelson shares her premature twins' SMA type 1 diagnosis
summary: Singer Jesy Nelson tells how her premature twin daughters were diagnosed with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) type 1 after months of appointments. SMA type 1 is the most severe form: it progressively weakens muscles including limbs, breathing and swallowing; untreated, life expectancy is under about 2 years.
Treatment is time-critical; her daughters were treated quickly even before full confirmation.
Trust your instincts and keep pushing if you feel something is wrong, even when told everything looks fine.
caution: Personal story; medical details are from a parent's perspective. Ask your doctor about newborn screening for SMA, which exists in some countries, and seek review for any baby with weak or floppy movements or worsening feeding.

author: noahbsimmons
title: KidNet: A DIY Ad-Free Digital Sandbox for Kids
summary: The creator introduces KidNet, a DIY project built on a Raspberry Pi that creates a closed, ad-free, and algorithm-free digital environment for children. It includes curated educational tools, creative apps, and a safe social space, designed to be an offline-style alternative to the open internet.
key_points: KidNet is a curated, offline-style digital sandbox for kids.
It runs on a Raspberry Pi connected to a monitor via HDMI.
Features include an offline Wikipedia, world map, creative tools, and a local social network.
The system is designed to be ad-free and algorithm-free.

products.name: Raspberry Pi
products.type: Single-board computer used to host the KidNet platform.

products.name: HDMI cable
products.type: Connects the device to a monitor for display.

caution: This is a DIY technical project; ensure proper setup and safety when using electronics with children.
transcript: I'm an uncle who deeply cares about his nephews, and for the past nine months, I've been building something to try and solve the brain rot epidemic, and it's called KidNet. It's a mini internet for kids, and I want to show you how it works. All you have to do is plug KidNet in and connect to its Wi-Fi the same way you would your home Wi-Fi. Then just go to kidnet.local to get to the homepage, and it works on tablets and phones too. We've settled into this elegant user interface that's kid-friendly but not too childish. Kids get to make their own avatars to make it feel more personalized, and they get to add cool little widgets to their board that they collect by exploring through KidNet. Kids have access to research tools, such as a simplified offline version of Wikipedia that's easy for them to read, a fully offline, zoomable map of the entire world, and a number of creative tools, such as our flipbook animator, our puppet show maker, and our storybook writer, just to name a few. KidNet is not connected to the internet but that doesn't mean they can't socialize with friends and family that their parents approve of. Kids can easily play multiplayer games across devices with their friends and siblings and it even has a mini social media called The Buzz where they can make posts and share things with their friends and family. There are tons of things to do in KidNet and we're spending a lot of time making it rewarding and encouraging exploration by making it endlessly deep with little Easter eggs and events that make kids happy. In a world full of subscriptions, we're going the complete opposite way. Every tool, app, and piece of software on KidNet is yours once you purchase it. If you want to be the first to know when it launches, join the waitlist in my bio.
onscreen: Outer space, commonly shortened to space, is the near-vacuum between celestial bodies. It is where all of the planets, stars, galaxies and objects are found. It is the expanse that exists beyond Earth and its atmosphere.

On Earth, space begins at the Karman line (100 km above sea level). This is where Earth's atmosphere is said to stop and outer space begins. This is not a natural boundary but is a convention used by scientists and diplomats.
Geospace is the region of outer space near Earth. It includes the upper region of the atmosphere and the magnetosphere. The Van Allen radiation belt lies within the geospace.
The space inside the magnetosphere is protected from radiation from the Sun, our closest star. It has a low level of electrically charged particles.

Interplanetary space is the space around the Sun and planets of the Solar System. It has the solar wind, a continuous stream of charged particles from the Sun. This stream creates a very thin atmosphere (the Heliosphere) for billions of miles or kilometers into space.

Interplanetary space has the magnetic field generated by the Sun. Planets such as Jupiter, Saturn, Mercury and the Earth also have Magnetospheres. These magnetic fields can trap particles from the solar wind and other sources, creating belts of magnetic particles such as the Van Allen radiation belt. The solar wind gradually strips off the atmospheres of planets without magnetic fields, like Mars.
Interstellar space is the physical space in a galaxy that is not occupied by stars or their planetary systems. It continues to the edges of the galaxy, where it fades into the intergalactic void.
Most of the mass in this space is made up of single hydrogen atoms, fewer helium atoms and a few heavier atoms formed in stars. Supernovae blow some of their atoms huge distances.

author: onesikhmom
title: Kids learn to say no to alcohol by watching parents refuse
summary: A mom tells how relatives pressured her non-drinking husband over 20 times to have a drink at a family party while their teenage daughter overheard from the next room. The daughter was angry at the disrespect but learned two lessons: adults get peer-pressured too, and if dad could resist that much pressure, so can she. Part of an alcohol miniseries from a Punjabi-Canadian family.
key_points: Children watch how you handle peer pressure, even when you don't realise it.
Politely and repeatedly declining alcohol ('No thank you, I'm good') models refusal skills for teens.
Showing that adults face peer pressure too helps teens feel less alone with it.
scripts: No thank you, I'm good.
dedupe: model saying no to alcohol peer pressure
transcript: You never know when your kids are watching you. Years ago my husband and I we went to a family party and my husband was asked to have a drink. I was also asked to have a drink by the ladies and I politely declined. My husband was surrounded by a group of men all of them being relatives and they continuously put pressure on him to have a drink. Over the years my husband and I we just stopped drinking alcohol. As our kids got older we made a decision to just stop drinking. So these people may not have known that. One individual in particular he was relentless. He must have asked husband about 20 times to have a drink and each time my husband said no thank you i'm good over 20 times i'm not exaggerating what my husband didn't know was that our teenage daughter was actually sitting in the room next to them and she could hear everything she was furious she hated how these people who were family were putting pressure on her dad and they wouldn't respect his answer of no but it taught her two things one adults get peer pressured too two if her dad was able to resist that amount of pressure, then it's possible that she can too.
onscreen: years ago my husband and I
I was also asked to have a drink by the ladies
on him to have a drink
we made a decision to just stop drinking
caption:
As a nondrinker, the pressure from family or friends to have “just one glass” can be heavy. Often times, the only nondrinkers in the room happen to be me & my husband. The persistence to drink reminds us of the same pressure put on us when we were teenagers.

This experience taught our daughter two things:
1- Adults can also get peer pressured into doing things we don’t want to do.
2- Saying no to alcohol in front of our children helps them realize that they can say no too.

Have your kids ever approached you regarding alcohol or your use of alcohol?

1/5 Alcohol Miniseries
Disclaimer: The stories we share are our experiences with alcohol as second generation immigrants in Canada. These videos are meant to start a discussion on alcohol’s use and abuse in your home & in the community.

title: L&D triage skit: itchy palms and soles at 35 weeks
summary: A nurse acts out a labor and delivery triage scene where a 35-week pregnant woman casually reports itchy palms and soles with no rash, and the nurse reacts with alarm, monitoring the baby and ordering bloodwork. The humorous skit highlights that this symptom pattern (possible cholestasis) is not 'normal pregnancy itch' and needs testing; the caption notes it's exaggerated but still concerning.
key_points: Itching only on palms and soles without a rash in late pregnancy can signal cholestasis and needs blood tests.
Don't assume it's dry skin; report it to your provider/L&D.
Expect fetal monitoring and bloodwork if you present with these symptoms.
caution: Dramatized; the real response is testing and possibly treatment, not usually an emergency.

author: cozybabysleep
title: Lay a sleeping baby down feet first to avoid the startle reflex
summary: A baby sleep consultant's short tip: when transferring a sleeping baby, lower them feet first (then bottom, then head) rather than head first, to avoid triggering the Moro/startle reflex and waking them.
key_points: Transfer a sleeping baby by lowering feet first, then bottom, then head.
Head-first lowering can trigger the startle (Moro) reflex and wake the baby.
Keep the baby close to your body during the transfer.
caution: Always place the baby on their back on a flat, empty sleep surface.

author: foodbyjenn
title: Layer crib sheets and pads for fast middle-of-the-night changes
summary: A mom shows the 'double layering' hack: put waterproof pee pads (bought cheaper in the pet section) on the mattress, then a fitted sheet, then repeat. When there's a leak or spill, rip off the top sheet and pads to reveal a clean bed underneath.
key_points: Layer: mattress → pads → fitted sheet → pads → fitted sheet.
For a quick change, strip the top sheet and pads; a clean set is ready underneath.
Pet-section pee pads are much cheaper than baby-branded ones.
Especially useful for night-time leaks, vomit or spilled bottles.

products.name: waterproof pee pads
products.type: Protects mattress from leaks and spills.

products.name: fitted sheet
products.type: Used for layering to allow quick changes.

caution: Safe-sleep guidance calls for a firm, flat, tight-fitting surface with nothing loose; make sure layered pads and sheets are completely flat and tightly fitted, and avoid loose pads for young babies (pet pads may also contain scents/gels).

ill.caption: Baby mattress with fitted sheet layered over a waterproof cover

transcript: If I could suggest any tip to any new mom out there, it would be this. Line your baby's mattress with pee pads before you put on the sheet and get them from the pet section. They're like double the price if you get them in the baby section. And once you've got that first layer on, do the exact same thing again with the second layer so that when it's time to change the sheets, especially if you have to do it in the middle of the night, all you have to do is rip off that top layer sheet, pull off the dirty pads, then you have a fresh and clean brand new sheet and pad set up underneath. author: sonshinemagazine
title: Let boys dress as female characters for Halloween
summary: A parenting-for-equality creator asks why parents happily let daughters dress as male characters but hesitate with sons dressing as female ones. She argues that shutting this down teaches boys that women aren't aspirational, and that affirming such choices helps sons see women as equals, while acknowledging the real fear of teasing.
key_points: Notice any double standard: girls as Harry Potter is fine, boys as Hermione often isn't.
Telling boys they can't be a female character can imply girls aren't worth looking up to.
Affirm your son's choice of female heroes to support seeing women as equals.
Caption: children often self-censor by about age 7, so start early.
If you worry about teasing, give your child tools to respond rather than banning the choice.
caution: Values-based opinion.
dedupe: boys dress as female characters halloween
transcript: Would you let your child dress as a character of a different gender for Halloween? Well, let's put that a different way. Would you let your daughter dress up as Harry Potter, Frankenstein and his monster, Captain America? And then, would you let your son dress up as Ghost Spider, Hermione Granger? What about Wednesday Addams? No one wants to be Pugsley. If you said yes to the first three, you said no to the second three. Do you know why? Did you feel a bit uncomfortable about it? Worried they'd be teased? Does it just feel wrong? When we tell our boys that they can't dress up like a female character, what exactly are we telling them? Is it that girls aren't aspirational? That girls aren't good enough for boys? If we want our sons to see women as equals, really simple things like just affirming their choices around being a female character for Halloween can have a huge impact. Our society tells boys absolutely everywhere that they should not look up to women. And I totally get it. We don't want our boys to be teased. But if we shut this stuff down, they'll take on that societal belief. And just to be clear, that societal belief is misogyny. I'd love to hear your thoughts. What would you do?
onscreen: Would you let your child dress as a character of a different gender for Halloween?
dress as a character of a
and then would you let your son dress up as ghost spider
did you feel a bit uncomfortable about it?
When we tell our boys that they can't dress up like a female character

caption:
Would you let your child dress as a different gender for halloween? I personally think if we want our sons to think women are equals we should be affirming this by upholding their choice of favourite characters, and giving those options without judgement... but it is really hard because society is telling us boys can’t look up to women or female characters ALL the time!
It’s tricky to go against societal norms, and the worry that they’ll be teased is real.
Often by the time they are 7 they’ll be self-censoring already so we need to start early! Teaching our young children that there’s something ‘wrong’ with boys dressing up as girls comes from fear - but what are we afraid of? Afraid they’ll be too girly? Afraid they’ll be gay? Afraid they’ll be trans? We have to confront our own biases and unpick them.
What would you do? Let them go as a female character? Give them some tools if they encounter teasing? Let me know - I’d love to hear your thoughts.

author: abigailprtr
title: Levator ani avulsion: a hidden birth injury (childfree creator)
summary: A childfree creator relays information from a pelvic floor PT about levator ani avulsion, where part of the pelvic floor muscle detaches from the pubic bone during vaginal birth. She says it affects about 1 in 5 people who give birth, ranges from partial to full on one or both sides, is often undiagnosed, raises prolapse risk, and is more likely with forceps delivery.
key_points: Levator ani avulsion = the levator ani muscle tearing partly or fully off the pubic bone, on one or both sides.
Claimed to affect roughly 20% of people who give birth vaginally; often undiagnosed.
It increases risk of pelvic organ prolapse and can affect quality of life.
Forceps-assisted delivery increases the risk.
If you have postpartum heaviness/bulging or pelvic floor symptoms, ask for a pelvic floor physiotherapy assessment.
credentials: none (childfree creator relaying a pelvic floor PT's video)
caution: Delivered with an anti-pregnancy, fear-based framing; 'everyone do Kegels' is oversimplified. Prevalence figures vary by study (often cited 10-36% of vaginal births). Discuss risks and postpartum pelvic floor checks with your provider.

ill.caption: Pelvic model showing how the levator ani muscle can detach from the pubic bone on one side during birth.

transcript: There's an injury that can happen during childbirth that I actually didn't even know about. Hi, I'm the girl with the list and I'm gonna make sure you know about these things. Actually affects around 20% of people who have given birth, one in five people and nobody has any idea that this injury exists. I wish I could tell you this surprised me. My highest viewed video to this date is when I learned what the epidural was and simultaneously learned that no one else knew what it was either. I had thousands of comments from moms who had had multiple epidurals who still didn't really understand what it was. The point is, nobody talks about these things, our education is severely lacking, and that's why I'm doing this. The thing that can happen during childbirth is that as that muscle stretches and as we have that baby, part of that muscle can actually tear off of the pubic bone. There are different levels of severity. They're just a little bit. It can tear fully on one side. It can tear a little bit on both sides. It can tear fully on both sides. So this is what's called a levator ani avulsion. And when I looked this up to learn more, I found that it is what's called a hidden birth injury that needs attention. and also that it significantly impacts your quality of life. If you have one of these, you're significantly more at risk for a pelvic organ prolapse. And if you don't know what a prolapse is, it's basically when your pelvic floor muscles are too weak to keep your organs in place, so they fall out. Everyone do five Kegels right now. According to the original video, you're more at risk for this type of injury if you have a forceps-assisted delivery. And if you don't remember the forceps, they call them the salad tongs. this is just another example of a childbirth related injury that is rarely talked about rarely diagnosed rarely taken seriously and an injury that i won't ever have because i'm not having kids take your birth control and do your key goals i'll see you next time

author: brooklin_dawn
title: Low-Effort Elimination Communication for Newborns
summary: A mother shares her 'lazy' approach to elimination communication (EC) with her 7-week-old baby. By observing morning grunting signals, she holds her baby over the toilet as part of their morning routine, which she finds helpful for the baby's comfort.
key_points: Observe consistent baby signals like grunting or straining.
Hold the baby with their back to your chest, hands under their thighs, over the toilet.
Keep the session short (30-45 seconds max).
EC can be done as a low-effort, once-a-day routine rather than full-time potty training.
caution: This is a personal parenting approach; ensure the baby is supported safely when held over the toilet.
transcript: My seven-week-old baby has pooped in the toilet three mornings in a row. What? So I'd heard of elimination communication when I was pregnant, and I thought that's kind of cool, but I'm not going to commit to doing that. But I'd heard somebody say, even if you do like a lazy version of EC, that it can be beneficial when you are trying to potty train down the road, because I'm not trying to potty train my seven-week-old baby. But every single morning without fail, when she wakes up she is grunting and upset and her tummy hurts and all of the things like just grunt grunt grunt grunt grunt grunt and so I figured I would give it a try like she obviously needs to go poop as soon as I put her in a bouncer she goes poop like there's a connection here that would be very easy to draw and so I held her just back to my chest you know you put your hands under their little thighs and sat backwards on the toilet and she pooped in it a lot and so I just figured I'd build that into part of our morning routine like when it's time to get up for the day we get her diaper off wipe whatever's there and then we go in the bathroom and we sit over the toilet for a couple seconds like 30-45 seconds max and she usually poops in the toilet it's it's crazy and honestly so cool am I gonna try to do this throughout the rest of the day absolutely not um I do not have the mental capacity for that however um helping her feel a little bit better in the morning and being able to like get what's going on with her that's that was kind of cool

Have a cold drink or snack ready for each child
Play calm music and keep the car comfortable and quiet
Regulate yourself so you don't need your child's reassurance about their day
Ask about the day later, once the child has decompressed

author: jillianfit
title: Managing pressure during labor and epidural risks
summary: A pre/postnatal coach shares her experience of being pressured by medical staff into an epidural during an unmedicated labor. She highlights the risk of rare but serious complications, such as persistent nerve damage and numbness, and advises parents to advocate for themselves and ask for follow-up if issues persist after birth.
key_points: You have the right to decline or delay medical interventions like an epidural.
Write your preferences in a birth plan and have an advocate present.
Ask medical staff for reasons, alternatives, and time to decide.
Report persistent numbness or weakness after birth to your doctor immediately.
caution: The video describes a rare medical complication; always consult your healthcare provider regarding birth interventions.

And the pressure became so much because they were saying things like this over and over and over again. author: agapedeng
title: Milk took 5 days to come in: colostrum was enough
summary: A first-time mother shares that her mature milk didn't come in until five days after birth; in between her baby got only colostrum. Encouraged by her lactation consultant and husband, she kept nursing rather than panic-supplementing with formula, since nursing signals the body to make milk. Her baby regained birth weight by week two and she later had an oversupply.
key_points: It's normal for mature milk not to come in for the first 3-5 days; colostrum is what the newborn needs then.
Newborns can lose up to 7-10% of birth weight and should regain it by around 2 weeks.
Frequent nursing (or pumping) signals the body to produce milk; replacing feeds with formula without milk removal can lower supply.
Colostrum volume is small, so you can't see much; the baby may seem unsatisfied and feed very often.
Supplementation is sometimes medically needed — decide with your healthcare team/lactation consultant.
caution: Personal experience; seek prompt medical/lactation help if weight loss exceeds ~10%, wet/dirty diapers are low, the baby is very sleepy or jaundiced — supplementing is sometimes necessary.
dedupe: colostrum enough before milk comes in
transcript: He was born on a Sunday, and my milk didn't come in until the following Friday. In between, I didn't feed him breast milk, and I didn't feed him formula. So if you're a first-time mom, you might be wondering, what in the heck did you feed your baby? And the answer is something called colostrum, which is something I never knew existed until I had my baby. It's normal for a baby to lose weight in the first three to five days. it's normal for your milk to not have come in yet in the first three to five days. Babies will lose weight and you might feel panicky like I did freaking out that I'm starving my baby but it's normal and they can lose some weight a few ounces up until seven to ten percent of their birth weight. By the second week they should have regained that birth weight and he did. In between I really wanted to supplement with formula. I was encouraged by my lactation consultant not to supplement with formula because I was producing cholesterol. That action of the baby nursing actually helps your milk to come in. I just let him suck. It was really hard because I couldn't see him drinking milk because it's not a large volume. And again, I'm just like feeding him and feeding him and he's hungry. He doesn't seem satisfied. So I understand if you want to bridge with milk, but now I am an oversupplier. Milk is great. He's great. It does get better. You're doing great.
onscreen: He was born on a Sunday and my milk didn't come in until the following
So if you're a first time mom you might be wondering what in the heck did
And the answer is something called colostrum
That action of the baby nursing actually helps your milk to come in

caption:
Another PSA for FTMs: don’t panic-supplement with formula like I almost did, if your milk doesn’t come in in the first 2-5 days, *as long as you are producing colostrum!* Colostrum is basically like an ultra-concentrated pre-workout sample that the body makes exclusively for newborns. 💪 

They call it liquid gold and it’s EXACTLY what baby needs those first few days. Milk production works on a supply-and-demand system. In those early days:

* Every time your baby nurses (or you pump), your body gets the signal to make more milk.
* If feeds are replaced with formula and there’s no nursing/pumping to replace them, your body receives FEWER signals to increase milk production, which can lead to a lower supply, hence becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy.😭

That said, there are many situations where temporary formula supplementation is medically appropriate so work with your healthcare team. For me personally, my anxiety kept me panic-reaching for the formula, but my husband and LC kept reminding me volume was not what baby needed right now, but all the nutrients in the colostrum. I’m still glad that I took some home from the hospital for peace of mind, but ultimately I didn’t need it, by latching baby continuously, my milk came in and I thankfully have no supply issues now!

title: Model respect first: teens back-talk when they don't feel respected
summary: A teen parenting coach challenges parents who wait for their teen to show respect first. She defines respect as regard for someone's feelings, wishes and rights, and argues rude back talk often signals a teen who doesn't feel respected. As the adult with the fully developed brain, the parent leads by listening, empathising and validating.
key_points: Respect is modelled, not demanded because 'I'm the parent'.
Back talk and rudeness can signal the teen doesn't feel respected.
Listen more and validate the teen's thoughts and feelings, even if you don't agree.
Notice if you grew up where respect was commanded and how that fuels your reaction.
caution: Claim that back talk is always due to not feeling respected is the creator's opinion; partly promotional.
transcript: Are you waiting for your teenager to respect you so that you can then respect them? Because if they're going to keep treating you with this backtalk and moody, rude spiciness, there's no way you're going to show them respect. And quite frankly, they don't deserve it. That's the first problem. You see, the definition of respect is to have a deep regard for the feelings, wishes, and rights of someone else, a feeling of deep admiration for someone, their abilities and qualities. And although your teenager's showing up super spicy and moody with backtalk, I can promise you it's because they don't feel respected. And if you're like me, you grew up in an environment where respect is demanded and commanded. So you are pissed because they are not respecting you. And how dare they? You're the adult in this relationship. That's my bad news for you. You model respect.
caption:
YOU: Why should I respect my teen when they don't respect me?!

If you're teen is rude, back talking, blaming you for everything, and being mean, respecting your them seems absurd.

What if I told you they don't feel respected either, and that's part of what you're seeing?

Respect is regard for someone's feelings not something you demand or command from your teen 'because you're the parent'.

You're the adult with the fully formed brain so you're the leader. When you model respect by listening more and empathizing and validating your teen's thoughts and feelings (you don't have to agree), you'll get more respect in return.... and a calmer house!
