author: elenpinsky
title: Why babies need emotional connection, not just physical care
summary: The post references René Spitz's 1940s studies of institutionalised babies who received food and nappies but no consistent loving caregiver, documenting loss of curiosity, developmental delays, blank stares and emotional shutdown. Footage contrasts babies freely exploring blocks with babies who flinch and stop playing. The message: responsive parenting is not spoiling; a baby needs to feel safe to explore and play.
key_points: Babies need responsive, emotionally available caregiving, not only feeding and changing.
Severe emotional deprivation (as in Spitz's institution studies) was linked to loss of curiosity, delays and shutdown.
A baby who feels safe explores and plays; a stressed baby shifts into self-protection.
Responding to your baby is not spoiling and does not create 'bad habits'.

products.name: blocks
products.type: Tool for infant exploration and play.

caution: Dramatised framing; the findings concern extreme institutional deprivation, not ordinary parents who are sometimes busy or stressed. The source of the baby footage isn't identified.
onscreen: This is what happens to a baby when love isn't safe.
She picks them up when they fall, and tries again.
Veronique lifts her hands to block the toy.
Every other baby would've knocked the tower with joy.
But the anxiety is too much.
caption:
This is what happens to baby development without emotional safety.

In the 1940s, psychoanalyst René Spitz studied babies raised in institutions, without one loving caregiver. where food and nappies were provided but connection wasn’t.

He documented the effects of emotional neglect:

👉🏻 Loss of curiosity
👉🏻 Delays in baby development
👉🏻 Blank stares, still bodies
👉🏻 Emotional shutdown

🧠 This is why baby development depends on more than care - it needs connection.

They were surviving.

Why?
Because without responsive parenting, a baby’s brain doesn’t feel safe enough to play.
It shifts from exploring to protecting.

Baby development starts with connection.
And responsive parenting isn’t spoiling. It doesn’t create “bad habits”.
It’s what protects babies from shutdown before they even have words.

author: msfab_learninglab
title: Why mixed-age groups help kids learn and socialise
summary: Educator Ana Lorena Fabrega argues that age-segregated classrooms don't resemble real-life socialising and put 'speed limits' on learning by grade. From student teaching in mixed-age schools in New York City, she saw younger kids attempt harder challenges by imitating older ones, while older kids consolidated learning by teaching, letting the teacher act as a guide.
key_points: Outside school, people rarely interact only with same-age peers; mixed-age settings mirror real life.
Telling kids they can't learn something 'until fourth grade' puts an artificial ceiling on curiosity; kids often crave a challenge.
Younger children attempt harder tasks when they can imitate older children.
Older children solidify their own understanding by teaching younger ones.
There are sensible age limits (not 18-year-olds with 4-year-olds), but mixed ranges create organic teaching and learning.
At home: let siblings/cousins of different ages play and learn together and let kids go beyond 'grade level' when interested.
credentials: educator (student-taught in mixed-age schools in New York City)
caution: Based on the creator's teaching experience and educational philosophy; she does not cite specific studies for mixed-age classrooms.

but really we're sending them to this environment where they're only with people their age and there are two things here it doesn't really resemble the way you socialize in the real world one and two when you tell kids you can learn math this unit up to here because you're in third grade by fourth grade we'll explain that but we're not there yet so you can't learn about that you're putting a speed limit and if there's something that i've learned by working with so many kids is that kids are capable of much more than we give them credit for and they actually crave a challenge the problem is that as adults we kind of sometimes don't realize this and we're constantly putting speed bumps we're like you're going to learn up to here oh no you're not old enough to try this but i've student taught in different mixed age groups in new york city and i actually got to see what happened when you remove the grades and when you have older kids with younger kids and of course there's a caught of age you're not going to put an 18 year old with a four year old but what you would see is the little kids wanted to imitate the older kids and so suddenly they were taking on these challenges that they otherwise wouldn't even have access to if they were in a traditional school where they have great levels and then you have the older kids who were motivated because they wanted to teach the younger kids they wanted to be that older kid that i know a little bit more than you and here's how you do it and one of the best ways to learn something is by teaching it that's when you really realize and you crystallize your learning and so there was just so much teaching and learning going on organically that the teacher could finally kind of like step out and do what she's supposed to do, which is a guide.

caption:
Mixed-aged grouping allows kids to interact at different social levels and in ways that resemble real-life interactions.

Think about it: Older kids benefit from teaching and helping younger kids (and research shows that the best way to learn something is to teach it, so they get to crystallize their learning) and younger kids learn more and faster because they attempt to do what older kids are doing… there are no speed limits. 

I got to student teach at several mixed-aged schools and I was always surprised by what the younger kids were able to accomplish when you removed the barriers (aka grades) 

Overall, it’s a more natural and effective way to learn and socialize.

title: Why new parents and new grandparents clash over advice
summary: A family therapist explains a common source of tension: grandparents expect to be valued for their child-raising expertise, while today's parents want support, not guidance. Because modern parents are older, more established and long independent, unsolicited advice, however well-meant, feels jarring.
key_points: Grandparents often expect to be appreciated for their expertise; many new parents want practical support instead of guidance.
Today's parents tend to be older, established in careers/homes and used to making their own decisions.
Seeing it as a generational/cultural difference in expectations can reduce conflict.
Talk explicitly with grandparents about what kind of help you want (support vs advice).
transcript: One of the biggest struggles I see between new grandparents and new parents as a family therapist is differences about expectations for the grandparent role. Grandparents often enter this role of grandparent with this expectation that they will be appreciated and valued for their expertise and competence in raising children. But for a lot of parents, especially parents of today's generation, they are looking to grandparents for support, not for guidance. And if you look at this difference in expectation as a cultural or generational difference, it makes a lot of sense because we are typically older than our parents were when they had us. So we bring a different level of maturity and intention to our parenting journeys. We've typically been out of the house for over a decade. We might own our own home or be established in our careers. And it's been a while that we've had a parent try to influence our decision-making. So when a grandparent comes along trying to tell us what to do, no matter how well-meaning their intentions are. And how well spoken this advice is, it's super jarring and just rubs us the wrong way.

title: Why teasing boys about girl friends is especially harmful

She argues that the same teasing lands differently because of wider socialisation: girls are raised to nurture, while boys get messages that anything feminine is bad. key_points: Don't tease any child about opposite-sex friends ('Is that your girlfriend/boyfriend?')—it makes them uncomfortable and can end valued friendships.
Context matters: boys often receive messages that femininity is shameful, so such teasing can reinforce contempt for girls.
Parents of boys have limited control over outside misogynistic messaging, so be diligent about not contributing to it at home.
She notes boys are often exposed to adult/pornographic material young, which can reinforce disrespect for women.
caution: Opinion/social commentary rather than research-based advice.

Make family values explicit: 'that's not what we do'.
Lessons on standing up for others can stay with a child for life.

onscreen: Zendaya talking about how her parents cussed her out in fifth grade, not for bullying a classmate, but for standing by as a silent bystander:
caption:
During an interview reflecting on her childhood, Zendaya shared that one of the biggest lessons her parents taught her came in fifth grade. She explained that they didn’t scold her for bullying another student-instead, they were upset because she stood by silently while someone else was being bullied. Her parents believed that staying quiet in the face of cruelty was also a failure to do the right thing, and they made sure she understood the importance of standing up for others.

Zendaya has said that the moment stayed with her throughout her life. It helped shape her values of empathy, accountability, and using her voice to support people who are being mistreated. As one of Hollywood’s most influential young stars, she has often spoken about kindness, inclusion, and speaking out against bullying, showing how that childhood lesson became a lasting part of her character.

title: 'Bad habits' as trauma responses from a toxic family upbringing
summary: A carousel reframes adult habits (procrastination, over-apologising, perfectionism, isolating, people-pleasing, hyper-independence, dissociation, overthinking) as survival responses learned in emotionally unsafe childhoods. Aimed at adults healing from their own upbringing; useful as a reminder of what children learn from criticism and conditional love.
key_points: Procrastination can stem from childhood criticism: avoiding starting to avoid judgment.
Over-apologising can come from conditional love: trying to stay safe from anger or rejection.
Perfectionism can be about avoiding shame/punishment when mistakes were 'unforgivable'.
People-pleasing and hyper-independence can develop when a child's needs didn't matter or support was unreliable.
Dissociation (zoning out) and overthinking can be responses to overwhelming or unpredictable homes.
For parents: emotional safety, forgiving mistakes and unconditional love help prevent these patterns.
caution: Pop-psychology generalisations; these habits have many possible causes and are not diagnostic of childhood trauma. Seek a therapist for personal concerns.

You didn’t develop these trauma responses because something is wrong with you.

You learned them in an environment where emotional safety didn’t exist.

You procrastinate because you grew up fearing that nothing you did would ever be good enough.
You over-apologize because you were taught that your feelings were a burden.
You strive for perfection because mistakes were never forgiven.
You isolate yourself because trust was broken too many times.
You please everyone around you because saying “no” was never an option.
You became fiercely independent because relying on others only led to disappointment.
You dissociate because your mind had to escape when life felt unbearable.
You overthink because you lived in constant fear of what might happen next.

These are not flaws.
These are the echoes of a childhood where you had to survive, not thrive.

But here’s the truth:
You’re not that helpless child anymore.
You are safe now.
You are allowed to heal.
You are allowed to unlearn.
You are allowed to take up space without apology.

Your survival responses got you here, but they don’t have to define your future.
Healing is possible—and you deserve every step of it.

title: 'They'll be children only once': take the time off and get in the water
summary: A text-on-screen reel responding to the '18 summers' debate: you'll be a mother forever but they're children only once, so take the paid time off. It says children value quality time more than fancy vacations and will remember you getting in the water, not how you looked in a swimsuit.
key_points: Use your vacation days for time with your kids.

YOUR CHILDREN DON'T CARE ABOUT FANCY VACATIONS, THEY CARE ABOUT QUALITY TIME.
YOUR CHILDREN WILL REMEMBER THE TIMES YOU GOT IN THE WATER, NOT HOW YOU LOOKED IN A SWIM SUIT.
caption:
The internet is divided by the whole concept that we only have 18 summers with our children. Coming from a person who still spends a lot of time with their parents as an adult and mother myself, I personally do not see it as something that should be stressful. I view it as a little reminder, the memories built as a child are not the same as adults.

So is the mist of all the chaos and hectic life, this is your gentle reminder:

⭐Take that PTO
⭐ Focus on quality time not these lavish summer vacations on your feed
⭐ Put on that bathing suit without body shaming ourselves to enjoy these summer days with them
⭐ Not every moment will be enjoyable but, this phase will pass

author: sincerely.brit
title: 3 ways for moms to stay grounded when overwhelmed
summary: A motherhood-identity creator offers three simple grounding habits: take one deep breath before reacting, keep a small ritual that's just yours, and end the day naming one thing you're grateful for instead of replaying what didn't get done. The caption also promotes a freebie.
key_points: Take one deep breath before answering, moving or fixing anything to interrupt the stress spiral.
Keep one small personal ritual (quiet coffee, solo walk, your playlist) to remember you exist beyond others' needs.
End the day with one small thing you're grateful for rather than your undone list.
caution: Light self-care tips; persistent overwhelm or low mood (especially postpartum) warrants talking to a professional.
dedupe: mom grounding tips breathe ritual gratitude
onscreen: 3 Ways to Stay Grounded When Motherhood Feels Overwhelming
caption:
The THREE ⬇️

➡️ Breathe before you react. 
One deep breath before answering, moving, or fixing anything. It’s simple, but it interrupts the spiral.

➡️ Have one small ritual that’s yours. 
A quiet coffee, a walk alone, a playlist that feels like you — something that reminds you you exist outside of everyone else’s needs.

➡️ End your day with presence, not pressure. 
Instead of replaying everything you didn’t get done, try naming one thing you’re grateful for — something small, real, and right in front of you.

These shifts didn’t fix everything overnight, but they made the heavy feel a little lighter.
And some days, that’s enough. 🤍

✨ I know how it feels to be stuck in survival mode. These simple shifts helped me breathe again and If you’ve been feeling lost in motherhood, you’re not alone.

I made something to help you start making time for you again — I made this for the mom who’s tired of feeling like she disappeared somewhere between the school runs and the laundry piles. It’s simple, honest, and exactly what helped me start finding me again.

✨ Comment SHIFT and I’ll send it your way!

summary: A pregnant creator carrying a large (99th percentile) baby shares the skincare routine she uses on her belly to prevent stretch marks. Step 4: Seal it in with a few drops of oil; she uses Josie Maran argan oil and says the type of oil doesn't matter much.
So far she has no stretch marks, but she has the linea nigra (the dark line on the belly).

author: kathleen.rowan.co
title: Baby sleep in Japan vs the US: a doula's observations
summary: An American doula who has parented for five years in the US and five in Tokyo shares anecdotal observations on why she thinks Japanese parents struggle less with infant sleep. She points to widespread room-sharing, later family bedtimes (baby joins a 10-11pm bedtime and sleeps until about 8am), and parents waiting a moment before picking up a crying baby. She says this is lived experience, not research.
key_points: Room-sharing is the norm in Tokyo, often for years, so there's no early push to move the child out.
Later bedtimes (around 10-11pm) with the baby joining family life, and sleeping until about 8am with a couple of night feeds, is her family's pattern.
She has seen Japanese and European mothers wait a beat before picking up a fussing baby, giving the baby a chance to settle.
Ask whether your sleep struggles come from the baby or from inherited cultural expectations.
caution: Explicitly anecdotal and not research-based; broad cultural generalisations. She sleeps with her baby, so if that means bed-sharing, follow AAP safe-sleep guidance (separate sleep surface in the parents' room). Late bedtimes won't suit every family. The video ends with a promo for a paid class.
dedupe: japan vs us baby sleep culture
transcript: I have been a mom for 10 years. Five of those years were spent in the U.S. and five of those years were spent here in Japan. And as a birth and postpartum doula, I've also worked with a lot of families in both countries and I've noticed something very striking about infant sleep. American parents are struggling so much more than Japanese parents and I want to talk about why. Number one, most families room share and this is really common especially in Tokyo because spaces are small so it's often out of necessity. I have friends with pre-teens and teens who still sleep all in the same room because that is just the cultural norm and nobody bats an eye i'm not saying that you should do that and i'm not saying that i want to do that i personally have my seven and ten year olds sleep in their own room and then i sleep with the baby right now but eventually of course i want him to move to his own room here's what i've noticed because japanese parents don't try to get their kids out of the room early they actually don't have the sleep struggles that we have in the u.s we've essentially built a sleep problem that doesn't exist here number two bedtimes are much later here than they are in the u.s in the u.s a lot of people put their babies down between 7 and 7 30 which sounds great until your baby's up at 4 a.m here it's normal for elementary school age kids to go to bed between 10 and 11 and i've noticed with our family the baby just kind of joins in on that so we're all doing things until bedtime at 10 or 11 he's kind of part of the hustle and bustle then he sleeps until about 8 a.m of course he wakes up for a couple feeds in the middle of the night but then he just goes back to sleep number three is anecdotal from my own work with mothers and babies i teach mom and babies pilates classes here and i noticed japanese moms wait a beat before picking up the baby when they're crying and actually a lot of the european moms do this too however i've noticed that my english-speaking clients pick up babies really quickly so this is like u.s canada uk australia whatever content we're consuming in english is having us pick up the babies really quickly it seems this moment that they're waiting to pick up the baby seems to be this trust that they can kind of settle themselves to a certain extent japanese kids are really calm and cued in in public and i wonder if it's starting in infancy there's no right way to approach infant sleep but i do think it's worth asking whether the challenges we're having with sleep are actually about the baby or about the expectations that we've inherited. If you land here by accident, hit follow and stick around for more content that makes you feel less overwhelmed for your pregnancy, birth, and postpartum and gives you the confidence that you can handle it all.
onscreen: AMERICAN BABIES SLEEP WORSE THAN JAPANESE BABIES
caption:
Baby sleep looks really different depending on where you live, and after ten years of parenting across two countries, I have thoughts. 🌸

A quick note before you watch: everything I’m sharing here comes from my own lived experience as an American mom raising kids in Tokyo, and from working with families in both countries as a doula. This is not research-based, and I’m genuinely not trying to make sweeping cultural statements. Japan is not a monolith. Our experience is specific to our community in Tokyo, and I know it can vary widely across the city and across the country.

That said, the differences I’ve noticed in how families here approach sleep, co-sleeping, bedtimes, and how quickly parents respond to a fussing baby, have made me think a lot about which of our sleep struggles are cultural, and which ones we might be creating for ourselves.

What’s your experience? Do you find that your sleep expectations came more from culture than from your baby?

P.S. If this got you thinking, I literally just taught a class on infant sleep inside The Beehive. Comment SOFTSTRENGTH below and I’ll send you a free trial so you can watch it.

author: celebritymidwife4
title: Bimanual uterine compression for postpartum hemorrhage (clinical demo)
summary: A midwife demonstrates on a training mannequin bimanual compression of the uterus, a life-saving maneuver used by clinicians for postpartum hemorrhage caused by uterine atony. One hand is inside the vagina pushing against the anterior fornix/lower uterine segment, the other presses the uterus from the abdomen, reducing blood flow and stimulating contraction.
key_points: Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is often caused by uterine atony – the uterus failing to contract after the placenta is delivered.
Bimanual compression is an emergency maneuver performed by trained clinicians: one hand internally, one on the abdomen, compressing the uterus.
It reduces bleeding and stimulates the uterus to contract.
For parents: heavy bleeding after birth is an emergency; maternity staff have procedures to manage it.
caution: Clinical training content for professionals, not something parents should attempt; mainly useful as background on PPH.
transcript: Guys let's do bimanual compression of the uterus. First of all what is bimanual compression of the uterus? It is a life-saving maneuver used in postpartum hemorrhage when bleeding is due to uterine atony or when there is failure of the uterus to contract immediately after the delivery of the placenta in mothers that have given birth. So what do you need to do? First of all, one hand is placed in the vagina to push up against the anterior phonics all over uterine segment, and the other hand is placed externally on the abdomen, pressing the uterus against the vagina wall. Immediately after that, this is going to help the uterus to reduce blood flow and to stimulate contraction. When you're done with doing that, please make sure the mother is comfortable.
onscreen: Bimanual compression of the uterus to stop hemorrhage in pph

author: theholisticpsychologist
title: Claim: father's stress passes to children via sperm epigenetics
summary: Dr. Nicole LePera argues that a father's sperm carries epigenetic markers shaped by his stress, trauma, relationships and nutrition, and that these can influence his child's anxiety and emotional patterns. She says these patterns can be changed by working on your own nervous system.
key_points: Claims a father's life experiences (stress, trauma, poor nutrition) alter epigenetic marks in sperm.
Suggests these marks may contribute to a child's anxiety or emotional patterns.
Message: inherited patterns are not fixed; you can work to change your nervous-system responses.
Relevant reminder that a father's health before conception matters too.
credentials: psychologist (Dr. Nicole LePera, 'The Holistic Psychologist', author of How to Do the Work)
caution: Overstates the science: paternal epigenetic inheritance is mostly shown in animal studies; human evidence that a father's emotions are transmitted via sperm is limited and preliminary.
transcript: Your father's sperm doesn't just pass on his DNA. It passes on his life experiences, his stress, his fears, and even his emotional patterns. Here's how it works. When your father created you, his sperm didn't just carry genetic material. It carried epigenetic markers that were shaped by his life. This means that every time he dealt with stress, faced trauma, or even lived through major life events, those moments didn't just affect him. They affected the sperm that created you. Let me put this into perspective. If your dad went through something like emotional hardship, unhealthy relationships, or even had poor nutrition, those experiences physically changed the way his genes were expressed. And those changes were passed down to you. So when you feel anxious, struggle with stress, or notice emotional patterns that just don't make sense, it's not just you. It could be the imprint of your father's nervous system and his emotional struggles living on inside you. And the most mind-blowing part, you can change it. You can rewrite the story of your nervous system, your emotions, and your reactions.
caption: It didn’t start with you… #epigenetics #trauma #healingjourney

summary: A mom plays a compound-word card game (labelled 3+) with her young daughter: two picture halves (e.g. star + fish, fire + truck, sun + flower, rain + bow) are shown and then flipped to reveal the combined word, delighting the child when she realizes two words make a new one. A light, fun activity idea with no explanation of benefits.
key_points: Compound-word picture cards (age 3+) show two pictures that combine into one word: star + fish = starfish, sun + flower = sunflower.
Ask the child to name each picture, then flip the card to reveal the combined word.
Simple word games like this build early language and phonological awareness through play.
scripts: A star and a fish - if you combine them together, what is it?

products.name: compound word flip cards
products.type: Builds early language and phonological awareness.

transcript: These are called compound words pairs. Are you ready? Yeah. Basketball. If you flip it, it's a? Basketball. What is this? A star. A star and a? Fish. If you combine them together, can you flip it? What is it? A star. Is that funny? I don't want to do that. Oh, all right. Fire truck. Okay, if you flip it. It's a? Fire truck. No. Fun. What do you think is that? It's a? Pancakes. Here, a butterfly. Okay, flip it. What do you call it now? A rainbow. A rainbow. I want one next Next, alright, let's do it again If you flip it, it's a Sunflower

author: dr.alex.lupoi
title: Cosmetic surgeries covered for children by the Romanian state
summary: A Romanian doctor, filming while driving, lists three cosmetic surgeries the Romanian state reimburses for children with a referral: otoplasty for protruding ears, rhinoplasty, and gynecomastia surgery for enlarged male breast tissue. The state's reasoning is to prevent bullying and social trauma, which he agrees with.
key_points: In Romania, otoplasty (pinning back protruding ears) is reimbursed for children.
Rhinoplasty is also reimbursed for children, for the same anti-bullying reason.
Gynecomastia surgery (removing enlarged breast gland tissue in boys) is covered.
A referral letter (bilet de trimitere) is required.
caution: Check current coverage rules and age criteria with a doctor or CNAS before relying on this.
transcript: Iată-mea, dacă toți sunt prins în trafic, hai să-ți zic niște operații de chirurgie estetică care sunt decontate la copii și de ce e importantă chestia asta. Prima este otoplastia, adică dacă ai urechile mai depărtate de cap, dar mai clăpăuge, poți să le apropii prin operația asta și este decontată la copii, pentru că statul consideră că ție foarte mult bully și îți dă o traumă socială, ceea ce este corect, copiii sunt foarte răutăcioși. A doua operație este rhinoplastia. Știu, weird, rhinoplastia e decontată la copii din același motiv. Da, ai gândi statul consider că atunci când devii adult nu mai poți să iei traumă pe această temă sau ți-a luat deja destulă și aia e. Și a treia este ginecomastia, adică practic dacă ai glanda mamare foarte mărită ca bărbat, poți să-ți faci aceste operatii să-ți reduci volumul al sânului, scoțând glanda mamară. Bun, sunt curios de două chestii. Ce părere ai de justificarea statului care mie mi se pare foarte bună și sunt profund surprins că statul român a făcut decizie bună? Și a doua este dacă știai că aceste operațiți se pot face la copii gratuit cu bilet de trimitere Și dacă știi pe cineva care vrea să-și facă operațiile astea
onscreen: viața mea, dacă tot sunt prins în trafic
adică dacă ai urechile mai îndepărtate de cap
caption: Estetică PENTRU COPII? 👀  Nu, nu e nimic ciudat, se practică chiar frecvent! author: elenaamatei
title: Cybex Lemo 4-in-1: newborn bouncer to high chair to learning tower
summary: A Romanian mom of two under two reviews the gifted Cybex Lemo system from Taticool Shop, which converts from a newborn seat insert (first 2-3 months) to a bouncer (until rolling), then a height-adjustable high chair for starting solids, a children's chair and a learning tower. She praises the posture and adjustable footrest for weaning and the space saved versus buying separate products.
key_points: The newborn insert has a head cushion, harness, breathable mesh back and 3 recline positions; she used it for the first 2-3 months.
The bouncer mode (3 recline levels) was used until the baby started rolling - stop using bouncers once babies roll.
For starting solids, a high chair with an adjustable footrest supports a correct, stable sitting position.
The seat and footrest adjust in height and depth without tools, so it can be shared between two children.
A multi-stage product can replace 5-6 separate items and save storage space.

products.name: Cybex Lemo 4-in-1 system
products.type: Adjustable high chair, bouncer, and learning tower.

caution: Gifted/sponsored product review (#gifted).
dedupe: cybex lemo convertible high chair review
transcript: Avem practic patru produse într-unul singur și, sincer să fiu, este produsul pe care îl recomand din tot sufletul și care mie mi-a făcut viața mai ușoară cu doi copii sub doi ani. Este vorba despre Cybex Lemo 4 nume de la Taticul Shop, un sistem cu patru configurații care se adaptează nevoilor copilului tău de la primele luni și până în copilărie. Primul oară am pus-o pe cea mică în acest suport, dar unde are și perniță pentru căpușor cu centuri și acea husă se dă la o parte și pe spate are o plasă în cazul în care transpiră. aici am ținut-o în primele două luni, două, trei luni, după care am schimbat, are și trei poziții de înclinare, el arată cam așa, după care partea de sus, da, pe care am încercuit-o, se pune în suportul pentru bouncer, deci după aia avem cel de-a doilea produs, bouncerul, care la fel are trei trepte de înclinare și aici am ținut-o până când a început să se rostogolească, pe mine m-a ajutat foarte mult pentru că am luat-o pe cea mică peste tot cu mine în casă, în funcție de vârsta pe care am avut-o, am adaptat acest produs și mi-a fost un mare ajutor pentru că a fost mereu prezentă acolo cu mine și cea mare și a văzut tot ceea ce se întâmplă. Iar în momentul în care am ajuns la diversificare, am schimbat și am mutat scaunul, alert, are doar două șuruburi pe care le folosești. În primul rând avem acest suport unde se pun picioarele, care după cum vedeți își modifică înălțimea în 100.000 de moduri, la fel și șezutul, care la fel și el se modifică și în afară de faptul ăsta se dă și în fază și în spate în funcție de mărimea copilului. După care am pus pătarul și deja, uite aici, avem un scaun de birou, dacă se poate sau puteți să-l puneți la masă direct cu voi. Acest suport se folosește pentru modul de turn de învățare și dacă stau bine să mă gândesc, cred că de fapt avem 5 produse în unul, dar noi acum suntem la diversificare, așa că pregătim scaunul pentru diversificare și vă zic că am mai avut alte două scaune și nu se compară cu Cybex Lemo. În primul rând poziția copilului este mult mai corectă în Cybex și un plus are suportul pentru picioare, este foarte important lucrul acesta în diversificare mai ales la început și faptul că își modifică poziția cum vrei tu. Pe lângă asta, eu pot să folosesc scaunul ăsta și pentru cea mare și pentru cea mică, fără să mă chinui prea mult, pentru că îi modific poziția din două mișcări. Nu am șuruburi și nu stau să mă chinui cu el. Mie îmi se pare că este un scaun foarte bun, ai foarte multe produse într-unul singur, nu trebuie să cumpere mai multe produse separat și să le depozitezi. Am uitat să vă menționez că se curăță extrem de ușor și de rapid.

author: parenting.playbook
title: Dad Advice: Play With Your Kids While They Still Want You To
summary: In a street interview, a dad says the hardest part of fatherhood is that kids soon stop wanting to play with you — his 13-year-old prefers friends. His advice to soon-to-be parents: put down the phone, TV, Netflix and YouTube and go outside to play catch with your kids while they still ask.
key_points: Say yes when young children ask you to play — the window is short.
Swap screen time (phone, TV, Netflix, YouTube) for active time with your kids, like playing catch outdoors.
By the teen years, kids often prefer friends over parents.

So instead of watching TV, looking at your phone, staring at your screen, watching Netflix, doing YouTube, you should instead walk away, go to your kids, and go outside and play some catch with them.

author: dadlifemichael
title: Dad does a love-language quiz with his young son
summary: A dad asks his young son a series of questions (hugs, gifts, praise, help, quality time) rating each as 'super loved', 'medium' or 'nothing' to discover his love language. The result is gifts (especially wrapped ones) and playing games. He plans to repeat the quiz over time to see how answers change.
key_points: Ask a child to rate actions as 'super loved', 'kind of loved' or 'doesn't do anything' to learn what makes them feel loved.
Mix items from the five love languages: hugs/touch, gifts, words of praise, acts of service, time together.
Repeat periodically because a young child's answers will change.
In this case the boy loved wrapped gifts, getting to pick something at the store and playing games together.

author: thebusinessessence
title: Dad makes daughter walk 5 miles to school after bus bullying
summary: A reposted viral video of a father whose 10-year-old daughter was suspended from the school bus for bullying a second time. Instead of driving her, he films her walking five miles to school in 36°F weather, arguing kids treat parents' help as a right rather than a privilege. He acknowledges many parents will disagree.
key_points: The father uses a natural/imposed consequence (no lift to school) after a repeated bullying suspension.
His reasoning: rides and help from parents are privileges, not entitlements.
The video does not address why the child bullied or how to repair harm with the victim.
caution: Punitive 'tough love' and filming/posting a child's punishment publicly is controversial and contrasts with gentle-discipline approaches; it may shame rather than teach empathy. Consider safety (cold, distance, traffic) and addressing the reasons behind bullying.
dedupe: dad makes child walk to school bullying punishment
transcript: This lovely lady is my 10-year-old daughter who has, for the second time this school year, been kicked off the school bus due to bullying another student. Let me make this extremely clear. Bullying is unacceptable, especially in my household. Friday, when my daughter brought home her paperwork for her bus suspension, she said, Daddy, you're going to have to take me to school next week. As you see this morning, she is learning otherwise. A lot of children today feel that the things their parents do for them is a right and not a privilege. So today, my beautiful daughter is going to walk five miles to school in 36-degree weather. I know a lot of you parents are not going to agree with this, but that is all right. Because I'm doing what I feel is right to teach my daughter a lesson and to stop her from bullying.
caption:
Tough Love: My Daughter Walks 5 Miles to School After Bus Bullying Suspension

My ten-year-old daughter has been suspended from the school bus for the second time this year due to bullying. Let me be absolutely clear: bullying is not tolerated in our family. When she brought home her suspension paperwork on Friday, she nonchalantly said, “Daddy, you’re going to have to take me to school next week.” Well, today, she’s learning a different lesson.
Too many kids today see their parents’ efforts as entitlements, not privileges. So, this morning, my beautiful daughter is walking five miles to school in 36-degree weather. I know some of you won’t agree with my approach, and that’s okay. As her parent, I believe this is the right way to teach her a valuable lesson about the consequences of her actions and to put an end to this bullying behavior.

author: dragosbuzzi
title: Dad sprays yard insecticide (Solfac) against ticks
summary: A Romanian dad says ticks are every parent's enemy in spring and that long socks and repellent sprays aren't practical for kids playing in a yard in summer heat. His solution is to spray the garden with an insecticide called Solfac using a garden sprayer.
key_points: Ticks are most active from spring; check children after outdoor play.
Personal repellent sprays may suffice for occasional park visits.
He treats his whole yard with the insecticide Solfac via a pressure sprayer.

caution: Solfac is a pyrethroid insecticide; follow label directions and keep children and pets off treated areas until dry. Yard spraying does not replace daily tick checks and proper tick removal.

I don’t want her to mistake a virtual world for real joy, or let something so small take away her peace. As a parent, all I want is to protect her—from addiction, from distraction, and from anything that could steal her innocence too soon. While she was crying, I hugged her tightly and explained that Roblox isn’t good for her. I told her that I only want what’s best for her. This mama has a very simple ask and that is that her baby receives all of their blood back from the placenta before the cord is cut. Now this birth worker, whether that be a nurse, OB, or midwife, is trying to rush the process by telling this mother that her placenta is wanting to come, therefore they need to cut the cord. author: crunchymommaelizabeth
title: Elimination communication from birth: baby using the toilet at 4 days
summary: A mother claims her baby used the toilet from 4 days old through elimination communication (EC), so they rarely change poopy diapers. The caption explains EC as reading the baby's cues and offering chances to go outside the diaper, not as infant potty training. The video itself gives no method ('how in the comments'), so the practical detail is missing.

The creator started EC as soon as they came home from the hospital
She reports long dry-diaper stretches between potty opportunities
The actual technique (cues, timing, holding position) is not shown in the video
caution: Anecdotal claim ('babies are born with the desire not to soil themselves') presented as fact; EC is a niche practice and the video gives no instructions. Not necessary for healthy development.
onscreen: Our baby could use the toilet by 4 days old
Meaning we don't change poopy diapers
Meaning you don't have to either
caption:
I don’t mean to potty talk but… 

We were told that there was no way this could work. That it would be too hard to potty an infant. That it would be too messy! Or that she wouldn’t be capable to do it. 

I know it sounds crazy that from birth babies actually have some intuition and preferences on their personal hygiene and when they need to use the bathroom. They are born with the desire to not soil themselves and have control over their bodily functions.

I hated the idea that my baby would have such little communication with me at birth. I also didn’t like the idea of her sitting in poo all day long. This is why I did a ton of research on elimination communication (EC). I found our babies have the ability to que when they need to use the potty. Their are also lots of awesome tricks to know when they need to go. EC is not infant potty training. It is communication between baby and caregiver with the opportunity to use the bathroom outside of the diaper. 

I was so excited to try it! We started once we got home from the hospital and couldn’t believe it actually worked! We have even had times where her diaper is completely dry in between times we take her potty. We have only had one messy diaper and that was due to an abnormality in our schedules where we were unable to potty her. Obviously we still have dirty diapers and it’s not a 100% potty trained at birth thing. It’s way less mess and so rewarding to see her respond to it all. 

It has been extremely rewarding and so freaking cool to see how intuitive it is for babies. Let me know if you want to learn more! I’m happy to share my experience and resources that got us going. 

#proudmommy #ec #pottytraining #baby #eliminationcommunication #potty #family #motherhood

author: flappynappies
title: Elimination communication: why start pottying in infancy
summary: A cloth-diaper brand argues it is easier to potty a baby than train a toddler, because newborns instinctively avoid soiling themselves and toddlers are more strong-willed. She suggests offering the potty once or twice a day from infancy by holding the baby in a squat over a potty and cueing with a 'ps-ps' sound. The video mainly promotes a paid tutorial.
key_points: Elimination communication: remove the diaper, hold the baby in a supported squat over a potty or toilet, and make a cue sound ('ps-ps-ps').
Offering the potty even once or twice a day can make it a normal part of life from early on.
Her claim: babies kept only in diapers lose the instinct not to soil themselves, and starting in toddlerhood brings more resistance.

products.type: Used for elimination communication to potty train early.

caution: Promotional content from a diaper brand selling a tutorial. Claims about babies 'losing the instinct' and EC being easier are the creator's opinion; mainstream pediatric guidance (e.g. AAP) favours child-readiness-based toilet training, usually from around 18-24 months or later.
transcript: So there are two main reasons why it's easier to potty train a baby versus a toddler. Reason number one is that babies are actually born with instincts to not soil themselves or you. If you take a newborn baby, remove the diaper, and hold your baby in a squat over a potty or a toilet and say, ps-ps-ps-ps, that baby will almost certainly instinctively pee and or poop. If you keep your baby in diapers, however, your baby will lose this instinct and learn to pee and poop in diapers. The second reason is that toddlers are much more willful and defiant than babies. Even just offering the potty once or twice a day to your baby allows the potty to become a normal part of your child's life from a young age. but if you exclusively use diapers until your child is a toddler and suddenly expect a new behavior from that child you are much more likely to have potty training drama and resistance. The learning curve.

title: How one mum turned her breech baby at 39 weeks (personal routine)
summary: A prenatal fitness creator says her baby was breech at 39 weeks and flipped head-down within 24 hours after releasing hip flexors, avoiding long sitting, doing supported open puppy pose, inversions, birth-ball hip mobility and swimming (including handstands). She attributes breech position to pelvic/ligament tension.
key_points: Her routine: hip-flexor release several times a day and avoiding long periods of sitting.
About 20 minutes in a supported open puppy pose (twice, including before bed).
Around 10 inversions held for 20-30 seconds / three deep breaths each.
Birth-ball pelvic mobility; swimming.
Her theory: tension in round and uterosacral ligaments limits space for the baby to turn.

products.name: Birth ball
products.type: Helps mobilize pelvis to encourage baby positioning.

caution: Anecdotal; evidence that exercises/inversions turn breech babies is weak. Inversions and handstands late in pregnancy carry fall/dizziness risks. Discuss breech options (e.g. ECV) with your midwife/OB first.

ill.caption: Supported open puppy pose as used in a self-reported breech-turning routine (check with your care provider first).

transcript: So at 39 weeks of pregnancy, I found out that my baby was breached and here's how I flipped the baby head down within 24 hours. I focused on releasing my hip flexors, which might have been tight and restricting space. And I did this multiple times throughout the day, as well as avoiding sitting for long periods. I then spent around 20 minutes in this supported open puppy pose. And I did this right before bed too. And I did around 10 or so inversions holding for three deep breaths for each one which helps to release the uterine ligaments and untwist or create space in that lower uterus and then I spent a lot of time on the birth ball mobilizing my pelvis for baby to find the space they need to flip and drop down into the pelvis head first hope this helps
caption:
How I flipped my breech baby at 39 weeks of pregnancy. 

If your baby is breech or in a less optimal positions it might be because of an imbalance or asymmetry in your pelvis or soft tissues, if there is uneven tension or twisting in your lower uterus it might be restricting space your baby to flip head down and get into position. We want to encourage baby into an optimal position down the birth canal for a smoother labor. 

A baby’s position is based on the space available to them so we can focus on releasing tension in the uterosacral and round ligaments during pregnancy to help create more space! Your uterus has several ligaments that attach to it and tension in these ligaments can twist or pull the uterus, decreasing space in the uterus for your baby to get head down. 

Here’s what I did within the 24 hours: 

✨Released my hip flexors 
✨Inversions for 20-30 seconds each x 10
✨20 minutes in a supported Puppy Pose x2
✨Birth Ball Hip Mobility
✨Went swimming in the pool and did handstands! 

I hope this helps!

title: How our daughter's PANS/PANDAS was diagnosed and treated (parent)
summary: A mother (not a medical professional) explains that a PANS specialist diagnosed her daughter with extensive bloodwork for active infections and antibodies (mycoplasma pneumonia, strep antibodies, tick-borne illnesses) and urine mycotoxin tests for mold. key_points: Diagnosis in their case involved a PANS-specialist doctor ordering extensive blood work: active infections and antibodies (mycoplasma, strep, tick-borne illnesses).
They also tested urine for mycotoxins (mold).
Treatment targets the underlying infection; several antibiotics were tried before one worked.
IVIG is commonly used for PANS/PANDAS; they also used supplements for immune support.
Healing is not linear and every child's treatment differs.

transcript: I've had a lot of people ask me questions similar to this one. How is it diagnosed? And also, how is it treated? Again, want to preface this. I'm no doctor. I'm no expert in PANS. I'm just a mom that's been through it. So how it's diagnosed, there's several different ways to diagnose it, I believe. Our doctor who specializes in PANS, he just did very extensive blood work. He tested for certain active infections and also certain antibodies. Just very in-depth blood work that we had never got done before. mycoplasma pneumonia, strep antibodies, tick-borne illnesses, also mycotoxins in the urine, which would be a sign of mold. Now how it's treated, from what I understand, the type of treatment is based off of what type of infection is in the body. For my daughter, she had several different things that were factors into her PansPandas, so it wasn't just one specific infection we were targeting so we tried several different antibiotics before we found the one that really worked for her that seemed to be a turning point did still take time to get her to where she is now healing is not linear it's very up and down very back and forth also ivig is huge a lot of kids with pans pandas get ivig done another thing for us that worked was just lots of supplements tons of different things just to keep her immune system strong and keep her from getting back into the place she was at. So that's just what we do. Like I said, everyone's different. Every journey is different and every treatment is different depending on the child, depending on what works for them, depending on the infection, lots of different things. Hopefully once Pans Pandas is more recognized amongst the medical community, it will be easier to diagnose and easier to treat. So yeah, that is how we got my daughter diagnosed and treated for Pans Pandas.

transcript: The internet was never designed for kids, and I got tired of waiting on it to fix itself. So for the past year, my team and I have been building a new kind of internet just for kids. It's called KidNet, and I want to show you how it works. KidNet is a fully offline device with an expansive, curated, kid-friendly world inside. It feels and functions like the actual web, but they're never actually connected to the big internet. To use it, just plug it up to an outlet and connect to it wirelessly with the devices you already own. Then go to kidnet.local to get access to everything KidNet has to offer. KidNet is full of all the good things from the internet and none of the bad. You won't find any advertisements or algorithms, and there's absolutely no data harvesting or strangers. We built KidNet around the concept of a treehouse. It's safely built by adults so that kids can explore freely without constant supervision. We knew that if this concept was actually going to work, we'd have to make it extremely fun and engaging for kids, which is exactly what we did. We recently started playtesting in our local schools, and we're pleasantly surprised to find out that kids are just as excited about KidNet as parents. caption:
Follow @thepositiveparenting to become a positive parent

Teaching Responsibility to Kids

Encouraging your child to help out and take on responsibilities is a key part of their development. It teaches them important life skills, builds confidence, and nurtures their sense of contribution.

It’s true—sometimes letting them help can be a test of patience. The process may be messy or take longer than expected, but allowing them to participate is worth it. After all, learning happens best through hands-on experience.

Remember, it’s about guiding them through these tasks and showing trust in their abilities. When they feel included, they develop a sense of pride and responsibility that lasts a lifetime.

And who knows? The smallest hands can indeed make the biggest difference!

title: Letting babies take physical risks before they walk
summary: An open-ended play coach shows a pre-walking baby exploring a rocking board, balance board, Pikler-style ladder, spinning toy and step stool. She argues that allowing safe risk-taking before age one builds problem solving, spatial awareness, confidence and resilience, not just the big milestones.
key_points: Development isn't only big milestones; the small skills between crawling and walking matter.
Give babies time and trust to test their limits on low climbing and balance equipment.
Risky play before age one supports problem solving, spatial negotiation, confidence and resilience.

products.type: Supports balance and physical development in babies.

products.name: balance board
products.type: Helps develop core stability and spatial awareness.

products.name: Pikler-style ladder
products.type: Encourages climbing skills and physical confidence.

products.name: spinning toy
products.type: Promotes sensory exploration and motor skill development.

products.name: step stool
products.type: Enables independence and reaching higher surfaces safely.

caution: Little practical detail; supervise closely and use stable, age-appropriate equipment on soft surfaces.
onscreen: She might not be able to walk yet...
But she's already figuring out exactly what her body is capable of.
caption:
We focus so much on those big milestones like walking and crawling, and we can sometimes forget all the little bits in between. 

We can forget the importance of allowing them take risks, even before they turn 1. 
We need to give them time and trust to figure out their limits and what their bodies capable of. 

Because even months before they walk, those two little feet, can gain so many skills that support their development in a ton of ways. 
From problem solving, space negotiation to building their confidence and resilience ✨❤️

author: floraguzman19601
title: Mayim Bialik on raising her babies without diapers (EC)
summary: In a 2014 Howard Stern clip, Mayim Bialik explains her kids didn't wear diapers thanks to elimination communication. Babies give signals before peeing/pooping; if parents learn and reinforce them, the signals get clearer. Her kids learned the sign for 'potty' and used it by 12 months, before walking or talking; she admits it's not for everyone.
key_points: EC is separate from attachment parenting, though some attachment parents practise it.
Babies give cues before eliminating; responding reinforces them, ignoring them makes them fade.
It's more about training the parent to read cues than training the baby.
Teach the sign-language sign for 'potty'; her kids signed it by about 12 months.
caution: Celebrity anecdote; EC is a niche practice, and 'no diapers at all' is not realistic for most families.

ill.caption: The sign-language sign for 'potty' used in elimination communication.

transcript: The kids do not wear diapers. Oh, no. So my kids did not wear diapers. That's called elimination communication. But it's actually separate from attachment parenting. Many people, some people who do attachment parenting do this. But yeah, so you, basically babies are born giving signals when they pee and poop, I promise. And if you learn those signals and reinforce them, they will give them stronger and clearer. And we taught our kids to sign. This is the sign language sign for potty. By the time they were 12 months old, they were signing for potty. They couldn't walk, talk, or eat solids. They only breastfed, but they could sign for the potty before they could even walk, talk. Is it the same theory with a dog? Like, dogs will teach, you can teach them to go to the bathroom outside. Right, so you're more training yourself to learn the cues that the baby will give. And if you don't reinforce them, a baby will stop giving those cues. And it's not for everyone, believe me. But yeah, especially with boys, it's easy. We just hold them up over a tree.

author: thealiceelms
title: Mom asks for help: baby's chin slumps to chest in car seat
summary: A first-time mum shows her sleeping baby in a car seat and asks for advice because she can't get a finger between the baby's chin and chest, even after repositioning several times. She is worried about the baby's breathing room. No answer or solution is given in the video.
key_points: The worry: the baby's chin rests on her chest in the car seat (no finger-width gap), which can restrict a young baby's airway.
Repositioning the baby several times did not fix it, which suggests the seat setup itself needs checking.
The video only asks the question and gives no solution.
caution: Chin-to-chest slumping in a car seat is a real airway risk for young infants. Check the seat's recline angle indicator and newborn insert against the manual, keep harness straps snug at or below the shoulders with the chest clip at armpit level, avoid aftermarket padding, and have a certified car seat technician check the setup.

author: tushapv
title: Only 2 hours a day with your kids: make them count
summary: A working mom cuts up a paper strip of the 24 hours in a weekday to show how sleep, school, homework, sports and dinner leave only about two hours with her daughters. She uses this to explain why she makes that time intentional: being kind, present, and letting the kids lead conversations so they feel special.
key_points: Map out your child's weekday: after sleep, school, homework, activities and meals, very little shared time remains (about 2 hours for her).
Treat that time as a priority: be present, kind and let the child talk about what they want.
Eat, talk and laugh together so the busy days still create good memories.
dedupe: limited daily hours with kids quality time
transcript: this is my kids 24 hours with me in a day monday through friday they sleep at 9 p.m and they wake up at 6 a.m we leave for school at 7 30 a.m and their school starts at 8 a.m they are in school from 8 a.m to 3 p.m this is what they have when they come home they relax they do their homework they have one hour of sports every day monday through friday and they eat dinner so this is these four things, which is going in three hours. So this is the time that they have Monday through Friday with me. And this is the time that I choose when I am kind to them, spend quality time with them, be nice to them, ask about what they want to talk. It is all about them because I want them to feel special. When they grow up, I want them to remember those times that the little time that we had. Those were the best times that they had in their day.
onscreen: 24 hours in a day... but only 2 with my girls...
caption:
I get about two hours a day with my girls.

The rest of the day is filled with getting ready, school, work, homework, dinner, showers and sleep.

When I really thought about it, I realized how little time we actually get together on a normal weekday.

That’s why my kids are a priority. Those two hours matter to me. I want them to remember that even when life was busy, we made time to talk, laugh, eat together and just be present with each other.

I can’t make the days longer, but I can be intentional with the time we do have. 💕

#Motherhood #Parenting #WorkingMom #FamilyTime #raisinggirls

author: jojohnsonoverby
title: Opinion: if you want to be 'Team Green', do it with baby #1
summary: A mother pregnant with her third child argues that parents who want to wait until birth to learn the baby's sex should do it with their first pregnancy. Her reasons: people ask fewer intrusive questions, and gender-neutral registry gifts are more practical and reusable for future children.
key_points: 'Team Green' means not finding out the baby's sex until birth.
Not knowing the sex reduced intrusive questions (e.g. about names) from others.
With the first baby, a gender-neutral registry yields practical gear that can be reused for later children.
She doesn't view a birth reveal as more special than other ways of finding out—it's personal preference.
credentials: parent (mother of two, pregnant with third)
caution: Personal opinion, not a recommendation either way.
dedupe: team green first pregnancy surprise sex
transcript: I have a parenthood hot take. And that is if you want to do team green in one of your pregnancies, I think you should choose your first one. You can choose all of them, obviously. But if you know for sure you want to experience it once, I think you should choose your first one. I think it is the superior choice. I'm currently pregnant with my third baby. Our first two, we were team green. We did not find out what we were having until they were born, laid them on my chest. My husband got to tell me it's a boy, it's a girl. Wonderful. Loved it. But if that interests you, even the slightest, the reason it's best to do it with your first one, a couple of different things. One, people don't ask you as many questions. We found out the sex of the baby this time. And I cannot believe how much more invasive the questions are. They want to know a name. They want to know, I don't know. That's the only thing I can think of right now. And that's like not. Two, you get more practical things off of your registry. When you do that with your first pregnancy and all of your gifting from friends and family and all those really supportive things that you get can apply to any child in the future, you're so much more set up. Now, again, not everybody wants to experience Team Green. They want to find out. And I am not of the camp that not finding out until birth is like the greatest surprise in life. I don't, I don't subscribe to that. Anytime you find out it's a surprise, like when you take a sneak peek at seven weeks, that's a surprise. If you do a gender reveal with family and friends, it's a surprise then too. And if it makes you feel more comfortable to prepare, whatever, that's not how it was for me. But this message is specifically to the people who think they're interested in being team green, but want to wait till they're having their second or third already knowing what they have at home under their belt. No, it's not the way to do it. Number one is the way to do team green.

author: drjabanmoore_
title: PANS/PANDAS warning signs infographic
summary: A functional medicine practitioner's infographic listing warning signs of PANS/PANDAS, pediatric neuropsychiatric disorders he says affect 1 in 200 children and are often overlooked. Signs include cognitive/learning changes (brain fog, sudden poor grades, loss of math skills, sleep issues, processing problems, confusion) and communication/behavior changes (new stuttering, peer trouble, angry outbursts, regression).
key_points: Cognition/learning signs: brain fog, sudden drop in grades, loss of math skills, sleep issues, auditory/visual processing problems, confusion.
Communication/social signs: sudden stuttering, trouble with peers, angry outbursts, regression in coping and social skills.
The key feature is a sudden onset; raise it with your pediatrician.
caution: Functional-medicine source; the 1-in-200 figure and broad symptom list are not settled science, and many listed signs are common and nonspecific. Discuss with a pediatrician.

author: larakellam
title: Parenting with BPD: the struggle to regulate yourself first
summary: A 22-year-old mum diagnosed with BPD/EUPD a few months postpartum describes how hard it is to regulate herself before responding to her 3-year-old son. She links it to never seeing her own mother regulate, explains that BPD keeps her near-constantly in fight-or-flight, and says she keeps trying for her child despite the guilt.
key_points: Self-regulation before responding to a child is important for every parent and especially hard with BPD.
Many parents never saw regulation modelled in their own childhood and have to learn it as adults.
Mental-health conditions can be diagnosed or noticed postpartum; seek professional support.
Mum guilt can stack on top of condition-related guilt; keep trying and be compassionate with yourself.
She mentions DBT skills (in hashtags) as part of her emotional-regulation work.
credentials: parent with lived experience of BPD/EUPD
caution: Personal experience, not clinical advice; her description of the amygdala and BPD is simplified. Anyone struggling should seek professional help.
transcript: Regulating your emotions when you're a mum who has BPD is one of the hardest things that I've ever done. So I was diagnosed with EUPD or BPD, same thing, back in 2023 when I was a few months postpartum from having my son. Now my son is three years old and I'm 22 and I've been living with BPD or EUPD for a lot longer than what's on my medical records. Although it's been years of me living with BPD and learning more and more about it every single day, the one thing that I still can't seem to do very well is regulate myself before dealing with my son. A lot of the time it's because we was treated like this as children too. I know for a fact my mum was not regulating herself before yelling and throwing wet cloths at me and I don't want to do the same with my child but because I never saw my mum regulate herself, I really don't know what i'm doing regulating yourself as a mom isn't more important when you've got a mental health condition like bpd it's always going to be important but for someone who has bpd where the amygdala part of the brain the survival part of the brain the fight or flight response it works in a different way which means i'm almost constantly in fight or flight so regulating my emotions becomes almost impossible and to be honest being a parent of bpd is almost like just forcing yourself to keep going. We've got one of the best reasons to be here and to keep trying and that's for our kids. So I'm never gonna stop trying but oh my gosh it's the hardest thing I've ever done in my life.

author: imdisabledrn
title: Post-hysterectomy recovery realities
summary: A registered nurse shares her personal experience with the unexpected physical and emotional side effects of a laparoscopic hysterectomy. She discusses organ shifting, hormonal changes, and recovery challenges, emphasizing that these experiences can be intense.
key_points: Organs may shift into the space left by the removed uterus.
Post-operative swelling of the vulva is common.
Expect significant fatigue due to healing and blood loss.
Hormonal changes can occur even if ovaries are retained.
Vaginal incision pain can be triggered by internal structures like the colon.
Abdominal binders can provide support during the initial recovery phase.

products.name: abdominal binder
products.type: Helps support body while organs relocate after surgery.

caution: This is a personal account of a specific medical procedure and should not replace professional medical advice.
transcript: Howdy, my name's Caroline, and I just had a hysterectomy. Here's seven things that I wish someone had told me before surgery. Number one, you can feel your organs sloshing around inside you. The uterus was removed, and that frees up some empty space, and your organs have to relocate themselves to account for that. You can feel that happening in your body. It's very disturbing. I used an abdominal binder for the first two weeks or so, until my body readjusted to where my organs' new positions are. Number two, immediately post-op, there is a lot of swelling of the vulva. My anatomy did not look like what it usually looks like, and that really freaked me out. But it turns out that's normal. Number three, continuing with the vulva and vagina, there's a lot of discharge happening. there was minimal post-op bleeding but there is just a lot more discharge than i was expecting i don't know it's not cervical mucus so like what is coming out of me but um you know we're three weeks post-op right now and there's still quite a bit every day which is fine i just wish that i had known and could have mentally prepared number four profound fatigue this is a phrase that my surgeon's PA used in my post-op appointment and god damn is that accurate. I am sitting here day in and day out doing absolutely nothing except watching tv shows and doing ugly artwork and I am still so fucking tired. My body is healing. That takes a lot of energy. That requires a lot of breasts. I guess I wasn't expecting there to be so much remodeling happening after they took my uterus out. In my post-op, they also explained that that fatigue is partially due to blood loss from the surgery. The uterus is a muscle, it's muscle tissue, and therefore it is vascular. So that's a whole organ worth of blood that is no longer in my circulatory system, and it takes your body a minute to adjust to that. Number five is hormonal changes. I did on some level know that this would be happening. I just wasn't expecting the symptoms to be as intense as they are. I retained my ovaries, so I figured that nothing much would really change, but it's mood swings. It's not your average depression. This is advanced depression. It's hot flashes and night sweats and crying all the time for no reason. I've been through medically induced menopause before so I kind of know the drill when it comes to this but I wasn't expecting to have menopause symptoms after the hysterectomy because I still retained my ovaries. Number six is pain at the vaginal incision. It's not the pain that you think. It's not just like a conic low grade like pain it's pain when any structure inside my body bumps up against that incision so when my colon is full and i need to have a bowel movement that kind of stretches it it bumps up against the incision and that hurts like a bitch which brings me to number seven which is that i am constantly shitting now i had a lot of bowel endo and a lot of bowel symptoms related to uh my uterus being very very hostile so like and when i say like serious i mean i had bowel movements once or twice per month which is not good but now that it's more like once or twice per day. What are normal people doing pooping all the time? I feel like it makes me kind of miss the constipation because I feel like I'm just pooping constantly now and I don't like it. So be warned if you're prone to constipation. So this is me warning you about things that may or may not happen after a hysterectomy. You're welcome. Oh, more careful tips.

title: Pre-pregnancy fitness: being active isn't the same as being ready
summary: A pelvic floor physical therapist explains in the caption that general fitness (running, lifting, yoga) often doesn't prepare the body for pregnancy's specific demands on the pelvic floor, core and hips. She assesses old injuries, muscle imbalances, hip mobility and stability, breathing patterns and joint load tolerance, and says these are best addressed before conception.
key_points: Being 'in shape' differs from being prepared for pregnancy's load on the pelvic floor, core and hips.
Common gaps: one hip working harder than the other, unequal oblique activation, breathing that doesn't reach the pelvic floor.
A pregnancy-readiness assessment looks at old injuries, muscle imbalances, hip mobility/stability, breathing patterns and joint load tolerance.
The window before pregnancy, before hormones change, is the easiest time to address these.

onscreen: "getting fit before pregnancy" means something different than most people think...
caption:
most women who come to me- a pelvic floor physical therapist- before pregnancy tell me they’re already active. they run, they lift, they do yoga. and they’re genuinely surprised when I tell them that most of the time that’s not enough to prepare for pregnancy.

being “in shape” and being truly ready for pregnancy are two different things. what pregnancy asks of your body — the load on your pelvic floor, the demand on your core, the stability requirements of your hips and pelvis — is very specific. and the general workouts most women are doing leave big holes where your body can compensate.

a left hip that works a little bit harder than a right hip. obliques that activate unequally. breathing that doesn’t quite reach your pelvic floor. 

small things that can create big problems during pregnancy 

as a pelvic floor PT, when I assess someone’s pregnancy readiness, I’m looking for old injuries that have not healed 100%, muscle imbalances, hip mobility and stability, breathing patterns, and joint load tolerance. 

the good news? all of this is completely addressable, especially in the window before pregnancy, before your hormones change and baby starts placing stress on your body. 

right now you have the time and the capacity to actually build the foundation that pregnancy will rely on!!

if you want to head into pregnancy feeling strong, prepared, and confident  🌱comment BEFORE 
and i’ll send you more info about my before pregnancy program, designed for women who are thinking about getting pregnant in the next 3-12 months

and for more preconception goodness, follow along @dr_kayla_dpt where we chat all things endocrine disruptors, pelvic floor PT, and pregnancy prep!!

title: Pregnancy myths a third-time mom no longer believes
summary: A Romanian mother pregnant with her third child lists beliefs she rejects (in the caption; the video is just mirror selfies with music). Second and third babies deserve photos, a baby shower and celebration just like the first.

Exercise in pregnancy is not automatically forbidden (caption is truncated after this point).

1. Ca bebelusul e „prea mare” si eu sunt prea ingusta in bazin si nu il pot naste. Mi s-a spus asta la ambii copii de cativa medici. Chiar daca eu am pornit de la 50 kg si ei au avut 3.850 amandoi, asta nu inseamna ca nu i-am putut naste. Exista si complicatii medicale, dar nu poti sa te uiti la o mama doar pentru ca e slabuta si sa-i spui: „tu nu poti”.
2. „Corpul tau nu va mai fi niciodata la fel” – corpul meu a aratat la fel de bine si dupa primul, si dupa al doilea bebe. Daca faci sport, te alimentezi cum trebuie si ai grija de tine, doar infloresti. A avea mai multi copii nu inseamna ca vei arata ca o epava dupa.. conteaza si geneticul, dar am vazut multe situatii in care femeile au invins genticul, prin munca. 
3. Fara poze, baby shower sau alte bucurii doar pentru ca este al doilea sau al treilea bebe? Bucuria e la fel de mare de fiecare data.
4. Hainele de maternitate ...sincer, sunt cam uratele. Nu avantajeaza corpul si nu sunt cool. Exista haine mai frumoase din materiale naturale la barbati sau femei cu marimi mai mari. Eu mi-am luat multe haine de la barbati: tricouri si blugi din bumbac, marimea L sau XL.
5. „Nu ai voie multe lucruri” nu ai voie sa faci sport daca nu erai sportiva inainte? Fals. Ai voie sa faci orice simti ca este natural si potrivit pentru tine si pentru bebe. A fi insarcinata nu inseamna ca ai un handicap – e o superputere.
6. „Mananci pentru doi” – nu e adevarat. Copilul are de unde sa se hraneasca, nu trebuie sa exagerezi.
7. „E cel mai greu cu 3 copii, ca sunt parintii in minoritate…” – nu am trecut inca prin asta, dar am avut 2 copii sub 2 ani, alaptati, care nu faceau la WC si nu vorbeau. Nu inteleg cum, acum ca ei sunt mari, comunica, sunt destul de independenti, se spala, mananca singuri, ar putea fi mai greu doar pentru ca vine inca unul. Dar sa speram ca nu voi plange prea mult dupa.

author: pinkpillrx
title: Pregnancy nutrition guidelines rely on studies that rarely include pregnant women
summary: The creator discusses a 2025 review of 122 nutrition publications that found only 4.6% of participants were pregnant or lactating, while 71.1% were men. She argues that nutrition recommendations for pregnant and postpartum women are largely extrapolated from non-pregnant (often male) adults plus calculated estimates of fetal and placental needs, rather than direct trials in pregnant populations.
key_points: A 2025 review of 122 publications found only 4.6% of participants were pregnant or lactating; 71.1% were men.
Pregnancy and lactation reference values are often extrapolated from non-pregnant adults rather than tested directly.
Factorial models estimate extra needs (e.g. what the placenta and baby require) for calories and micronutrients.
Treat pregnancy nutrition guidance as a best estimate and discuss individual needs with your provider.
caution: Critiques the research base but gives no alternative recommendations; the cited review is not named in the video. Keep following your provider's prenatal nutrition guidance.
dedupe: pregnancy nutrition research excludes pregnant women
transcript: Nutrition recommendations are given to pregnant women and postpartum women. What percentage of nutrition research do you think actually includes them? 3%. Actually, you're kind of close. What is it? 4.6%. I was close. See, I have learned things. You want to know what percentage were men in these studies? Oh, 83%. 71.1%. A 2025 review of 122 publications found that only 4.6% of all participants were pregnant or lactating, while 71.1% were men. Here's the problem. We give women nutrition advice based on these studies that don't include them. Just like pharmaceuticals. So, yeah, that's a problem. You know what? You'd think they would care because half those babies are boys. They just say, you know what? add one third on, or they do estimated calorie expenditure, like the extra calories that it might take. So it's all quantitative, not qualitative. Or they use factorial models where they calculate, oh, how much like a placenta would need and how much a baby needs to be sustained. It's just straight up calories. It sounds like it's all caloric. Well, no, because they do, I'm talking about micronutrients too.
onscreen: Nutrition guidelines for pregnancy & postpartum are mostly based on studies done on men.
caption: Large reviews of the studies used to set dietary recommendations have found that women (and especially pregnant and lactating people) are consistently underrepresented.  In many cases, reference values for pregnancy are extrapolated from non‑pregnant adults (often male‑dominant studies) plus estimates of fetal and placental needs, rather than from direct trials in pregnant populations. #womenshealth #evidencebased #pregnancynutrition #feminist #postpartumjourney

title: Reflections on religious upbringing and tolerance
